Honestly, sometimes I wonder if I should have just stayed a librarian. Speaker_2: Librarians are quiet. You’re not quiet. You shout sometimes when I leave my toys everywhere. Speaker_1: (Smiling) That’s true. I do occasionally raise my voice. It’s a family trait, I suppose. Anyway, regarding the skiing, I’ve checked the baggage allowance. We can probably squeeze everything in one case each, but we’ll need to be ruthless. No extra shoes! Speaker_2: But I need my sparkly shoes! For the hotel! Speaker_1: We’ll see. We can always wear the boots on the plane… (She winks) Just kidding. We’ll figure it out. I've also pre-booked ski hire, so that’s one less thing to worry about. It’s all starting to feel real now, isn’t it? Speaker_2: Yeah! Will there be snow? Real snow? Speaker_1: Oh, yes. Plenty of snow, I promise. And hot chocolate, and maybe even a snowball fight. Are you excited? Speaker_2: (Jumping up and down) YES! Can we go *now*? Speaker_1: Not quite now, darling. Finish your bolognese. And maybe…just maybe…help me find the oregano. Speaker_2: (Immediately starts searching through the spice rack) Oregano! Oregano! Found it! Speaker_1: (Sighs happily) That’s my girl. Speaker_2: Mummy? Speaker_1: Yes, love? Speaker_2: Will there be a snowman? A really, really big snowman? Speaker_1: (Smiling warmly) We can certainly *try* to build a really, really big snowman. We will.

Speaker_1: Ugh, honestly, Food Tech is *killing* me. Mrs. Davies is obsessed with soufflés. Soufflés! Who even makes soufflés regularly? Speaker_2: Seriously! And she’s like, “It’s a fundamental skill!” No, it’s a skill for people who want to spend their lives stressing over eggy bubbles. I’d rather make pasta, like, every single day. Speaker_1: Exactly! And it’s always the same recipe. Vanilla soufflé. Every. Single. Week. I think I’m starting to dream about vanilla. Speaker_2: I’m dreaming about getting a decent mark in Maths. Mr. Harrison is setting, like, impossible equations. Did you get the homework on quadratic equations? Speaker_1: Oh god, don’t even. I spent two hours on it last night and still only managed to answer half of them. It's just…letters everywhere! x and y and z. It's like he *wants* us to fail. Speaker_2: I know, right? It’s so different from how he explains it in class. He makes it look so easy, then gives us this monstrosity as homework. I think I’m going to ask Lily for help. She’s a maths whiz. Speaker_1: Good idea. I might do the same. Although, honestly, I'd rather spend the evening practicing my Spanish. Speaker_2: Oh yeah? You're getting good at that, aren’t you? I'm thinking about dropping it next year, actually. It’s just… so much grammar. Speaker_1: No way! You should stick with it! Think about it, we could go to Spain together, or South America. It’d be so cool. And it’s actually really useful, even just for understanding things when you hear Spanish music. Speaker_2: Hmm, maybe. I just don’t see myself using it much. I’m thinking about doing Computer Science instead. Apparently, they're looking for students to help with coding the school website. Speaker_1: Oh, that sounds… practical. You’re good at that sort of thing. I'm still trying to figure out what I want to *do* with my life. I liked History last year, but I'm not sure what jobs you can even *get* with a History degree. Speaker_2: My mum said something about museums or archiving. Or teaching, if you’re brave enough. Remember Mr. Peterson’s stories? He seemed to really love his job. Speaker_1: Yeah, he was pretty good. Though, thinking about jobs is stressing me out already. I’m only fifteen! Speaker_2: Tell me about it. I was talking to Josh yesterday, and he's already thinking about apprenticeships. He wants to be an electrician. Speaker_1: Josh! Wow. He’s so sorted. I’m just trying to survive this week, one soufflé and quadratic equation at a time. Did you finish that English essay on 'Romeo and Juliet'? Speaker_2: Almost. I'm stuck on the conclusion. I keep rewriting it, but it just sounds rubbish. It’s about how Shakespeare uses light and dark imagery, and it’s just… complicated. Speaker_1: I got feedback on mine today. Miss Thompson said I needed to ‘develop my analysis’. Which basically means “you didn’t say enough.” Seriously, what does she want me to write, a novel? Speaker_2: Classic Miss Thompson! She always says that. Ugh, I need a break. Fancy going to Millie’s after school? Her mum said we can have pizza. Speaker_1: Yes! Absolutely. Pizza sounds a million times better than another vanilla soufflé. And maybe Millie can help me with my English too. It’s worth a shot, right?

Speaker_1: Honestly, darling, I don’t know what they’re *doing* with films these days. It’s all… noise and explosions. Nothing like a good story anymore. Speaker_2: (stirring sugar into her tea) You mean like, proper character-driven stuff? Yeah, I get what you mean. It feels like everything's a franchise or a superhero movie now. It’s exhausting. Speaker_1: Exactly! Remember those films with…oh, what was his name? James Mason? Such a handsome devil. And the stories! So subtle, so well-written. Not this… *bang* *crash* *vroom*. Honestly, I need a lie down after some of them. Speaker_2: James Mason! Good shout. He was in ‘North by Northwest’, wasn’t he? Hitchcock. Classic. I actually watched ‘Rear Window’ last week. Still holds up, even though it's ancient. Speaker_1: Hitchcock. Oh, he knew how to build tension. None of this jump-scare nonsense. It was all about the atmosphere, the music... and Grace Kelly, of course. She was *gorgeous*. Speaker_2: She was. I tried to get my flatmate to watch ‘Vertigo’ with me the other day, but she wasn’t having it. She said it was too slow. Too… psychological. Speaker_1: (scoffs) Too psychological! They want everything handed to them on a plate, these youngsters. No imagination. No patience. You have to *think* when you watch a good film, you know? Speaker_2: I know, right? It’s like they want constant stimulation. I was telling Ben – you know, from work? – about ‘The Third Man’ the other day. He’d never even heard of it! Speaker_1: ‘The Third Man’! Orson Welles! In Vienna! Oh, that’s a good one. All shadowy and mysterious. You wouldn't get that now. Everything’s so…bright. And loud. Speaker_2: He just looked blank. Said it sounded “depressing.” Apparently, everything needs a happy ending now. Speaker_1: Depressing? Life is depressing sometimes! Films should reflect that! Not everything's sunshine and roses. Though, mind you, I did enjoy ‘Paddington 2’. That was rather sweet. Speaker_2: (laughs) Okay, I can get on board with ‘Paddington 2’. That’s genuinely a lovely film. Hugh Grant’s villain was brilliant. Speaker_1: Oh, he was! Such a silly performance. They really let him camp it up. It was a refreshing change. I do wish they’d make more things like that, though. Good, wholesome entertainment. Speaker_2: Maybe we should have a film night? We haven’t done one in ages. We could pick something classic. Speaker_1: Oh, that’s a lovely idea! We could have popcorn, and…and those little chocolates I like. The ones with the orange cream inside. Speaker_2: Deal. I’ll make a list of suggestions. And you can veto anything that's too…noisy. Speaker_1: (smiling) Excellent. Though, if you pick anything with subtitles, you’re on your own. My eyes aren’t what they used to be, you know. Does this meet your requirements? Do you want me to continue the conversation, or perhaps shift the topic slightly? Speaker_1: (smiling) Excellent. Though, if you pick anything with subtitles, you’re on your own. My eyes aren’t what they used to be, you know.

Speaker_1: Honestly, Mum, the traffic was *brutal* getting here. I left ages ago, and it was just… stationary for a good twenty minutes on the A38. Speaker_2: Oh, love, you didn’t! That road’s a nightmare, always is. Should’ve gone the other way, through Sutton Coldfield, even if it's a bit longer, it’s usually smoother. You know I always say that. Speaker_1: I did think about it, but the satnav insisted this was the quickest route. I swear these things just make things worse sometimes. Still, here I am, coffee smells lovely. Thanks. Speaker_2: You’re very welcome, petal. It’s a new blend, from that little shop on High Street. Says it’s ethically sourced, which is nice, isn't it? Cost a fortune though, I tell you. Everything’s going up, isn’t it? Speaker_1: It is. I was looking at energy bills yesterday, and I nearly choked. I’m trying to be good, turning everything off, but… it just feels endless. Anyway, enough about doom and gloom. How was court yesterday? Anything interesting? Speaker_2: Oh, the usual. A lot of young lads, trouble with the police. Makes you sad, really. One poor lad, barely eighteen, charged with shoplifting. Said he needed the money for his mum’s birthday. Breaks your heart. The judge was firm, though. Sent him down for a month. Speaker_1: That *is* sad. It’s just… a cycle, isn’t it? Then everything’s so stressful for everyone involved. Is Mr. Henderson still being a grump? Speaker_2: (chuckles) Always! Thinks he’s God’s gift, that one. Keeps going on about his cricket days. Says he was nearly professional. Nearly! He’s a right wind-up merchant, but underneath it all, he's alright. Speaking of sport, did you catch the football on Saturday? Absolutely dreadful. Speaker_1: Awful! I tried to watch it, but I ended up reading a book. I just couldn’t bear another ninety minutes of that. I’m starting to lose interest, to be honest. It’s all just money and diving these days. Speaker_2: Tell me about it. It's not like it used to be. Remember when it was all about skill and passion? Now it’s just… well, it’s a business. Honestly, I'd rather watch gardening. Speaker_1: (laughing) That’s true! You and your roses. Are they still doing well? Speaker_2: Oh, they’re blooming lovely, actually. I’ve got a new variety, a pale pink climber, absolutely gorgeous. I’ll show you when we go out into the garden later. We should get out there if this rain holds off. It’s supposed to get warmer later. Speaker_1: That sounds lovely. I'm free all afternoon, so we can potter about. What about next weekend? Were you thinking of coming down to see me in Hitchin? Speaker_2: Oh, that would be nice, love. I’d like that. But the car… it’s making that rattling noise again. I’m worried about driving that far. I really need to take it to the garage, but they always charge a fortune… Speaker_1: Oh, Mum. It’s always something with that car. I could maybe drive up, pick you up, and we could both come down? It’s not *that* far. Speaker_2: Oh, would you? That would be a lifesaver, honestly. I'd really appreciate that. Oh and I haven't even asked, how’s Buster? Is he still shedding everywhere? Speaker_1: (groaning) Don’t even get me started! The vacuum cleaner is my best friend. He's lovely, but the fur... It's like living with a cloud! But he's a good boy, all cuddles and wags.

Speaker_1: Honestly, that seminar was… draining. Three hours on post-structuralism before five pm is just cruel and unusual punishment, don't you think? Speaker_2: (Chuckles) You and your students. They didn’t seem to be suffering *too* badly, though. I popped my head in to see how you were getting on, and they all looked remarkably engaged, even the one who’s perpetually scrolling on their phone. Speaker_1: Engaged with the *idea* of engagement, perhaps. I suspect half of them were mentally composing shopping lists. Which, actually, reminds me. I need to get milk. And bread. And possibly… are we out of coffee? Speaker_2: Pretty sure we are. I finished the last of it this morning, bracing myself for marking essays all evening. It was a close call. Maybe we should grab some on the way in? There’s that little shop near the noodle place, they do a decent French press blend. Speaker_1: Good thinking. And I saw a new fabric shop opened up near the market yesterday, the one Mrs. Chen was telling me about. I really need to find some silk for that waistcoat I'm trying to make. The pattern arrived last week and it’s just sitting there, mocking me. Speaker_2: Silk, huh? Getting ambitious, are we? I thought you were still perfecting your embroidery. Speaker_1: Well, embroidery is… therapeutic. But the waistcoat is a *project*. A statement. Plus, I’m terribly bored of wearing cardigans. It feels like all academics own approximately seven cardigans. It’s a uniform. Speaker_2: (Laughing) It is, isn’t it? It's the academic equivalent of a builder's van. It signifies... competence and a willingness to be comfortable. Speaker_1: Exactly! I want to break free from the cardigan tyranny. Though, realistically, it’ll probably take me six months to finish the waistcoat. And I’ll end up wearing a cardigan *over* it in November. Speaker_2: Likely. Still, good on you for trying. What about dinner? Are we feeling noodles or something a bit more… adventurous? I saw a new Uyghur restaurant opened up a few blocks back. Speaker_1: Ooh, Uyghur? That sounds amazing. We haven’t had proper *laghman* in ages. Let's do that! I’ll text Li Wei and see if she and David are free to join. They were saying they wanted to try it too. Speaker_2: Perfect. And I’ll make a list of things we need from the shop. Coffee, milk, bread… anything else? Speaker_1: Hmm… maybe some oranges? I’m craving Vitamin C. And those little sesame balls from the bakery down by the park. Treat ourselves after a day of post-structuralism and essay marking, eh? Speaker_2: Sounds like a plan. Come on, let’s pick up the pace. It’s getting dark, and I don't fancy navigating these streets in the pitch black. Plus, the *laghman* is calling my name. Does this conversation fit your requirements? Shall I continue it, or perhaps modify it in any way? Speaker_1: You know, I think Professor Zhang asked me to sit on a committee for the new curriculum changes. Another thing to add to the pile. It's… exhausting, isn’t it? All this administrative stuff. It takes away from the actual teaching and research. Speaker_2: Oh, brilliant. More meetings. I swear, half my life is spent in meetings discussing meetings. They really need to streamline things. Have you thought about saying no? Speaker_1: Tempted. Very tempted. But he was quite insistent. And it’s… difficult to refuse directly. You know how it is. The whole face-saving culture. Speaker_2: Oh, I do. It's exhausting navigating those unspoken rules. You could always try a polite deferral? Say you're already overcommitted? Steer clear of a flat 'no'. Speaker_1: That’s a good idea.

Speaker_1: Right, so, Mrs. Peterson said she absolutely *cannot* do Saturday night. Something about her book club having a crisis meeting – honestly, you’d think the world was ending! Speaker_2: (Small voice, poking at a bowl of flour) But… you promised I could have a sleepover with Lily on Saturday. Speaker_1: I know, sweetie, and we’ll still *try* for Saturday. I’m just texting Sarah now. She mentioned she might be free. It’s just… finding someone reliable last minute is a nightmare. Speaker_3: (Holding up a picture book) Mummy, look! The dinosaur has *massive* teeth! Bigger than my hand! Speaker_1: Wow, that *is* a big dinosaur! Okay, one minute, let me finish this text. (Types rapidly) Okay, sent. Fingers crossed. Now, what were we saying about dinosaurs? Speaker_2: I want to make cookies! Chocolate chip ones, with sprinkles! Speaker_1: Okay, cookies sound good. But after we finish reading this dinosaur book, alright? We need to get dinner sorted too. I was thinking spaghetti bolognese? Speaker_3: Yeah! And can I help stir? Speaker_1: Of course you can help stir! You’re excellent stirrers. Although, maybe not with the hot sauce. Remember last time? Speaker_2: (Giggles) You made a funny face! Speaker_1: I did, didn't I? Right, Sarah just replied! She says she’s tentatively free, but she’s having her hair cut on Saturday afternoon, so it depends how long *that* takes. Speaker_3: What’s ‘tentatively’? Speaker_1: It means she might be able to do it, but it’s not definite yet. It’s a grown-up word, darling. Speaker_2: Will Lily come then? Speaker_1: We’re still working on it, love. Look, how about this? We’ll see what Sarah says, and if she can’t do it, we can have a really fun family night? We could build a fort, watch a movie, and *definitely* make those chocolate chip cookies. Speaker_3: A fort?! A *big* fort? Speaker_1: The biggest fort you’ve ever seen! We’ll use all the blankets and pillows. Speaker_2: And can we take photos in the fort? Like a photoshoot? Speaker_1: That’s a brilliant idea! We can dress up and everything. I have that silly feather boa somewhere… Speaker_3: I want to be a dinosaur in the photoshoot! Rawr! Speaker_1: You can absolutely be a dinosaur! Right, let's get this dinosaur book finished, then we’ll start prepping for dinner and maybe do a little cookie dough mixing. Does that sound like a plan? Speaker_2 & Speaker_3: (In unison) Yes! Speaker_1: Good. Now, where were we? Ah yes… “Once upon a time, in a land filled with volcanoes…”

Speaker_1: Honestly, this canteen food is…an experience. I think that’s the polite way to put it. It’s like they actively *try* to make beige food. Speaker_2: (Laughing) You're not wrong! It's all shades of sad, isn’t it? I swear the pasta sauce is just watered-down tomato puree. I brought a sandwich today, thankfully. You should’ve done the same. Speaker_1: I thought, “Oh, I’ll be a responsible student and support the university canteen.” Massive mistake. I’m regretting my life choices with every bite of this…chicken? Is that even chicken? Speaker_2: It *looks* suspiciously like reformed poultry. Anyway, are you still up for that night out on Friday? Chloe was saying she’s managed to get a table at Pryzm. Speaker_1: Pryzm?! Oh god, is that still a thing? Last time I was there, I think I lost a shoe. And my dignity. Speaker_2: (Grinning) Classic you! Well, Chloe reckons they’ve done it up a bit. Apparently, it's less sticky floors and more…themed rooms now? Speaker_1: Themed rooms doesn’t really reassure me. Still, I suppose it beats staying in and writing that essay on Post-Structuralism. My brain physically hurts just thinking about it. Speaker_2: Tell me about it. I’m completely stuck on the Foucault section. It's just…words. Fancy words. All over the page. Speaker_1: Right?! It’s like he’s deliberately trying to confuse everyone. My tutor said we need to “deconstruct the inherent power structures within the text.” I nearly choked on my coffee. Speaker_2: Oh, those tutors! Always with the big words. My mum keeps asking me what I actually *do* at university. I tried to explain it to her, and she just started talking about proper jobs. Speaker_1: Same! My nan asked me if I was learning to type. A *typewriter*! Honestly. She thinks university is just a fancy typing school. Speaker_2: (Chuckles) Bless her. Maybe we should just tell our families we’re training to be professional club-goers. Seems more relatable. Speaker_1: That's a brilliant idea! “Yes, Gran, I’m mastering the art of responsible alcohol consumption and flawless dance moves.” Speaker_2: Exactly! We could even get qualifications. “Level 3 Certificate in Social Fluidity.” What do you reckon? Speaker_1: (Laughing) I'm in. Speaking of fluid, I need a drink. This canteen coffee is actively depressing me. Fancy grabbing a proper coffee after this? There's that little place on Eden Street... Speaker_2: Oh, definitely. Their oat milk lattes are a lifesaver. And maybe we can plan our Pryzm survival strategy. Shoe security is paramount. Does this conversation fit the context and your expectations? Do you want me to continue it, or change something? Speaker_1: What exactly does it mean? Speaker_2: That you should. Speaker_1: I'm honestly thinking of just doing a gap year and working at a ski resort. Speaker_2: That sounds really good. Speaker_1: The food is incredible. Speaker_2: Where exactly? Speaker_1: Val Thorens. It's actually the highest resort in Europe. Speaker_2: Wow. Speaker_1: It is a bit pricey but the work is easy and the après-ski. Speaker_2: When will you do that? Speaker_1: I'm thinking next year. Speaker_2: That's great. Definitely.

Speaker_1: Right, so I was thinking, for next year, we should actually *do* a proper holiday. Like, not just a weekend in York or something. Somewhere hot. Speaker_2: Hot sounds good. I’m so tired of grey. Though, honestly, anywhere that isn't actively raining feels like a holiday after this winter. Remember that trip to the Lake District last year? Pure, unadulterated drizzle. Speaker_3: Oh god, don't remind me. I think I permanently smell of damp sheep after that one. Though, in fairness, the pub lunches were alright. Speaking of which, have you two tried that new Thai place near the station? It's lethal. Speaker_1: No! Is it actually decent? I always read the reviews and they’re either raving or saying it gave someone food poisoning. There's no in-between. Speaker_2: I went with a mate last week. Really good. Proper spicy, though. I ordered a 'medium' and nearly cried. I'm a pathetic excuse for a spice enthusiast, I know. Speaker_3: You and me both. I’m a ‘mild’ kinda guy. Anything beyond that and my internal organs stage a full-scale rebellion. Anyway, back to holidays... what were you thinking, hot-wise? Spain? Greece? Somewhere a bit more adventurous? Speaker_1: I’ve always fancied Croatia. I saw some pictures online and it looked stunning. Loads of little islands, crystal clear water… plus, it’s meant to be relatively affordable. Speaker_2: Croatia’s a good shout. I was looking at Portugal last year, but everything was booked up. It's becoming the new Spain, apparently. Everyone and their nan is going there now. Speaker_3: Portugal is lovely. My auntie and uncle went last year, spent ages in the Algarve. Said the golf was world class, if that's your thing. I’m more of a ‘lie on a beach and read a terrible book’ kinda holidaymaker. Speaker_1: Sounds perfect to me. Speaking of terrible books, have you seen that new series everyone’s banging on about on Netflix? The one with all the dragons? Speaker_2: Oh, *that* one. My sister's obsessed. She keeps trying to get me to watch it, but I’m not really a fantasy fan. Too much CGI, not enough actual story. Speaker_3: I gave it a go. Got about three episodes in and realised I was actively bored. Plus, all the knights look suspiciously like they’ve wandered off the set of ‘Game of Thrones’. It's just…derivative. Speaker_1: Fair enough. I’m hooked, though. Completely pointless escapism. It's like eating a whole packet of biscuits when you know you shouldn’t. Anyway, back to practicalities. If we're thinking Croatia, we should probably start looking at flights soon. Are we talking a week? Ten days? Speaker_2: Ten days, definitely. A week feels… rushed. And we need time to recover from the inevitable sunburn. Speaker_3: Agreed. Ten days minimum. And we *must* promise to try and find a local restaurant that doesn’t serve tourist menus. I’m sick of bland pasta and overcooked steak when I go on holiday. Speaker_1: Right, Operation Find Proper Food is a go. And… I’ll start looking at potential dates. Maybe July? August’s usually a bit chaotic, isn’t it? Speaker_2: July sounds good. Just… no Lake District. Please. My waterproof jacket has had enough. Speaker_3: Absolutely no Lake District. I second that motion. Let’s aim for sunshine and reasonably priced seafood.

Speaker_1: Right then, finished that crossword. Took me ages with 23 down, "Maritime vessel," six letters. Eventually twigged it was ‘yacht’. Speaker_2: Good for you, Arthur. I’m still trying to decipher what Maureen said on the phone earlier. Something about a new fangled washing machine… honestly, these modern things! Speaker_3: (Chuckles) You and technology, Mum. It’s a never-ending battle. Speaking of battles, did you two see that football match last night? Absolutely brilliant! Villa were on fire. Speaker_1: Football? Bah. All running about and shouting. Give me a good horse race any day. Saw Old Man Hemmings down the pub, reckons his mare is looking good for the Newmarket meeting. Speaker_2: Oh, Arthur and his horses. Honestly, you’d think they were your children. Though I suppose they’re more reliable than some children! Remember young Timothy, the one I used to mind? Always getting into trouble, that one. Speaker_3: I remember. He ended up going to that youth hostel in Cornwall, didn’t he? Said it changed his life. Though I suspect the surfing had more to do with it than any kind of self-discovery. Speaker_1: Cornwall… Lovely place. We went there years ago, stayed in a little B&B near St. Ives. Prices have gone through the roof since then, I reckon. Everything’s so expensive now. Speaker_2: Tell me about it! We’ve been looking at selling this house, you know. Prices are good, apparently. But where would we go? Everything's so small these days. Speaker_3: Selling the house? Really? I thought you were happy here, Mum. It's got all your memories. Speaker_2: We *are* happy here, dear, but it’s getting too much to manage. The garden, the stairs… It's a bit much for us now. We'd like something smaller, more manageable, perhaps closer to you. Speaker_1: Closer to David? That’ll be the day! He’s always gallivanting about London. Remember when he tried to convince us to sell everything and buy a flat there? Madness, I tell you. Absolute madness. Speaker_3: It was a bit ambitious, Dad. London’s not for everyone. Though I have to admit, I had a good weekend there. Went to a conference on new teaching methods. Interesting stuff, though tiring. Speaker_2: Speaking of tiring, your father’s been on at me to list some his old bits and bobs on eBay. Apparently, he’s got a collection of commemorative spoons that are 'worth a fortune'. Speaker_1: They *are* worth a fortune! Some of them are silver! I tell you, that eBay is a racket. They take a ridiculous cut. I tried selling my old model railway once, and they took nearly half the price! Speaker_3: You have to factor in the fees, Dad. It’s part of the game. Though I’m not sure anyone will be queuing up for a collection of spoons. Speaker_1: Don't you underestimate it, lad! People collect all sorts these days. What about that election coming up? Any idea who you’re voting for? Speaker_3: Thinking about it carefully. It’s all a bit depressing, isn’t it? Promises, promises… and nothing ever changes. Speaker_2: That’s the truth. Still, at least we have the television. Good distraction, eh? Though the news is enough to give anyone a headache. I saw an advert for a new car the other day… a lovely little thing, but far too expensive. Speaker_1: Cars are just money pits. You're better off with a good pair of walking boots. Fresh air and exercise, that’s what you need. Now, who’s for a cup of tea?

Speaker_1: Honestly, I’m starting to feel like a dairy cow. Just… attached. It's relentless. Speaker_2: Tell me about it! It's all everyone talks about, isn't it? "Is she feeding well?" "How long is she feeding for?" Honestly, I feel like people think my entire existence is now just providing milk. Speaker_1: Exactly! And the judgement! If you bottle feed, you’re a bad mum. If you breastfeed for longer than six months, you're… also a bad mum, apparently? There’s no winning. Speaker_2: Oh, absolutely. Auntie Carol had a little comment the other day about how ‘a good strong baby needs proper food, not just milk’. Honestly, the cheek! She didn’t even *have* children! Speaker_1: Oof, Carol is the worst. She's always got an opinion, hasn't she? Remember when she tried to tell me how to decorate my flat? Speaker_2: Oh god, yes! The beige curtains. Traumatic. But seriously, this feeding stuff... little Leo was cluster feeding all evening, and I felt like I was living on the sofa. Speaker_1: Oh, Lyra did that last week. Just relentless. I barely moved from the armchair. Ben tried to be helpful, bringing me endless cups of tea, but honestly, I just wanted him to take the baby and *do* the feeding himself, just for five minutes! Speaker_2: (Laughs) Oh, Ben. He's a good egg, but they never truly understand, do they? Mark just looks terrified whenever I detach. Like I’m some kind of dangerous, milk-producing machine. Speaker_1: It's hilarious and pathetic all at once. And then there’s Mum. She keeps asking if I’m getting enough iron. As if the answer isn’t “No, Mum, because I'm constantly nourishing a tiny human being!”. Speaker_2: Oh, mine’s worse. She keeps comparing Leo to your cousin Emily’s baby, like it’s a competition. “Oh, Emily’s baby slept through the night at six weeks, is Leo doing that?” Speaker_1: Ugh, the comparison game! It's… it’s exhausting. Honestly, sometimes I just want to hide under the duvet. Speaker_2: Me too. It’s wonderful, obviously, having him, but sometimes... it's just *a lot*. Have you spoken to Sarah about how’s she coping? She had Elsie a week before us. Speaker_1: I texted her yesterday. She said she’s struggling with the lack of sleep. Speaker_1: …and young Timmy, bless ‘im, he came home from school the other day, lookin’ right downcast. I watch Alcaraz and Djokovic, and they make it look *easy*. Like, the power and spin they get… it's insane. Speaker_3: They are exceptional, of course. But they’ve been working at it since they were tiny. Alcaraz, I read, barely did anything *but* tennis as a kid. It’s a dedication you rarely see. Speaker_1: It's not just dedication. It’s natural talent too, isn’t it? Though, Djokovic’s work ethic is legendary. He’s completely changed the game, really. The physicality he brings… and that return of serve! Speaker_2: Yeah, his return is mental. I tried to copy it once, ended up hitting the ball into the net every time. Speaker_3: (Chuckles) It takes years of practice, Leo. Don’t get discouraged. Focus on the basics. Mr Davies will have you sorted. Have you seen Sinner play recently? Speaker_1: Oh, Sinner’s brilliant, isn’t he? Such a smooth player. And so calm under pressure. Reminds me a little of Federer, actually, the way he moves. Speaker_2: Federer’s the best, though. Don't even argue. The elegance… he made it look like art. Speaker_1: He *was* incredible. A true genius. But Djokovic has the stats, doesn’t he? The sheer number of Grand Slams… Speaker_3: It’s a different era. They all play a very different game. It’s hard to compare across generations. What about you, Leo, who’s your favourite player right now? Besides Alcaraz and Federer, obviously. Speaker_2: Hmm… probably Rune. He’s a bit of a showman. And he's good, obviously, but he’s just really… entertaining to watch. Speaker_1: (Smiling) Oh, a bit of a rebel, are we? Well, a bit of flair never hurts. Now, are you going to help me chop these vegetables or are you just going to stand there analysing tennis pros all evening? Speaker_3: Let him dream a little, love. Good players often have idols, it’s inspirational. Just make sure you practice what Mr Davies tells you, Leo. That's what truly matters.

Speaker_1: Honestly, these napkins… they look like someone’s already… used them. And then folded them. Speaker_2: (Chuckles) Oh, don’t be daft, Liam. They’re just floral. A bit…busy, maybe. But perfectly clean. Speaker_3: They *do* have a strange shape, though. A bit…brief-like, don't you think? Speaker_4: Right, we’re not going there. Focus on the turkey, it’s looking good, Mum. How long was that in for? Speaker_5: Four hours, love. And it’s perfect. Just like your Grandad used to make it. Remember how we always had Christmas dinner at 1pm sharp? No matter what. Speaker_1: I remember having to wear a shirt and tie even if I didn't want to! Speaker_2: Well, it was special! And afterwards, we’d always watch the Queen’s Speech. Though I swear she says the same thing every year. Speaker_3: It’s a tradition, isn’t it? It’s weird to think this is probably the last one with… well, with things being different now. Speaker_4: Don’t be morbid, Sarah. Let’s enjoy the day. Speaking of traditions, anyone done any proper Christmas shopping yet? I still need to get something for Uncle Barry. He’s impossible to buy for. Speaker_5: He always says he doesn't want anything. Then he complains if he doesn’t *get* anything. Men! Speaker_1: I'm gonna go and listen to some tunes. Has anyone heard the new Wham! song? It's banging. Speaker_3: It's alright. Bit nostalgic, isn't it? Reminds me of when you and Josh used to call each other ‘George Michael’ and ‘Andrew Ridgeley’ back in year seven. Speaker_1: (Grumbling) Don’t remind me. That was mortifying. Josh still brings it up. Speaker_4: You two were always a pair. Remember that dance routine you tried to learn for the school disco? The one that involved a lot of… enthusiastic flailing? Speaker_2: Oh, I remember! It was… memorable. Although, 'dance routine' is perhaps a generous description. Speaker_5: My Doris and I used to love those old musicals. Though I never could pick up the steps. Doris was a natural dancer; she could have been in a show, she really could. Speaker_3: Speaking of musicals, the music in *Wonka* was really good. It reminded me of some of the songs from those old films. Speaker_4: Good soundtrack, yeah. I've been listening to a lot of soundtracks lately. Helps me focus when I’m working. Speaker_1: Dad, you never tell us what you *actually* do at work. “Service Manager” sounds… vague. Speaker_4: It is vague. It means I put out fires. Mostly involving computers and grumpy people. Speaker_2: And you come home exhausted. You should have gone to Florida with your sister, dear. Speaker_5: Oh, that reminds me, how *was* Florida, Sarah? Did you have a good time? All that sun... Speaker_3: It was amazing! So hot, though. Getting through the airport was a nightmare, though. So many people. And the security… honestly. Speaker_1: I'd love to go to America one day, but the flights are so expensive. Speaker_2: It's not just the flights, Liam. It's everything. And the way they treat people over there, sometimes. It's different. Speaker_4: We should all be kinder to each other, really. It’s been a… a challenging year, hasn’t it? Let's make a wish on the wishbone later, and hope for a better one.

Speaker_1: Honestly, this shepherd’s pie is amazing, Mum. You’ve outdone yourself. Speaker_2: Oh, you’re sweet, love. It’s just a bit of mince and mash, isn’t it? Though I did use a proper stock cube this time. Makes all the difference, apparently. Speaker_3: (Chuckling) A proper stock cube, eh? Sounds scandalous! Back in my day, it was all bones and water. Built character, it did. Speaker_1: Character and probably a lot of grit. So, Dad, how’s the farm doing? Still battling the weather? Speaker_3: You wouldn’t believe it. Torrential rain all week. The barley’s looking a bit waterlogged, but the sheep are thriving, thankfully. They’re not fussy. As long as they’ve got grass and a dry patch to lie on, they’re happy. It’s the price of lamb that’s the worry now, though. Keeps going down. Speaker_2: Oh dear. It’s just the way things are going, isn’t it? Everything’s getting more expensive, except for what you *sell*. I was talking to Brenda at school today, she’s complaining about the energy bills again. Says they’re threatening to close the greenhouse. Speaker_1: That’s awful! Is there nothing they can do? Maybe a fundraiser or something? Speaker_2: She’s looked into it. Apparently, there are grants, but the paperwork is a nightmare. She's got enough on her plate with the exams coming up. Speaker_1: Exams… Ugh. That sounds stressful. How are you coping, Mum? You always seem so calm amidst the chaos. Speaker_2: It’s… busy. The kids are all under pressure. And honestly, dealing with some of the parents is a full-time job in itself. This one mother, she's convinced her son’s predicted grade is deliberately low because the teacher doesn’t like him. Speaker_3: Sounds like a right drama queen. People put too much pressure on these kids. Used to be, you passed or you failed. Simple. Speaker_1: It’s different now, isn’t it? Everything’s so competitive. It’s exhausting just *thinking* about it. Speaking of exhausting, how’s the hunt for a flat going? Have you found anything remotely affordable in London yet? Speaker_2: (Sighs) Don’t even ask. It’s… grim. Everything’s either a shoebox or costs the earth. I saw one yesterday, supposedly ‘cosy’, it was literally under a railway arch! Speaker_3: London! What did you expect? It's a rip-off. You’re better off staying here. Plenty of space, fresh air. Speaker_1: I know, Dad, but I need to be in London for work. It’s just… the money. I thought I’d be further along by now. Starting out as a project coordinator isn't exactly rolling in it. Speaker_2: Don’t be so hard on yourself, darling. You’re doing brilliantly. It takes time to build a career. And you have a lovely little flat now, it’s just a bit small. Speaker_1: It is small. And the neighbours are…enthusiastic partiers. Last night, I swear they were having a rave until 3am. Speaker_3: (Laughing) Rave, you say? You need to join them! Let your hair down, lass. Speaker_1: Maybe. Or maybe I just need a decent night’s sleep. Oh! I almost forgot. Sarah told me she’s finally split with Mark. Speaker_2: Oh, no! Poor Sarah. I always thought he was a bit of a… user. Speaker_3: Good riddance, I say. She deserves better. Should give her a ring, see if she’s alright. Speaker_1: I will. I was thinking of inviting her down for the weekend. A bit of fresh air might do her good.

Speaker_1: Right, onions are softening nicely. You’re sure you don’t want mushrooms in this pasta sauce? I’ve got a lovely punnet. Speaker_2: No, honestly, I’m good. Mushrooms… they’re just… textural issues. How was your appraisal today? Did the Big Boss finally acknowledge your existence? Speaker_1: (Chuckles) A little bit. She said… and I quote… “Your accuracy is consistently high, which is valuable.” Valuable! Like I’m a slightly chipped antique. No raise, naturally. Speaker_2: Ugh. The usual. They’re all the same, aren’t they? Telling you how valuable you are while simultaneously underpaying you. Did you at least threaten to unleash a transcription rebellion? Speaker_1: I considered it. Briefly. Mostly I just nodded and smiled politely. Thinking about ordering a pizza actually. I’m too tired to properly cook. Speaker_2: Good shout. Have you seen the new Marks and Spencer food adverts? They're doing those posh pizzas now, the ones with the fig and balsamic glaze. Speaker_1: Ooh, tempting! We could get one of those. Though I’m still slightly scarred by that smoked salmon and horseradish pizza we tried last year. Such a disaster. Speaker_2: Okay, fair point. Perhaps we’ll stick to something a little… less adventurous. Speaking of Marks and Spencer, I need new trousers. All mine seem to have mysteriously shrunk in the wash. Speaker_1: They don’t shrink, darling, you’ve just…expanded slightly. (Winks) Speaker_2: (Laughs) Very funny. I saw something on Facebook about the appalling conditions some horses are kept in. Absolutely dreadful. Makes my blood boil. Speaker_1: It’s heartbreaking, isn’t it? That’s why I donate to the World Horse Welfare. Just a little each month, but it feels like something. Did you finish that crossword? The one from Saturday? Speaker_2: I got most of it. Stuck on 17 across – ‘a small island chain’. Any ideas? Speaker_1: (Concentrating) Hmm… The Faroes? Speaker_2: Yes! Of course! You’re amazing. I’ve got a bottle of wine in the cupboard, a Rioja, but I think it's… seventeen years old? Or maybe fourteen. It’s been lurking there a while. Speaker_1: Fourteen-year-old wine. Bold. Are we sure it’s still drinkable? We might need the blender to turn it into something resembling sangria. Actually, the blender's making a funny noise. I think it's finally giving up the ghost. Speaker_2: Another thing to add to the list of things to replace. You know what I’ve been watching? *Trapped*. That Icelandic detective series. It's brilliant. So bleak. Speaker_1: Oh, I’ve heard good things. I’m still slogging my way through *The Walking Dead*. It’s just… so relentlessly depressing. Speaker_2: *Trapped* is depressing, but in a beautiful, windswept, fjord-filled way. Speaking of bleak, have you seen Winston today? He's been particularly aloof. Speaker_1: He was draped across the sofa, judging everyone, as usual. He probably disapproves of our pizza plans. He’s a cat of refined tastes, you know. Speaker_2: Absolutely. A tiny, furry overlord. So, pizza then? And a slightly ancient bottle of Rioja? Speaker_1: Sounds perfect. Now, about those onions… Speaker_2: I'll get the pizza menu.

Speaker_1: Right, honestly, I've been staring at my wardrobe for half an hour. I have *nothing* to wear. Absolutely nothing. Speaker_2: You always say that, love! What's the occasion anyway? Is it just a general getting-glammed-up-for-a-night-out situation, or is there a specific…vibe? Speaker_1: Just a night out, yeah. Sarah’s birthday, at that new place downtown. I was thinking something…sparkly? But not *too* sparkly, you know? I don’t want to look like a Christmas tree. Speaker_3: Ooh, sparkly! I’m feeling a black dress, classic. Though, knowing us, we’ll end up in trainers by the end of the night. Heels are just… cruel. Speaker_4: Preach! I wore heels last week and genuinely thought I was going to faceplant into someone’s chips. I just can't do it anymore. They're instruments of torture. Speaker_5: You lot are weaklings! I’m a heel pro. Though, I *do* pack a pair of flats in my bag, just in case. Smart move, really. Speaker_1: You're showing off now, Chloe. What are *you* wearing then? Bet you’ve already got an outfit planned, you organised soul. Speaker_5: Guilty as charged. Burgundy bodycon, with black heels. Simple, effective. And, importantly, comfortable enough to dance in… for a bit, anyway. Speaker_2: Oh, nice! I was thinking about a jumpsuit. I got a really cute navy one in the sales last week, but I keep worrying it makes my legs look a bit…stumpy. Speaker_3: Stumpy? No way! You’ve got great legs, Liv. Jumpsuits look amazing on you. You just need to find the right shoes - wedges might balance it out. Speaker_4: Speaking of shoes, anyone else spend three hours scrolling through ASOS last night and end up buying nothing? It’s a talent, honestly. Speaker_1: Oh my god, that's literally me. I added like, twelve pairs of boots to my basket and then panicked about the returns process. It's too much effort. Speaker_2: It is! Honestly, shopping online is a nightmare. I much prefer actually *being* in a shop, trying things on. Although, then you have to deal with the changing room lighting... always terrible. Speaker_3: Don’t even get me started on changing room lighting. It's designed to make you feel awful about yourself. Plus, you’re always battling for a mirror. Speaker_5: This is why I just order everything in three different sizes and return what doesn't fit. It’s easier, even if it’s slightly wasteful. Speaker_1: You are a menace, Chloe. A glorious, stylish menace, but still. Anyone fancy pre-drinks before we go out? I've got some prosecco chilling. We need to fuel up for a night of questionable dance moves. Speaker_4: Prosecco sounds *amazing*. I'm in. Just promise me we’ll all look out for each other and make sure no one ends up talking to a lamppost. Speaker_2: Oh, that’s happened… let’s just say I've seen things… Also, pacing ourselves is key. We don't want a repeat of last time. Speaker_3: Right, Operation: Don't End Up Regretting Everything Tomorrow is officially in effect! Let the prosecco flow! Does this fit what you were looking for? Let me know if you'd like me to continue the conversation, or adjust anything.

Speaker_1: Honestly, the way Mark just *dominates* every conversation… it’s exhausting. You’d think, after twenty years, he’d learn to let someone else get a word in edgewise. Speaker_2: (Sighs, stirring his coffee) He’s always been like that, hasn’t he? The ‘expert’ on everything. It's a confidence thing, I think. Deep down, he's probably terrified of being seen as… ordinary. Speaker_1: Terrified of being ordinary? He runs a plumbing business! There’s nothing ordinary about fixing burst pipes in January! It’s just… a need to always be right. It’s draining. Speaker_2: It is. Remember that time we went to that historical reenactment in Warwick? The Victorian one? He spent the *entire* day correcting the actors on the accuracy of their accents. Speaker_1: (Laughing) Oh god, yes! And the poor woman playing the scullery maid, she looked genuinely tearful. He was going on about the regional variations in dialect! Like she wasn’t already dressed in layers and pretending to scrub floors! Speaker_2: He’s got a genuine fascination with detail, though. That’s part of what makes him… him. It’s just not always appropriate. It’s like he’s on a constant spiritual journey to discover the perfect historical fact. Speaker_1: A spiritual journey? You're being generous. I think he just wants to prove he’s smarter than everyone else. It makes me wonder about soul mates, actually. Do you think they’re real? Or just a really good marketing ploy by the romance industry? Speaker_2: I don't know. I used to be very cynical about it all. Then I met you. Speaker_1: (Smiling) Oh, you smooth talker. Speaker_2: No, honestly. It's not about finding someone perfect, because nobody is. It’s about finding someone who understands your… quirks. Who doesn’t mind when you spend three hours researching the best type of teacup. Speaker_1: (Chuckles) Guilty. And who puts up with you endlessly tinkering with the home network, convinced you’re preventing a cyberattack? Speaker_2: Precisely. Speaking of which, I *am* thinking of setting up a separate network just for the smart speakers. They're a security nightmare. Speaker_1: Oh, here we go. Can we *please* not talk about IT first thing on a Saturday? I was hoping we could at least pretend it’s a day off. Speaker_2: Sorry. Force of habit. I was just thinking… If we could throw a party, but invite people from different periods in history, who would be on the guest list? Speaker_1: Oh! Ooh, that’s a good one. Right. Definitely Jane Austen. And Cleopatra, obviously. Maybe Leonardo da Vinci, for the entertainment value. Although, knowing Mark, he'd be interrogating him about the engineering of his flying machines. Speaker_2: And a Viking? A proper, bearded Viking. Speaker_1: Yes! A Viking, definitely. Though we’d need to hide the silverware. And Elizabeth I, she’d run the whole show. Absolutely dominate the conversation. Mark would have a field day…or a breakdown. Speaker_2: It would be chaos. Delicious, historical chaos. Look, I’m really sorry for bringing up Mark’s… tendencies. I didn't mean to start the day with a complaint fest. Speaker_1: It’s alright. It’s just… sometimes it gets to me, you know? But honestly, even with all his quirks, I wouldn’t change him. Especially not if it meant missing out on imaginary parties with historical figures.

Speaker_1: Honestly, the amount of paperwork for that little craft stall is ridiculous. You wouldn’t believe. It's like running a FTSE 100 company, the hoops you have to jump through just to sell a knitted penguin. Speaker_2: A knitted penguin? Seriously? That sounds… adorable, actually. But yeah, I get the paperwork thing. Even applying for a blue badge was a nightmare. Mountains of forms. Speaker_3: Penguins, eh? You’re branching out from the scarves then, Carol? Last time I saw you, it was a rainbow of woolly neckwear. Speaker_1: Scarves are steady trade, don't get me wrong. But penguins are *selling*. Apparently, everyone needs a knitted penguin. I'm thinking of expanding, maybe little knitted corgis. Though I’m worried about getting the ears right. Speaker_2: Corgis are a good shout. Everyone loves a corgi. Especially since… well, you know. Speaker_1: (Sighs) Don’t remind me. It's just…it feels a bit insensitive to capitalise on royal sadness, even with knitted dogs. Still, bills need paying. Speaker_3: You’re overthinking it, love. People want a little bit of comfort, a little bit of joy. A knitted corgi isn’t glorifying anything. It’s…craft. Pure and simple. Speaker_1: Maybe you’re right. Though I did have old Mrs. Higgins giving me the side-eye at the church fete. Said it was ‘disrespectful’. Honestly, some people. Speaker_2: Oh, bless. Mrs. Higgins is always finding something to disapprove of. Remember when she complained about my bright pink hair? Said it ‘wasn’t becoming of a young lady’. Speaker_3: That was hilarious! You handled her beautifully, love. Just said, “It matches my personality!” Speaker_2: Had to! Honestly, the things people comment on. It’s always something. Makes you wonder if they’ve got nothing better to think about. Speaking of better things to think about, how’s work? Still battling the endless reports? Speaker_1: Oh, don’t even *start* me on the reports. Brenda called in sick again. Apparently, a bad curry. That’s the third time this month. I’m starting to suspect she just really likes a good takeaway. I swear, half my job is covering for Brenda. Speaker_3: Brenda. Always a drama. I’ve got a staff member off on ‘stress leave’. Apparently his goldfish died. A *goldfish*! I had to approve it. HR are going mad for authorisation. Speaker_1: A goldfish?! Oh, that's… something. You’d think they’d just get another one, wouldn’t you? It’s not like it’s a beloved family pet. Speaker_2: It’s the principle, innit? Loss is loss, apparently. Though, I'm honestly starting to think people just take the mickey sometimes. My cousin went off on sick leave because she broke a nail. Speaker_1: No! You're joking! Speaker_2: I wish I was. A *nail*. Said she couldn’t type. Honestly. It's a different language sometimes, the world of work. And the excuses people come up with. Speaker_3: It’s appalling. Reminds me of that time my Uncle George tried to claim on his insurance because a squirrel stole his sandwiches. Speaker_1: (Laughing) Oh my god! George? That’s brilliant! He’s always been a character. Speaker_2: Right? I told you, Peterborough is a special place.

Speaker_1: Honestly, I’m starting to think living with Liam is a mistake. A massive, student loan-funded mistake. Speaker_2: Woah, what happened? Last I heard you were bonding over obscure FIFA teams. Speaker_1: That *was* last week, before he decided his bedroom was a biohazard zone. Like, genuinely, I can smell it from the hallway. And he’s just… leaving plates everywhere. Dirty plates, Jamal! Speaker_3: (Entering, carrying a grocery bag) Oh god, don’t even get me started on flatmate hygiene. Chloe in my halls uses the communal kitchen as a personal dumping ground. I swear I saw a science experiment growing in her sink yesterday. Speaker_2: Sounds… delightful? But seriously, Liam? You’ve known him ages, I thought you'd be able to handle a bit of mess. Speaker_1: It’s not just the mess! He keeps ‘borrowing’ my oat milk. Like, subtle sips, then suddenly half the carton’s gone. And then he has the cheek to ask if *I’ve* been using his shower gel! Speaker_3: That's next level. The oat milk is a crime against humanity, though. It's expensive! Did you ask him about it? Speaker_1: I tried! He just gave me this puppy-dog look and said he was ‘really craving a creamy coffee’. A creamy coffee funded by *my* student loan! Speaker_2: (Laughing) Oh, Liam. He's a professional user of puppy-dog eyes. Remember that time he convinced Mrs. Henderson to extend the deadline for his essay? Speaker_3: Oh, *that* was legendary. He told her his nan was ill, which, in his defence, she was, but he’d already finished the essay and was just trying to get a weekend free for a football match. Speaker_1: Don’t remind me. He’s going on about the derby this weekend, needing ‘tactical support’. Which means he wants me to make him snacks whilst he yells at the TV. Speaker_2: Speaking of the derby, I’m going with Ben and Aisha. Want to come? It’ll be a good distraction from the oat milk bandit. Speaker_1: Hmm… tempting. Although, I'm supposed to be doing that reading for Dr. Davies’ lecture. It’s on tax law, and honestly, my brain is already glazing over thinking about it. Speaker_3: Tax law? Ugh, that sounds… thrilling. I’ve got to start looking into student council elections. Sophie's trying to get me to run for treasurer. She says I’m “good with numbers,” which is a polite way of saying I’m obsessively good at budgeting because I'm perpetually broke. Speaker_2: You'd be amazing! You're the most organised person I know. Plus, think of the power! You could influence where the uni spends its money. Maybe get them to invest in… better kitchen cleaning supplies for Chloe? Speaker_3: (Smiling) Now *that’s* a campaign promise I can get behind. Though, honestly, just managing to afford groceries this week feels like a major victory. Did either of you check out that new market on Tuesday? They had really cheap fruit. Speaker_1: No, I totally forgot. I spent all afternoon trying to decipher HMRC’s website. Apparently, I have to register as self-employed for that freelance design work I did last summer. It’s a nightmare! And I'm pretty sure I'm going to owe them money. Speaker_2: HMRC is evil. Pure evil. I swear they invent rules just to torment students. Maybe Liam could use his puppy-dog eyes on them? Speaker_1: (Scoffs) Don’t even joke. They'd probably just audit him, and then we’d *all* be in trouble.

Speaker_1: This seafood risotto is *amazing*. Honestly, the best thing I’ve eaten all week. Speaker_2: (Smiling) Glad you like it, love. Croatia does seafood so well, doesn’t it? Much better than anything you get back home, even at that fancy Italian place you like. Speaker_3: It’s alright. I just wish they did chips. All this…fishy stuff. Speaker_4: (Chuckles) You and your chips, lad. You’ll broaden your horizons eventually. Try a bit of this, it’s actually quite mild. Speaker_1: Dad, don’t pressure him. It's a holiday, let him eat what he wants. Anyway, I was telling Mum about university applications. I've narrowed it down to Manchester and Leeds. Speaker_2: Manchester, eh? That's not far. Good for getting home easily. What are you thinking of studying? Still psychology? Speaker_1: Yeah, still psychology. Leeds has a really strong course on forensic psychology, which I’m really interested in, but Manchester is closer to… well, everything. And I know more people there. Speaker_3: Can I go to Manchester with you when you go to uni? Speaker_1: (Laughing) Not for a good few years yet, little brother! You’ve still got school to worry about. How’s year seven treating you? Speaker_3: It’s okay. There’s this lad, Liam, he’s got a tattoo… on his ARM! Speaker_2: (Scoffs) Year seven and tattoos? Honestly. They’re getting younger and younger. I saw a girl, probably fourteen, with a full sleeve the other day. Speaker_4: It's the times we live in, I suppose. Though I still think it's a bit rash for anyone, let alone a teenager. Speaking of rash decisions - remember young Daniel getting on that moped in Corfu? Nearly gave your mother a heart attack. Speaker_2: Don’t remind me! He was speeding around like a maniac. Honestly, I thought he was going to end up in the hospital. Which brings me to my day - absolute chaos. Little old Mrs. Higgins went into labour two hours early. Had to practically sprint to her house. Speaker_1: Wow, sounds stressful! Speaker_2: It is, but rewarding. It’s just… the paperwork afterwards. Mountains of it. And then trying to explain to young patients the importance of iron levels and healthy eating – it’s like talking to a brick wall sometimes. They’d rather be on Facebook, scrolling through influencers than listening to me. Speaker_4: (Smiling) Sounds familiar. Trying to explain market analysis to clients can be equally frustrating. They all think they know best, until the numbers tell a different story. Although, I did have a very interesting meeting today about the potential redevelopment of that supermarket site down on Bridgeman Street. They’re thinking of building flats. Speaker_1: Oh really? That would be good, wouldn’t it? That supermarket’s always so crowded. Speaker_3: Can we get a dog when we get back? Please? A big one, like a Labrador? Speaker_2: (Sighs) We’ve been through this, love. We don't have the time to look after a dog properly, not with my shifts at the hospital. Speaker_4: And remember the last time we tried getting the bus into town? Absolute nightmare! Packed like sardines. Speaker_1: Oh god, don't even get me started on the Bolton buses. It’s an experience, alright. Speaker_2: This wine’s lovely though, isn’t it? We really needed this break. England feels a million miles away.

Speaker_1: Right then, cups of tea all round, I think. Good to be back in a proper chair, eh? That YHA bunk was…functional. Speaker_2: Functional is a kind word, Arthur. It was a bit like sleeping in a tin box. But honestly, Cornwall was lovely. Thanks for suggesting it, dear. And David, good of you to come collect us, wasn't it? Saved us wrestling with the suitcases on the train. Speaker_3: No problem at all. Glad you both had a good time. Though, judging by the faces, the journey back wasn’t entirely smooth sailing? Speaker_1: Smooth sailing? Ha! Tried to tell her about that cycle race. “Yorkshire in a Day” they called it. Absolute madness. All those lycra-clad lunatics going up hills. Nearly got run off the road twice. Speaker_2: Arthur only wanted to point out a particularly steep incline. He’s been on about hills ever since we visited that lighthouse. Stunning, wasn't it? Lizard Point. Though good heavens, the wind! Thought my hair would blow right off. Speaker_3: Lizard Point, brilliant. I’ve always wanted to go. Did you get any good photos? I’m attempting a presentation on coastal landscapes for the school, and decent visuals are proving elusive. Speaker_1: Got plenty. Mostly of Maureen trying to stand upright in a gale. She looked like a scarecrow. And a surprisingly large number of crabs. Little blighters were everywhere. Tried to steal my pasty, one did. Speaker_2: He’s exaggerating slightly. It *looked* at the pasty. Anyway, I have loads of photos too, David. Let me get my phone. Oh, and some of that YHA. It wasn’t *all* bad. The views were spectacular. Though I did spend a good hour trying to work out how to share a bathroom with fourteen teenagers. Speaker_3: Sounds…challenging. You two volunteering was a good idea though, providing a bit of support for the YHA. I admire that. It’s good to give back. Speaker_1: Give back? Foot ache is what I gave back! That coastal path… endless steps. Didn’t realise I was still capable of walking that far.
