I checked the app before we left, said ‘slow but moving’. ‘Slow but moving’ is a generous description, wouldn't you say? At this rate, we'll be lucky to get to Manchester before tea time. Speaker_3: It’s the M6, love. Expect nothing less. Still, at least we’re all together. And you’ve got a good supply of biscuits, Moira. That’s the main thing. Speaker_1: (Chuckles) Always prepared. Though I’m starting to think *I’ll* be the one needing the comfort of a biscuit before long, staring at these brake lights. Speaking of needing things...did you manage to sort out that quote for the removal van, David? Speaker_3: Aye, I did. Got a surprisingly good price, actually. Old Mr. Henderson from down the road recommended a company. Apparently his daughter used them when she moved to York. Seemed decent enough on the phone. Said they're very careful with furniture. Reminded me of when we moved to Walsall… absolute chaos, that was. Remember that antique sideboard your mother loved? Speaker_2: Oh, don't even start! I've heard that story approximately fifty times. The one where it nearly went over the M5 embankment? Speaker_3: (Laughing) It was a close call! The straps gave way, and it was wobbling like a jelly! Luckily, young Timmy – bless him – managed to brace it with his foot. Saved a family heirloom, he did. Speaker_1: Well, let’s hope *this* move is a little less eventful. I’m already stressed enough about downsizing. So many years in that house, so much… stuff. It’s overwhelming. Speaker_2: You'll be glad to be rid of it, honestly. Remember your back troubles last year? All those stairs weren't helping. A nice, level bungalow will be much better for you. And closer to us, which is a bonus. Speaker_1: True, true. Proximity to my favourite people is a definite perk. Though I'm dreading the entire airport palaver. I haven’t flown in… goodness, must be ten years now? Speaker_3: Airports are a nightmare these days, aren't they? All queues and security checks and lost luggage. I used to travel all the time for work, used to be a bit more civilised. Now? It's just stressful. I much prefer a nice, long drive, even one like this one. Speaker_2: At least we can control the music in the car. And stop for biscuit refills. Though I do feel a little guilty about leaving the car at home, you know? It's been sat on the drive for months with barely a journey since you retired, David. Speaker_3: Don't you worry about the car, love. It's had a good run. Besides, I'm enjoying being able to rely on public transport for once. Forces me to walk a bit more, which can’t hurt. Though my knees aren’t what they used to be. Speaker_1: Oh, your knees! Are they playing up again? Did you take your glucosamine tablets? Speaker_3: Aye, I did. Just a bit of a niggle. Damp weather, you know? Always affects them. Good job we're heading towards Manchester and not further north, eh? I heard it's been pouring up in the Lake District.

Speaker_1: So, you won’t *believe* what happened with the bike. Speaker_2: Oh no, don’t tell me it's… worse? I thought you said the police hadn’t had any luck. Speaker_1: Well, they hadn’t. But Mrs. Henderson from number 32, she recognised it! She saw a lad riding it down towards the seafront yesterday afternoon. She said she was pretty sure it was yours, with the stickers and everything. Speaker_2: No way! Did she… did she say anything? Speaker_1: She did. Apparently, she followed him – really bravely, actually – and kept an eye on where he went. He ended up leaving it chained up outside the amusement arcade. She called the police straight away. Speaker_2: Seriously?! That’s amazing! So you’ve got it back? Is it alright? Speaker_1: Yep, picked it up just an hour ago. A little scuffed, but nothing major. The lock they used was rubbish, honestly. I reckon I could have just snapped it with my hands. Speaker_2: That’s brilliant! I was so gutted when it went missing. I was starting to think I’d have to walk to college every day. It’s miles! Speaker_1: I know. And with the hills! Honestly, it was giving me stress just thinking about it. I told you not to leave it unlocked, though. Speaker_2: I know, I know, Mum. I just popped into the shop for like, two minutes! It's just… it happens so fast. Have you seen on TikTok, there’s this whole trend of bike thefts going around? Apparently, Hastings is a hotspot. Speaker_1: TikTok? Honestly, you and that TikTok. It’s probably just making you more paranoid. Still, good to be aware, I suppose. Right, fancy some lunch? I made a massive pasta bake. Speaker_2: Ooh, yes please! That sounds amazing. Is it the one with the cheesy crust? Speaker_1: The very same. I even put in extra cheese, knowing how much you love it. Speaker_2: You’re the best! I’m still buzzing about the bike, though. I'm definitely investing in a seriously good lock now. Maybe one of those ones that beep if someone tries to move it? Speaker_1: Good thinking! And try not to post pictures of it all over social media, advertising where you live, yeah? Just a thought. Speaker_2: Ugh, you’re right. Mum’s always looking out for me. Maybe I’ll just stick to posting about the pasta bake instead. Speaker_1: Now *that* is a good plan. Come on, let’s go eat before it gets cold. And after, we can go for a little cycle – maybe just around the park, to test it out properly. Speaker_2: Perfect! A celebratory cycle with extra cheesy pasta… couldn’t ask for more. Thanks, Mum. You always sort things out. Speaker_1: Nonsense, dear. That’s what mums are for. Now, let's eat! Speaker_2: Okay! Speaker_1: (slightly under her breath) Honestly, TikTok… Speaker_2: (laughing) I heard that! Speaker_1:Just saying!

Speaker_1: Right, I’m officially declaring myself starved. This Ticket to Ride is deceptively energy-consuming. Speaker_2: (Chuckles, placing down a train card) Tell me about it. Strategising is *hungry* work, you know? Though, to be fair, I did have a rather large elevenses. Speaker_3: Elevenses? You’re turning very English, Gareth. Next thing you know you’ll be demanding scones with clotted cream. Speaker_2: (Feigning offense) Hey! A Welshman can appreciate a good scone. It’s the jam-first debate where things get really heated. Speaker_4: (Without looking up from the board) Jam first is the *only* way. Anyone who argues differently is a heathen. Speaker_5: Oh, don’t start that again, Bryn. We’ve had this argument every family holiday for the last decade. It’s exhausting. Speaker_1: (Laughing) You’re all wonderfully predictable. Right, food. What are we thinking? I was fancying a proper pub lunch tomorrow, maybe? Somewhere with a roaring fire? It's definitely that sort of weather. Speaker_3: Sounds good to me. Though, I'm warning you, I'm craving a Sunday roast. Yorkshire puddings are non-negotiable. Speaker_2: Oooh, ambitious. A good Yorkshire pudding is a thing of beauty. Speaking of ambitious… I’m attempting to complete the Trans-Siberian Railway route. It’s proving…challenging. Speaker_4: The Trans-Siberian? Good luck with that! It’s a monster. You need to think about momentum, you see. Like a real train. Speaker_1: (Raises an eyebrow) Oh, here we go. Prepare for a lecture on train dynamics, everyone. Speaker_4: It’s not a lecture! It’s applied physics! You need to factor in the gradient, the weight of the carriages, the resistance from the tracks… It’s a delicate balance. You can’t just haphazardly lay down routes. Think about George Stephenson's Rocket! Speaker_5: (Smiling fondly) Oh, Bryn and his trains. He’s been obsessed since he was a little boy. Used to dismantle anything with wheels. Speaker_3: I remember one Christmas, he took apart my brand new train set to “understand how it worked.” My mum nearly had a fit. Speaker_4: (Defensively) It was for educational purposes! I rebuilt it, eventually. Mostly. Speaker_2: Right, well, clearly I'm not approaching this with enough scientific rigour. I'll need to factor in the gravitational pull of the coloured plastic trains. Speaker_1: (Chuckles) Absolutely essential. Do you want me to start calculating wind resistance? Speaker_2: Please do! While you're at it, could you research the optimal coal-to-water ratio for steam engines? You know, for strategy purposes. Speaker_3: I think we need to change the subject before we both end up researching Victorian engineering. Anyone fancy helping me collect more train cards? I’m desperate for blues. Speaker_5: Happy to. Though, if we’re talking about journeys, I’m dreaming of a train journey through the Italian countryside. The food alone… Speaker_1: Oh, now *that* sounds perfect. We should definitely do that one day. Right after a Sunday roast with enormous Yorkshire puddings. And jam-first scones. Speaker_2: (Placing down another train route) Right, I’ve secured Edinburgh to Newcastle. Progress! Though honestly, it feels like I’m building a railway network across Siberia with a toothpick.

Speaker_1: Right, your go. Honestly, this game is taking *forever*. I thought ‘Ticket to Ride’ would be a quick evening activity after your mum’s roast, not a three-hour strategic battle for railway dominance. Speaker_2: (Chuckles, studying the board) It *is* taking a while, isn’t it? Though, I’m thoroughly enjoying it. It’s a good change from marking essays. And besides, Mum’s roast deserves a lengthy wind-down. She puts so much effort in. Speaker_1: True, true. She did outdo herself with the Yorkshire puddings. Still, I’m starting to feel like I need a map just to figure out where everyone is trying to go. You’re awfully quiet, what nefarious plan are you hatching? Speaker_2: No plan. Just…considering my options. Strategizing. It's funny, isn’t it, how seriously people take board games? I was reading an article the other day about the German *Spiel des Jahres* award – apparently, it’s a massive deal. Like, national news level. Speaker_1: Really? That’s…intense. I always assumed board games were just a bit of fun, a rainy-day activity. Germans seem to take everything very seriously though, don’t they? Even their leisure time? Speaker_2: It’s a whole culture, apparently. They have these huge board game conventions, and it’s considered a perfectly acceptable adult hobby. A lot more sophisticated than Monopoly and Cluedo, though. They’re all about intricate mechanics and long-term strategy. Speaker_1: Hmm. Sounds exhausting. I prefer something a bit lighter, honestly. We should dig out 'Carcassonne' next time we’re here. It’s a lot more… pastoral. Less about resource management and more about building little medieval landscapes. Speaker_2: Good shout. You know, it’s a weird contrast to the drinking culture here, isn’t it? In Germany, it's all about the games being the *focus*. Here, a ‘games night’ often feels like a thinly veiled excuse to get progressively more tipsy. Speaker_1: (Laughs) Oh, you’re spot on. Especially with Uncle David involved. It starts innocently enough with a bit of Scrabble, then someone suggests cards, then it’s ‘never have I ever’ fuelled by gin and tonics. It escalates quickly. Speaker_2: Precisely! And don't even get me started on family charades. It’s less about acting out clues and more about deliberately obtuse interpretations to wind everyone up. Speaker_1: Oh God, yes. And Dad *always* chooses incredibly obscure historical figures. No one has a clue what he's doing. It's purely designed to frustrate us. Right, I’m claiming the blue route to Plymouth. Take that! Speaker_2: (Sighs dramatically) You fiend! You’ve completely blocked my access to the southwest. You realize this means war, don't you? A quiet, strategic railway war, fought across the map of Great Britain. Speaker_1: Bring it on. Though, just so you know, I’m already thinking about the wine Mum’s stashed in the cellar for after the game. That's my real strategy. Speaker_2: You’re terrible. Absolutely terrible. Though, fair point about the wine. A little Burgundy might just be the fuel this railway empire needs. Speaker_1: Exactly. A little fortification for the final push. Speaker_2: Okay, okay. My turn, then. Prepare to be outmaneuvered. Speaker_1: I'm suitably prepared. And slightly caffeinated from that second cup of tea. This is going to be good.

Speaker_1: Honestly, this shepherd’s pie is amazing, Kerrie. You’ve outdone yourself. It's even better than last time. Speaker_2: It really is fantastic. What’s the secret this time? More Worcester sauce? Speaker_3: (Chuckles) Just a good pinch of nutmeg, boys. That’s all. My grandmother always said a pinch of nutmeg makes all the difference. And proper lamb mince, never beef. Speaker_1: Nutmeg! That’s clever. I always forget the little things like that. I tried making a stew last week and it was… well, it was edible. But not *this* good. Speaker_2: I’m still trying to get my head around moving all the white goods. It’s a nightmare. The washing machine alone feels impossible. Speaker_3: Oh, that’s a headache, isn’t it? Did you get quotes for removal firms? They’re expensive, but worth it if you’ve got a lot to move. Speaker_2: I did, and horrifyingly so! I was hoping to just bribe a couple of strong friends with beer and pizza, but I think I might actually need professionals. The staircase in the new place is *narrow*. Speaker_1: You really should get professionals. It’s not worth risking injury, or damaging your stuff. Remember what happened to Sarah when she tried to move her sofa herself? Speaker_3: Oh, don't remind me. A trip to A&E and a very expensive sofa repair! She learned her lesson, that one. Speaking of which, how’s Sarah’s back? Last I heard, she was still having trouble. Speaker_1: She’s a lot better, thankfully. Physiotherapy seems to be doing the trick. She’s back to doing her pottery, which has really cheered her up. She’s making some beautiful little planters now. Speaker_2: That’s good to hear. She puts so much effort into it. It’s always nice to see people doing things they enjoy. I’m just… stressed about all this moving stuff. And the bins! Apparently, the collection schedule is completely different in the new area. Speaker_3: Oh, bins are *always* a source of contention. Honestly, I spend half my life trying to figure out which bin is for what. It changes every year! And don’t even get me started on the council’s website… Speaker_1: It’s designed to be purposefully confusing, I swear. I’ve spent ages trying to find out what day our recycling gets collected. It feels like a conspiracy. Speaker_2: It does! And the new place… it’s got a tiny kitchen. I’m going to have to get rid of half my gadgets. I just bought a new pasta maker a month ago! Speaker_3: Oh dear. Well, you can always store some things here for a bit, if you’re really stuck. I’ve got a spare room, though it's currently a bit of a storage room itself. I keep meaning to sort it out, but then something always comes up. Speaker_1: That’s really kind of you, Kerrie. Honestly, you’re a lifesaver. I’m still trying to convince my brother to help me with the furniture. He claims he's 'busy', but I suspect it's just an excuse to avoid manual labour. He’s got all those fancy qualifications, you'd think he’d be able to lift a sofa! Speaker_2: Classic. Everyone underestimates how much physical work is involved in moving. It’s not just about logistics, it’s about sheer muscle power.

Speaker_1: Honestly, Mum, this traffic is mental. Feels like we’ve barely moved in the last ten minutes. Speaker_2: It always does around here, darling. Especially heading towards the North Circular. Remember when your father used to get absolutely *furious*? Full-on road rage. Speaker_1: (Chuckles) Oh yeah, the horn was his second voice. He’d be laying into people left, right, and centre. I try to just… zen out. It’s not worth the stress. Speaker_2: Wise lad. Though a little assertive honking never hurt anyone, within reason. Are you still enjoying the car, by the way? Your Grandad would be chuffed to see you driving it. Speaker_1: Yeah, it’s good. Properly comfy, actually. Still getting used to the parking, though. It’s a beast. Though I think it’s more the London drivers I need to get used to. Speaker_2: They’re a special breed, aren’t they? So, how was that meeting with your supervisor yesterday? Still feeling good about the dissertation? Speaker_1: Yeah, it’s going alright. He gave me a couple of pointers on the methodology, which was helpful. It’s just… enormous. Feels like I’m drowning in research sometimes. Speaker_2: Well, you’re a clever boy, you’ll get there. You always do. Speaking of enormous, I had the most dreadful email from a prospective author this morning. Thought he was submitting a manuscript to the *TLS* – completely missed that we only do reviews. Speaker_1: Oh, bless him. People don’t read the submission guidelines, do they? Speaker_2: Apparently not! It’s a constant battle, that. And then the debate about digital versus print. Everyone’s convinced print is dead, but we still get a surprising number of subscriptions. Speaker_1: I get that. I still prefer proper books. The *feel* of them, you know? Though, I confess, my Kindle does get a fair bit of use. Especially on the commute. Speaker_2: It’s convenient, I’ll give it that. But there’s just something about holding a beautifully bound volume… Although, shipping costs are killing us. It’s getting ridiculous. Speaker_1: Right? Everything’s getting more expensive. You’d think they were sending the books by private jet. Speaker_2: Practically! Oh, speaking of expense, I need to pick up a birthday present for your Aunt Sarah. Any ideas? She's impossible to buy for. Speaker_1: Hmm… she mentioned wanting to go back to France, didn’t she? Maybe a nice French cookbook? Or a voucher for a French wine tasting? Speaker_2: That’s a good thought, actually. She’s always going on about her trip to Provence. And a wine tasting… she’d love that. I’ll look online later. You know, she’s fitted those new driving sensors in her car. She was petrified to go over the M25. Speaker_1: Good. Reliable. Safety first. She's a good driver, but it gives everyone peace of mind. Speaker_2: Exactly. Oh, look! We’re almost there. Just need to navigate this roundabout… careful now, someone’s trying to merge without indicating. Honestly! Some people… Speaker_1: (Sighs) Here we go. Zen mode engaged. Speaker_2: You’re a good boy, you are. A very good boy. Now, remind me, are we picking up that frame for your sister or… Speaker_1: The frame. Yes. For the photo from graduation. She loved that picture.

Speaker_1: Right, so then the seagull *actually* swooped down and tried to steal the chips right out of her hand! Honestly, I’ve never seen anything like it. Old Mrs. Higgins nearly had a heart attack. Speaker_2: (Laughing) No way! Classic Blackpool. They’re proper aggressive them seagulls, aren’t they? They’ve no shame. Speaker_3: It’s true! My little cousin lost a whole sausage roll to one last year. She was devastated. The seagull didn’t even look sorry. Just perched on the tower, smug as anything. Speaker_4: You get that in Scarborough too, honestly. One tried to take my ice cream. I had to physically wrestle it off him. Nearly ended up with a beak mark! Speaker_5: Wrestling a seagull? You’re braver than you look, love. Speaker_4: I was fuelled by raspberry ripple, alright? It was a matter of principle! Speaker_1: Speaking of risking life and limb for snacks, remember that time Liam tried to climb the lamppost at Southport Pleasure Beach to get a better view of the fireworks? Speaker_2: (Groaning) Oh god, don’t remind me. My dad nearly killed him. He was absolutely furious. Speaker_3: He thought he was Spider-Man! He was shouting “With great power comes great responsibility!” as he was halfway up. Speaker_5: He’s always been a bit dramatic, our Liam. I remember when he convinced himself he was a pirate for a whole month after that trip to Alton Towers. He wouldn't answer to anything but "Captain Blackheart." Speaker_4: (Smiling) Oh, I'd forgotten about Captain Blackheart! He made us all walk the plank – which was just a piece of wood across the garden, but still. Speaker_1: And he insisted on wearing an eye patch, even to school. Mrs. Davies had to have a word. Speaker_2: Poor Mrs. Davies. She's seen it all, hasn’t she? Remember when I tried to convince everyone I could speak fluent Welsh after that school trip to Snowdonia? Speaker_3: (Bursting out laughing) Oh my god, yes! You just kept saying “Shwmae” and hoping for the best! Speaker_1: The look on the sheep farmer’s face was priceless. He clearly had no idea what you were on about. Speaker_5: It was the sheer confidence that made it so good. You totally committed to the bit. Speaker_4: I think we were all a bit… experimental at school, weren’t we? Trying to figure out who we were. Speaker_2: Definitely. I went through a goth phase, remember? All black clothes, pale makeup, the whole nine yards. Speaker_1: Oh yeah, the one where you insisted on calling everyone “darling”? Speaker_2: It was a *look*. And it suited me, thank you very much! Though my nan wasn’t impressed. She kept telling me I looked like I was attending a funeral. Speaker_3: My mum still brings up my obsession with My Little Pony. I had, like, a hundred of them. Speaker_5: A hundred? That’s commitment. I was more of a Pokémon cards guy myself. The hours I spent trading those things… Speaker_4: It’s amazing how much time we wasted on… well, everything, really. But it was good fun, wasn’t it? Speaker_1: Absolutely. These are the stories we’ll be telling our grandkids, you know? “And then your Auntie Sarah nearly lost her chips to a seagull…”

Speaker_1: Honestly, the best thing about a proper winter camp, you know, when it’s *really* cold… is the silence. Utter, absolute silence. Speaker_2: (Chuckles) Sounds… bracing. I’m quite happy with central heating and a good book, thank you very much. Though I suppose I can appreciate the appeal, in a purely theoretical sort of way. Speaker_3: Dad’s right, it’s incredible. It’s a different kind of quiet than you get anywhere else. People just… don’t *go* out when it’s like that. You've got the whole landscape to yourself. It's a bit like feeling like the first person to ever see the place. Speaker_1: Exactly! Last February, up in the Cairngorms… snow was coming down sideways, wind howling like a banshee, and not a soul for miles. You build your snow shelter, get the stove going… and then just *listen*. It's incredibly grounding. Speaker_2: A snow shelter? You build a snow shelter? Good heavens, Arthur, you’re a brave man. Or possibly slightly mad. I’m imagining something out of an Arctic survival manual. Speaker_1: (Laughing) Not quite as dramatic as that, Moira. It’s a quinzee. You pile up a huge mound of snow, let it sinter for a couple of hours, then hollow it out. Keeps you remarkably warm. It’s about the physics, really, the way the snow insulates. Fascinating stuff. Speaker_3: He’s a bit obsessed with the physics of it all, Mum. But it really works. I've been doing it with him since I was a kid. You wouldn’t believe how warm it gets inside. And it forces you to be… efficient. You can’t take unnecessary things. Every ounce counts. Speaker_2: That sounds… challenging. I'd be worrying about everything freezing – toes, fingers, vital organs… Speaker_1: Proper kit, Moira, proper kit. Merino wool base layers, down sleeping bag rated for -20… it's an investment. But it's an investment in your well-being, truly. It’s about stripping things back to basics, reconnecting with… well, with yourself and the natural world. Speaker_3: It's a good mental reset, too. Being completely self-reliant for a few days, solving problems as they come... it's a good antidote to the constant stimulation of modern life. Plus, you see wildlife you’d never normally see. Tracks in the snow, ptarmigan blending into the landscape… Speaker_2: Ptarmigan? Are those the ones that change colour? Speaker_3: Aye, they do. White in the winter, mottled brown in the summer. They’re remarkably well camouflaged. I saw a golden eagle circling overhead last year, it was breathtaking. Speaker_1: They’re magnificent creatures. The whole experience… it’s exhilarating. It’s a bit like… pushing yourself to the edge of your comfort zone, and then finding out that the edge isn’t where you thought it was. Speaker_2: I think my comfort zone involves a roaring fire and a nice cup of tea. But I appreciate hearing about it. It sounds… intensely alive. Perhaps a bit too intensely for me, but alive nonetheless. I'm content observing the wildness from a distance, thank you. Speaker_3: No pressure, Mum. It’s not for everyone. But Dad’s trying to get a small group together for a weekend in March. Might be a good opportunity to try a gentler version – a base camp with day hikes, rather than a full-on overnight quinzee build.

Speaker_1: Honestly, I’m still reeling from that film last night. “Everything Everywhere All at Once”. What *was* that? Speaker_2: (Chuckles) Right? A complete sensory overload. Brilliant, though. Utterly brilliant. I haven't thought about hot dog fingers since…well, since last night. Speaker_1: Hot dog fingers! Don't even. It’s just…so much. My brain feels like it needs a lie-down. Did you actually *follow* all the universes? Because I was losing track after the raccoon chef. Speaker_2: No way. I just went with it. Tried to appreciate the sheer creativity, you know? It’s one of those films where trying to understand it logically detracts from the enjoyment. It’s more about the *feeling* it gives you. Speaker_1: That's fair. It definitely evoked *a feeling*. Mostly, bewilderedness. Though I did love Ke Huy Quan. He was amazing. Proper comeback story. Speaker_2: Totally. And Michelle Yeoh just absolutely carried it. She’s incredible. Reminded me a bit of…have you ever read any Ursula K. Le Guin? Speaker_1: Vaguely. Something about Earthsea, wasn’t it? Ages ago in uni. Why? Speaker_2: There’s a similar kind of… philosophical depth, I think. Le Guin explores these vast, complicated worlds, but the heart of the story is always very human. Like with “Everything Everywhere”, it’s all these crazy sci-fi concepts, but ultimately it’s about a mother-daughter relationship. Speaker_1: Ooh, I see what you mean. That makes sense. I might have to revisit Le Guin then. I remember liking the writing, just being a bit… lost in the world-building at the time. Speaking of needing comfort after a confusing experience, fancy grabbing some Thai tonight? There’s that new place on the High Street everyone’s raving about. Speaker_2: Thai sounds perfect. I’m craving a proper Pad See Ew. It’s been too long. Did you manage to get any of that mango sticky rice last week when we went to that other place? Speaker_1: Oh, disappointingly not! They'd sold out. I was gutted. Honestly, it’s borderline obsession at this point. I need to hunt down some decent mango sticky rice. It's a mission. Speaker_2: We will find some. We *must*. It’s a fundamental human right, surely? Speaker_1: (Laughing) Absolutely. Right up there with free healthcare and decent public transport. Speaker_2: Speaking of missions, I’ve got that site visit tomorrow morning. Dreadful journey, all the way out to… well, somewhere near Melton Mowbray. Speaker_1: Oh, dear. Melton Mowbray? The pork pie capital of the world. At least the drive won’t be *totally* wasted. You can stock up. Speaker_2: (Grimaces) Tempting, but I’m trying to be good. Though…a Melton Mowbray pork pie *is* a cultural experience, isn’t it? Speaker_1: It absolutely is. You’re a consultant engineer, you deserve a pork pie. Think of it as… fieldwork. Speaker_2: (Chuckles) You're enabling me. Fine. One pork pie. For research purposes. Speaker_1: Exactly! Research. It’s important. Right, Thai tonight, pork pie potential tomorrow, and potentially re-reading Ursula K. Le Guin. Sounds like a plan. Speaker_2: Sounds brilliant.

Speaker_1: Right, so then the giant… he didn’t actually *eat* the little boy, you know. That’s what I thought when I first read it, but he just… tickled him until he couldn’t breathe from laughing! Speaker_2: (Giggles) Tickled him? Like, really, really tickly? Speaker_1: Oh, *incredibly* tickly. Apparently, giants have really rough hands. Like sandpaper. Can you imagine? Speaker_3: Sandpaper hands would hurt! Could you build a giant with Lego, do you think? A really, really big one? Speaker_1: Mmm, that’s a good question. It would need a *lot* of Lego, wouldn’t it? And you’d need to reinforce it, because all those blocks would make it wobbly. Speaker_2: I could make the head! I have lots of grey bricks. Speaker_1: You could definitely make the head! And maybe you, Leo, could do the feet? They’d have to be huge. Like, bigger than this bedroom! Speaker_3: I could! But then it wouldn't fit in the room. Would it? Speaker_1: No, it definitely wouldn’t. It’d be a garden giant! Speaking of big things… remember Mrs. Higgins at Brownies last night? She was going on about the Brownie Promise, and how important it is to do a ‘good turn’ every day. Speaker_2: I said I helped tidy up my toys! Does that count? Speaker_1: That absolutely counts, sweetheart. That's a brilliant good turn. Leo, did you do a good turn? Speaker_3: I shared my PlayStation time with Finn. He wanted to play the racing car game. Speaker_1: Oh, that was very kind of you. See? Good turns don't have to be huge things. It's just being helpful and thoughtful. You know what *isn't* very helpful or thoughtful? My computer at work. It's been playing up all day. Speaker_2: What’s wrong with it? Speaker_1: It just keeps freezing. I was trying to make a spreadsheet in Excel – you wouldn’t believe how many numbers I have to put in! – and it just… stopped. I had to start all over again. It makes me want to throw it out the window. Speaker_3: Can’t you just get a new one? Like a really fast one? Speaker_1: We'll see. They’re quite expensive. It reminds me of Grandpa's old typewriter. Remember that? Speaker_2: The clicky one? Speaker_1: The clicky one! It was so loud, but he loved it. He said it made a satisfying sound. He wouldn’t have understood computers, I don’t think. He was a very practical man. He built things with his hands, not with… with algorithms and spreadsheets! Speaker_3: What’s an algorithm? Sounds like a dinosaur. Speaker_1: (Laughs) It *does* sound like a dinosaur, doesn’t it? It's… well, it’s a set of instructions for the computer to follow. It tells it what to do. It’s complicated. But you don't need to worry about algorithms right now. Speaker_2: Can we read another story? A really scary one? Speaker_1: Maybe tomorrow night, darling. It’s getting late. Time for sleepy thoughts now. Let's talk about what you’ve both enjoyed today. Leo, what was your favourite part of the day? Speaker_3: Building the spaceship! And sharing my PlayStation. Speaker_1: Lovely. And you, Lily? Speaker_2: Making pictures with glitter! And talking about giants. I like giants.

Speaker_1: Honestly, Arthur, you look like you’ve slept in your clothes. Not that it matters here, of course, but still… a bit of effort never hurt anyone. Speaker_2: (Chuckles) Oh, come off it, Margaret. Comfy is the aim of the game at my age. Besides, you’ve barely fared much better with that… is that a gravy stain? Speaker_1: It is *not* gravy! It’s… a remnant of the rhubarb crumble from last night. And it's perfectly respectable. More coffee? I made a fresh pot. Speaker_2: Don't mind if I do. Speaking of rhubarb, I was driving past that old farm near Skipton yesterday - the one we used to get our rhubarb from, remember? It’s all gone to seed. Or rather, to weeds. Sad to see. Used to be a thriving place. Speaker_1: Oh, that’s a shame. They had beautiful fruit. It's the same with so many places around here. You start looking into the history, and you realise half of West Yorkshire is built on or around deserted medieval villages. Incredible, isn't it? All those lives, just… vanished. Speaker_2: Vanished and replaced with roadworks, apparently. I spent a good hour yesterday crawling along the A650, thanks to some essential repairs. Essential to whom, I wonder? Certainly not to me and my blood pressure. Speaker_1: Don’t start on the roadworks. I had to navigate a minefield of cones just to get to the shops yesterday. And then they had the cheek to send me a leaflet advertising their services! Junk mail, the bane of my existence. Speaker_2: Tell me about it. It’s a constant stream of offers for things I neither need nor want. And the phone! Constant calls about PPI, or extending my car warranty on a car I sold five years ago! It’s driving me round the bend. Speaker_1: I just put the phone down on them now. Rude, perhaps, but effective. Though sometimes they ring back on a withheld number. It's a conspiracy, I tell you. A conspiracy! Are you enjoying your toast? I made the damson jam last week. Speaker_2: Lovely jam, Margaret, truly. You’ve got a gift for it. Far better than anything you can buy in the shops. You should think about selling it. Speaker_1: Oh, don’t be daft. I just enjoy making it. Like my herbs, you know? I’ve got basil, rosemary, thyme, mint… all thriving on the windowsill. It's therapeutic. Keeps me busy. Speaker_2: Speaking of busy... any progress on the house sale? Have you had any more viewings? Speaker_1: One last week. A young couple, nice enough. Seemed quite keen, but they’re apparently waiting for their mortgage to be approved. Honestly, the entire process is exhausting. I just want to be done with it and move on. It feels like… like letting go of a part of my life, you know? Even though it’s just bricks and mortar. Speaker_2: I understand. It's a big step. But you’re doing the right thing, downsizing. It’ll be much easier to manage, and less of a worry. Besides, you can always come and visit. My spare room is always open… though you might have to navigate the junk mail to get to it. Speaker_1: (Laughing) I might just take you up on that. Now, finish your coffee, you scruff! We have a walk planned this afternoon, remember? Speaker_2: Ah yes, the bracing Yorkshire air. Lead the way, Margaret! Just let me find my… respectable shoes.

Speaker_1: Honestly, this new hand cream is a lifesaver. My skin was getting *so* cracked with all the handwashing at work. It's lavender and chamomile, smells divine. Speaker_2: Lavender and chamomile, eh? Sounds… calming. Though I still reckon a good dollop of Vaseline does the trick. More economical, at least. You've gone all fancy on me, haven’t you, love? Speaker_1: Oh, don’t be such a scrooge! It was on offer at Boots. And it’s not just about the smell, it actually *works*. You’ve still got that redness on your knuckles, haven’t you? Speaker_2: Just a touch. It’s character building. More importantly, did you manage to get those new blood pressure tablets sorted? The chemist said they were waiting for a delivery. Speaker_1: Yes, picked them up this morning. Though they tried to push me towards the ‘own brand’ again. Honestly, I told them I’d rather walk to Spain than take a cheaper version of my medication. Speaker_3: (Laughing) Walk to Spain? Mum, you’re dramatic. Speaker_1: Well, I am a nurse! I know what I need. Besides, I’m planning something a little more exciting than walking to Spain. I was looking at holidays… maybe Greece next year? Speaker_2: Greece? Nice. Always fancied Santorini. Though getting around those islands… nightmare. All those winding roads. Remember that time we got lost in Cornwall? Speaker_3: Oh god, yes! Dad tried to navigate using Facebook directions. It led us down a farmer’s track barely wide enough for the car! Speaker_2: It did! And I’m pretty sure we ended up in someone’s greenhouse. Honestly, these phones are supposed to make life easier, but… Speaker_1: Speaking of phones, have you seen what Auntie Maureen’s been posting on Facebook? Another one of those chain letters about changing your profile picture to a landmark. Honestly, she believes everything she reads. Speaker_3: Oh, bless her. She still thinks emojis are ‘hieroglyphics’. Speaker_1: Exactly! It’s endearing, but… frustrating. I tried to explain to her that it’s just a silly fad, but she said it was ‘showing support’ for… something. I honestly didn’t listen after that. Speaker_2: It's a distraction tactic, that's all. Keeps her busy. Did you get anything good for Christmas? Apart from luxury hand cream, obviously. Speaker_1: Oh, you know… the usual. Socks, chocolates… you got me that lovely scarf, which is perfect. What about you? Speaker_2: I got a new gadget for the garden. Apparently, it automatically waters the plants. I’m hoping it’ll save me some backache. Though knowing my luck, the squirrels will just set up a water park. Speaker_3: (Smiling) You and your squirrels, Dad. You’re constantly at war. Speaker_1: Speaking of animals… how’s Winston been? Is he still shedding everywhere? Speaker_2: Everywhere. The house is coated in golden retriever fluff. But he’s a good boy. And Luna seems to have accepted him, which is a miracle. Remember when they first met? It was like watching two tiny dictators negotiate a peace treaty. Speaker_3: Oh yes, Luna looked *furious*. She thought Winston was trying to steal her throne. Speaker_1: (Chuckling) That’s Luna all over. Queen of the household, she is. Right, anyone fancy a cup of tea? I made a fresh batch of ginger biscuits this morning. Speaker_2: Can’t say no to that. Especially after all this talk of walking to Spain. I need a sugar boost. Speaker_3: Me too! And maybe we can convince Mum to show us some photos of the Greek islands later. Speaker_1: It’s a deal. Just promise me, no Facebook directions if we actually go!

Speaker_1: Honestly, this week has been *wild* at work. New client, total nightmare. They want everything to sound like a motivational Instagram post, even for… industrial plumbing supplies. Speaker_2: (Laughing) Oh my god, seriously? That sounds awful. What’s the brief, like, “Reach for the pipes!”? Speaker_1: Don't even joke! Something equally cringe. It’s exhausting trying to inject enthusiasm into…fittings. I spent three hours yesterday crafting copy about ‘robust drainage solutions’. Robust! Speaker_2: Oh, the joys of copywriting. I’m starting to think my PhD is less stressful. Although, honestly, the data sets are making my brain melt. I'm programming a survey about public trust in the media right now, and everyone just seems incredibly cynical. Speaker_1: No surprise there, is there? Have you seen what’s been happening with… well, everything? The whole thing with the water company dumping sewage? It's beyond belief. Speaker_2: It’s horrific. And then the Tories just… deflect. My mum was going on about it at dinner last weekend, saying it's just blatant corruption. Honestly, trying to have a sensible conversation with her is impossible. She goes straight to conspiracy theories. Speaker_1: Oh, mums. Mine’s obsessed with that show, ‘Escape to the Country’. Keeps trying to convince me I need to buy a cottage in the Cotswolds and ‘find myself’. Like, I’m currently trying to ‘find’ a decent salary in London, Mum. Speaker_2: (Smiling) Bless her. My parents are convinced I’m having a crisis because I haven't secured a ‘proper’ job after finishing my Masters. They keep subtly suggesting I apply for teaching. Speaker_1: Ugh, the pressure. Are you still seeing Ben, by the way? I haven’t properly caught up since… well, since everything with Chloe happened. Speaker_2: We’re… on a break. A very long, uncomfortable break. He’s still processing, I think. It was all a bit messy. Turns out Chloe and my flatmate were secretly besties. The betrayal! Speaker_1: Oh, wow. That’s… a whole other level of awkward. I'm so sorry. That’s awful. Honestly, people can be so awful. Speaker_2: Tell me about it. It's just... draining. Anyway, enough of my drama. How are *you* doing, actually? Anything exciting happening, aside from the plumbing copy? Speaker_1: Not much. I’m trying to save up for a deposit on a place, which feels impossible. London rent is ridiculous. I’ve started meal prepping to try and cut down on costs, but I keep accidentally burning things. Speaker_2: Oh no! Are you alright? Speaker_1: Yeah, just a slightly charred attempt at roasted vegetables. It’s a skill, really. Should probably just stick to toast. We should definitely do this again soon. Maybe next week? We could actually go *to* the cinema instead of just complaining about our lives in a pub. Speaker_2: Definitely. A cinema sounds amazing. Let’s aim for next Tuesday? I’m free then. And maybe we can revert to complaining about our lives *during* the film to make it more interesting.

Speaker_1: Honestly, I’m absolutely shattered. Did absolutely nothing all day except transcribe that dreadful interview about pigeons. Pigeons, honestly! Speaker_2: (Chuckles) Pigeons? That *is* a niche topic. Could be worse, though. Could be tax law. Speaker_3: You’re both lucky you can relax at home. I’ve been staring at this blank page all afternoon. Writer’s block is a genuine physical ailment, you know. Feels like my brain’s turned to concrete. Speaker_1: Oh, I know the feeling. Though mine’s more likely turned to pigeon facts. Did you manage to get a walk in today, David? You were talking about trying to get back into running. Speaker_2: Not today, no. Rain came on just as I was about to head out. And honestly, after dealing with spreadsheets all day, the thought of pushing myself physically… it just didn't appeal. Maybe tomorrow. What about you, Sarah? Any venturing out? Speaker_1: Just to the shops. Needed milk. And avoided eye contact with Mrs. Higgins, she cornered me last time to talk about her grandson's GCSE results for half an hour. Speaker_3: Oh, the neighbourhood watchdogs! They mean well, but…a captive audience is never pleasant. Speaking of neighbourhoods, have you seen what that house on Elm Street sold for? The one with the awful garden gnomes? Speaker_2: No, really? Don’t tell me it went for over asking. Speaker_3: Over asking, and by a *significant* amount. Apparently, it was a bidding war. Nearly half a million. Honestly, it’s ridiculous. Speaker_1: Half a million for *that* house? They must be mad. It needs a complete gutting. Honestly, the market is completely bonkers. I sometimes wonder if we should just move somewhere rural. Speaker_2: Rural? You'd miss your shops, Sarah. You and your Mrs. Higgins avoidance tactics. Speaker_1: (Laughs) True. Though a little peace and quiet does sound appealing. But then you look at house prices *outside* the city…it’s just as bad. Speaker_3: It’s a terrible position to be in. I'm thinking I should just build an extension and stay put. Though last time I attempted anything DIY, it involved a trip to A&E. Speaker_2: I can imagine. You have... a certain enthusiasm for projects, don't you, Margaret? Speaker_3: Enthusiasm is one word for it. Chaos is another. Right, I think I need to make a cuppa. And possibly contemplate the meaning of life while I do. Or, you know, just think about what to make for dinner. Speaker_1: Good idea. I’m thinking of attempting that Moroccan tagine recipe I found online. It looks incredibly complicated. Speaker_2: Oh, be careful with those. They always look deceptively easy in the photos. And require about twelve different spices you don't have. Speaker_1: True. Maybe I'll just stick to spag bol... safe and reliable. Although, even that feels like a huge effort right now. Pigeons have really drained me. Speaker_3: Spag bol is perfectly acceptable. Don't underestimate the power of comfort food. Tell you what, I’ll bring round some shortbread tomorrow… if I manage to wrestle my brain into submission and actually finish writing something. Speaker_2: That sounds excellent, Margaret. Shortbread always sorts things out. Speaker_1: That’s very kind, thank you! Now, if you’ll excuse me, I think I’m going to lie down before the pigeons start haunting my dreams.

Speaker_1: Right, so basically the whole department’s in a bit of a flap because of this new budgeting thing. Apparently, they’re expecting us to cut… well, everything. Speaker_2: Oof, sounds cheerful. Is that across the whole Uni, or just your little corner of it? Speaker_1: Seems pretty widespread, yeah. Apparently, fewer students are applying, or something, and funding’s been cut. Means no new software, delayed maintenance on the archives… the usual. It’s stressful. I spend half my day just cataloguing ancient documents, the other half arguing why we *need* a new scanner. Speaker_2: Classic. Bureaucracy at its finest. I’m getting the same sort of vibes at work, although it's more about justifying project costs. Every single item needs three quotes now, and a full risk assessment. It's slowing everything down. Especially infuriating when a bolt costs, like, three quid. Speaker_1: Three quid! Honestly. You’d think they’d trust you lot to build things that don’t immediately fall down without needing to micromanage the bolt budget. Speaker_2: You’d think. Though, to be fair, I did hear about Old Man Hemmings’ bridge design last year… apparently, didn’t quite account for the river’s tendency to *flood*. Speaker_1: (Laughs) Oh, no! Hemmings? He’s the one who always wears the tweed and smells faintly of pipe tobacco, isn’t he? Speaker_2: The very same. Still, it makes it easier to understand why they’re being so cautious. Anyway, enough about work. You were telling me you went to see a musical? Speaker_1: Oh aye! Went to see “Six” at the Cambridge Theatre. Honestly? Brilliant. I didn’t really know much about it before, just that it’s about the six wives of Henry VIII, but it’s done like a pop concert. Each queen gets her own song, and they're all belting out these amazing tunes. Speaker_2: Sounds… intense. A bit different from the sort of things I usually go to. I was considering seeing “Hamilton” when it comes to London, but it’s so expensive. Speaker_1: It *is* pricey, but “Six” is much more affordable and honestly, really fun. It’s not highbrow theatre, it’s just… good. Loads of energy. You’d enjoy it. Did you see anything good lately? Speaker_2: Not really. Been mostly heads-down with work, unfortunately. Though I did catch a documentary about trainspotting the other night. Surprisingly gripping. Speaker_1: (Raises an eyebrow) Trainspotting? Really? That’s a… niche interest. Speaker_2: I know, I know. It was on iPlayer, and I was flicking through. Turns out there’s a lot of dedication and history involved. Plus, the scenery’s rather nice. Much better than staring at spreadsheets, that’s for sure. Speaker_1: I’ll stick to glittery Tudor queens, I think. Though, a nice train journey *does* sound lovely… Maybe we could go to York one weekend? Speaker_2: York? That's not a bad idea. I’ve heard they’ve got a really good railway museum. And a decent pub or two, I imagine. Speaker_1: Essential criteria. Definitely essential. Speaker_2: Right, well let's start looking at dates, and maybe, just maybe, I'll get Hemmings to design a train set for me. A flood-proof one, naturally.

Speaker_1: Right, that’s the fence posts sorted, more or less. Just need a good coat of paint and they’ll look as good as new, eh? Though, honestly, looking at the state of next door’s garden… it’s a losing battle. Speaker_2: Tell me about it. Old Man Hemmings, isn't it? Let it go completely, he has. I drove a bloke past there last week, potential buyer, fancy house up the road, and he nearly choked when he saw it. Said it brought the whole street down. Speaker_1: It's a shame. I heard he's got a bad hip, though. Can't get about like he used to. Still, shouldn’t let it become a jungle. All those developers sniffing around, you know? They’ll be wanting to flatten everything and build flats. Speaker_2: You’re not wrong there. They’re already building those monstrosities down by the docks. Looks like concrete boxes stacked on top of each other. No character at all. Used to be a thriving market, that place. Speaker_1: It’s horrifying, isn't it? The relentless march of…progress. Speaking of relentless, did you see that new film, “The Lighthouse”? The one with Willem Dafoe and Robert Pattinson? Speaker_2: Can’t say I did. I was working all weekend. Picked up a bloke from the airport, then a hen party. Honestly, the things I hear in this job. Speaker_1: Oh, it’s brilliant. Properly unsettling. Two lighthouse keepers going slowly mad. Dafoe is incredible, just completely loses himself in the role. It reminded me a bit of that Beckett play we saw, *Waiting for Godot*, but with more seagulls and… existential dread. Speaker_2: Sounds a bit heavy, that. I prefer a good action film, something to switch the brain off. Like that *John Wick* one. Bang, bang, bang. Job done. Speaker_1: Different strokes, I suppose. I’ve been trying to get back into painting, you know. Haven’t touched a brush in ages. Found a really cheap easel in that charity shop on Smithdown Road last week. Absolute bargain. Speaker_2: You always were a good artist. Remember that portrait you did of me, years ago? My mum still has it up on her wall. Speaker_1: Oh, God, that was awful! I was still learning. It made you look like a right villain. Speaking of charity shops, I was wondering… would you mind if I borrowed your ladder for a couple of days? These gutters need a proper clean before winter, and mine's missing a couple of rungs. Speaker_2: No worries, mate. It's out in the shed. Just be careful with it, yeah? It’s seen better days, that ladder. Almost as old as me. Speaker_1: Will do. Promise. Hey, listen, I’ve been thinking. I really need to start sorting out my life a bit more. I mean, I enjoy the lecturing, but it feels… stagnant. I need a project. Something to really sink my teeth into. Speaker_2: You thinking of writing another book? That one about the German Romantic poets was a good read, even if I didn’t understand half of it. Speaker_1: Maybe. Or maybe I should take that pottery class I’ve been eyeing up. You know, just something completely different. What about you? Any goals, beyond surviving another shift in that taxi? Speaker_2: (Chuckles) Well, I’d like to finally get that classic car I’ve been saving for. A proper vintage Jag, you know? Something to cruise around in on a sunny day. And maybe retire a bit earlier. These knees aren't what they used to be. Speaker_1: That sounds good, very good. A Jag… that’s a proper ambition. Right, back to the painting then. Do you think this shade of green is too lime-y? I was aiming for something a bit more… subtle.

Speaker_1: Honestly, this scenery is just… relentless, isn’t it? Fields and fields. Beautiful, of course, but after a while, it all blends into one green blur. Are we sure we didn’t miss a turning for something a bit more… dramatic? Speaker_2: (Chuckles) Dramatic? Auntie Carol, relax! We're in rural Poland, not filming a blockbuster. It’s *meant* to be peaceful. Besides, it’s nice to just… be. No deadlines, no parent-teacher meetings, just the open road. And look, that little church steeple. See? Not entirely devoid of interest. Speaker_1: Easy for you to say, you’re the one driving! I’m just observing the endless expanse of… crops. Though, a little detour wouldn’t kill us. Remember that medieval castle we saw advertised near Krakow? Speaker_2: We’ve got Tarnow booked, remember? And we agreed to stick to the plan. Though, speaking of plans… have you worked out exactly how much this trip is costing us? I’m trying to keep a record for budgeting, and the campsite fees are adding up. Speaker_1: Oh, dear. Not another financial reckoning. Honestly, I’m trying not to think about it too much. All this ‘freedom’ comes at a price, doesn’t it? I did transfer you some money yesterday, though. Was it enough? Speaker_2: Yeah, that was brilliant, thank you. It covers the fuel for a good chunk of the journey, I think. We’re doing okay, but I’m worried about food costs. Polish supermarkets are… interesting. Trying to navigate the sausage aisle is a whole adventure in itself. Speaker_1: (Laughing) Oh, I can imagine! I’m happy to stick to bread and cheese, if that helps. Less linguistic challenge involved. And are you still in touch with Sarah and Liam? I was thinking about them the other day. Haven’t heard from them properly since… well, ages. Speaker_2: Yeah, I messaged Sarah just last week. Liam's still working crazy hours at the hospital. They’re talking about trying to get away for a weekend in the Lake District in October. I told them about the van – they were a bit jealous, naturally. Speaker_1: Good. They deserve a break. Though, honestly, this van is a bit of a revelation. I’ve been meaning to declutter the spare room for years, and this is the impetus I needed. Anything not absolutely essential has been donated or sold. It’s quite liberating, actually. Speaker_2: See? Travelling does good things for the soul. And for storage space. Speaking of decluttering…did you remember to bring the extra phone charger? Mine’s playing up, and I need it for the GPS. Speaker_1: Oh, bother. I *thought* I did, but… let me have a look. (Rummages in a cupboard) Hmm… no. Definitely no. I’m hopeless with electronics. You know, back in my day, we navigated with maps! Speaker_2: (Smiling) Back in your day, dinosaurs roamed the earth, Auntie Carol. Okay, no worries, I packed a spare travel adapter, which might work in a push. Oh, look! Someone’s hitchhiking up ahead. Speaker_1: Oh, goodness. Don’t even *think* about it. Absolutely not. We don’t know who that is! It’s a bit risky, isn’t it? Speaker_2: I wasn’t seriously considering it! Just observing. Though, it’s amazing how many people still try it, isn’t it? Especially around here. It feels very… old-fashioned. Speaker_1: Old-fashioned and potentially dangerous. Honestly, it reminds me of that time… never mind. Let’s just focus on the scenery and getting to Tarnow in one piece, shall we? Do you fancy stopping for coffee when we get there? I could really use a proper cappuccino.

Speaker_3: Right, just off the M55 now, onto the A6. Should be alright, shouldn’t it, love? You’ve got the Sat Nav, haven’t you? Speaker_2: Yes, Dad, I’ve got it. It's telling me to exit at the next junction. Honestly, you worry like a new mother. Speaker_1: He just doesn’t like getting lost, do you Dad? Remember that time in the Lake District? We ended up on a farm track. Speaker_3: (Chuckles) Don't remind me! Thought we were going to need a tractor to get us out. Your mother… she wasn’t best pleased. Still, a nice view though, weren’t it? Speaker_2: Beautiful, but a bit stressful at the time. Speaking of stressful, how are those revision notes coming along, Elsie? Exams getting close now. Speaker_1: Ugh, don’t even mention it. History is just… a lot. So many dates. I keep mixing up Henry VIII’s wives. Speaker_3: Six wives, wasn’t it? A right messy business. Your grandma used to be brilliant at history. She could rattle off monarchs for fun. Used to tell us stories about ’em too, not just dates. Speaker_2: She did have a gift for storytelling. I remember her telling me about the Queen when I was first learning English. Made it so much easier to understand the whole monarchy thing. Speaker_1: It’s weird thinking about the new King now, isn't it? Feels like it was only yesterday we were all glued to the telly. Speaker_3: Aye, it does. Seventy years she reigned. A lifetime. They don’t make ‘em like that anymore. Speaker_2: No, they don’t. Oh look, there’s a Waterstones coming up. Do we need anything from there? I was thinking of getting something for my mum, she's been talking about the Hay Festival. Speaker_1: Ooh, Hay Festival sounds amazing! I saw something on TikTok about it. Loads of authors and book stalls. I wish I was going. Speaker_3: It’s good, that festival. A bit pricey though, isn't it? Your Auntie Brenda went a couple of years ago. Spent a fortune on books she ended up giving away. Speaker_2: (Laughing) Sounds like Brenda! She's got a good heart. I saw a really good biography of Marie Curie, might grab that. Elsie, are you reading anything good at the moment? Aside from history textbooks, of course. Speaker_1: I’m trying to get through ‘Circe’ by Madeline Miller. It's really well-written, but quite slow. It's a bit… dense, you know? Speaker_3: Dense? Like your Uncle Arthur trying to explain cricket? Speaker_1: (Giggles) Yeah, exactly like that! Speaker_2: We should probably think about dinner while we’re out. I was hoping to go to that new Italian place near the shops, but I heard it’s really busy. Maybe just get something from Sainsbury’s? Speaker_3: Sainsbury’s it is then. Although, I keep meaning to try that Turkish place. Remember that one we went to in Bolton? Now *that* was good. Speaker_1: Oh yeah! With the massive portions and the free bread? Speaker_3: The very same. Right, nearly there. Just past this road, then left at the roundabout… Ugh, these train strikes are a nightmare, aren’t they? Heard Mrs. Higgins couldn’t get to visit her daughter.

Speaker_1: Well, I never! Honestly, you two, keeping a whole visitor a secret? I thought I’d lost my hearing, not my ability to detect a conspiracy! Speaker_2: (Chuckles) Oh, Mother, you’d have found out eventually. We wanted it to be a surprise. You haven’t been to Thirsk in ages. And Leo’s been wanting to see you properly. Speaker_3: Hi Gran! It’s good to see you. Did you have a nice journey? Speaker_1: Lovely journey, thank you, Leo. Though that sat nav tried to take me through a farmyard at one point! Honestly, these modern gadgets… they’re clever, but they lack common sense. Remind me to tell you about the time a computer told me a perfectly good recipe involved beetroot in a trifle. Beetroot! Speaker_2: (Smiling) Oh, don’t start on the technology again, Mum. Leo’s quite the whiz with it himself, you know. He’s building some sort of…what was it, Leo? A gaming computer? Speaker_3: It’s a PC, yeah. I’m trying to get it built for next month’s LAN party. It's complicated, but really fun. Speaker_1: A “LAN party”? Sounds like something out of a science fiction programme. Still, as long as it’s keeping you occupied. Though I do worry about young people spending too much time staring at screens. It can’t be good for the head, can it? Speaker_2: It's a balance, isn’t it? We try to encourage him to get out and about. He plays rugby, thankfully. Keeps him fit. Speaker_1: Rugby! That’s proper exercise, that is. Not like… tapping away at buttons. So, what have you two been up to? This house looks…different. You’ve been clearing out, I see. Speaker_2: We have. Trying to declutter. It’s a never-ending task. Your visit was actually a good excuse to tackle the attic. Found some…interesting things. A whole box of your old hats, for starters. Speaker_1: (Eyes light up) My hats! Oh, good Lord. I'd forgotten all about those. Some of them were rather stylish, you know. Before everyone started wearing baseball caps. Speaker_3: Mum says there's a really weird one with feathers and...stuff. Speaker_1: (Slightly wistful) Ah, yes. That was for the races, years ago. Your Grandfather insisted. Thought I needed to make a statement. He was a good man, your Grandfather. Though a bit oblivious sometimes. Speaker_2: He was. Listen, Mum, how are *you* doing? You seem…pale. Are you feeling alright? Speaker_1: Oh, I’m fine, dear. Just…a bit tired, that’s all. It’s this time of year, isn't it? The light fades so quickly. It gets to you, you know? Especially being so far from home. It’s easy to feel isolated. Speaker_2: I feel the same. You’re one of the few people I can actually talk to about… stuff. Without feeling like I need to filter everything through ten different layers of polite conversation. Plus, you introduced me to pierogi

Speaker_4: I once bought a place in France, you know. A little cottage in the Dordogne. The oddest transaction, though. No solicitors, no land registry… just a handshake and a

Speaker_1: Right, so we’re agreed – the Aussie sun is definitely impacting my brain cells. I’ve been staring at this whiteboard for an hour and all I’ve written is ‘EdTech’ in massive letters. Speaker_2: (Chuckles) It’s the jet lag, darling. And the novelty of house-sitting a place with a pool. Don't worry, brain cells recover. EdTech *is* broad though. We need to niche down. Speaker_2: Better quality is a baseline, isn’t it? It needs to be *different*. I’ve been toying with the idea of curated case studies. The legal side would be a headache, though. Fair use, licensing… all that jazz. We’d need to be very careful. Speaker_2: Absolutely. That's where my expertise comes in. Speaker_1: It’s funny, isn’t it? How different the sea is depending on where you are. I mean, North Norfolk – that’s bracing. It slaps you in the face, all grey and wild. She misses her family, but he… he thrives in the bustle of the city. He needs the energy, I think. And the specialist cheese shops. Speaker_2: (Smiling) Fair enough. Although, I suspect he could find specialist cheese shops anywhere if he really put his mind to it. That man has a nose for artisanal dairy products. Speaker_1: You're not wrong. It's terrifying. Speaker_3: Oh, actually, before we get totally distracted by terrible TV fashion, did either of you see that Zara sale preview? They've got some amazing boots. Speaker_1: No way! I haven't! I’m trying to be sensible and invest in some quality pieces this autumn, rather than fast fashion, but those boots…they're a really good shape, aren't they? Speaker_1: They looked fairly chunky, yeah? I'm really into the chunky boot trend at the moment. It’s comfy *and* stylish. A winning combo. Speaker_3: Definitely chunky. And they had a couple of really nice trench coats too. I’m thinking I need a proper autumn coat this year. One that isn't just a lightweight mac. Speaker_2: Oh, a trench is a good idea. Classic and you can throw it over anything. I just bought a Barbour jacket, secondhand, which I

Speaker_1: Mum, look at this photo I took in art today. It’s supposed to be abstract, but Mr. Davies said it looks like a splattered raspberry. Speaker_2: (Chuckles) Oh, darling. It’s… vibrant. Very, very vibrant. What were you *going* for? Speaker_1: I was trying to capture the feeling of being overwhelmed, you know? Like, all the pressure with the mock exams coming up. What’s your biggest fear about the exams? Besides failing, obviously. Speaker_1: Um… I think just… disappointing you. And Dad. You both want me to do well. Speaker_2: We're still looking. Dad keeps changing his mind. One minute he wants to go to Scotland, the next he's talking about a cruise. Honestly, I'd rather stay home and read. Listen, about the exams… have you thought about asking Mr. Jones for some extra help with history? He's really good at explaining things. Speaker_1: Maybe. I just feel silly asking for help. Like I should already know it. Speaker_2: Nonsense. There's no shame in asking for help, darling. Everyone needs it sometimes. Now, how about we ditch the serious talk and I make us some hot chocolate? And you can show me some more of your… vibrant… art.

Speaker_1: Right then, lovely to see you both. Cup of tea? I’ve just put the kettle on. Speaker_2: Oh, that’d be lovely, Arthur. Thank you. Bit of a trek from Harrow, mind you! And then there's the bit about ‘digital literacy’. What even *is* that? Speaker_3: It’s basically how comfortable you are using computers, Dad. I could take a look for you if you like? Honestly, it's enough to keep a man up all night. And I *have* been up all night, actually. That cockerel next door. Cock-a-doodle-doo at 4 AM! Drives me mad. Speaker_2: Oh, that cockerel. I heard it when I walked past yesterday. Dreadful! Poor thing probably thinks it’s doing a good job. Still, doesn’t make it any easier to sleep. Speaker_3: You'd think someone would do something about it. Speaking of noisy things, little Tom Wilkins in Year 3… honestly. He's a handful. Currently fixated on building a fort out of chairs during maths. Speaker_1: Problem children, eh? They've always been around. Remember young Derek Plunkett? Used to steal plums from Mrs. Higgins’ orchard. Little terror. Speaker_2: Oh, Derek! He ended up a dentist, didn't he? Imagine that! Funny how things turn out. Look, while we’re on the subject of things turning out… have you seen those baby birds in the nest in your apple tree, Arthur? Speaker_1: I have! Little cheepers they are. Mum and Dad are working hard bringing them worms. It’s a miracle, really, when you think about it. Tiny creatures, all relying on their parents. Speaker_3: Nature's brilliant, isn’t it? I’ve been getting into 3D printing lately. Made a little model railway engine for my nephew. Keeps me occupied. Speaker_2: Oh, that sounds clever! What sort of things can you make? Reliable things, I hope? Not like Arthur's drive… Speaker_1: (Grumbling good humouredly) I told you, it wasn’t *my* drive! Anyway, what are you two up to for your birthdays? Coming up soon, aren't they? Speaker_3: Mum's is next month. We’re thinking a weekend away somewhere. Maybe the Cotswolds? Somewhere peaceful. Speaker_2: Yes, that’s the plan. Arthur, are you doing anything special? Or just avoiding that application form? Speaker_1: I told you about that form! And no, nothing special. Just a quiet day, I suppose. A bit of gardening, maybe watch the football. Though, I tell you what, the state of Norwich these days…

Speaker_1: Honestly, Arthur, the thought of it all is quite exhausting. Just… the sheer logistics. Speaker_2: You’re overthinking it, Margaret. You always do. It’ll be wonderful, having Isla here. Truly. Speaker_1: Wonderful for *whom*, Arthur? Wonderful for me, shuffling around trying to make space, dealing with the inevitable culture shock, and, frankly, the added expense? She’s been in Australia for fifteen years! Fifteen! She’s built a life there. Speaker_2: She *wanted* to come here. She said so, quite clearly. And she’s not a child anymore, Margaret. She’s a capable woman. She's not expecting you to run everything for her. Speaker_1: But she's my daughter, aren’t you listening? And she’s…adjusting. She's leaving a sunny climate, friends, a job she enjoys…for rainy Brighton and… well, us. And the National Health Service, bless its heart. Speaker_2: Oh, here we go. Don't start on the NHS again. It served you well enough. And Brighton isn't *that* bad. The pier is lovely, you know. Speaker_1: The pier is full of seagulls and sticky toffee apples, Arthur. Not exactly a sophisticated welcome to Britain. And she’s used to…space. Houses in Perth are enormous. Here, we’re crammed in. I’ve already started shifting things around, trying to clear the spare room and… it’s just depressing. Speaker_2: We've managed perfectly well in this house for thirty years, Margaret. A bit of shifting won't kill us. We can always get rid of some of your…collections. Speaker_1: (sharply) My ‘collections’ are memories, Arthur! Each one represents something! And it’s not just the space. It’s… I’m worried she’ll be unhappy. What if she regrets this? What if she quickly realises she’s made a mistake? Speaker_2: She wouldn’t have come if she thought that. She said she misses family, she wants to be closer. She wants… well, you, Margaret. She’s missed *you*. Speaker_1: She calls. We video chat. It’s not the same. And what about finding work? She’s a graphic designer. The market is flooded here! She might end up flipping burgers. Speaker_2: Now you’re being dramatic. She’s brilliant at what she does. She’ll find something. And even if it takes a while, we'll help. That’s what family does. Speaker_1: I suppose. It’s just… it feels like such a big upheaval. After all these years of quiet, of just us… it’s a shock to the system. Speaker_2: Life is full of upheavals, Margaret. You of all people should know that, having been a teacher for so long. You dealt with teenagers, for heaven’s sake! This will be easier. Speaker_1: Teenagers *are* easier. They’re temporary chaos. This is… permanent potential chaos. And I haven’t even started to think about the visa applications and all the paperwork! It’s a nightmare. Speaker_2: We’ll tackle the paperwork together. Don’t worry. I'll help. And look, think about the positives. Grandchildren… eventually. Long walks on the beach with your daughter… Speaker_1: (a small smile) Brighton beach, with seagulls and sticky toffee apples. Speaker_2: Exactly! It’ll be lovely. Trust me.

Speaker_1: So, did you catch much of the Scottish referendum coverage yesterday? Absolute nail-biter, wasn't it? Speaker_2: Nail-biter is putting it mildly! I was glued to the television, frankly. Thought for a good while there it was going to be a ‘yes’. Quite a relief, I think, for a lot of people, though I can understand the disappointment north of the border. It’s a messy situation, all round. Speaker_1: It really is. And the fallout… the political manoeuvring already begun is exhausting just to watch. Makes you wonder what the next few years will hold. Anyway, enough about politics depressing us both. How did your interview go on Friday? You were a bit cagey about it afterwards. Speaker_2: Oh, the interview. Right. Well… it was… an experience. It wasn't terrible, not terrible at all, but I don’t think I shone, if I’m honest. They were very keen on someone with more experience leading large, funded research projects. Which, as you know, isn’t exactly my forte. Speaker_1: Ah, bugger. That’s a shame. You’ve got plenty of experience, just not *that* kind of experience. Who was interviewing you, anyway? Was it old Professor Davies? He’s a bit of a stickler. Speaker_2: It was Davies, and his deputy, Dr. Albright. Albright was the more… probing, shall we say. Kept asking about quantifiable outcomes. I felt like I was back in undergraduate statistics. Davies was mostly nodding and making encouraging noises, which didn't exactly fill me with confidence. He’s utterly hopeless at reading a room, that man. Speaker_1: Sounds about right. He’s a brilliant academic, no doubt, but people skills… not his strong suit. Look, don’t beat yourself up about it. There’ll be other opportunities. Besides, you’re a valuable asset to the department as you are. Speaker_2: You’re very kind, old boy. I appreciate that. Although, truthfully, I’m beginning to wonder if I should just stick it out until retirement and avoid the whole job-hunting circus. It's rather draining. Speaking of draining… how's your daughter? Still loving university? Speaker_1: She is! Absolutely thriving, actually. She's joined the debating society, apparently. Can you believe it? Little Emily, the shrinking violet, now arguing the toss about… well, everything. She was telling me all about her latest debate – something about the ethics of AI. It went on for hours. Speaker_2: Good for her. It's wonderful when they find something they're passionate about. It gives them a focus. My Sarah’s just turned thirty, can you believe it? Seems like only yesterday I was teaching her to ride her bike. It’s flown by. Speaker_1: It does, doesn't it? They grow up far too quickly. Are you seeing her much these days? Speaker_2: Not as much as I’d like, unfortunately. She's got a demanding job in London. She’s a solicitor. Always busy. We speak on the phone every week, though. She sent me a lovely text this morning, actually. Saying she’s thinking of coming down for the weekend. Speaker_1: That’s nice. Well, you deserve a bit of family time. Listen, are you free for a pint next week? We could commiserate about the referendum and your interview. My treat. Speaker_2: I'd like that very much. How about Tuesday evening? The Red Lion? Speaker_1: Perfect. Tuesday it is. I'll book a table. It will be good to get out and chat properly, away from all this… present situation.

Speaker_1: Right, so the spoon goes…no, absolutely not, Leo! It needs to be balanced, not hanging off the edge. Honestly, you'd think a chef would understand balance! And aggressively patriotic. Everything was about America being the best. It was charming, initially, but after a while… Speaker_3: It must have been a culture shock. You’re used to British understatement. Speaker_5: I always found the American healthcare system a bit baffling, from what George described. The expense, the insurance…it all seemed so complicated. Speaker_2: It’s a constant worry for people over there, isn't it? I had to deal with a colleague who nearly bankrupted herself trying to cover her son's medical bills. I briefly considered applying for a position with the embassy in Washington a few years back. Good money, but ultimately… Speaker_1: You wouldn’t have lasted a week. Too much enthusiasm required. You’d be politely declining invitations to baseball games and pretending to enjoy apple pie. Speaker_2: Precisely. I’d be spending my evenings craving a decent cup of tea and a quiet evening. Speaker_4: (Suddenly) Right! I think I’ve got it! Spoon…lever…book…Dominoes… Speaker_3: (Watching intently) This is either going to be brilliant or a catastrophic failure. Speaker_1: Right, okay, so… operation ‘wardrobe refresh’ was largely successful. Speaker_2: (From another room, a slight chuckle) Oh really? Did you bankrupt us entirely? Speaker_1: It’s not retail therapy! It’s… sensible acquisition. The conference next month, remember? And I realised I have absolutely nothing appropriate to wear. Everything feels… stale. Or covered in cat hair. Or both. Speaker_2: The conference in Shanghai? You have a perfectly good navy suit. Speaker_1: Navy is so… predictable. And it wrinkles. Immediately. I got a really lovely teal dress. It’s silk, so it drapes nicely. And a cream blouse, really soft. Speaker_2: Teal and cream. Sounds… bright. You usually go for more muted tones. Speaker_1: I’m branching out! Trying to be a bit more adventurous. I also got a really nice pair of trousers – wide-legged, black, incredibly comfortable. They practically feel like pyjamas. Speaker_2: Practical *and* stylish. Excellent. Did you manage to resist the lure of shoes? Because that’s usually where things get dicey. Speaker_1: (Avoiding eye contact) Maybe… a small pair. They were on sale! And they’re incredibly versatile. Black block heels. You can wear them with everything. Speaker_2: "Small pair"? That sounds suspiciously like code for "at least three pairs". Speaker_1: (Sighs) Okay, fine. Two pairs. One is a little more… sparkly. For evenings. Speaker_2: (Laughing) Sparkly? You’re going to blind the entire academic delegation. Speaker_1: Don't be ridiculous. It’s subtle sparkle. It’s… sophisticated sparkle. And I needed something for dinner, didn't I? We're going to that nice restaurant near the Bund, remember? Speaker_2: Oh, right. That *is* a bit more of an occasion. Still, let's have a look at this haul, shall we? Before our credit card statement arrives. Speaker_1: (Starts unpacking the bags) Alright, alright. Don't judge. They're much nicer in person, honestly. And they were a *bargain*. Speaker_2: (Smiling) I'm not judging, darling. Just curious. And slightly apprehensive. Now, where's my coffee? This requires serious evaluation. Speaker_1: Coming right up! Then prepare to be amazed by my impeccable fashion choices. Speaker_2: I highly doubt that, but I’m willing to be entertained. Speaker_1: (Smiling) Just you wait. Speaker_2: (Chuckling) I always do. Speaker_1: I'll get the coffee started. Speaker_2: Perfect. Speaker_1: Do you have anything planned this evening? Speaker_2: The old admin for tomorrow, but I'm sure I can get it done tomorrow before lunchtime. Speaker_1: Great. Speaker_2: That's good. Speaker_1: Shall we order a Chinese then? Speaker_2: Sounds great! Speaker_1: Great! Speaker_2: Yeah. Speaker_1: I'll order it. Speaker_2: You do that. Speaker_1: Perfect.

Speaker_1: Ah, that was a match and a half, wasn’t it? Jesus, the last ten minutes… I thought we were done for. Speaker_2: It was brilliant! That try by Mack Hansen was *amazing*. He just flew past everyone. Speaker_3: It was a bit stressful watching, I have to admit. My heart was going a mile a minute. Though, honestly, anything with a lot of shouting and running around keeps me awake these days. Speaker_4: Aye, it was a good show. We had a rugby taster session at school today, actually. I got to try tackling—it’s harder than it looks! Speaker_1: Harder than it looks alright! It’s a proper man’s game. Speaker_2: Okay, okay, peas coming. Is it the one with the dinosaur on the front? Speaker_3: The very one. Your grandmother chose it. She’s terribly proud of you, you know. Especially now that you’re getting into sports. It’s good to see you active. Speaker_4: It is. Better than staring at those screens all day. Though, I suppose even rugby gets shown on the telly these days. When I was teaching, sports day was the highlight of the year! Rounders, egg and spoon races… simple joys. Speaker_1: Right, right. Simple joys. We should do something like that with Oisin, more often. Maybe a picnic in the park this weekend? Speaker_3: That sounds lovely. But first, cards. And then, bedtime. He’s yawning already. It's getting late. Speaker_2: Can I have five more minutes? Please? Speaker_1: Five minutes, then straight to bed. And no arguing. Speaker_4: Once he's tucked up, maybe we could go outside and have a look at the stars? It's a beautiful clear night. I always loved showing the children the constellations. Speaker_3: Oh, that's a wonderful idea, Moira! I've been meaning to get a telescope. Maybe we could look for planets? Speaker_1: Absolutely. After the cards and Oisin's bedtime, we can all head outside. I'll grab a blanket. We can have a hot chocolate too, yeah? Speaker_2: Hot chocolate *and* stargazing? Best birthday ever! Speaker_3: Alright then, peas finished, card signing station set up. Let's make this a good one. And then, sleep, young man. Speaker_4: Aye, a good one indeed. It’s good to have everyone together. Speaker_1: It is. Right, where did I put that pen…? Speaker_3: It's right there, darling, next to the cards. Now, Oisin, tell Auntie Moira what you're hoping to get for your birthday… Speaker_2: A new rugby ball! And a dinosaur! Speaker_4: A dinosaur, eh? A fine choice indeed! Speaker_1: That’s my boy! Speaker_3: Right. Let’s get signing. And then a very sleepy little boy.

Speaker_1: Honestly, I’m starting to feel like all I talk about is nappies and sleep schedules now. It’s… consuming. Speaker_2: (Laughing) Oh, you’ve joined the club!
