Speaker_2: Oh, the one with the riverside views? I think my aunt mentioned it. She said it's seriously expensive though. London prices creeping outwards, I suppose. Are you and Tom thinking about moving anytime soon? Speaker_1: Not yet. We’re quite happy where we are for now, small as it is. Although… I’m starting to realise Leo is going to need his own dedicated space eventually. Tom keeps joking about converting the shed! We were having a clear out in the loft yesterday, though, and I unearthed a bunch of clothes I haven't worn in ages. Proper vintage stuff. Speaker_2: Ooh, send them my way! Seriously. I'm trying to avoid buying loads of new stuff and just reusing what I have. And your taste is always brilliant. Remember that floral dress you wore to Sarah’s wedding? I was so jealous. Speaker_1: Oh, that one! It’s probably lurking somewhere… I’ll definitely have a sort and send anything that fits. You've got a much better eye for styling things than I do anyway. Although, I'm definitely dressing for comfort these days. Tracksuits are my friend. Speaker_2: Tell me about it! Comfort is key. It’s so strange, though, isn't it? We were talking about learning Italian just a few years ago, planning that trip to Rome, and now… it’s all baby talk and house hunting. Speaker_1: It is a world away. Though, I'm still trying to keep up my Spanish, even if it's just Duolingo for five minutes a day. It feels important to keep a part of *me* going, you know? Leo might need a bilingual mum someday. Speaker_2: That’s a good point. It’s easy to lose yourself when everything revolves around a tiny human. My brother’s just started a German course – he’s hoping to move to Berlin next year. He wants to completely reinvent himself, apparently. Speaker_1: A complete reinvention! Good for him. Maybe we all need a little bit of that. Speaking of reinventions… have you tried that new cafe on Trumpington Street? The pastries are incredible. A tiny bit of self-care, perhaps? Speaker_2: Ooh, yes! I’ve heard amazing things. That sounds perfect. Lead the way! Maybe we can discuss Leo's impending toddlerhood over croissants. Speaker_1: Excellent plan. And maybe we can plot your sister’s escape from the London property market.

Speaker_1: Right, so then old man Hemmings, he’s going on about how “proper Bedfordshire folk” don’t pronounce the ‘h’ in ‘house’. Proper ridiculous, innit? Like, who cares? Speaker_2: (Chuckles) Oh, Hemmings. He’s a lost cause, that one. Still banging on about the old ways. It’s just dialect, man. Natural evolution. My nan used to drop her ‘h’s all the time. Speaker_3: My yiayia, she didn’t even *have* an ‘h’ to drop. Everything was just…different. Proper Cyprus stuff. Though she picked up a bit of Luton slang over the years, bless her. Used to call everything "chuffed". Speaker_1: Chuffed? That’s northern, isn’t it? I thought that was Yorkshire. Speaker_2: Nah, it’s spread. Luton’s a melting pot. You get a bit of everything, especially with the airport. You hear accents here you wouldn't believe. Remember that Finnish guy who used to come into the pub? Speaker_3: Oh god, yeah! The one who tried to order a pint of…what was it… “sadness”? Thought he was asking for a dark beer. Speaker_1: (Laughing) Sadness! That’s brilliant. Speaking of pints, I’m thinking of getting back into learning guitar. Dust off the old six-string. Speaker_2: Good on ya! I always admired people who can play. My attempts ended with a lot of frustration and stringed fingers. You still doing artwork? Saw some of your stuff online, looked wicked. Speaker_1: Yeah, still plugging away. Freelance stuff mostly. Keeps me busy. Pays the bills, sort of. It’s just…finding the clients is the killer. And then dealing with the ones who think graphic design is just ‘messing about on the computer’. Speaker_3: Tell me about it. Gardening’s the same. People think it’s just mowing a lawn. It’s a science, man! Soil composition, pruning techniques… and the sheer physical graft. I'm considering a bit of MMA training actually, for self-defence, you know? Seen a few… questionable characters about lately. Speaker_2: MMA? Serious? That’s a bit intense, isn’t it? Though I get it. Confidence and all that. I've been trying to learn some basic self-defense techniques just from YouTube. It feels a bit pathetic. Speaker_1: YouTube is alright for a start, I guess. Though nothing beats proper training. My cousin did a course, says it’s changed his whole outlook. He used to be a right pushover. Now he's…calm, but you wouldn’t want to cross him. Speaker_3: Speaking of crossing people, anyone fancy a game of Monopoly later? My mum’s got that really ancient version with all the wooden houses. Speaker_2: Monopoly? You trying to start a family feud? That game is notorious for destroying relationships. Speaker_1: I’m in, though. I'm ruthless. I’ll bankrupt you all. Just saying. Anyone got any tobacco? I’ve run dry. Speaker_3: I think I've got a rollie left somewhere…and a lighter. Hold on. Though, fair warning, it's a bit whiffy… my mum's been on about my smoking again. Speaker_2: Honestly, you two. It’s a wonder your lungs haven’t turned black. Have you guys seen that new nature documentary on Netflix? The one about orangutans? It was heartbreaking. Speaker_1: Nah, not yet. Been binging that new sci-fi show. Total escapism. Speaker_3: I’m trying to cut down on screen time, actually. Feeling a bit… sluggish. Might take the bike out tomorrow. See if the weather holds up. Speaker_2: Good idea. Fresh air’s always a winner. Though, knowing Bedford, it’ll probably be raining by lunchtime.

Speaker_1: Right, onions are sizzling. You okay to chop the peppers while I do this? Speaker_2: Yeah, no problem. Though honestly, this kitchen is freezing. Feels like winter again. Speaker_1: It is a bit nippy, isn't it? Should we put the heating on? Speaker_2: Nah, let's not. Trying to save a bit, remember? Especially with… well, everything. Speaking of saving, have you thought any more about getting a smaller car? Speaker_1: (Sighs) We’ve been over this, haven’t we? I *like* the Mini. It’s fun to drive. Speaker_2: I know, I know. It is a nice little car. But the insurance is killing us, and the petrol… Honestly, the commute is costing a fortune. I'm spending almost £200 a month just getting to and from Peterborough. Speaker_1: Okay, £200 is a lot. But you *could* cycle a couple of days a week? You always said the cycle path is pretty good. Speaker_2: It is, when it's not pouring with rain. And when I don’t have to carry a load of project documents with me! Seriously though, a more economical car would make a huge difference. Something like a… a Toyota Yaris? Speaker_1: (Grimaces) A Yaris? That sounds… sensible. A bit *too* sensible, perhaps? Speaker_2: Sensible is good! We’re trying to be responsible adults, remember? Think of the holiday we could afford if we weren’t throwing money at a car. Speaker_1: You are relentless. I suppose you’re right. It's just… I feel like I’ve only just paid it off. Getting rid of it feels like a waste. Speaker_2: It's not a waste if it saves us money long term. We could look at selling it privately, get a bit more for it than going through a dealership. My mate, Liam, sold his old Ford like that. Got a really good price. Speaker_1: Hmm, okay. That's a thought. Maybe we could browse AutoTrader tonight, just to get an idea of prices? No commitment. Speaker_2: Deal! And while we’re being responsible, I’ve been looking at energy providers. Think we could switch and save a bit on the bills? Speaker_1: (Chuckles) You're on a roll! Okay, okay. Let’s have dinner first. All this talk of saving is making me hungry. Actually, remember that time your old Fiesta broke down on the A1? Speaker_2: (Groans) Don't remind me! That was a disaster. I had to call the AA at like midnight. And then wait two hours in the freezing cold. Speaker_1: I remember! You were livid. You said you’d never buy another British car again. And then you bought a… well, never mind. Speaker_2: (Smiling) Hey, it was a good car, apart from that one little issue! And it got me to work, which is the main thing. Now, those peppers… are they finely chopped? You know I like them small. Speaker_1: Yes, Mother! They’re perfectly diced. Now, stirring or seasoning? Speaker_2: Stirring… definitely stirring. And maybe a pinch more chilli flakes. You know how I like it. Speaker_1: (Laughs) Naturally. You and your obsession with spice. Speaker_2: It’s a flavour sensation! Now, about that Yaris… Speaker_1: (Sighs dramatically) Let's eat first, please.

Speaker_1: Right, now then, love, you’ve had a good brew, haven’t you? Grandad, more biscuits? You look like you’re rationing yourself again. Speaker_4: (Chuckles) Never rationing, lass. Just savouring. These ginger nuts are proper good, they are. Not like them factory ones, all crumbly and tasteless. Speaker_3: He says that about *everything* factory made, doesn’t he? Says the butter doesn’t taste the same. Honestly, Arthur, you’d think they put sawdust in it. Speaker_4: Well, they practically do! It’s all additives and… stuff. Yorkshire butter, that’s what you want. From a proper farm. Speaker_2: (Entering the room, balancing a stack of books) Can I just quickly ask about the Wi-Fi password? Mr. Henderson wants us to upload the history project tonight. Speaker_1: Oh, bless you. It’s the usual, love. “YorkshireRose2023”, all one word. Though, honestly, I’m thinking of changing it. Everyone seems to know it now! Speaker_3: Changing it to what, then? “Arthur’sGingerNuts”? Speaker_4: Now you’re talking! That’s a secure password. Nobody’d guess that. Speaker_1: (Rolling her eyes good-naturedly) Don’t encourage him, Doris. Honestly. Anyway, are you sure you’ve got everything for your rugby training, lad? Warm coat, gloves… it’s turning nippy out there. Speaker_2: Yeah, Mum, all good. Got my kitbag packed. I’m meeting Tom at the bus stop. Speaker_1: Good. And text me when you get there, won’t you? Just so I know you’re safe. This traffic has been awful lately. Speaker_3: It’s always awful around here. Used to be lovely and quiet, used to be. Before they built that bypass. Speaker_4: Bypass didn’t solve anything, did it? Just moved the traffic further down the road. Speaker_1: That’s progress for you, eh? Speaking of progress, I’m trying to work out the heating schedule. It’s costing a fortune. I think I need to lower the temperature overnight. Speaker_3: You’re always freezing, though, aren’t you, love? You have to be warm. Old bones need warmth. Speaker_1: I’ve got me thermal vest! And a hot water bottle. I’m set. The main thing is to try and be sensible. Those electricity bills are frightening. I was marking GCSE papers today, and honestly, some of them couldn't work out percentages! You’d think they’d at least know how to figure out a discount on a jumper… Speaker_2: (Grinning) Don’t tell me you had another one trying to divide by zero? Speaker_1: (Laughs) Oh, you know it! At least two this year. They just… don’t *think*. It’s a lost art. Speaker_4: It always was, if you ask me. Just a bunch of youngsters glued to those little screens… Speaker_3: (Patting Arthur's hand) Oh, Arthur, don’t start. They’ve all got to learn somehow. And those screens are good for keeping in touch, aren’t they? Otherwise, we wouldn’t get to see your granddaughter in Australia last week. Speaker_4: That’s true, that’s true. Though I still don’t trust it. All that… digital nonsense. Give me a good book any day.

Speaker_1: Right, so Captain Blackheart’s ship has just run aground on a coral reef, and… oh, for goodness sake, Leo, are you trying to eat your pirate eye patch? Speaker_3: (Muffled) But it smells like…chocolate! Speaker_1: It *looks* like black liquorice, darling, and absolutely does not taste like chocolate. Honestly! Elsie, are you drawing a map? A treasure map? Speaker_2: Mmm-hmm! It’s to find the sparkly jewels! They’re hidden on… erm… Rainbow Island! Speaker_1: Rainbow Island! Excellent. Very creative. Now, after we rescue Captain Blackheart from the reef, we need to think about Shakespeare week. It’s starting Monday, isn’t it? Speaker_2: Shakespeare? Is that the man with the frilly collar? Speaker_1: That’s the one! He wrote lots of plays, very famous ones. We might even try and go to Stratford-upon-Avon if the weather’s good. Wouldn’t that be exciting? Speaker_3: Is there a pirate ship in Stratford? Speaker_1: (Chuckles) Probably not a pirate ship, sweetheart. But there’s Shakespeare’s house, and the Royal Shakespeare Theatre… we could see a play! Maybe *A Midsummer Night’s Dream*? It has fairies and magic in it. Speaker_2: Ooh, fairies! Can we wear fairy wings? Speaker_1: Absolutely. We can dress up! And speaking of exciting things, remember the circus workshop we booked? The one in the real circus tent? Speaker_3: YES! I want to be a trapeze artist! I’m going to swing really high! Speaker_1: That’s wonderful. Elsie, what will *you* be at the circus? Speaker_2: I want to ride an elephant! A sparkly pink elephant! Speaker_1: (Smiling) A sparkly pink elephant. That sounds… spectacular. Right, who wants some pineapple? It’s looking a bit like pirate treasure, all golden and chunked up. Speaker_3: Pineapple! Yes! Are we doing the Easter pictures tomorrow? Speaker_1: We are! We're going to decorate eggs and then I’ll take photos of you two looking all Easter-y. Remember the little bunny ears? Speaker_2: I want glitter on my egg! Lots and lots of glitter! Speaker_1: (Sighs playfully) Lots and lots of glitter it is. Honestly, this house will be covered in glitter for weeks. Elsie, did you finish that stop-motion animation you were working on? The one with the Lego pirates? Speaker_2: Almost! Captain Bluebeard needs to find the treasure, but he keeps losing his sword. Speaker_3: I can help him find it! I’m good at finding lost things. Speaker_1: That’s very kind of you, Leo. Maybe you can be Captain Bluebeard’s first mate. Now, eat your pineapple before it sails away like a pirate ship! Speaker_1: Honestly, all this talk about pirates and magic. It’s exhausting! But it’s good, isn’t it? They’re having fun. Speaker_1: Oh, and by the way, I’m trying a new recipe for the Easter cake. It involves orange blossom… I hope it doesn’t taste too… floral. We shall see. Speaker_1: They’ve got such imaginations. It's a lovely thing to witness, really. Speaker_1: Now, if only I could get Leo to stop attempting to eat the furniture...

Speaker_1: Honestly, Roger, you wouldn’t *believe* the fuss. Jeddah to Cyprus, I tell you. Perfectly sensible plan, clear skies… or so we thought. Speaker_2: (Chuckles) Sensible? Dorothy, attempting to sail the Red Sea in a… what was it, a thirty-foot yacht? With Bernard at the helm, no less? Speaker_3: Ah, but it’s the *story* that matters, isn’t it? Bernard always did have a talent for attracting trouble. Remind me again, what was the official charge? Speaker_4: Attempting to leave port without proper clearance, as I recall. And, crucially, ignoring repeated requests from the harbourmaster to… well, stay put. Something about unseasonal winds. Though the real issue, I suspect, was Bernard’s insistence on a full English breakfast *on* the deck just moments before setting off. Speaker_1: It wasn’t just the breakfast! It was the fact they didn’t understand we had provisions! They thought we were trying to smuggle something. Goodness knows what. I tried to explain, in my best Arabic, that we simply wanted to sail to Cyprus. Speaker_2: And they responded with…armed guards? I heard you ended up in a cell. Speaker_1: Not a cell, precisely. More of a holding room. Very clean, surprisingly. But filled with bewildered-looking fishermen and a rather insistent camel. The camel kept trying to eat my handbag. Speaker_3: (Laughing) A camel! Only you, Dorothy. You manage to get arrested with a camel involved. This is prime material for your next book. You *are* writing another one, aren't you? Speaker_1: I’m toying with the idea. It’s rather difficult, you see. Getting the tone right. It wasn't frightening, exactly, just… extraordinarily inconvenient. And hot. Terribly hot. Speaker_4: Saudi Arabia and its peculiar charms. I remember you telling me about the difficulty obtaining even a thimbleful of sherry while teaching there. Speaker_2: Ah yes, the restrictions. Completely different to my stint in Spain. Wine flowed like water, practically. One had to be careful not to get carried away, naturally. Though a little Rioja with tapas never hurt anyone. Speaker_3: It's all relative, isn’t it? My sister-in-law spent a year in Iran during the seventies. She told me they used to distill alcohol from dates. Apparently it was potent, and strictly forbidden, so naturally everyone made it. Speaker_1: Dates, you say? That actually sounds rather appealing. Better than some of the… concoctions I was offered in Jeddah. They had this local drink made from fermented milk. Honestly, it tasted like sour socks. Speaker_4: Saudi Arabia *was* a bit of a culture shock, wasn't it? Though, speaking of sailing, it reminded me of a rather unfortunate incident off the coast of Greece… involving a rather large wave, a stack of *British Dental Journal*, and my dentures. Speaker_2: (Raises an eyebrow) Your dentures? Don’t tell me… Speaker_4: They flew out, Roger! Right into the Aegean! I spent a good half hour fishing around with a boat hook. Thankfully, I retrieved them. Though they were covered in seaweed and rather salty. Speaker_3: (Roaring with laughter) Good heavens, Arthur! You are a treasure. Lost dentures and dental journals... it’s a tale for the ages. Speaker_1: Goodness me. Well, it’s certainly been a colourful evening. Another glass of wine, anyone? Perhaps we can steer clear of maritime disasters for a while.

Speaker_1: Honestly, the state of that bathroom this morning… I don’t know what goes on in there. It looked like a bomb had hit it. Speaker_2: Oh, tell me about it. Remember when Liam was that age? Exactly the same. Everything ends up… everywhere. It’s a teenage boy thing, I reckon. No spatial awareness, no concept of ‘putting things back.’ Speaker_3: (Muttering from another room) I *did* put the empty shower gel bottle in the bin! Speaker_1: (Calling back) Yes, dear, well done. But the clothes on the floor, the wet towel draped over the… everything else. It's just relentless. Speaker_2: It is a phase. They eventually learn. Mostly. Though Liam’s bathroom still needs a good scrub when he comes home from uni. Speaking of which, have you started looking at holiday options for August yet? Speaker_1: A little. I was thinking maybe somewhere in Cornwall? Nice beaches, relatively easy to get to. Though honestly, part of me just wants to stay here and avoid the stress of travelling with a teenager. Speaker_3: Cornwall would be… okay. Can we take the bodyboards? Speaker_1: Possibly. We’ll see. It depends on your behaviour between now and then. And whether you promise to at least *attempt* to tidy your room occasionally. Speaker_2: You’ve got to offer incentives, you know. Remember when I used to bribe Liam with extra pocket money if he helped with the gardening? Worked a treat. Speaker_1: Hmm, tempting. Though I’m trying to instill a sense of responsibility, not just rewarding him for basic chores. He needs to start thinking about work experience, doesn't he? It's looming. Speaker_3: Ugh. Work experience. Ms. Davies said we need to start thinking about it. It’s so boring trying to find stuff. Everything’s either stacking shelves or helping in a charity shop. Speaker_2: Now, that’s not true. Liam did work experience at a garage once. Got covered head-to-toe in grease. He hated it, of course, but it was *something*. Speaker_1: I was hoping he might find something a bit more…creative. He’s quite good with computers, could maybe volunteer somewhere helping with IT. I’ve been having a look online. It's finding something suitable and within travelling distance that's the tricky part. Speaker_3: Actually…Emily’s dad works with computers. He builds websites and stuff. Maybe I could ask him? Speaker_1: That’s a brilliant idea! See? Sometimes things just fall into place. Speaking of Emily… how are things going with her? You seem quieter than usual when she's mentioned lately. Speaker_3: (Slightly mumbled) It’s fine. Speaker_2: “It’s fine” usually means it’s *not* fine. Are you two having a little disagreement? Speaker_1: Don’t tell me he’s broken another girl’s heart. Honestly, you’d think he'd learn. Though, I suppose at your age, it’s all a bit of a learning curve. Speaker_3: Look, it’s nothing. We just…had a bit of an argument about who should referee the Year 7 football match on Friday. She thinks *I* should, but I don't want to! It’s a nightmare! They’re all awful at football. Speaker_1: (Laughing) Oh, that’s it? A football refereeing dispute? That’s a relief. I thought it was something serious! Speaker_2: See? Sometimes it’s the little things. It’s good he’s getting involved though, refereeing. Builds character. Though I wouldn't fancy that, those parents can get loud.

Speaker_1: Honestly, this scenery is unreal. Like, absolutely stunning. Didn’t realise Croatia was *this* green. Speaker_2: It is lovely, isn’t it? Much nicer than the motorway back home. And the air smells… clean. Not like Bolton sometimes, you know? Everything smells of diesel and chips. Speaker_3: (From the back, engrossed in his phone) Can we stop for ice cream soon? I'm starving. Speaker_4: (Driving) We had a massive breakfast, Liam. Though, yes, we can look for a gelateria in the next town. This whole truffle thing is making me hungry again, actually. Speaker_1: Oh, speaking of truffles, did I tell you about that chef I follow on Instagram? He does a truffle mac and cheese. *Truffle mac and cheese*. It’s obscene. Speaker_2: (Scoffs lightly) Obscene is right. Truffles are wasted on mac and cheese, love. They need something… elegant. A proper risotto, maybe. Or shaved over pasta. Speaker_4: My client, David, he’s a bit of a foodie. Went on and on about a truffle hunt he did in Italy last year. Said it was life-changing. Cost him a fortune, naturally. Speaker_1: Sounds like something Mark would be into. Remember Mark and his… everything being artisanal? Speaker_2: (Chuckles) Oh, Mark. Honestly, he'd have a nervous breakdown if he saw me having a cigarette. Though, to be fair, I’m trying to cut down. It’s just… holidays and having a smoke. It goes hand-in-hand. Speaker_3: Gran, you told me they were really bad for you! Speaker_2: I *am* trying to stop, darling! One a day isn’t going to kill me. It’s stress relief, okay? Dealing with expectant mothers all day is…a lot. Speaker_4: You’re a saint, honestly. Dealing with all that. Reminds me, saw something fascinating on TV the other night about stem cell research. Apparently, they’re making huge breakthroughs with treating complications in pregnancy. Speaker_1: Oh yeah? That’s amazing! It's mad how quickly science is moving. Feels like yesterday we were all freaking out about Dolly the sheep. Speaker_3: Who’s Dolly the sheep? Speaker_1: Oh, you wouldn't remember. It was a big thing when we were kids – the first mammal cloned from an adult cell. Speaker_2: It's all a bit scary when you think about it, isn’t it? Still, good to see advancements that can help people. Speaking of helping people, did you hear old Mr. Henderson’s grandson is off to university in America on a football scholarship? Speaker_4: Really? Good for him. That’s fantastic. Shame about the state of English football at the moment though. Utterly depressing. Speaker_1: You and your football! Honestly, you’d think it was a matter of national security the way you talk about it. Speaker_4: It's important, El! It’s… culture. Tradition. Speaker_2: He’s just passionate, love. Don't wind him up. Are you driving alright, dear? This road's a bit bumpy. And slow down a bit will you; I don't want us ending up in a ditch before we even get to try the truffle pasta. Speaker_3: Can we put some music on? My ears are popping. Speaker_1: Good call, Liam. Anything but Dad's classic rock, please.

Speaker_1: Honestly, this canteen food is…an experience, isn’t it? I think I’ve identified at least four different shades of beige on my plate. Speaker_2: (Chuckles) You’re being kind. It’s functional, I suppose. Fuel for the afternoon. Though I’m starting to suspect the ‘chicken’ is actually tofu in disguise. Speaker_3: Definitely tofu. I tried to spear a piece with my fork and it just…slid off. Like trying to catch smoke. Speaker_1: Oh god, yes! Exactly. I’m clinging to the hope that the salad bar will offer some redemption. Although, judging by the wilted lettuce, that's a long shot. Speaker_2: So, how's the dialect data coming along, Amelia? Still drowning in recordings of Norfolk vowels? Speaker_1: Pretty much. It's fascinating, genuinely, but transcription is…slow. Especially when people decide to just trail off mid-sentence, or slur everything into one long sound. You wouldn’t believe the number of “hmmms” and “ahhs” I’ve had to code for. Speaker_3: Sounds intense. I’m still mostly just making spreadsheets and chasing people for updates on the Peterson project. Less intellectually stimulating, let's say. Though, I did manage to convince Malcolm to finally approve the budget for the new server. Small victories. Speaker_2: Nice one, Ben! That’s a proper win. Malcolm’s notoriously tight-fisted with the funds. I’m currently battling the algorithm on the new ad campaign. It keeps trying to target 70-year-olds with gaming laptops. It's… challenging. Speaker_1: (Laughing) Oh, that’s brilliant! The algorithm clearly hasn’t grasped target demographics. Speaker_3: Sounds about right. The AI revolution is clearly still a work in progress. Are you two heading to the Arts Festival this weekend? I saw they’ve got a photography exhibition on, thought it might be good. Speaker_2: I was thinking about it. I’ve been meaning to get out more. Uni life gets a bit…claustrophobic sometimes, you know? Just bouncing between the office and my flat. Speaker_1: I'm definitely up for it! I need a break from phonemes and spectrograms. A bit of visual stimulus sounds perfect. Plus, I heard there's a decent gin bar nearby. Speaker_3: Excellent! Gin is always a good plan. We could grab tickets for that film screening too, the one about the Cambridge punting history? Speaker_2: Oh, that sounds… incredibly Cambridge. I'm in. Anything to lean into the stereotype, right? Speaker_1: Absolutely. Embrace the punting. It's practically a requirement for living here. Although, I still haven't actually tried it myself. Speaker_3: You haven’t?! Amelia, that’s a scandal! We *have* to rectify that. Speaker_1: I know, I know! It’s on the list. Right after ‘learn to navigate Cambridge without looking at Google Maps’. Speaker_2: Maybe we can make it a triple threat: punting, the festival, and a lesson in Cambridge orienteering. Speaker_3: I think we have a plan. Now, has anyone managed to find a remotely edible component to this lunch? I'm starting to think my stomach is staging a protest. Speaker_1: I’m officially declaring the potato wedges salvageable. They’re slightly overcooked, but marginally less terrifying than the ‘chicken’. Speaker_2: Good call. Potato wedges it is, then. Fuel for our adventures.

Speaker_1: Right, so are you absolutely sure about the directions, love? It all looks a bit… uniform out here. Fields and fields and more fields. Speaker_2: Positive, Auntie Carol. Google Maps says another five kilometres, then a left turn onto a little side road. Apparently, Kasia’s place is practically hidden. She says everyone gets lost the first time. Speaker_1: Hidden is one thing, driving into a ditch is another! Honestly, this campervan is lovely, but it’s not exactly built for navigating Polish farm tracks. Are you sure we’ve got enough clearance? Speaker_2: Relax, it’ll be fine. I checked the reviews of the campsite Kasia recommended, and someone specifically mentioned getting a larger vehicle down that road. Plus, I’m a pretty good driver now, remember? Been doing this for a couple of years, trekking around Europe with students. Speaker_1: Trekking around Europe with students is very different to a Polish backroad in a borrowed campervan, dear. Though, good for you, being so adventurous. It just…it feels a long way from Cambridge, doesn’t it? Speaker_2: It is a long way! Which is the point, isn’t it? Kasia’s been going on about this for months, wanting us to come and see her new garden. And honestly, after the last year, a bit of Polish countryside is exactly what we need. Speaker_1: Yes, well, the countryside is nice. I’m more concerned about this ‘little side road’. Is it… paved? Speaker_2: I think so? The satellite view wasn’t super clear. But Kasia said it's generally okay, just bumpy in places. We'll take it slow. And if we *do* end up in a ditch, at least it’ll be a scenic ditch. Speaker_1: (chuckles) Always the optimist. Right, well, let's just hope it’s not a particularly muddy ditch. This borrowed campervan’s owner would have my hide. He’s a lovely man, but very particular about his vehicle. Speaker_2: Don't worry, we'll be careful. Did you remember to pack the Polish phrasebook? Kasia said her English isn't brilliant when she's explaining complicated things about fertiliser and… beetroot. Speaker_1: Oh, yes, it’s in the little bag beside you. Though I suspect 'Where is the nearest shop?’ and ‘Do you accept card?’ will be the extent of my Polish vocabulary this trip. Speaker_2: That’ll probably cover most emergencies! Actually, she mentioned there’s a little market in Tarnow on Saturday. We could stock up on pierogi. Speaker_1: Pierogi! Now *that* sounds promising. A good pierogi can solve most problems, I think. It’s just…I’m terrible at remembering names, you know? I’ll probably spend the whole weekend calling Kasia ‘Katarina’ or something equally embarrassing. Speaker_2: You won’t. Just focus on the pierogi. And I’ll gently correct you if you slip up. Don't stress, Auntie Carol, it’s going to be a lovely weekend. Relax and enjoy the… fields. Speaker_1: Alright, alright. I'm trying. Just point out when we’re getting close to this ‘little side road’, will you? And maybe check the Google Maps one more time? Just for peace of mind. Speaker_2: Will do. Nearly there – five kilometres, then left. And I promise, no ditches. Probably. Speaker_1: (muttering) 'Probably' is not reassuring…

Speaker_1: Honestly, that was a dodgy call. They’ve been letting Villa play far too easily, haven’t they? You’d think with all the money they’ve splashed, they’d be… more dominant. Speaker_2: Aye, a bit. But listen, speaking of money splashing, did you see the new Liverpool kit? Absolutely dreadful. That colour… it’s like someone spilled a pint of Guinness on a white shirt. Speaker_1: No way! Really? I haven’t even looked. I avoid looking at football strips these days. It's just…corporate greed on nylon, isn’t it? They churn them out every year, make a fortune, and half the time they’re objectively awful. Speaker_2: Objectively is a strong word, but… yeah. This one’s pushing it. And the sponsor. Another betting company. Honestly, it's relentless. When did football just become one giant advert? Speaker_1: It's been a slow creep, hasn't it? Remember when it was breweries on the shirts? At least that felt a bit… local. Now it's all global gambling conglomerates and vaguely defined 'financial services'. Speaker_2: Exactly! And they pay these players millions to *wear* the logos. It’s just… baffling. Makes you wonder what’s actually driving the sport these days. Is it passion, or just revenue? Speaker_1: Probably revenue, if we’re being realistic. Though, I reckon there's a tipping point. People are getting fed up with it. They *will* switch off. Speaker_2: Maybe. No-one wants a hospice looming over their garden. Speaker_1: Thinking about the demographics, there's a surprisingly high number of ex-pats around here. Lots of retired professionals. They have excellent facilities, but they’re stretched. We can offer a more localised, community-focused approach. Speaker_1: And they're good at navigating the complexities of the health budgets, aren’t they? Honestly, trying to understand the commissioning process is like wading through treacle. I've been on the phone all morning trying to get a clear answer about funding for integrated care pathways. Speaker_2: It's a deliberate obfuscation, I suspect. Keeps everyone on their toes. Though, I have a contact at the Clinical Commissioning Group… might be worth a discreet phone call. We need to be clear about the cost-benefits. Preventing unnecessary hospital admissions, reducing A&E visits… that’s where the financial argument lands. Speaker_1: Right. Okay. So, deadline for drafting the full business case is next Friday? Can we arrange a follow-up meeting on Wednesday to review the patient story drafts and refine the location rationale? Speaker_2: Wednesday is perfect. 2 pm? And let’s bring in Sarah from finance then – she can sanity-check the budget projections. This has to be watertight. It’s not just a building, it’s…well, it’s about giving people the best possible end to their

Speaker_1: Oh, look at this one! Us at Sarah’s wedding. God, that feels like a lifetime ago. Everyone was so… optimistic. Speaker_2: Optimistic and slightly tipsy, if I remember correctly. Old Man Hemmings nearly took a tumble trying to do the Macarena. Speaker_3: (Peeling potatoes) Haha! I vaguely remember that. How’s the job hunt going, by the way, Chloe? Any interviews lined up? Speaker_3: Actually, yes. I have one on Friday, for a content creator role at that digital marketing agency in Canterbury. It sounds pretty good, the work seems really creative. Speaker_1: Oh, wonderful! That’s brilliant, love. Are you nervous? Speaker_3: A bit. It's the first real interview I’ve had since graduating. Though she also said he was terrible at cooking. Speaker_1: Terrible is an understatement. He once tried to make shepherd’s pie with peas instead of carrots. The less said about it, the better. Speaker_3: (Laughing) I think we’re safe on that front. Unless you’ve secretly substituted peas for carrots. Speaker_1: Don't even joke!

Speaker_1: Right, so are we actually gonna watch this, or are we just gonna sit ‘ere talkin’ about how scared we are? 'Cause I’m gettin’ a right neck ache lookin’ up at the telly. No, honestly, I’m just worried it'll be all jump scares. I hate jump scares. Makes me jump. Obvious, innit? Speaker_2: It’s supposed to be slow burn. Atmospheric. That’s why I picked it. And try not to spill the popcorn all over the sofa. Speaker_1: No promises on that front either. Speaker_2: Right. Shhh! It’s starting… Speaker_1: (Immediately grips Speaker_2’s arm) Oh god, this music is already awful. Speaker_2: It’s supposed to be! Speaker_1: I knew I shouldn't have agreed to this. Speaker_2: Just breathe. It's only a film. Speaker_1: Easy for you to say, you aren’t afraid of clowns! Speaker_2: (Quietly) Yet… Speaker_1: What was that?! Speaker_2: Nothing! Nothing yet. Speaker_1: Oh… right.

Speaker_1: Right, well, almost bedtime for me I think. Just finishing this cup of tea. You alright, Grandad? Speaker_2: Oh, aye, fine, fine. Just been flicking through the channels. Nothing but rubbish on these days, you know. All shouting and flashing lights. Give me a good old book any day. Speaker_1: I know what you mean. Though, I did order a new book *online* last night. Especially for things like books. Though I was looking at Airbnb too, thinking about a little weekend away somewhere. Have you ever considered that? Speaker_2: Airbnb? What’s that then? Speaker_2: Oh, that’s kind of you, dear. But no, I’m alright. Had a nice bit of cheese and a biscuit earlier. You enjoy. Reminds me, your cousin Emily rang today. Said she’s coming down next week. Speaker_1: Oh, lovely! I’d forgotten she was planning a visit. How long is she staying? Speaker_2: A few days, I think. Said she wanted to see the garden. She’s always liked your garden, hasn’t she? Speaker_1: She has. I'm trying to rearrange the living room a bit. I was thinking of selling that old armchair. It's just taking up space. Have you seen anyone looking for furniture recently? Speaker_2: Not that I’ve noticed. Old Mrs. Higgins down the road mentioned needing a new sofa, but she’s more of a floral print type of woman, and your armchair is…well, it’s quite masculine, isn’t it? Speaker_1: It is, isn't it? Right. Well, I think I’ll take a picture and put it on that selling website you showed me, Gumtree. It's all a bit daunting, all this technology. I got another seventeen emails today, mainly from school though. Speaker_2: Seventeen! Goodness me. What do they *want*? Speaker_1: Just updates, mostly. Parent communications, policy changes… endless stuff. I wish they’d just stick to letters. Speaker_2: Me too. Give me a nice, handwritten letter any day. More personal, you see. Speaking of personal, are you using that iPad I got you? Speaker_1: Every day! It’s brilliant for reading, and checking emails. I'm just trying to work out how to video call Mum and Dad, but it’s a bit fiddly. Speaker_2: I can show you tomorrow if you like. I had a go on it, trying to watch a cricket match. Didn't quite grasp it though. Speaker_1: That’s kind. Right. I really should head up to bed. Long day tomorrow. Speaker_2: Alright, dear. Sleep well. Don't let the bedbugs bite!

Speaker_1: Aye, honestly, that Kerouac’s been sittin’ on my shelf for months now. *On the Road*. Everyone raves about it, says it changed their life, but I just… can't get into it. Feels a bit boyish, doesn’t it? All that romanticising of hitchhiking and bein’ a beatnik. Speaker_2: (Chuckles, stirring his coffee) Boyish? Coming from *you*, Alistair? The man who once spent three weeks backpacking through the Highlands with nothing but a rucksack and a copy of poetry by Burns? Speaker_1: That was different! That was… a spiritual journey! Kerouac just feels like a well-meaning lad trying to be profound. Besides, the Highlands are a bit more forgiving than some dusty American highway. I reckon I lost a good stone just fighting the midges. Speaker_2: You always exaggerate. Still, I see your point. It *is* a bit… performative, isn’t it? Though I did enjoy the sheer energy of it. It made me want to just hop on a train and disappear. Which, ironically, is exactly what I *didn't* do. Had essays to mark, remember? Speaker_1: Ah, the glamorous life of a Director of Studies. Chained to your desk while the rest of us are out exploring the world. Speaking of exploring, you still heading to Japan next year? Speaker_2: Aye, all being well. Planning on going in cherry blossom season. Supposedly breathtaking. I've been reading a lot about Kyoto, trying to get a feel for the place. It sounds… refined. A bit less chaotic than somewhere like Tokyo, eh? Speaker_1: I've heard the same. I was in Tokyo for a conference a few years back and it was… overwhelming. Brilliant, but overwhelming. The sheer density of people, the noise… it was incredible. Though I did manage to find a tiny little ramen shop down an alleyway that was heaven on earth. Speaker_2: Those are the best finds, aren't they? The bits you stumble upon. I'm hoping to spend a couple of weeks just wandering, getting lost, seeing what happens. Though I’m trying to learn a few basic phrases, just to avoid completely embarrassing myself. My Japanese extends to… *konnichiwa* and a rather enthusiastic ‘arigato’. You really do find trouble, don’t you? I’m more worried about the etiquette. Apparently, there's a whole world of unspoken rules about how to behave, how to present yourself… Speaker_1: Don't overthink it. Just be polite, respectful, and try not to stick your chopsticks upright in your rice. That’s apparently a big no-no. I read that somewhere. Speaker_2: Upright chopsticks… noted. Right, I’m adding that to the list. Though honestly, I might just stick to tea. I hear they have some incredible teas in Japan. Speaker_1: They do. Proper ceremony and everything. I’ve got a mate who went last year, he came back a fully converted tea enthusiast. He’s now judging people based on their brewing technique. Speaker_2: (Smiling) Sounds… intense. Well, I’m hoping to come back with a few good memories, and maybe a decent book or two, rather than a lifetime obsession with tea.

Speaker_1: Honestly, Mum, the interview felt…weird. Not bad weird, just…off. Speaker_2: Off how, love? Was it the people? The building? You were saying it’s a really prestigious firm, wasn’t it? It was the fluffy stuff that threw me. Speaker_2: Well, that’s good then, that the work speaks for itself. Listen, don’t beat yourself up about it. These things happen. And I've been applying for jobs for months now. It's starting to feel a bit disheartening. Speaker_2: I can imagine. Have you heard anything back from that smaller firm, the one in Shoreditch? The one doing the eco-housing project? Speaker_1: Not yet. I sent a follow-up email last week, but nothing. I'm starting to think they've gone with someone else. They’re a lot smaller, so maybe they just didn't have the budget to hire. Actually, I completely forgot to tell you - I also applied for that role at the National Trust, doing conservation work. Speaker_2: Oh, that sounds lovely! That’s more your speed, isn’t it? Preserving beautiful buildings, not necessarily designing gleaming new ones. Speaker_1: It is, yeah. But the salary is…significantly lower. I'm starting to think I need to revise my expectations. Maybe I'm aiming too high right away. Speaker_2: Don’t sell yourself short, darling. You've got a brilliant degree, you’re talented, and you’ve worked really hard. But a little realism is good too. It’s a tough market out there. Look, why don’t we go for a proper walk tomorrow? Get out of this flat, breathe some fresh air. We can talk it through properly. And I promise, no talk of ‘emotional connections to concrete’. Speaker_1: (Laughs) That sounds amazing, actually. Thank you, Mum. That means a lot. Perhaps a walk *and* a really large slice of cake? Speaker_2: Absolutely. My treat. Now, tell me about this woolly jumper your aunt knitted for you… it’s a bit…bright.

Speaker_1: Right then, settle yerselves. Cup of tea, Doris? Arthur, you’ll have your usual, I expect? Speaker_2: Aye, please, Bernard. A nice strong brew. Been a long drive, even just coming from Costessey. Traffic was somethin' awful around the roundabout. Speaker_3: Oh, don't even *mention* the traffic, Arthur. I came round earlier and it was nose-to-tail all the way from Harrow. Honestly, you’d think everyone decided to go shopping at the same time. Speaker_1: They probably did. Everything's gotten busier, hasn’t it? Used to be able to get anywhere quick as you like. Remember that, Arthur? When you could drive into Norwich and find a parkin’ space without a palaver? Speaker_2: Aye, those were the days. Before all these fancy one-way systems and cycle lanes. Makes a fella dizzy just tryin' to navigate the city now. Though, I must say, that new supermarket on the edge of town is handy. Good prices, too. Speaker_3: I went there last week. It's alright, but they seem to move everything around every time you go. You spend half an hour just lookin' for the biscuits! Speaker_1: They do that on purpose, Doris. It’s a tactic to get you to buy things you don’t need. They call it ‘consumer journey optimisation’ or some such nonsense. Speaker_2: Consumer what-now? Sounds like a load of balderdash to me. They just want yer money, that’s all. Speaking of money, did you see what they’re sayin’ about house prices now? Still goin' up, apparently. Speaker_1: Absolutely ridiculous. Young folks haven't a chance these days. I remember when you could buy a perfectly decent semi for a few thousand pound. Now they’re payin' half a million for a shoebox. Speaker_3: It’s criminal, it is. My granddaughter’s savin’ up, but she says it'll take her a lifetime to afford anything. And even then, it'll be somethin' tiny. Speaker_2: They should build more council houses, that's what they should do. Like they used to. Good quality, affordable homes. Not these flimsy things they stick up now. Speaker_1: They won't do that though, will they? It's all about profit these days. Speaking of buildin' things, I was readin’ about that new road they’re plannin' to build through the countryside. Says it’ll cut journey times, but I reckon it’ll just ruin the landscape. Speaker_3: Oh, I heard about that. It's a shame. Norfolk’s lovely and green, we don't want it covered in concrete. And what about the wildlife? Where will all the birds and animals go? Speaker_2: They don't care about that, Doris. Progress, they call it. Always progress. My old man used to say, progress is just makin' things worse, slower. Speaker_1: Your old man was a wise man, Arthur. A very wise man. He always had a good head on his shoulders. Remember his old Austin A35? Now *that* was a car. Built to last. Speaker_2: Ah, Bessie. Good old Bessie. She took us everywhere. She wasn’t much to look at, but she was reliable. Unlike these modern cars, full of electronics and things that go wrong. Speaker_3: My son’s got one of those self-driving cars. Scares me to death even thinkin’ about it. What happens when it malfunctions? Whose fault is it then? Speaker_1: Exactly. Too much reliance on technology, I say. Give me a good old-fashioned engine any day. Now, who wants another biscuit with their tea? I’ve got some lovely ginger snaps.

Speaker_1: Right, so I was chatting with Old Man Hemmings from the community garden this morning, and he's really keen on utilising that little nook by the fire escape on the ground floor. Speaker_2: The one we were thinking of for storage? Honestly, I was hoping to get some shelving in there, we’re bursting at the seams with all the event kit. We need to be thinking about how we maximise every inch of this building. Speaker_1: That’s what I said to him! Gently, of course. We could market those really well on social media. ‘Grow Your Own!’ – very Brixton. Have you checked the fire regulations for that space though? It’s right next to the escape route. We don’t want plant pots obstructing anything. Speaker_1: I already flagged it with Barry, the fire safety bloke. He said as long as there’s clear access and the plants aren’t flammable, we should be okay. He did remind me, for the tenth time, about the boxes blocking the corridor near the kitchen. Speaker_2: Oh, *that*. Right. I’ll get onto that after the meeting with the new yoga teacher. Apparently, she’s wanting to book the hall every Tuesday evening. Speaker_1: Excellent! That’s a good consistent income stream. Is she paying the going rate? I don’t want us getting undercut again. Remember what happened with the pottery class? Speaker_2: I’ve already negotiated with her, she’s aware of our rates. She’s offering to run a free taster session for some of the families we work with too. Good PR. Speaker_1: That’s brilliant, actually. Good thinking. Although… free sessions eat into profit, don’t they? We need to track those accurately. Speaker_2: I am, I am. I’ve built it into the spreadsheet. Speaking of which, have you sorted holiday cover for the front desk? I’m off for two weeks in August. Speaker_1: I’ve asked young Maya if she's available. She’s finishing her A-Levels and said she’d be keen. She’s good with people, really efficient. But she’ll need training on the booking system, naturally. Speaker_2: She’s reliable, that one. Right, what about furniture? We desperately need new chairs for the waiting area. These ones look like they’ve been through a warzone. Speaker_1: I’ve been looking online. There’s a company doing refurbished office furniture, reasonably priced. I thought we could go for something more… colourful? A bit less corporate. Speaker_2: Definitely. Something that reflects the vibe of the place. And maybe a small coffee table? People are always balancing mugs on their knees. Reminds me, I need to remind maintenance about that leaky drainpipe, it’s dripping directly onto the bike shed. Speaker_2: I'll add it to the list. Right, yoga teacher imminent. Let's hope she’s organised. I swear, some people treat this place like it's a free-for-all.

Speaker_1: (Smiling, pushing a plate towards Speaker_3) Honestly, Ben, you *have* to try this chutney. It’s ridiculous. Mrs. Davies from the village made it - apparently, it’s a family recipe. Plum and something… fiery. Speaker_3: (Takes a generous spoonful, chews thoughtfully) Oh. *Woah*. Right. Fiery is…an understatement. It’s like a tiny dragon just breathed on my tongue. Just a knob of butter and a splash of milk. My grandmother swore by it. She said it's all about treating them gently. They’re sensitive little things. Speaker_3: Sensitive potatoes, eh? Speaker_3: (Groans) Don't even *mention* the paella. It looked like something dredged from the bottom of the sea. And tasted… vaguely of sadness. Speaker_4: (Laughing) It was memorable, at least! Speaker_5: (Looking at Speaker_6) Margaret, are you enjoying? You haven't said much. Speaker_6: Oh, I am! Lovely meal. It's just…nice to be *away*. Away from work, away from everything. Speaker_1: Honestly, the hospital… it’s just a conveyor belt, isn’t it? In, examined, out. Barely a human touch. John knows that. He’s just… lost. And trying to be ‘the rock’.

Speaker_1: Right, well that was a lovely dinner. Honestly, that dauphinoise potatoes were *almost* worth the effort. Almost. Speaker_2: (Mouth full) They were good! Can I have some more pudding? Speaker_1: Right, okay, this one… this is absolutely dreadful quality, isn’t it? Taken on that little disposable camera we had on the Japan trip. Speaker_2: I did not scream! I emitted a… startled yelp. A perfectly reasonable reaction to a wild animal attempting a home invasion. Speaker_1: …and honestly, the pub quizzes in Galway were *intense*. Like, people were taking this seriously. Proper serious. Someone almost came to blows over the capital of Burkina Faso. Apparently, there’s this new zombie virus… Speaker_3: Oh, don't even *start* with the zombie apocalypse talk, Chloe. Speaker_3: (Laughing) Questionable is putting it mildly! You nearly poisoned us all. Honestly, leave the gefilte fish to the experts. Speaker_1: Honestly, I’m convinced you’ve got a sixth sense for finding the *worst* peanuts in any pub. These are… dusty. Speaker_2: (crunching thoughtfully) Dusty? No, they’ve got character. Speaker_2: (choking on a dusty peanut) *What?!* Live finches in… You're kidding. Speaker_1: I wish I was! Apparently, they’re quite a delicacy in some parts of Asia. The poor birds. Speaker_2: Right. Haven't noticed a huge difference yet, but I'm keeping my fingers crossed. Speaker_3: Glucosamine? Poppycock! You need a good liniment. My mother swore by it. And stop driving that little Mini. Speaker_1: Honestly, you two look so relaxed! Belgium clearly did you good. How was it overall? Speaker_2: Oh, Brighton’s a bit… brisk, after Bruges, I tell you. It was lovely, really lovely. Faster to a demolition derby, maybe. Speaker_1: (Laughing) Oh Dad! You and technology… never a good mix. Did you at least manage to see some sights? Mum, you were saying something about the markets? It's in my bag, don't peek. Speaker_1: Oh, Mum, you shouldn’t have! You really didn’t have to. Speaker_2: And the chocolate! Don't even get me started on the chocolate. I swear, I came back two stone heavier. Daphne kept buying me pralines… supposedly for ‘medicinal purposes’. Speaker_3: They were fueling your sightseeing, Harold! You needed the energy after complaining about the sat nav. Honestly, that thing. It wasn't even picking up road signs properly. We ended up in a farmyard at one point! Speaker_1: A farmyard?! Seriously? Speaker_2: Serious as a heart attack. A cow looked at me like *I* was the one who was lost. And then trying to reverse out... the road was covered in, well, you can imagine. Speaker_1: Oh, Dad! That sounds… chaotic. You should’ve just stopped and asked for directions. Speaker_2: Asked for directions? From *Europeans*? They’d have given me a ten-minute lecture on the history of the road before even pointing me in the right direction! No thank you. Speaker_3: That's a bit harsh, Harold. Most people were very helpful, actually. Except for that waiter… the one who brought me the mussels. Speaker_1: What about the mussels? Were they bad? Speaker_3: Not bad, darling, just… small. And they didn't serve them with enough chips! It's just not the same with a handful of frites. And the service was so slow! I was practically waving my arms to get his attention. Your father was asleep by the time they arrived. Speaker_2: I was resting my eyes! It had been a stressful drive, thanks to the aforementioned technological marvel. I found a new route along the coast, it’s supposed to be beautiful. Speaker_3: Oh, I'd love that, darling. As long as Harold promises not to take the lead and get us lost. Speaker_2: I’m retiring from leading expeditions. Permanently. Speaking of which, I finally got a new mobile phone. One of those fancy smartphones. Speaker_1: Oh, brilliant! Can you actually use it? Speaker_2: That… remains to be seen. It’s got more buttons than a spaceship. I accidentally video-called someone in Kazakhstan earlier. Speaker_1: (Bursting out laughing) You *what*?! Oh, Dad! You are unbelievable.

Speaker_1: Right, onions are softening nicely. Honestly, I think this ragu is going to be *good*. Maybe even worthy of a second helping. Which, let’s be realistic, happens rarely with my cooking. Now, about that wine… Speaker_1: Perfect. Speaker_2: Although...you do sound a bit like my Auntie Morag when you're talking about smells. Speaker_1: Honestly, this pierogi is… unexpected. I mean, good unexpected, but not what I anticipated in a vegan restaurant. It’s… beetroot and horseradish? Honestly, sometimes I just want to sit in silence. Speaker_2: That sounds blissful. I’ve been trying to get into meditation, but I just end up thinking about my to-do list. Speaker_2: True. Perspective. Although I bet she had her own anxieties. Maybe about knitting patterns or the price of butter.

Speaker_1: Right, so swimming is definitely on for Saturday morning, agreed? Unless someone has a sudden aversion to chlorine. Speaker_2: (Excitedly) Can I take Finley? Speaker_1: Right, so then she was saying, like, he just… doesn’t anymore. And she’s proper stressed, yeah? Like, really upset about it. Speaker_2: Oh, no. That sounds awful. How old are they both? Speaker_1: Early thirties, I think. Him maybe a bit older. She’s been with him for, like, eight years, so you’d think… you know? It's just, she's worried it's something *she’s* doing, but her mate was saying it’s probably just… you know. Speaker_2: Erectile dysfunction? Is that what she thinks? Speaker_1: She didn’t say the words exactly, but that’s definitely what she meant. She was all roundabout, like "it just doesn’t happen how it used to" and “he seems… distant”. She said his work’s been quiet lately. Speaker_2: Ugh. It's a tricky one. They really should talk to a doctor about it, shouldn't they? There's stuff they can do. All those adverts on telly… Speaker_1: She said she tried to suggest it, but he just brushes it off. Says he's “just tired”. Men, honestly. Always pretending everything’s fine when it clearly isn’t. It’s like, just *go* and get it checked out! Speaker_2: It's a pride thing, I reckon. A lot of them are embarrassed to even talk about it. Which makes it worse, obviously. It’s not like breaking a leg, it feels… personal, I suppose. Speaker_1: Yeah, that makes sense. But it's affecting their relationship! She was saying they've barely been intimate for months. It’s causing a proper rift between them. Speaker_2: Months? That’s a long time. It’s understandable she’s upset. I mean, sex is a big part of a relationship, isn't it? Speaker_1: She thinks so. She was saying she feels rejected and unloved. It’s just… sad, innit? You want your friends to be happy. Speaker_2: It is. And it’s really hard to offer advice when you don't know all the details. It's like, you don’t want to say the wrong thing and make it worse. Speaker_1: Precisely. I just kept nodding and saying things like “That sounds really tough” and “I hope it gets better”. Speaker_2: That’s probably the best you can do, really. Just listen. Sometimes that’s all people need. Though honestly, I’d be pushing him towards a doctor if I was her. A good, honest conversation and a medical check-up… that’s the way forward. Speaker_1: Maybe. I just feel a bit out of my depth with stuff like this. It’s all a bit much. Speaker_2: I get it. It's not exactly light conversation, is it? Still, good on her for talking to someone about it. It must have taken a lot of courage. Speaker_1: It did. She's a good lass. Hopefully, they can sort it out.

Speaker_1: Right, so I was thinking, for tonight, we could do the chilli with the rice, but I'm really trying to keep the Healthy Extra B choice down, you know? And rice doesn’t *quite* cut it. Speaker_2: Mint chocolate chip? Okay, that *is* a bit decadent. But you deserve it! I’ve been eyeing up some of those flavored syrups for ages. Are they actually any good or do they taste artificial? Speaker_1: I haven’t tried it yet, but it smells amazing. It's one of those Skinny Syrups ones. Apparently, they’re surprisingly good. Speaking of treats, are we still on for treat day on Saturday? I'm thinking maybe a small portion of cauliflower cheese with the roast. Speaker_2: Oh, yes! Cauliflower cheese is non-negotiable. Treat day is essential for sanity. I'm currently trying to decide if a small biscuit is worth 5 syns. It's a *really* difficult decision. Siri just told me the calendar says I have a dentist appointment next Tuesday, which I completely forgot about. Speaker_1: Siri is so unhelpful sometimes. Honestly, "remind me to book a dentist appointment" clearly isn't enough for her. I’ve just been looking at veg box deliveries, to try and save a bit of money and get more veg in. They seem a bit pricey though, even if it's all seasonal stuff. Speaker_2: Yeah, they can be. I was looking into those too. And have you started thinking about tax returns for the freelance work? I’m dreading it. So much paperwork. It’s the worst part of being self-employed. Speaker_1: Oh god, don’t even mention it. I’m putting it off as long as humanly possible. It feels like a mountain. I’ve been trying to hit my steps target at work, though. Pharmacy is surprisingly good for that, constantly walking backwards and forwards. Speaker_2: Really? I thought you’d be mostly standing. I'm trying to get back into running but I keep making excuses. Honestly, this weather doesn’t help. I think I need a new playlist. Oh and the Quorn

Speaker_1: Honestly, I’m starting to think Italy’s a disaster waiting to happen. Just…the logistics of getting around, the crowds… Speaker_2: Disaster is a strong word, love. A little cottage, the sea air, cream teas… Speaker_2: Cornwall? That’s…surprisingly sensible. I was bracing myself for Iceland. Though I did always fancy seeing the Northern Lights… Still, Cornwall sounds…nice. We could finally get around to visiting that pottery place you’ve been talking about for years. Speaker_1: Oh, the one near St Ives? Yes! And we could walk the coastal path. And maybe…just maybe…I could finally finish that short story I started about the lighthouse keeper's daughter. Speaker_2: The one with the mysterious ship? Still going with that? Speaker_1: It’s evolving. Now it involves a smuggled parrot and a surprisingly complex blackmail plot. I’m thinking of entering it into that local writing competition. Speaker_2: Go for it! You’ve got a real knack for that sort of thing. Though, perhaps tone down the parrot. It sounds a bit…fluffy. Speaker_1: It’s symbolic! The parrot represents…freedom! And a bit of squawking chaos, admittedly. Speaking of chaos, have you been following this latest political debacle? Honestly, they’re all at it. Speaker_2: Briefly. I try to avoid the news. Gives me a headache. It's all just shouting and pointing fingers. Speaker_1: Exactly! And then they wonder why no one trusts politicians anymore. It’s a self-fulfilling prophecy. It's making me rethink everything. Maybe I should just give up being a PA and become a full-time novelist and live in that Cornish cottage writing about parrots. Speaker_2: (Chuckles) Now *there's* a career change. Though, who would manage me then? I’d need a PA. Speaker_1: Good point. It's a vicious circle. Oh, and something else I’ve been thinking about. Speaker_2: Oh dear. Here we go. Speaker_1: Remember Sarah from book club? She’s just got a new tattoo…a full sleeve, apparently. And it actually looks really good. Speaker_2: Sarah? Really? She always struck me as more of a floral-print cardigan type. Speaker_1: Exactly! But it’s changed her. She seems…bolder. I’ve been secretly browsing tattoo designs online. Just looking, mind. Speaker_2: Oh no. Don’t you dare. You'll be wanting a dragon winding around your arm next. Speaker_1: Don’t be ridiculous. It would be something small. Maybe a little forget-me-not, behind my ear? Speaker_2: A forget-me-not? Very symbolic. Or maybe you're just forgetting what it feels like to have un-inked skin? Just promise me no parrots. Speaker_1: (Laughing) No parrots. I promise. Now, back to Cornwall… and potentially, my rebellion against the political establishment via feathered smuggling.

Speaker_1: Right, so, the 18th is definitely free then? For your mother’s birthday lunch? Speaker_2: Aye, completely. Cleared it with the boss months ago, truth be told. She knows how much family means to me. Though she did give me a look when I said it was for a lunch, not a full-blown party. Speaker_1: (Chuckles) Well, your mother isn't one for fuss, is she? Is that where they make pasta? Speaker_1: Amongst other things, yes. They also have very steep hills. Look at that view though, Dad's right, it's beautiful. Still, I reckon you could fly over all that quicker, you know, like Bear Grylls. Speaker_4: Bear Grylls isn’t known for his punctuality, is he? More for eating bugs and surviving in the wilderness. And speaking of surviving, how’s the Law conversion course going, Sarah? Are you still thinking it was a good idea after the EU referendum fallout? It’s all got so much more complicated. You'd think after all those science lessons… Speaker_3: Why do we have miles *and* kilometers? It’s so confusing! Speaker_4: It's a legacy of empires, basically. Different systems. Honestly, you’d think we’d have unified everything by now. It’s like the whole debate about metric versus imperial. It's ridiculous. Speaker_1: You know what else is ridiculous? The price of petrol these days! Seriously, it's highway robbery. And then the parking… trying to find a space in Bolton is a nightmare even *without* all the extra Christmas shoppers. Speaker_2: Don’t get me started on shopping. I had a lady in labour the other day who was convinced the supermarket was conspiring against her by hiding the chamomile tea. Said it was a sign from God. Speaker_4: (Raises an eyebrow) A sign from God? That's a new one. Has to be said, religion’s become a bit… intense lately, hasn’t it? Speaker_3: Miss, can we listen to some music? I’m bored. Speaker_1: Good shout. Terry Wogan, anyone? Bit of nostalgia? Speaker_2: Oh, lovely! Terry Wogan always cheered me up after a long shift. A proper gentleman. Speaker_4: Actually, before we commit to Wogan, anyone seen the new Mercedes C-Class? Thinking about trading in the old Volvo…It just feels… well, feels a bit like something out of Shakespeare, doesn’t it? All pondering and indecision. Plus I saw a programme about nudists the other day. Quite enlightening, actually.

Speaker_1: Honestly, this lentil shepherd’s pie is hitting the spot. I was *craving* something proper comforting. Speaker_2: It is good! Though, honestly, I still think you put too much rosemary in everything. It overpowers everything else. Speaker_1: (Scoffs) Never! Rosemary is a gift from the gods. It elevates everything. Besides, you ate, like, three helpings. Speaker_3: I’m with El on the rosemary front. It’s… assertive. But good pie, genuinely. Really filling after a twelve-hour shift. Speaker_1: Fair enough. Anyone else thinking about that documentary we watched last night? About the cultured meat? “Shmeat”, as they called it. Speaker_2: Ugh, don’t even. I’m still processing. It’s… unsettling. Like, meat without the animal, which is the whole point, but… it feels *wrong*, somehow. Speaker_3: I thought it was pretty fascinating. And logically, it makes a lot of sense. Way less environmental impact, no animal cruelty... It solves a lot of problems. Speaker_1: Exactly! I mean, I'm vegetarian, obviously, but even if I wasn’t, I’d seriously consider it. All this talk about animal welfare… it’s just horrific. Seeing the conditions in most abattoirs… Speaker_2: Yeah, but is it really *that* different? You’re still essentially… growing meat. It’s not like suddenly everyone's going to stop wanting burgers. It’s still satisfying that same primal urge, just in a lab. Doesn’t feel like progress if we’re just replacing one form of exploitation with another. Speaker_3: That's a good point, actually. It kind of sidesteps the issue of why we eat meat in the first place. It doesn’t challenge the idea that animals are just resources for us. Speaker_1: True. But think about the hunting argument. People romanticise hunting, say it’s “natural”, but a quick, clean kill in the wild is probably less suffering than most factory farming. And this is… even cleaner. No suffering at all. Speaker_2: Hunting is still terrible though! Taking a life for sport? It's just…oppressive. And it’s often not quick or clean, let’s be real. My uncle used to hunt, and the stories he told… Speaker_3: (Changing the subject) Speaking of unpleasant things, anyone seen the new series of *Curb Your Enthusiasm*? It's absolute gold. Larry David is a horrific human being but I can’t stop watching. Speaker_1: Oh my god, yes! The one with the coffee shop and the muffin top? I was cringing so hard. Speaker_2: He *always* manages to make the most mundane situations into epic conflicts. It's a masterclass in awkwardness. It’s almost soothing, knowing someone else is causing that much chaos. Speaker_1: It really is. It makes my day-to-day seem remarkably… normal. Plus, it makes me feel less guilty about being slightly judgemental. Speaker_3: Speaking of normal, have either of you been taking your vitamin D tablets? It’s been weeks since we’ve seen the sun. I feel like I’m turning into a cave dweller. Speaker_2: Oh god, you’re right! They’re in the kitchen, somewhere. I keep meaning to. Winter just drains all motivation. Speaker_1: Same. I'm practically hibernating. Although, I did read an article about getting enough iron if you're vegetarian, so I might start on those too. All this ethical eating requires supplementation, apparently!

Speaker_1: Right, that was a proper rubbish ending, wasn't it? Honestly, all that build-up for *that*? Speaker_2: Tell me about it. I knew something was gonna happen with the dog, didn’t I? Speaker_2: Playstation? You're already thinking about Christmas presents in October? It's a bit early, isn't it? Speaker_1: Never too early! Especially when it’s a good deal. Anyway, I’ve been meaning to ask, Daniel, have you applied for any jobs yet? Proper ones, not just…you know. Speaker_2: (Sighs) A few. Got another rejection email yesterday. "Highly competitive applicant pool." Translation: someone with a bit more experience. It's brutal out there, init? Speaker_3: You've got a good degree though! A First! They can’t just ignore that. Speaker_2: Apparently, they can. Keeps saying I lack “relevant experience”. What relevant experience am I supposed to have at 23, living in Whitehaven? Been to Uni, worked at the chippy, that’s about it. Speaker_1: You could put down your…er… extreme Minecraft skills? Speaker_2: (Sarcastically) Oh aye, that'll impress 'em. “Proficient in block building and virtual resource management.” I can see it now. Speaker_3: Honestly, you're underselling yourself. You're smart, you're capable… it’s just finding something. Speaker_1: Maybe you need to broaden the search? Like, look further afield? Speaker_2: Further afield? Where? London? I'd need to win the lottery to afford a shoebox apartment there. Speaker_3: I was thinking maybe Newcastle, or even Manchester. Not *that* far, and more opportunities. Speaker_1: Manchester's alright. Went to a gig there last year, decent night. Though getting the train back was a nightmare. Remember that? Stuck at Preston for three hours. Speaker_2: Don't remind me. That was a disaster. I thought we were gonna be sleeping on the platform. Speaker_3: Still, could be worse. Mum sent a picture of Dad attempting to put up the Christmas lights already. The whole garden looks like a tangled mess of fairy lights and extension cables. Speaker_1: Oh, lord. That sounds like a health and safety hazard waiting to happen. Speaker_2: He's been talking about getting one of those… smart thermostats. Says it’ll save a fortune on the heating bill. Speaker_3: He won’t even be able to work the remote for the TV, never mind a smart thermostat! He’ll end up freezing the house solid or setting it on fire.

Speaker_1: Honestly, this free buffet is a lifesaver. After that panel on legal tech, my brain was properly fried. Did you manage to catch any of it? Speaker_2: A little bit. I drifted in and out, mostly during the bit about blockchain. It all felt… a bit much, if I’m honest. More interesting to see who everyone ended up becoming, though, right? Did you spot Amelia Finch?
