Remember old Mr. Henderson saying “Think of the salary!”? Perhaps he had a point. Though, personally, I’m much happier with the research side of things. Still using my brain, but in a less… cutthroat way. Speaker_1: Exactly! I feel the same. Though, I won’t lie, sometimes I fantasize about winning the lottery and just travelling the world. Speaking of which, how was your trip to Italy last month? You were raving about Tuscany before you went. Speaker_2: Oh, Tuscany was incredible. Truly. The food, the wine, the countryside… it was just perfect. We stayed in this tiny little agriturismo, ran by a family for generations. I’m trying to convince Ben we need to go back next year. He’s more of a ‘beach holiday’ kind of guy, though. Speaker_1: Ah, the classic holiday debate. I'm firmly team ‘culture and history’. I’m thinking Portugal next. I’ve been reading about Lisbon, and it sounds amazing. Plus, it’s relatively cheap, which is always a bonus. My aunt went a couple of years ago and said it was transformative. Speaker_2: Portugal’s on my list! My cousin lives near Porto, so I keep meaning to visit. Family gatherings are… an experience, though. My grandma still asks me every single time when I'm going to "settle down and find a nice doctor". Speaker_1: (winces) Oh, the pressure! Mine's a bit different. Whenever I mention my job, my Uncle Barry inevitably launches into a monologue about how I should have gone into teaching like his wife. “So stable,” he says. “So rewarding.” Speaker_2: (laughs) Sounds familiar. They just don't *get* it, do they? They think anything academic is just… procrastinating with books. Speaker_1: Precisely! Though, I do miss the student life sometimes. Just the freedom to… not have any responsibilities. Now it’s spreadsheets and ethical approvals all the way. Speaker_2: Don’t remind me! Although, honestly, I wouldn’t trade my job. I love the research, and the team are brilliant. And it’s definitely a step up from the endless essay crises of undergrad. Speaker_1: True. Still, sometimes a girl can dream of sun-drenched beaches and not having to worry about data protection regulations. Right, I’m going to grab another mini quiche. Fuel for more networking, I suppose. Speaker_2: Good idea. I'll join you. And then we *must* try to find Amelia Finch. I want to hear all about Geneva. Speaker_1: Deal. Maybe she'll offer us a job! (laughs) Speaker_2: (laughing) Now *that* would be a holiday from reality.

Speaker_1: Right, honestly, that lecture this mornin’…absolute state it was. Dr. Ainsworth just droned on and on about…well, I don’t even *know* what he was on about, to be fair. Just endless dates and names. Speaker_2: (Chuckles) Sounds about right for Ainsworth, does it? He's a lovely bloke, but captivating, he is not. What was it on again? The Tudors? Speaker_1: Aye, the Tudors. But it wasn’t about the juicy bits, like Henry VIII and all his wives. It was about…parliamentary acts. Parliamentary *acts*, Liam! I’m tryin' to get a degree in English Literature, not become a politician. Speaker_2: Harsh. Did you take notes at least? You're a champion note-taker, you are. Speaker_1: I *tried*. But he speaks so monotone, I kept losin’ my place. Ended up drawin' little doodles of corgis instead. Honestly, I reckon I know more about the royal canine family than I do about sixteenth-century law right now. Speaker_2: (Laughing) Oh, brilliant. You'll be an expert on corgis by Christmas, then. Seriously though, is it all the lectures that are gettin' you down, or just Ainsworth? Speaker_1: It's...buildin' up, innit? Like, the seminar yesterday was good, but then I had that awful one. And I’ve got two more tomorrow. I’m startin’ to feel like all I do is sit in stuffy rooms listenin’ to people talk *at* me. Speaker_2: You need a break, love. You’ve been workin’ so hard since term started. Speaker_1: I know, I know. But there's so much to do! Essays, readings… it's relentless. Speaker_2: Look, I was thinkin'...remember how you were sayin’ your shoulders have been a bit achy? Speaker_1: Yeah, a bit. From all the bendin’ over books, I reckon. Speaker_2: Well, I saw a flyer for that new place in Headingley, "Zen Den" or somethin'. They do proper massages. Like, proper deep tissue stuff. Speaker_1: Oh, really? That actually sounds…amazing. I could really use one of those. Speaker_2: I thought so. I was thinkin’ maybe we could go on Saturday? After you’ve finished that essay on Brontë sisters? Reward for finally tackling that monster. Speaker_1: (Smiling) You’re readin' my mind. Oh, that sounds absolutely perfect. A proper relaxing afternoon. That's just what I need. Speaker_2: Sorted then. It'll do you good. And listen, if Ainsworth’s drone is gettin’ *too* much, skip a lecture. Seriously. Your mental health is more important than knowin’ the intricacies of the Statute of Uses, or whatever it was he was rabbitin’ on about. Speaker_1: You always know what to say, don’t you? Thanks, Liam. You’re the best. Speaker_2: Just lookin’ out for my favourite corgi enthusiast. Now, tell me more about these doodles…were they wearin’ little crowns? Speaker_1: (Laughing) Absolutely. And tiny velvet jackets! Speaker_2: Perfect. Speaker_1: Good, and maybe we could grab a chippy tea after the massage? I really need some proper grub. Speaker_2: Now *that* sounds like a plan.

Speaker_1: (Chewing thoughtfully) Right good roast, this. Honestly, Mary, you’ve outdone yourself. Yorkshire puddings are almost… perfect. Almost. Speaker_2: (Smiling) Oh, Dad, you always say that. I aim for ‘almost perfect’. Keeps me striving. And you’re just being polite, you always say the roast is good. Speaker_3: It *is* good, Arthur. Don't be so cynical, love. It's lovely to have a proper family lunch like this, isn’t it? So rare these days. Speaker_1: Rare indeed. Everyone rushing about. Speaking of rushing, has young Thomas sorted out that holiday with his girlfriend? He mentioned something about Spain? Speaker_2: I think so. He was on the phone last night arranging it. Something about cheap flights to Malaga. He’s very keen on finding a bargain, that one. Speaker_3: Good for him. He deserves a break. Teaching is exhausting. Though, honestly, I'm starting to wonder if *I* deserve a break. The workload is just… relentless. Speaker_1: You’ve been saying that for ten years, Brenda. You enjoy it, deep down. Don't pretend you don't. Remember Mrs. Higgins? She retired and lasted a week before she started volunteering at the library. Drove her husband mad. Speaker_2: (Chuckles) That’s true. Mum does thrive on being busy. Still, it’s good she’s considering slowing down a bit. Though, what *would* she do with herself? Speaker_3: Honestly? I think she’d garden. She talks about it constantly. A proper vegetable garden, she says, to ‘be self-sufficient’. Speaker_1: Self-sufficient? At our age? Honestly. Though I suppose it beats watching the news. Did you see what’s happening in Calais again? Dreadful. More boats. Speaker_2: It’s awful, isn’t it? I read something online about the conditions they’re living in. It’s just… heartbreaking. Makes you feel so helpless. Speaker_3: It does. And the politicians just bicker. No one’s actually *doing* anything constructive. It’s all posturing. Speaker_1: That's politics for you. Always has been. Always will be. Now, about future plans… I've been thinking. We should look into that cruise we talked about. The Mediterranean one. Speaker_2: The one in October? Oh, that sounds lovely, Dad. But isn’t that awfully close to Thomas's wedding? We should probably wait and see when they're finally setting a date. Speaker_3: She’s right, Arthur. We don’t want to miss that for a cruise. Though, a bit of sun would be nice. It’s been a damp summer. Speaker_1: Fair point. Fair point. Maybe next year then. Although, next year… well, who knows what next year will bring? We need to be proactive. Speaking of proactive, Mary, more gravy? This is all disappearing rather quickly. Speaker_2: Coming right up, Dad. You’re a bottomless pit. Speaker_3: You two and food! It’s a wonder you both still fit into your clothes. Speaker_1: (Grinning) A gentleman never discusses his weight, Brenda. Speaker_3: (Rolling her eyes affectionately) Oh, Arthur. You haven’t been a gentleman in years. Speaker_2: (Passing the gravy boat) Here you go, Dad. And Mum, more potatoes? Speaker_3: Yes please dear!

Speaker_1: Right, another Monday. Honestly, I’m fuelled entirely by caffeine at this point. How was your weekend, Gareth? Anything exciting happen beyond marking essays? Speaker_2: (Chuckles, stirring his coffee) Exciting? Not exactly. Utterly consumed by domestic chaos, more like. We finally started the bathroom renovation. Good Lord. Speaker_1: Oh dear. Renovations. A Pandora’s Box of stress, aren’t they? I remember when we did the kitchen… it was a nightmare. Dust *everywhere*. Speaker_2: Dust is the least of it, Idris. The plumber turned up two hours late, looking like he’d slept in his van. And then he tried to convince me we needed to move the entire soil stack! Speaker_1: Move the *soil stack*? Good heavens. What did you say? Speaker_2: I nearly choked on my tea, I can tell you. Apparently, it wasn’t ‘up to code’. Which, as far as I could gather, meant he hadn’t bothered to read the plans properly. I had to get his supervisor involved. Honestly, finding reliable tradespeople is like searching for unicorns these days. Speaker_1: Tell me about it. We’re thinking of redoing the downstairs loo, just a cosmetic job really, new tiles, that sort of thing. But already the thought fills me with dread. Do you know a decent tiler? Speaker_2: Actually, yes. Old Dai Evans. He did a fantastic job for Bronwen Lloyd – you remember Bronwen, History department? – completely transformed her hallway. Bit of a character, mind you. Always talking about rugby. Speaker_1: Bronwen, yes, of course! Good egg, Bronwen. Rugby… that’s a small price to pay for a well-tiled floor. I’ll have to get her number from someone and ask about Dai. Speaker_2: He’s worth a call. Though, be warned, he only works on Tuesdays and Thursdays. Says it’s lucky days for grouting. Speaker_1: (Laughing) Only on Tuesdays and Thursdays? That’s… dedicated. Or possibly eccentric. Either way, I'll bear it in mind. This bathroom of yours – are you gutting the whole thing? Speaker_2: Pretty much. New suite, new flooring, the whole shebang. My wife, Carys, has been pinning ideas on Pinterest for months. I swear she’s single-handedly keeping the bathroom tile industry afloat. It’s going to look lovely, eventually. Though I suspect our savings account will be weeping. Speaker_1: Pinterest is a dangerous place. My daughter got us into it. Suddenly, our living room needed a ‘feature wall’ and ‘mood lighting’. It’s a slippery slope, I tell you. Speaker_2: Exactly! And then there’s the kitchen. We’re thinking of doing that next year. Completely new kitchen. Carys wants a proper Aga. Speaker_1: An Aga? Crikey. That’s a commitment. They’re beautiful, of course, but… they roar, don’t they? And heat up the whole house. Speaker_2: That’s what I’m saying! I’ve tried to point this out, subtly, of course. But she’s adamant. “A farmhouse kitchen is what we need, Gareth,” she says. “A farmhouse kitchen!” We live in a semi-detached in suburbia, Idris! Speaker_1: (Smiling) You have my sympathy, my friend. Wives – a wonderful, perplexing species. Speaking of perplexing species, did you hear about Professor Armitage? Apparently, he’s taken up competitive ferret legging. Speaker_2: (Spitting out a little coffee) *Ferrets?* Legging? You’re joking! Speaker_1: I assure you, I am not. Apparently, he’s quite serious about it. He was telling me all about the specialist trousers he’s had made. The world is a strange place, Gareth. A very strange place.

Speaker_1: Right, so who wants more curry? This is a good one, isn’t it? A proper vindaloo. Speaker_2: Yeah, it’s good! Not *too* spicy, though. Speaker_3: It’s lovely, actually. A bit much with the rice, though, I think. My stomach’s already rumbling. Speaker_1: Ah, you’re a delicate flower, so you are. Now, Liam, you’re polishing off your plate, good man. Don’t be shy about asking for more. You’re growing like a weed. Speaker_2: Dad, you always say that! Speaker_1: Well, it’s true! Feels like only yesterday you were trying to eat… what was it? A key? Speaker_3: (Laughing) Oh, don’t remind me! He was convinced he could eat metal and gain superpowers. He actually swallowed a small screw! Speaker_2: It wasn’t a *small* screw! It was a fairly big one. And I didn’t swallow it! I got it stuck on the roof of my mouth and panicked. Speaker_1: Panicked is putting it mildly. You were screaming the place down. I thought you were choking! We had to drag you to the doctor. Speaker_3: And they said it would pass. Just…pass. Can you imagine? Speaker_4: (Babbling excitedly, pointing at his mouth) Baa! Me eat! Speaker_1: (Chuckles) No, little man, *you* are not eating metal. You stick to the puree. Speaking of which, is Leo behaving himself tonight? Speaker_3: He’s finally asleep. Took ages. He’s been obsessed with night deposit boxes all week. Apparently, they're "secret treasure holes". Speaker_2: A night deposit box? Where did he even hear about those? Speaker_3: Honestly, no idea. Probably some YouTube video. He saw me using one the other day and went wild. He kept trying to put his toy cars in the slot. Speaker_1: Kids are peculiar, aren’t they? Right. Liam, your birthday is coming up fast. Any thoughts on what you’d like to do? Speaker_2: I’m thinking maybe that big park event in Fitzgerald’s Park? The one with the bouncy castles and the face painting? Speaker_1: That sounds good. We can invite a few of your friends. And what about afterwards? A few slices of cake? Speaker_2: Yeah, that'd be great! Speaker_3: Maybe we could get that horrible history science book you were looking at? The one about, what was it, Victorian surgery? Speaker_2: Ugh, Mum! That sounds… gross. But yeah, actually, I kind of want it. It's funny. Speaker_1: Strange lad, you are. Alright, a park event and a gruesome history book it is. Now, speaking of gruesome… I was reading an article about the human body the other day and the sheer complexity of it. Biology is incredible isn’t it? Think of everything that has to happen just for us to, you know, *be*. Speaker_3: It is. Makes you think, doesn’t it? Like, what actually causes pain? The nerve signals…and how the brain interprets them. It's… unsettling. Speaker_1: Unsettling but fascinating. And don’t get me started on the liver! The things that organ does… It’s a miracle we’re all still functioning. Right, who’s for another glass of wine? I think I need one after that conversation. Speaker_2: Maybe just a small one, Dad. Speaker_3: I'll join you. A small one is a good idea. Leo will be up again soon, guaranteed.

Speaker_1: So, Elsie, how's the little’un doing with school? Still enjoying it, are she? Speaker_2: Oh, she’s a good girl, Amy is. Bit quiet, mind you. But she’s doing well enough. Just started a new project on… well, what *was* it, now? Something about volcanoes, I think. Speaker_3: Volcanoes, eh? That sounds exciting. We’re doing the Stone Age at the moment with my Year 5s. Always a hit, that. Lots of cave painting and pretending to hunt mammoths. Speaker_4: (Rolling her eyes) Ugh, the Stone Age is *so* boring. We just did that last year in Year 4. It's all just rocks and furs. Speaker_1: Now, now, young lady. Don't be disrespectful. History's important. Especially learning about where you come from. You wouldn’t want to live in a cave, would ya? Speaker_4: No! Definitely not. But it's just… repetitive, you know? Speaker_2: She’s right, Arthur. It does get a bit repetitive. Though I suppose it’s good they’re learning something. Bit different to when *I* was at school, wasn’t it? More about sums and sewing, if you ask me. Speaker_3: It's always a balancing act, isn't it? Trying to cover everything. Speaking of which, did Amy ever go back to those horse-riding lessons she was doing? She seemed to really enjoy that. Speaker_2: Oh, she did! She absolutely loved it. But it got a bit expensive, to be honest. And then the weather turned, and… well, you know Norfolk winters. It’s a bit bleak for riding. Speaker_1: Aye, bleak it is. I remember when I was a lad, winter meant staying indoors and playing dominoes. No fancy horse riding for us! Though I always fancied a good gallop, I did. Never had the money for it though. Speaker_4: My friend Chloe goes horse riding every week. She got a new pony for her birthday. It's called Sparkle. Speaker_3: Sparkle! That’s a good name. I bet that’s a treat. Do you ever go with her? Speaker_4: Nah, it’s kinda girly. And I'm not really into ponies. Speaker_2: Oh, Amy would have loved a pony! She was always talking about them. We even visited a farm a few times to just… look at them. Speaker_1: Remember that place near Attleborough, Elsie? The one with all the animals? Used to take the kids there years ago. Had a lovely little tea room, too. Speaker_2: Oh, yes! Farmer Giles’ place! We went there with the grandchildren. Lovely memories. It's all gone now, unfortunately. Turned into another housing estate. Speaker_3: That's the way of things, isn't it? Everything’s getting built on. Makes you wonder where it’ll all end. Speaker_4: There's a new amusement park being built near North Walsham. My mum says it's going to be huge. With a rollercoaster and everything. Speaker_1: A rollercoaster? Goodness me. Things have changed. When I was a lad, a rollercoaster was a bumpy ride on a horse cart! Speaker_2: Halloween is coming up soon. Are you two doing anything? Amy's already planning her costume, she wants to be a witch, naturally. Speaker_3: We usually hand out sweets. Bit of a tradition. I might put on a spooky playlist. Speaker_4: I'm going trick-or-treating with my friends. We’re going to try and get loads of chocolate!

Speaker_1: Honestly, this traffic is ridiculous. I thought we’d be there by now. It's just… stationary. Speaker_2: (Sighs) It always is, love. Steam Fair always brings it to a standstill. Everyone and their mother decides to come. Remember when we first came, what, twenty years ago? Wasn’t half this bad. Speaker_3: Twenty five, Dad. And it *was* bad then! My mate, Arthur, he’s been on the council list for years. He needs somewhere smaller, you know, now the kids have flown the nest. Speaker_3: It’s the council housing that’s the problem, isn’t it? There just isn't enough of it. They keep saying they’re building more, but it's never enough to meet the demand. And what about older people, like Arthur? Somewhere safe, with a little garden… It shouldn't be so hard to find. Speaker_1: It's awful, isn't it? I was reading about assisted living places, and they’re so expensive. Mum would never be able to afford that. Speaker_2: Assisted living… robbery, that is. Charging a fortune for a bit of help. And half the time, the staff are rushed off their feet. No time for a proper chat. Speaker_3: It’s true. I see it all the time at work. They try their best, the staff do, bless 'em. But they're so short-staffed. It’s heartbreaking. And then you get families complaining… but it's not the carers’ fault. Speaker_1: Speaking of heartbreaking… look at that space over there. Is that… disabled parking? Right at the front? Speaker_1: Honestly, I’ve been spending hours online looking at allotment layouts. It’s a rabbit hole, isn’t it? You’ll need to think about pest control too. Things like netting to keep the pigeons off, and maybe some companion planting to deter unwanted bugs. Marigolds are supposed to be good for that. Speaker_1: Pigeons are *the worst*. They’re like feathered bandits. I'll definitely look into that. Companion planting...right, more rabbit hole research. Do you have any recommendations for good gardening books, or websites? I feel a bit overwhelmed by all the information. Speaker_2: Oh, absolutely. The RHS website is brilliant – loads of advice. And there's a really good book called ‘The Vegetable Gardener’s Bible’ by Edward Smith. It's really comprehensive, but not too intimidating. Although, honestly, a lot of it comes down to just experimenting and seeing what works for you. Speaker_1: That’s true. You just have to get stuck in, don’t you? I’m a bit worried about the time commitment, though. I’m teaching full-time, and I don’t want the allotment to become another source of stress. Speaker_2: I get that. Don’t try and do too much in the first year. Start small, and build up gradually. It's meant to be relaxing, remember. Plus, you can always enlist help! I’m happy to lend a hand when I can. We could make a day of it, a proper allotment work party. Speaker_1: Oh, that would be amazing! Seriously, I'd love that. A work party sounds perfect. Maybe even

Speaker_1: Right, so I’m officially breaking up with the idea of trying to make friends with anyone on my course. It’s a lost cause, honestly. Speaker_2: Oh no, why? I thought you were getting on alright with Chloe? The one who always steals your pens. Speaker_1: Chloe’s a menace, a delightful menace, but… no. I feel like it’s been ages since you mentioned *anyone*. Speaker_2: Don’t even start. I had a disaster date last week. He spent the entire evening talking about his Warhammer collection. Speaker_1: (bursts out laughing) Oh, no way! Seriously? Speaker_2: Seriously! I tried to steer the conversation towards, like, world events or his favourite film, but he’d always loop it back to miniature figurines and dice rolls. It was… intense. Speaker_1: Oh, bless. That’s a *very* specific hobby. I’m officially thanking my lucky stars I’m single and can dedicate all my energy to avoiding bogs and protecting Yorkshire slang. Speaker_2: You should be. We need to make plans for this weekend, though. Absolutely essential. Just us, a Greggs sausage roll, and probably a good moan about uni. Speaker_1: You are speaking my language. Sausage roll secured. Moaning rights automatically granted. Let’s do it. Does this meet your requirements? Let me know if you'd like me to adjust or continue the conversation further. Speaker_1: Right, honestly, that last raid was a disaster. Absolute shambles. Liam, you just kept running into walls! Speaker_2: (Laughing) He was a bit… distracted, wasn’t he? Speaker_3: You’re a lifesaver, Chloe. Literally. I used like, half my supply just keeping everyone alive long enough for Liam to… commune with wildlife. And potentially humiliating. Mostly potentially humiliating. Speaker_1: It'll be legendary, to watch anyway. Right, back to Eldoria Online then? I wanna see if we can redeem ourselves. And maybe… gently steer Liam away from any further badgers. Do you want me to continue the conversation? Or perhaps change the scenario? Let me know! That was longer, and hopefully captured the dynamic a bit more. Let me know if you'd like any adjustments.

Speaker_1: Honestly, Doreen next door, you wouldn’t believe. She’s started one of her ‘detox’ diets again. All juice and…well, I didn’t quite catch what else, but it smelled of spirulina. The whole hallway did! Speaker_2: (Chuckles) Oh, Doreen. She’s a character, isn’t she? Still going on with those things then? I thought she gave up after the cabbage soup debacle of ‘21. Speaker_1: You’d think! But no. Apparently, this one’s “life-changing.” She was telling me it’s going to realign her chakras. I just nodded. Honestly, I just wanted her to stop talking about her insides. Speaker_2: (Smiling) Sounds…intense. I’m glad I just stick to trying to eat my greens. Did you hear back from Brenda about the cinema? We were thinking of seeing that new Wes Anderson film. Speaker_1: Oh, yes, Brenda messaged. She can’t make Friday. Said something about a bridge night commitment. Honestly, bridge! What is it with her and bridge? She’s obsessed. Speaker_2: Right? It feels like every time you suggest something, it’s “Oh, I’ve got bridge.” I swear she’s building a fortress of card tables in her living room. Speaker_1: Exactly! So, Friday’s no good. How about Saturday afternoon? It's supposed to be raining, anyway. Perfect cinema weather. Speaker_2: Saturday’s good for me. I’ve got that deadline looming at work, but I can sneak out for a few hours. Is it the one with Timothée Chalamet? Speaker_1: That’s the one! I’ve heard good things. Apparently, it’s very…pink. All the sets are pink. Speaker_2: Oh, brilliant. Wes Anderson being Wes Anderson. I love his films. They’re so meticulously crafted, aren’t they? Like little worlds. Speaker_1: They are. Reminds me of that one we saw, what was it… *The Grand Budapest Hotel*? That was a good one. Funny, and beautifully done. Speaker_2: Oh, loved that one! Ralph Fiennes was *amazing*. Have you seen anything good lately? Besides Doreen’s internal struggles, of course. Speaker_1: I finally got around to watching that documentary about Bowie, *Moonage Daydream*. Honestly, it was breathtaking. Just a wonderful tribute. I was a right Bowie fan back in the day, you know. Speaker_2: Oh, I’ve heard about that! I need to add it to my list. I’m currently slogging through a really bleak Scandinavian crime drama. It's good, but…it’s a lot. It requires serious concentration and a strong cup of tea. Speaker_1: Oh, dear. Sounds a bit grim. Sometimes you just need something lighthearted, don't you? Like a good old Cary Grant film. Speaker_2: Absolutely. Or something with Audrey Hepburn. Pure escapism. Right, I should probably get back to work. This deadline is breathing down my neck. But let’s firm up those cinema plans for Saturday? Speaker_1: Yes, let's do. We'll text Brenda to let her know we've gone without her…again! Speaker_2: (Laughing) Sounds like a plan! Speaker_1: Alright, off you pop then. And don't let the spreadsheets defeat you. Speaker_2: I’ll try my best! Bye! Speaker_1: Bye, love!

Speaker_1: …and then she just *launched* into a detailed explanation of the rules for ‘Wingspan’. Like, a twenty-minute rules explanation for a bird-collecting board game. It was intense. Speaker_2: (Laughing) Oh, bless her. She does love a good, complex board game, doesn’t she? Is she still going on about getting everyone to play ‘Gloomhaven’ next month? Speaker_1: You know it. She's already making a spreadsheet. Honestly, it’s like preparing for a military campaign. I said I might be busy, and she looked genuinely hurt. I think she's trying to fill the void since… well, you know. Speaker_2: Since Liam moved to Manchester? Yeah, poor thing. She's always been someone who needs a project, hasn't she? It's good she's got hobbies, at least. Did you manage to avoid actually *playing* Wingspan? Speaker_1: I pleaded a headache. A very convincing headache, I might add. I used the excuse that I had that awful interview this morning. Speaker_2: Oh, how did that go? The one for the research position at the university? Speaker_1: It was…fine. A lot of behavioural questions. "Tell me about a time you failed." "Describe a situation where you had to work in a team." You know the drill. It was a panel of three, and one of them looked like she hadn't smiled since 1987. Speaker_2: Oh, those are the worst! It's like they're actively looking for reasons to reject you. Speaking of things that are stressful, I finally booked us that spa day for next Saturday! Speaker_1: Oh my god, amazing! I need that so badly. I’ve been running on fumes lately. What did you book? Speaker_2: It’s at that place in Shoreditch, the one with the thermal suite. Massages, facials, the whole shebang. We can just lie there and moan about everything. Speaker_1: Perfect. I'm already mentally preparing my moan list. It's extensive. Did you see ‘The Undateables’ last night? Speaker_2: I did! Oh my gosh, the gentleman who collected garden gnomes! That was…something. Speaker_1: I know! Bless him. It’s just lovely to see people being so open and hopeful. Although, his expectations were… ambitious, considering. Speaker_2: A little. I was rooting for him, though. It reminded me I really need to catch up with Sarah. I haven’t seen her since Christmas. She’s been really busy with work. Speaker_1: Oh, how is she? Last I heard she was editing that cycling magazine? Speaker_2: Still is! Apparently, they're restructuring and she's worried she might lose her job. It’s a lot of pressure. She’s always been brilliant at what she does, though. Speaker_1: She is! I remember when she got her first article published. She was so thrilled. Has she started collecting DVDs again? Speaker_2: (Laughing) Oh, don’t even get me started. Her flat is basically a DVD fortress. She's got a whole room dedicated to them now. Apparently, she's trying to complete her collection of classic Hitchcock films. Speaker_1: That…is dedication. Right, I’m going to make a massive pot of tea. Fancy one? Maybe a biscuit, to plan our moan-list for the spa? Speaker_2: Yes, please! Definitely a biscuit. And extra tea. And maybe we should start brainstorming potential moan-topics now, just to get a head start?

Speaker_1: Right, I’m officially declaring war on this washing machine. It’s eating socks again. It's a black hole for single socks, I swear. Speaker_2: (Chuckles from the other room) Oh, not again. Is it the same one as last week, the blue striped one? Speaker_1: No, this is a black one. A perfectly good, perfectly reasonable black sock. Vanished. I've checked inside the drum, behind it, even inside other washing loads. Gone. It's a conspiracy. Speaker_2: Maybe it’s clinging to something else? Sometimes they get stuck inside duvet covers, that sort of thing. Speaker_1: I’ve turned the duvet cover inside out like a forensic investigator! Nothing. Honestly, I’m starting to suspect a tiny sock-gnome lives inside it. Speaker_2: (Walking into the kitchen, carrying two mugs of tea) A sock-gnome? Now *that* explains a lot. Here, drink your tea. You’re getting worked up over a sock. Speaker_1: It’s the principle of the thing! And it’s a perfectly good sock! Plus, I’m starving. Did you manage to grab anything from the shop earlier? I was up to my elbows in laundry detergent and existential dread. Speaker_2: Yeah, got some pasta and that pesto you like. I was thinking we could do a quick carbonara? Unless you fancy ordering something? Speaker_1: Carbonara sounds perfect. Though, quick is good. I need to at least *attempt* to make a dent in these research papers tonight. Dr. Evans is having a field day with my methodology. Speaker_2: Ouch. Still, you’re brilliant at what you do. He’s just being a… well, you know Dr. Evans. Pedantic. Speaker_1: That’s putting it mildly. He once spent twenty minutes critiquing my use of the Oxford comma. Twenty minutes! It's a comma, James! Speaker_2: (Laughing) Oh, God. Sounds about right. How are your mam and dad doing, by the way? I haven’t spoken to them in ages. Speaker_1: They’re good, actually. Mam’s taken up pottery. Apparently, the kitchen table is now permanently covered in clay. Dad's trying to learn the guitar, which, according to my sister, is torturing the neighbours. Speaker_2: (Smiling) Sounds like them. They’re good at finding new hobbies, your parents. What about your sister? How is little Leo? Speaker_1: They’re both fine. Leo is currently obsessed with dinosaurs. Apparently, he roars at the postman. Speaker_2: Oh, bless him. Sounds adorable. We should really try and get up to Sunderland soon. It's been too long. Speaker_1: Definitely. Although prepare for an extended pottery demonstration and a lot of enthusiastic, but probably off-key, guitar playing. Have you seen anything good lately? Any films? I need to switch my brain off later. Speaker_2: I saw that new Wes Anderson film. It was… very Wes Anderson. Lots of symmetry and muted colours. Visually stunning, but a bit… empty, if that makes sense? Speaker_1: Oh, I get that. Sometimes his style overwhelms the substance. I might just stick to something brainless, like a cheesy rom-com. Or maybe a documentary about sock-gnomes. You never know. Speaker_2: (Grinning) Good plan. And, just for the record, I’m officially on the sock-gnome investigation team. We will find your sock!

Speaker_1: Honestly, the price of houses these days… it’s beyond belief. We were looking at something in Penrith, just a little cottage, you’d think it was a palace with the asking price. Speaker_2: It’s the same down south, Mum. Absolutely bonkers. I was helping a friend look in Guildford, and everything's inflated. It's all London money flooding outwards. You’d get a decent semi here for what a garden shed costs them. Speaker_3: It’s the ‘premium’ isn’t it? Everything south of… well, Birmingham, really, carries a premium just *because* of where it is. Doesn’t matter if it's structurally unsound or built on a landfill. It’s the postcode. Speaker_1: Exactly! And all this talk about leveling up… absolute nonsense. They’re not leveling anything up, they’re just shifting the inequality around. It’s just… frustrating. We thought maybe a little bungalow near the lake, you know, for retirement. Now? Forget about it. Speaker_2: Did you see that article about the VW scandal again? It popped up on my newsfeed this morning. Something about further compensation claims? Speaker_3: Oh, that’s been rumbling on for years, hasn’t it? The sheer scale of it… deliberately cheating on emissions tests. Incredible. And they still get away with it, more or less. Speaker_1: It’s the arrogance of these big companies. Thinking they can just do whatever they want and get away with it. It’s the same with the housing developers. Building cheaply, squeezing every last penny out of everything. Speaker_2: I read somewhere that VW were actively trying to delay payouts as long as possible. It’s not necessarily the initial fine, it’s the long-term compensation to people who were misled. The impact on resale values etc. Speaker_3: It's a pattern, isn’t it? Accountability seems to be optional for large corporations. It's all lawyers and loopholes and kicking the can down the road. Makes you wonder what else they're getting away with. Speaking of getting away with things…have you seen what they’re charging for petrol now? Speaker_1: Don’t even start me on petrol! It’s daylight robbery. And then everyone complains about the price of avocados. Priorities, people, priorities! This whole country is becoming unaffordable. I remember when you could buy a perfectly lovely house in Penrith for under fifty thousand. Speaker_2: That sounds like a different lifetime. My parents told me stories about buying their first house in Birkenhead. They scrimped and saved for years, but it was *possible*. Now… a deposit alone is a fortune. Speaker_3: It's the intergenerational wealth gap, isn’t it? Those who benefitted from the post-war boom – affordable housing, secure jobs – are able to help their children, and those who didn’t… well, it’s a much harder climb. Speaker_1: It is. And it’s not like the wages have kept up. Even *with* two people working, it’s a struggle. I keep thinking, what are young people supposed to do? Speaker_2: It’s bleak, isn’t it? I’m lucky, I can work remotely, so the location has a bit less bearing on my job. But even then, the rent is crazy. Speaker_3: Perhaps we should all move to Scotland. I hear the house prices are more reasonable up there. And the scenery is stunning. Speaker_1: (Chuckles) Now there’s an idea. Perhaps we should all pool our resources and buy a small croft together. Speaker_2: I’m in, if you’re both serious. Imagine, escaping all this… mess. Speaker_3: It's a thought, certainly, a thought. Let’s at least look into it. Anything's better than accepting this as the new normal.

Speaker_1: Honestly, Doreen, you wouldn’t believe the fuss old Man Hemmings is kicking up now. About the bins again. Speaker_2: Not the bins! What's he on about *this* time? He’s a right misery, that one. Always has been. Speaker_3: Honestly, you two. Always moaning about someone. It's exhausting just listening to you. Speaker_1: It’s true though, isn't it? He went round Ms. Periwinkle, complaining that her recycling bin was overflowing. Overflowing! The poor woman's just got a bad hip, can’t get out there every week. Speaker_2: Serves her right for getting one of those fancy blue ones. Should've stuck with the grey. Less noticeable. Speaker_3: Frank, honestly! That's dreadful. She's entitled to a blue bin if she wants one. You’re encouraging him, you are. It's just upsetting people for the sake of it. Speaker_1: I’m just saying, it’s causing a right palaver. And it’s all because he's got nothing better to do since his pension started. Too much time on his hands, that’s what it is. Speaker_2: Speaking of pensions… mine’s landed, thankfully. Though it’s not nearly as much as they said it would be. Inflation, they say. Always inflation. Speaker_3: Mine's the same, Geoffrey. It’s a disgrace. Barely enough to cover the heating these days, never mind anything else. Speaker_1: They say we’re all supposed to be grateful we even *have* a pension. I heard young Tim down the pub telling his wife she’ll be lucky to get anything. Speaker_2: Tim’s just started that new job in IT, hasn’t he? All computers and clever stuff. I wouldn't trust a computer to tell me the time, let alone manage my pension. Speaker_3: You say that, Geoffrey, but you were asking me just last week how to set up that online banking. Speaker_2: That was… different. I just wanted to see if it *could* be done. Didn't mean I was going to start relying on it. It’s all a bit frightening, isn’t it? Everything online now. Speaker_1: It is. Reminds me of that holiday we took to Cornwall. Remember that little B&B we stayed in? The one run by that lovely couple? Speaker_2: Oh, yes! The one with the wonky stairs and the full English breakfast? Lovely place. Speaker_1: They were wishing they hadn’t started letting their place out to strangers after some builders moved in. Apparently, they were up all hours, playing loud music, and tracking mud everywhere. Speaker_3: See? People. Always something. That’s why I’m glad I’m retired from childminding. I couldn’t deal with anyone else’s… chaos. Though, sometimes I miss the little ones. Speaker_2: Still, you had your hands full with young Daniel and his obsession with digging up the garden, didn’t you? Speaker_3: Oh, don't remind me! That was a nightmare. Although, he did grow into a very polite young man. Speaking of gardens, I saw they’re building more of those new houses out by the old airfield. Speaker_1: They are. Absolute eyesore. Just concrete and new builds. Ruining the countryside, they are. And they’ll all be needing bins, won’t they? Perhaps that’s what's got Hemmings so worked up. Speaker_2: Probably. He'll be complaining about the traffic too, I expect. It's getting worse every year. Speaker_3: Honestly, you two. Why don’t you come and sit down? I’ll put the kettle on. A nice cup of tea will do you both good. And maybe we can talk about something other than complaining for five minutes.

Speaker_1: Honestly, this Biology essay is killing me. “Explain the evolutionary advantages of altruism.” Like, what even *is* altruism, beyond being a fancy word for being nice? Speaker_2: Dude, it’s basically doing stuff for others even if it doesn’t benefit you. Like, risking your life to save someone. Evolutionarily, it doesn’t make sense, right? Shouldn’t it be survival of the fittest, *me* first? Speaker_3: That’s what I thought! Mr. Davies was going on about kin selection. Apparently, you’re more likely to be altruistic towards family because they share your genes. So it’s still selfish, just…indirectly. Speaker_4: Ugh, Davies. He loves a good complicated explanation. He spent like twenty minutes last lesson explaining how peacock feathers evolved. Twenty minutes! Speaker_1: Seriously? It’s just… shiny feathers. Birds like shiny things. End of. Speaker_2: Nah, apparently it’s about demonstrating genetic fitness. Like, “Look how healthy I am, I can afford to grow these massive, impractical feathers!” It’s all about attracting a mate. Speaker_3: Sounds exhausting. All that posturing. Humans aren't much better, are they? All the flexing on Instagram. Speaker_4: Speaking of Instagram… did you guys see that video of old Mr. Henderson falling over in the fruit aisle? It’s gone viral. Speaker_1: No way! Mr. Henderson? The one who always yells at us for blocking the biscuit aisle? Speaker_2: Yeah! Someone filmed it and put it on TikTok with that sped-up music. It’s hilarious. He was trying to grab a pineapple and completely lost his balance. Speaker_3: Oh my god, send me the link. That’s amazing. Though, kinda feel bad for the guy… a little bit. Speaker_4: Don’t feel too bad. He’s earned it. He gave me grief for accidentally knocking over a display of avocados last week. Said I was a menace to society. Speaker_1: Menace to society! Over avocados? That’s ridiculous. It's always the older generation judging us. Speaker_2: It's like they think everything was better in their day. Honestly, they probably didn't even *have* avocados when they were our age. Speaker_3: You know what I hate though? When people start going on about how ‘woke’ everyone is now. Like, calling out sexism or racism is suddenly a bad thing? Speaker_4: Tell me about it. My aunt tried to explain to me why feminism isn’t “necessary” anymore. Said women have “equal rights”. Speaker_1: Oh, here we go. The classic ‘but women can vote now!’ argument. Speaker_2: It’s like they miss the point. It’s not just about legal rights, it’s about societal expectations and ingrained biases. And the wage gap, obviously. Speaker_3: And the fact that women are still disproportionately represented in positions of power. Like, look at Parliament... it's still mostly blokes. Speaker_4: It’s frustrating because when you *do* point these things out, you get labelled as ‘aggressive’ or ‘sensitive’. Speaker_1: Exactly! It’s a no-win situation. It's like if you're not outraged about injustice, you just don't care. But if you *are* outraged, you're a drama queen. Speaker_2: It's exhausting trying to navigate all that. Honestly, sometimes I just want to scroll TikTok and forget about the state of the world. Speaker_3: Mood. Anyone want another biscuit? This cake looks pretty good too.

Speaker_1: Honestly, the whole thing was a blur. Woke up in recovery, feeling… well, not exactly *right*. They said the operation went well, thankfully. No complications, they kept repeating. But it’s just… unsettling, isn’t it? Speaker_2: Unsettling is an understatement, love. Having anything poked and prodded inside you… I wouldn't wish it on my worst enemy. How’s the pain now? Are you keeping up with the tablets? Speaker_1: The pain's manageable, thankfully. Still a little tender, obviously. And yes, religiously taking the antibiotics and the painkillers. Though they make me feel a bit spaced out, if I'm honest. I nearly put salt in my tea this morning. Speaker_3: (Chuckles) Salt in your tea! Oh, you *are* feeling it then, eh? Remember when your grandad tried that? Said it brought out the flavour. Nearly gave your nan a heart attack. Speaker_4: He was a stubborn old fool, your grandad. Always had to have his own way. Still, a good man. Though I never understood the salt in the tea. Speaker_1: Times have changed, Grandad wouldn’t last five minutes these days. Anyway, the consultant said the infection markers are coming down, which is the main thing. He wants to see me again next week, just for a check-up. Speaker_2: Good, good. Regular check-ups are key. You need to look after yourself. You’re always rushing around, doing things for everyone else, you forget about number one. Speaker_1: Easier said than done, isn’t it? Especially with Mum needing so much help these days. Speaking of which, did you manage to sort out that appointment with the acupuncturist for her back? Speaker_2: I did, yeah. Tuesday afternoon. She’s a bit skeptical, bless her, but I told her to give it a go. Anything's worth a try, eh? It can’t hurt. Speaker_3: Acupuncture? Hmph. Poppycock. Give her a hot water bottle and a bit of liniment, that’s what she needs. That's what *we* used to do. Speaker_4: Your mother always was one for a good liniment rub. Remember how strong she used to make it? Nearly knocked you off your feet, Maggie. Speaker_1: I remember! It smelled like turpentine. Anyway, how are *you* two doing? Anything exciting happening in your world? Speaker_2: Not much excitement here, just work, work, work. Mrs. Henderson's house was a right state this week. Dust everywhere. Honestly, people live like pigs sometimes. Speaker_4: You don’t say. Still, honest work is honest work. Keeps you busy. I’ve been trying to get hold of young David. He promised to come round and help me with the car. Needs new tyres, and the MOT’s due next month. Speaker_3: David's always busy with that rugby. Constantly training, or playing, or travelling. He’s a good lad, though. A proper athlete. Speaker_1: He is. He’s really taking it seriously. He's talking about trying to get scouted by a professional team. Speaker_4: That'd be something. Remember when I used to play? Bit of local stuff, nothing fancy. Never had the knees for the big time. Though I was quite good on the ski slopes, back in the day. Speaker_1: Ah, the skiing holidays! Those were fun. Remember that time you ended up in a snowdrift, Dad? We were looking for you for hours. Speaker_2: And you, Maggie, nearly broke your arm. Always being a daredevil. Speaker_3: Oh, we had some laughs, didn’t we? Good times. Those were good times. Now, more coffee, anyone? I'll put the kettle on.

Speaker_1: Right, so we were talking about why learning about difficult things, like slavery, is important, even though it’s really upsetting. Do you two understand a little bit about what slavery was? Speaker_2: It was…when people weren’t free? And they had to work for other people? Speaker_1: That’s a good way to put it, sweetheart. They weren’t free, and they were forced to work for others, often in terrible conditions, without getting paid. It happened a long, long time ago, mostly, but it’s important to remember it so it *doesn’t* happen again. Speaker_3: But why did people *do* that? That’s mean! Speaker_1: It is very mean, isn’t it? It’s a really complex question, and there isn’t one simple answer. Some people thought they were better than others, which is completely wrong, of course. Others wanted to make money, and they didn’t care how much suffering they caused. Speaker_2: Like… bad guys in a story? Speaker_1: In a way, yes. But these were real people, doing real, awful things. And it wasn’t just a long time ago. Even more recently, people fought wars over whether slavery should be allowed. Speaker_3: Wars? Like with guns and bombs? Speaker_1: Yes, sometimes. Wars are also about different ideas and beliefs. America had a big war, called the Civil War, partly about whether people could own other people as slaves. It was a really brutal war, with lots of people getting hurt. Speaker_2: Did the good guys win? Speaker_1: Eventually, yes. Slavery was made illegal in America. But even after that, people still faced a lot of unfairness and discrimination. It takes a long time to fix things when something has been wrong for so long. Speaker_3: Discrimination? What's that? Speaker_1: That’s when people aren’t treated fairly because of who they are – their skin colour, where they come from, what they believe. It's still a problem today, sadly. That’s why it’s important to learn about history, so we understand how things got to be the way they are and how we can make them better. Speaker_2: So… learning about all these sad things can help people not be mean anymore? Speaker_1: Exactly! It can help us understand other people's feelings and learn to be kinder and more respectful. It also shows us how brave people have been in fighting for what's right, even when it was really difficult and dangerous. Speaker_3: Was it dangerous to try and stop slavery? Speaker_1: Very dangerous. People who tried to help slaves escape, or who spoke out against slavery, were often punished very harshly. They could be beaten, or even killed. Speaker_2: Wow. That’s scary. Speaker_1: It is. It’s a scary part of history. But remembering it helps us appreciate how far we’ve come, and how important it is to keep fighting for fairness and justice for everyone. Now, does anyone have any questions? It's okay if it's a tricky one. Speaker_3: So… did the people who were slaves get to go home? Speaker_1: That’s a really good question… It was… complicated. For many, home was taken away from them when they were captured. And even when slavery ended, rebuilding their lives was incredibly difficult. It’s a story full of sadness, but also of incredible strength and resilience. We can talk more about that later, if you like. Speaker_2: Can we read a book about it now?

Speaker_1: Honestly, I’m still reeling from that *Great British Bake Off* final. Poor Rahul! He looked like he was about to faint the whole time. Speaker_2: (Chuckles) He’s a lovely lad, Rahul. A bit… flustered, perhaps. But a very good baker. I thought Kim-Joy had it in the bag though. Her gingerbread scenes were phenomenal. Speaker_3: They *were* amazing! I saw pictures of them online. Did you see the article about Prue Leith’s new cookbook? Apparently, she’s put a recipe in for a Victorian sponge that uses mayonnaise. Speaker_4: Mayonnaise?! In a cake? Good Lord. That sounds… questionable. Speaker_5: Mayonnaise! That’s what they used to do back in the war, you know. When eggs were rationed. My mum used to make cakes with it. Didn’t taste of mayonnaise, apparently. Just made it nice and moist. Speaker_1: Still, sounds a bit odd to be deliberately doing it now. Speaking of odd, did you hear about old Mrs. Higgins next door? Apparently, she’s convinced the foxes are holding meetings in her garden. Speaker_2: (Laughs) Oh, not again! She told me last week they were planning a revolution. Said they were tired of being underestimated. Speaker_3: She’s a character, isn't she? Though, they *are* getting bolder. I saw one strolling down the high street the other day as if it owned the place. Speaker_4: They’re a menace. Honestly. Digging up the lawn, leaving… presents. I’ve been trying to fox-proof the garden, but it's a losing battle. Speaker_5: You need a good terrier. That’s what you need. They’ll sort them out quick as a flash. Remember Buster? He’d chase ‘em up a tree without a second thought. Speaker_1: Oh, Buster! Good times. He was a proper little scamp. We really miss him, don’t we? Speaker_2: We do. Though, I’m secretly relieved not to be scooping up dog poo at 6 am anymore. Remember that time he… well, never mind. Speaker_3: (Smiling) Oh please, tell the story! Speaker_2: No, no, it's too embarrassing. Let's talk about holiday plans. Are you two still thinking of going to Italy this year? Speaker_4: We are, yes. Tuscany, hopefully. We've booked flights, but haven't nailed down the accommodation yet. It’s proving surprisingly difficult to find somewhere that takes dogs. Speaker_1: Oh, that *is* tricky. Italy is beautiful though. Have you ever been to Lake Como? It’s stunning. Speaker_5: Beautiful? It's full of posh birds and fancy cars! Give me a pint in a proper pub any day. I saw George Clooney there once, you know. Just walking along the promenade. Didn't say hello, though. Too important. Speaker_3: (Teasingly) Oh, so you were expecting a personal invitation to his villa, were you? Speaker_5: Well, it wouldn’t have hurt! (Everyone laughs) I’m just saying, it’s overrated. Give me a good shepherd's pie and a quiet evening any day. Speaker_1: You and your shepherd's pie! It's all you ever talk about. Speaker_2: It is a good shepherd's pie though, admittedly. Right, who’s for another cup of tea? I’ll put the kettle on.

Speaker_1: Right, okay, dishwasher duty team. Poppy, you’re on plates, Leo, you’re tackling the cutlery. And please, *gentle* with the glasses, remember what happened last time? Speaker_2: (Grumbling) But plates are *boring*. Can I do the forks instead? They’re pointy! Speaker_1: No pointy forks, Poppy. Plates. I’ll help you with the big ones. Leo, are you managing? Speaker_3: (Clattering sounds) Yep! Found a spoon! It’s a *really* big spoon! Speaker_1: That’s… good, Leo. Just make sure it goes in the right section. Oh, and no playing with the knives, please. Speaker_2: Mummy, did you read me a Harry Potter chapter last night? The one with the… the whatchamacallit… the scary forest? Speaker_1: The Forbidden Forest? Yes, I did. And you were very brave listening, weren’t you? Even when Voldemort was… well, being Voldemort. Speaker_3: Voldemort’s silly. He has a funny nose. Speaker_1: (Chuckles) He *does* have a rather distinctive nose, doesn’t he? You two are surprisingly critical literary analysts. Speaker_2: Is Harry Potter real? Speaker_1: That’s a good question. He’s real in the stories, of course. But he's a character someone *wrote* about. Like… like George Stephenson. Speaker_3: Who’s George Stephenson? Speaker_1: Oh! He was a very clever man. He lived a long, long time ago, before cars and planes. He invented… well, he really improved steam locomotives! Trains! Speaker_2: Trains? Like the one we took to London? Speaker_1: Exactly like that one! But the first trains were very different. They puffed a lot of smoke and were quite slow. He was called the ‘Father of Railways’ because he made travelling much easier for everyone. Speaker_3: Did he drive the train himself? Speaker_1: He did sometimes! And he spent years building the railways, figuring out how to make them strong enough and safe enough. It was really hard work. Imagine trying to build a track all the way from here to… I don’t know, to Norwich! Speaker_2: That’s a looong way! Speaker_1: It *is* a very long way! He was a proper inventor, though. Very determined. Not at all like… well, not like Draco Malfoy. Speaker_3: Draco Malfoy is a bad guy! Speaker_1: He is a bad guy. George Stephenson was a good guy. Now, how’s the cutlery coming along, Leo? And Poppy, have you rescued any plates yet? We need to get this done before dinner! I hope this meets your requirements! Let me know if you'd like any adjustments or further conversation. Is there anything else I can help you with?

Speaker_1: Right, so I’m officially losing to Amelia on Words With Friends. It’s ridiculous. She just throws down a ‘quixotry’ for triple word score. Who *knows* those words?! Speaker_2: (Stirring a pot on the stove) Oh, she's a menace. Honestly, Amelia could win Scrabble with a dictionary tied behind her back. You need to start strategically using those blank tiles, Leo. That’s the key. Speaker_3: (Chopping vegetables at the kitchen island) Speaking of strategic, anyone else think old Mr. Henderson is getting seriously dodgy with his supper club? He’s been advertising on that new website, ‘Eat Local London’, and I heard he didn’t have the correct food hygiene certificate last time. Speaker_4: (Wiping down the counter) Dodgy as in… not declaring income dodgy, or actual food poisoning dodgy, Bex? Because that’s a very different level of dodgy. Speaker_3: Both, actually. Apparently, someone complained to the council about him not paying his taxes, and now he's trying to fly under the radar with the supper club. It’s a bit of a mess. Speaker_1: Oh god. That’s… a lot. I always thought he was a bit eccentric, but not a tax evader. He always offered me extra cake. Is that a bribe? I don’t know anymore. Speaker_2: (Laughing) Don’t overthink it, Leo. He probably just likes cake. Although, Bex has a point. It's important to be legit, especially with food. Remember when I was looking into getting a food hygiene qualification? It was a nightmare wading through all the legal stuff. Speaker_4: Yeah, I had to do that for the café. Honestly, the forms were designed by someone who actively hates people. Took me a week, and I’m fairly sure I’m still technically breaking some obscure regulation. Speaker_1: Speaking of jobs… anything new on the front with that publishing internship, Clara? Still waiting to hear back? Speaker_2: They said they’re swamped with applications. Apparently, everyone wants to work in publishing. Which, fair enough. It’s… a thing. I’m just trying to distract myself by perfecting my sourdough. Honestly, the hydration levels are *crucial*. You need 78% hydration, no less. Speaker_3: I swear, you talk about sourdough like it’s a newborn baby. Speaker_2: It’s practically is! It needs nurturing! It needs love! And precise temperature control. Actually, can someone check the oven? I think it’s supposed to be at 220, fan assisted. Speaker_4: On it. (Checks the oven) 218. Close enough. Smells amazing in here, by the way. Seriously, you’re a wizard, Clara. Speaker_3: You should bottle that smell and sell it. "Clara's Kitchen: The Essence of Happiness." Speaker_1: I’d buy that. Right now. Especially if it could distract me from Amelia’s winning streak. She just played ‘jazz’ on a double letter score. How is that even fair? Speaker_2: You know, I saw Sarah from uni the other day. She’s a lawyer now, specializing in intellectual property. Maybe she could advise Mr. Henderson… if he’s actually breaking the law. Speaker_4: Oh, is she still with Mark? They were inseparable back then. Speaker_3: I think they split up ages ago. Apparently, he opened a vegan cheese shop, and she couldn’t handle the constant talk about cashew nut fermentation. Speaker_1: (Gasps dramatically) *That* is a tragedy. A vegan cheese shop is perfectly respectable. Especially if the cashew nut fermentation is on point.

Speaker_1: Honestly, this canteen food is…an experience, isn’t it? I swear the gravy has a life of its own. Speaker_2: (Chuckles) It’s…robust. It’s certainly filling. My babushka would say it needs more dill, though. Everything needs more dill, according to her. Speaker_1: Your grandmother sounds like a woman after my own heart! I’m Sarah, by the way. We’ve worked together a few months now, haven’t we? I feel terrible, I’m rubbish with names. Speaker_2: Anna. It’s nice to properly meet you, Sarah. And yes, a few months. I’m still getting used to the British school system, it’s very different from anything I experienced growing up. Speaker_1: It *is* a bit of a beast, isn't it? Especially covering for so many different teachers. How are you finding it? And how’s the IT admin side going? Speaker_2: The IT side is fine, quite logical. I enjoy fixing the printers, honestly. It’s… satisfying. The covering is… unpredictable. Today’s Year 7s were particularly energetic. One tried to convince me that rubber ducks were a legitimate form of currency. Speaker_1: (Laughing) Oh, bless them! They’re brilliant at that age. Always testing the boundaries. My youngest, Liam, he’s eight, and he’s currently obsessed with building miniature castles out of cardboard boxes. The living room is a hazard zone. Speaker_2: Cardboard castles are good! My little cousin, back in Tomsk, he built an entire city. It took up the whole living room. My aunt was not pleased. Do you have other children? Speaker_1: Just Liam. My eldest, Emily, is at university studying history. Keeps me on my toes, that one. Always debating something. What about you, Anna? Any family back home? Speaker_2: I have a younger brother, Dmitri, studying engineering. And my parents, of course. We video call often, but it’s not the same. I miss my mother’s cooking terribly. She makes the best pelmeni - little meat dumplings. Speaker_1: Oh, that sounds amazing! I love trying new foods. I’m a bit of a disaster in the kitchen myself, though. I can burn water, honestly. My husband does most of the cooking. He makes a fantastic roast dinner. Speaker_2: Roast dinner is very British! I have tried it – Yorkshire pudding is… interesting. I’m getting better at cooking though. I’ve started to make sourdough bread. It's a slow process, but very rewarding. Speaker_1: Sourdough! That sounds impressive. I've attempted it once, it ended up looking like a hockey puck. Maybe I should stick to toast. It’s good you have a hobby, it’s so important to have something to switch off with. What do you do when you’re not saving us from rogue printers and Year 7s? Speaker_2: I paint, mostly. Watercolours. Landscapes, usually. It’s a good way to remember home, I think. And you? Anything you enjoy doing? Speaker_1: I used to do a lot of gardening, but Liam's football practice takes up most of my weekends now. And honestly, I'm happy to just curl up with a good book if I can get a quiet five minutes. It’s rare these days! This job is… well, it’s never dull, is it? Speaker_2: No, certainly not dull. It keeps life interesting, at least. Perhaps we can swap recipes sometime? I can show you how to make pelmeni, if you’re brave enough to attempt it.

Speaker_1: Right, so are we definitely going the right way? Because this doesn’t look like… Mothercare way. It looks like we’re heading towards the docks. Speaker_2: (Chuckles) Trust me, darling. I know Preston better than you think. We need to go past the docks, then take a left at the next roundabout. It's a bit of a detour, but avoids all the city centre traffic. Honestly, it's chaos around there right now. Speaker_3: Aye, she's right, love. That city centre’s a nightmare. Especially on a Saturday. Still, it’s good to get out, isn’t it? Been cooped up all week with that surveyor poking around the house like we’ve got something to hide. Speaker_1: Tell me about it. It was so awkward. He kept asking about damp patches, like, excuse me sir, this house is perfectly fine! Except for maybe the… well, the bit in the bathroom. Speaker_2: (Smiling) The ‘bit’ in the bathroom that requires a full renovation? That’s why we’re doing the survey, isn't it? To find all the ‘bits’. Speaker_1: Yeah, okay, fair point. But honestly, he was really focusing on this tiny stain on the ceiling. Like it’s a massive structural issue. Speaker_3: They always do that, lass. Gotta justify their fees somehow. Did he say anything about the garden? I’m worried about the fence. Old Man Hemmings next door’s always complaining it’s leaning into his garden. Speaker_1: He mentioned it. Said it needs… securing. Which I think is code for “replacing the whole thing”. Speaker_2: It does need doing. We’ve been putting it off. Right, turn left here, and we’re golden. Oh! Did you see that blanket in that shop we passed? The really fluffy cream one? That would be *perfect* for the baby’s room. Speaker_1: Ooh, yeah! It was really nice. But probably ridiculously expensive. Everything in Mothercare is ridiculously expensive. Remember when I was little and you used to get me blankets from… what was that shop? The one near the market? Speaker_3: Woolworths! Aye, Woolworths. You could get anything there. Pick ‘n’ Mix, stationery, blankets… a proper institution. She used to have the best little knitted cardigans, your mum did. Speaker_2: It’s a shame they’re all gone. But we want the best for this little one, right? Safety and comfort. Speaking of which, are you drinking enough water? You look a bit pale. Speaker_1: I’m fine, honestly. Just tired. College is exhausting. All the revision for my mocks is killing me. I swear, if I have to write another essay on Victorian poetry… Speaker_3: Mocks, eh? That brings me back. I were awful at poetry. Never understood a word of it. Give me a good maths problem any day. Speaker_2: You always were practical, darling. What about university? Are you still thinking about doing history? Speaker_1: Yeah, I think so. I mean, it’s what I’m good at. But it feels a bit... pointless sometimes. Like, what am I even going to *do* with a history degree? Speaker_3: You’ll be alright, love. Plenty of jobs for clever folk like you. Not like my days, mind you. Left school, went straight into a factory, never looked back. Different world altogether. Though I did get a bit of a reputation for being a bit of a rogue… Speaker_2: (Raises an eyebrow) Oh really? Do tell. Speaker_3: (Laughing) Best not to, love. Some stories are best left buried. Let’s just say I wasn’t always the model citizen. Did a bit of everything in my youth. A few scrapes, a few… let's just call them 'misunderstandings.' Speaker_1: Oh god. Dad

Speaker_1: Ugh, I’m so stuck on this level of ‘Astral Ascent’. It’s *impossible*. Speaker_2: Astral… what now? Sounds stressful, love. Are you sure you shouldn't be doing your homework? Speaker_1: Mum! It *is* homework, kind of. Mr. Davies wants us to analyse game design, and I chose this one. But seriously, the boss is just… unfair. He one-shots me every time. Speaker_3: (Chuckles, looking up from his phone) One-shotting? Dramatic. What class are you playing? Maybe you need to adjust your build? Speaker_1: I’m Zale, the spirit-walker. And I *have* tried different builds! It's not the build, it's the timing. It's like the game is actively trying to mess with my head. Speaker_2: Mess with your head? Oh, don’t start down that rabbit hole. It’s just a game, sweetheart. Speaker_1: No, but it’s designed to keep you hooked, right? All the colours and the sounds… and the frustration. I read an article saying game developers use psychology to make you addicted. Speaker_3: Yeah, there’s definitely a lot of behavioural science baked into game design. Reward systems, variable schedules… It’s all designed to trigger dopamine release. It’s clever, actually. Speaker_1: See! It's evil! I feel terrible after playing it and yet I keep going back. It’s… exhausting. Speaker_2: Well, maybe a break is in order. Have you thought about Christmas yet? Are you making a list? Your auntie Maureen keeps asking. Speaker_1: Ugh, Christmas. Everyone asks what I want, and I have no idea. I don’t *need* anything. Except maybe a strategy guide for ‘Astral Ascent’… Speaker_3: You know, we could actually *go* somewhere for Christmas this year. Not just stay here. Remember that hiking trip Dad was talking about in the Lake District? Speaker_2: Oh, that sounds lovely! Though your father would need to book it soon, everything gets snapped up. And the weather… it could be freezing. Speaker_1: The Lakes? That sounds… cold. And probably no Wi-Fi. Speaker_3: That’s the point! Disconnect a little. Remember what fresh air smells like. Speaker_2: He's got a point. You’re always glued to that screen. Though, I suppose I spend enough time online too, chatting with my sister. She's trying to get me to understand TikTok. Honestly, it’s all just people dancing, isn’t it? Speaker_1: (Smiling slightly) Mostly. Although there’s a lot of science stuff on there too, actually. Like little experiments and explainers. Speaker_3: Speaking of science, how’s university going? Found any research opportunities yet? Speaker_1: I’ve been looking. There’s this one professor in the biology department, Dr. Hayes, who’s doing really cool stuff with genetic sequencing. I sent her an email, but haven’t heard back yet. It’s really competitive. Speaker_2: Don’t worry, love. You’re a bright spark. She’d be lucky to have you. You get that from your father, always tinkering with something… even if it usually ends up broken. Speaker_3: Hey! I resent that. I’m a practical man. And, speaking of work, I think I might finally apply for that assistant research position at the institute. I've been putting it off. Speaker_1: Really? Go for it! It's perfect for you. It’s just…well, it’s a bit intimidating. Speaker_3: Intimidating is my middle name. Just kidding. But yeah, it's a step. Now, about that ‘Astral Ascent’ boss…let me see some gameplay footage. Maybe I can spot something you're missing.

Speaker_1: Right, so, copper is pretty easy to find in Minecraft, isn’t it? Loads of it just…underground. But it’s not *that* useful on its own, is it? Unless you’re making…lightning rods. Speaker_2: (Excitedly) Lightning rods are SO cool! I made a whole tower just for lightning! It zapped all the time! Speaker_3: But diamonds are the best! You need diamonds for everything good. Swords, pickaxes… Speaker_1: Yes, diamonds are amazing. But they’re *hard* to find. You have to go really, really deep down. It took me ages to find enough for a full set. It’s way harder than finding copper. Speaker_2: I found a diamond once! But a zombie took it. It was *so* unfair! Speaker_1: Oh no! That is unfair. You need to build better defenses against the zombies then. Maybe a wall made of…hmm…what’s a strong material in Minecraft? Speaker_3: Obsidian! Obsidian is super strong! You need a diamond pickaxe to even break it! Speaker_1: Exactly! See, you two are Minecraft experts. Now, thinking about real materials…what’s stronger, steel or bronze? Speaker_2: Steel! Definitely steel! It’s shiny and you can make really good swords and armour with it. Speaker_1: That’s a good answer. Steel *is* stronger, because it has carbon added to the iron. Bronze is iron and tin mixed together. It was important a long time ago but it's not as strong. Speaker_3: What about velvet? Is velvet strong? Speaker_1: (Chuckles) Velvet isn’t about strength, darling. It’s about being soft and fancy. It’s made of silk, or sometimes cotton, and it’s really nice to touch. Like…a really posh cushion. Speaker_2: Grandma has a velvet dress! It’s purple! Speaker_1: Oh, yes! That’s a beautiful dress. Right, so while we’re talking about inventing things…I’ve been thinking about a new legend. Speaker_3: A legend? Like…with dragons? Speaker_1: Possibly dragons. But this one’s about a magical forest, and a girl who can talk to trees. She has to protect the trees from… a grumpy gnome who wants to turn them all into furniture. Speaker_2: (Giggles) A grumpy gnome! That’s silly! Speaker_1: He’s very grumpy. And he has a tiny axe. She needs to find a special berry…the glowberry…to make the trees invisible. Speaker_3: Ooh, glowberries! Can you make glowberries in Minecraft? Speaker_1: You can make glow berries in Minecraft, yes! Which is probably why my brain decided to include them. Are you both taking your vitamins? Grandma sent those chewable ones, didn’t she? Speaker_2: I had mine this morning! They taste like strawberries! Speaker_3: I forgot! Can I have it now? Please? Speaker_1: Yes, you can have it now. But only if you promise to tell me more about your Minecraft adventures later. I need to learn all the best strategies. Speaker_1: And maybe we can all build a lightning tower together… if the grumpy gnome doesn’t get in the way. Speaker_2: Yes! A lightning tower! And we can make it out of obsidian! Speaker_3: And protect it from zombies with diamond swords! Speaker_1: Sounds like a plan. Now vitamins first, then Minecraft!

Speaker_1: Right, so then she just… vanished. Like, completely. Didn’t reply to a single message. Speaker_2: No way! After all that talk about being best mates forever? What happened? Speaker_1: Dunno! That's the frustrating bit. I tried calling, texted, even messaged her on Insta, nothing. It's proper weird. Makes you question everything, doesn’t it? Like, what did I do wrong? Speaker_2: People are strange, aren’t they? Honestly, sometimes I think I prefer my own company. Less drama. You know, less chance of getting left hanging. Speaker_1: Tell me about it. It’s just… we’d been friends since primary school. Years! It's not like a boyfriend going all silent, this is a *friend*. Speaker_2: Yeah, that's different. Did anyone else hear anything? Maybe she just needed space? Speaker_1: I asked around. No one’s seen or heard from her. It’s like she just…poofed. It’s just… creepy, innit? You hear stories about people disappearing, and you think 'that'll never happen to me'. Makes you think about all those weirdos online too. Speaker_2: Don’t go down that rabbit hole, aye. You’ll end up thinking everyone’s a paedophile. Seriously, it’s not helpful. Speaker_1: I know, I know. It’s just…seeing stories on the news, it just makes you wary. Anyway, speaking of weirdos… did you see old man Hemmings trying to chat up Sarah at the bus stop yesterday? Speaker_2: Ugh, *him*. Always lurking. I swear he thinks anyone under 30 is fair game. Sarah dealt with him, though, didn't she? Speaker_1: She told him she had a boyfriend who was a boxer. He scarpered proper quick. Speaker_2: Good on her. Right, enough about creepy people. What's been happening with you? Still messing about with that guitar? Speaker_1: Yeah! I finally managed to learn the intro to 'Wonderwall'. It’s still a bit clunky, but getting there. Speaker_2: Proper! Oasis are legends. I tried learning guitar once, but my fingers just wouldn't cooperate. I'm more of a lyrics kinda guy. Speaker_1: You always were good at writing. Remember that terrible poem you wrote about our PE teacher? Speaker_2: (Laughing) Oh god, don't remind me. Mrs. Peterson was terrifying. It was a masterpiece of passive aggression, though. Speaker_1: Absolutely. So, what bands are you into at the moment then? Anything new? Speaker_2: Been listening to a lot of Idles lately. They're proper shouty, but good. And Fontaines D.C. You’d probably like them. Bit…moody. Speaker_1: I’ll check them out. I’ve been stuck on Wet Leg. They’re brilliant. So dry and sarcastic. Speaker_2: Ah, good choice. They’re cracking. Me and Jamie saw them live last month. Brilliant gig. Speaker_1: Oh yeah? I’m gutted I missed it. Maybe next time. I've been trying to get back into painting as well, but I just…can’t seem to find the time with uni work. Speaker_2: I know the feeling. It's always something, isn't it? Still, gotta have *some* kind of hobby. Keeps you sane.

Speaker_1: Honestly, this weather is *mint*. Proper sunshine. Makes a change from Slough drizzle, eh? Speaker_2: Seriously! I was dreading being stuck inside all half-term, but this is perfect. You still on for that exhibition in London on Friday, Kai? The one with the street photography? Speaker_3: Oh yeah, the one Leo was banging on about? I’m in. Though knowing Leo, he'll probably want to spend three hours analyzing one picture of a bin. Speaker_1: (Laughing) That sounds about right. He *is* a bit… intense about art. Did you guys finish that history assignment? Mrs. Davies is gonna murder us if we haven’t. Speaker_2: Nearly. Just the conclusion left. It’s a slog though, isn’t it? All that research on the Industrial Revolution… feels a bit pointless. Speaker_3: Tell me about it. I’m way more stressed about my EPQ. Trying to get interviews for my research is proving impossible. Everyone ignores my emails. I’m doing it on the ethics of fast fashion, you know? It’s a big topic. Speaker_1: That sounds… ambitious. I went for something a bit simpler. Building a gaming PC. Less reliant on people actually replying to me. Speaker_2: Smart move. Speaking of ambitious, did you see Maya’s Insta story? She’s practically living in Montenegro. Beaches, mountains, fancy restaurants… it's ridiculous. Speaker_3: Ugh, don’t even. It’s just…flaunting. Her dad owns half of Wembley, it’s hardly a relatable holiday. Speaker_1: Fair point. Still, looks nice. Thinking about uni applications… have you guys got any ideas beyond “somewhere with a decent student union”? Speaker_2: I’m leaning towards Bristol, maybe. Good music scene, not *too* far from home. Thinking about doing Economics. You? Speaker_3: I’m torn. I really like the idea of studying Anthropology at York, but… it feels a bit… impractical? Like, what jobs do you even *get* with an Anthropology degree? My mum keeps suggesting teaching. Speaker_1: Teaching’s alright, I guess. My uncle does it. Says the kids are the worst part. Honestly, I haven't got a clue. Probably just pick whatever has the lowest entry requirements. Speaker_2: Harsh! You're capable of more than that, Kai. Remember when you made that amazing paella for Sarah's birthday? You're practically a chef! Speaker_1: That was one time! And I nearly set the kitchen on fire. Plus, my mum did half the chopping. Speaker_3: (Smiling) You’re just humble. You should totally do something food-related. Maybe culinary school? Speaker_1: Nah. Too stressful. Plus, my cousin Ben went vegan last week and now won't shut up about the ethical implications of eating eggs. I don’t need that drama in my life. Speaker_2: Oh, *Ben*. He’s always got to be… something. Remember when he tried to learn to juggle and just kept hitting himself in the face? Speaker_3: (Laughing) Oh my god, yes! He looked like he was auditioning for a slapstick comedy routine. It was epic. Speaker_1: Good times. Anyone fancy grabbing a Greggs? I’m starting to get peckish. Maybe a sausage roll to fuel our existential university crisis? Speaker_2: Lead the way! Sausage roll sounds perfect. Speaker_3: Definitely. And then we can debate the merits of Montenegro some more.

Speaker_1: Honestly, this kitchen is a disaster zone. I walked in earlier and someone had left a half-eaten pot noodle on the counter… for *days*. It was actively growing something. Speaker_2: Tell me about it. I swear, living here is a breeding ground for germs. And the passive-aggressive notes? Don't even get me started. "Please clean up after yourselves!" Like we’re five years old. Speaker_3: (Chuckles) It’s uni life, innit? A bit of chaos is par for the course. My mum would have a heart attack if she saw this place. She's obsessed with cleanliness. Literally has a cleaning schedule for everything. Speaker_4: My nan is the same. She'd inspect every surface with a white glove. She keeps asking when I'm going to 'settle down' and get a proper job. Like being a student isn't a proper job! Speaker_1: Oh, the “settle down” question. My auntie Maureen brought that up at Christmas. Said I should be thinking about a 'sensible career' and 'finding a nice young man'. As if those two things are mutually exclusive. Speaker_2: Ugh, relatives. Always with the unsolicited life advice. Mine are obsessed with how much everything costs at uni. Constantly asking how much my rent is, how much books are... They think I'm rolling in it just because I moved away for university. Speaker_3: It's expensive, though, isn’t it? I'm already dreading the overdraft at the end of term. My dad keeps sending me articles about budgeting, like I haven’t heard it all before. “Cut back on takeaways!” he says. Easy for him to say, he's got a fully stocked fridge. Speaker_4: Rent is insane. I’m working part-time at the campus bar just to keep my head above water. It's not glamorous, but it pays the bills. And the tips aren't bad, especially on student nights. Speaker_1: I’m considering getting a second job. But then I’d have no social life. It’s a vicious cycle. I'm trying to save up for a trip to see my family back in Cornwall over Easter, but it feels impossible. Train tickets are daylight robbery. Speaker_2: Cornwall? Lucky you! Mine are up in the Lake District. It's a trek, and mum always makes me feel guilty for not visiting enough. Says I only call when I need money. Which…is sometimes true. Speaker_3: (Smiling) Mothers, eh? Always know how to make you feel small. My mum’s currently trying to set me up with every eligible girl in Bolton. She keeps sending me pictures through WhatsApp. Speaker_4: Oh god, no. My mum tried to do that with a girl from her friend’s yoga class. Sent me a full profile, including her A-level results. It was mortifying. Speaker_1: A-level results? That’s dedication! Speaking of mortifying, did you hear about Liam from the history course? He accidentally sent a very… enthusiastic message meant for his girlfriend, to the group chat. Speaker_2: (Gasps) No way! What did it say?! Speaker_3: Oh, this is good. Spill the tea.
