Speaker_4: Liam? Seriously? He always seemed… reserved. This is juicy. Speaker_1: Apparently, it involved a detailed description of his feelings and a lot of fire emojis. The screenshots are going viral. Speaker_2: Oh, poor Liam. That’s brutal. Although, a little bit funny. Speaker_3: I think it's a lesson to everyone: double-check who you're sending to. Especially when feelings are involved. Speaker_4: Definitely. And maybe don’t send anything you wouldn’t want your mum to read. Just a general rule of thumb.

Speaker_1: Honestly, Mum, the kids are already driving me round the bend about Christmas. Leo’s decided he *needs* a drone this year. A drone! Speaker_2: (Chuckles) Oh, boys and their gadgets. Your father would have been the same, always wanting the latest bit of technology. Remember that video camera he saved up for, the one that weighed a ton? Speaker_1: Vaguely. I mostly remember him fiddling with it and filming us all looking miserable. But a drone is a different league. They’re expensive, and potentially dangerous. I’ve told him he can ask Santa, which feels like a polite fob-off, but what else can I do? Speaker_2: Santa’s a good buffer. Distances you from the ‘no’ a little bit. Though, knowing your brother, Richard, he’ll probably promise Leo one anyway. He’s always the indulgent uncle. Speaker_1: Oh, don’t even get me started on Richard. He rang last week boasting about taking the kids to Lapland. Lapland! I’m trying to get through December without completely losing my mind and he’s whisking them off to the North Pole. Speaker_2: Oh, he does love to show off, doesn’t he? But he means well. Remember when he tried to build that treehouse for them in your garden? Nearly gave your Dad a heart attack. Speaker_1: (Laughing) Oh, God, yes! It was a death trap. Entirely unstable and leaning precariously over the shed. Dad spent a week dismantling it while Richard kept suggesting “structural improvements”. Speaker_2: Speaking of things needing improvement, how’s the teaching going? Still battling with teenagers who think grammar is optional? Speaker_1: It’s…a challenge. I’ve got a new group of beginners, mostly Spanish and Italian, and it’s lovely seeing them learn, but getting them to understand prepositions is like pulling teeth. Then there’s Signor Rossi, who insists on correcting *my* pronunciation. He thinks he’s a linguistic genius. Speaker_2: Oh, the audacity! You’re the teacher! Speaker_1: Exactly! Though, honestly, some days I feel like I'm learning more from them than they are from me. It’s good though, keeps me on my toes. It's just… tiring. I'm starting to think that holiday in Portugal next spring is going to be absolutely essential. Speaker_2: It sounds wonderful. We should try and go with you. I’d love to spend some proper time with the grandchildren. Actually, Mrs. Peterson from my yoga class was telling me about a lovely little villa she rented near Lagos last year. I could get you her number… Speaker_1: Oh, that would be brilliant, Mum. That would *really* be brilliant. I’m already exhausted just thinking about the Christmas rush. A little sunshine sounds like heaven. Speaker_2: Well, we’ll see. Though, Richard will undoubtedly try to hijack the whole holiday and turn it into some sort of ‘family adventure’. Rest assured, I’ll pack my earplugs. Speaker_1: (Smiling) You’re a lifesaver, Mum. A complete lifesaver. Now, another cider? Speaker_2: Don't mind if I do. And tell me, how's young Daniel been? Is he still showing promise with that art of his? Speaker_1: Oh, he's amazing. He's just started a new project – sculpting – and I'm having to ban him from raiding the kitchen for tin foil! It’s quite the spectacle. Speaker_2: (Laughing) Always something with that one! It's lovely to see him with a passion.

Speaker_1: It’s just… good to actually *see* you, Dad. Feels like ages. Two years is a long time, isn’t it? Speaker_2: Feels like a lifetime, lad. A lifetime. Good to see you too, honestly. Thought the M25 would swallow me whole getting here, though. Absolutely rammed. Still, better than relying on trains these days, eh? Did you have a nightmare getting here? Speaker_1: Nah, not too bad. Actually, I was messing with a new phone app that analyses driving – tells you if you’re braking harshly, accelerating too fast… all that. Quite addictive, actually. It felt like being back in driving lessons! Speaker_2: (chuckles) Sounds like one of those things that'll just stress you out, doesn’t it? Everything's a data point these days. Speaking of driving… they've put another speed camera up near the old library, you know. Absolute racket. And apparently, they're thinking of lowering the limit *again*. Speaker_1: Seriously? They just did that! It's like they *want* people to lose their licenses. Remember Uncle Barry? Got done doing 33 in a 30 zone and lost his for a month. Nearly had a heart attack. Speaker_2: Aye, that was a mess. He was fuming. Speaking of messes...how’s work going? Still teaching the… what are they, the Japanese businessmen? Speaker_1: Yeah, mostly. It’s alright. Keeps me busy. Though it’s…interesting, trying to explain the nuances of English idioms to people who've already mastered everything else. Trying to explain ‘raining cats and dogs’ is always a highlight. What about you? Still dealing with angry customers all day? Speaker_2: You wouldn’t believe it. Had a bloke yelling at me for a solid ten minutes about a delayed parcel. Said I’d personally ruined his birthday. Honestly, some people. I’ve been feeling a bit under the weather lately, too. Just a nasty cough that won’t shift. Doctor said it’s probably just a bug, but it's dragging me down. Speaker_1: Oh, that’s rough. You need to look after yourself, Dad. Really. Remember what happened to old Mr. Henderson? Worked himself into the ground and then… well. Speaker_2: Don’t remind me. Awful business. I’ve been thinking… maybe Brighton isn’t such a bad idea, actually. Mum always liked the sea air. Maybe a little flat, a bit of a change of scenery. Speaker_1: Brighton would be nice. A bit more going on than Crayford, that’s for sure. What about the family? Has Auntie Maureen been up to her usual mischief? Speaker_2: Oh, you *know* Maureen. Apparently, she entered a competitive baking competition. And lost. Said the judges were biased. Claims her Victoria sponge was “a work of art”. She sent me a picture of it. Looked… questionable. Speaker_1: (laughing) Classic Maureen. Remember that trip to Tanzania we took when I was a kid? She tried to barter for a zebra. Speaker_2: (roaring with laughter) Oh god, yes! The guide was mortified. I've put on a bit of weight, haven't I? Speaker_1: A bit. But you still look good, Dad. Honestly. Speaker_2: Don’t patronise me, lad. I’ve noticed. Still, talking of trips, how was that recording thing you were doing with your mates? The podcast? Speaker_1: It was chaotic. Absolute chaos! Trying to get four people to agree on anything is impossible. We spent an hour arguing whether Jon Snow was a good leader in *Game of Thrones*. Speaker_2: Jon Snow? Bit of a wet blanket, if you ask me. Shouldn't have been king. But back to flights, have you checked prices for getting out to see me once you're settled? I've been looking at some potential dates for December.

Speaker_1: Honestly, the supermarket was *mental* today. I swear everyone decided to do their weekly shop at exactly 2pm on a Tuesday. Speaker_2: Oh, don’t even. I popped in on my lunch break, thinking I’d be quick, and it was the same. Packed. People abandoning trolleys everywhere. It’s chaos. Did you at least manage to get everything? Speaker_1: Mostly. I had to swap brands of pasta three times before I found one they hadn’t completely decimated. And they were out of oat milk. *Out* of oat milk! It’s a national crisis, I tell you. Speaker_2: (Chuckles) A crisis indeed. I'm switching to almond, myself. Not as good for a latte, but at least they seem to keep it in stock. Speaking of stock… did you see the PR fallout from that band, ‘Static Bloom’? Ugh, disaster. Speaker_1: Oh, the ones who had that awful tweet about… well, everything? Yes. It’s fascinating, isn’t it? How quickly things can unravel. My media ethics students are having a field day dissecting it. Apparently, the PR team is scrambling, trying to issue a non-apology apology. Speaker_2: A non-apology apology! Brilliant phrasing. That’s exactly what it is. It's always the same, isn't it? Trying to walk the line between acknowledging wrongdoing and not actually admitting fault. Speaker_1: Precisely. It's exhausting just *watching* it unfold, let alone *being* the PR person in that situation. I feel for them, honestly. Though, a little foresight could have prevented this mess. Speaker_2: True. Although, I’m starting to think foresight is a rare commodity these days. Did you hear anything more about the funding bid for the new music tech lab? Speaker_1: I did. It’s looking… optimistic. We should hear something definitive by the end of the week, apparently. Professor Davies is pretty confident. He's been schmoozing all the right people. Speaker_2: Good. That lab would be transformative for the department. We could finally get students hands-on experience with some proper kit. Are you going to that gig on Friday? The Jazz Collective at The Waterfront? Speaker_1: Oh, I’d forgotten about that! I completely meant to get tickets. I’ve been so swamped with marking. Is it a good line-up? Speaker_2: Apparently, pretty good. Liam’s been raving about the saxophonist. Said she's phenomenal. I’ve already got a ticket. Fancy coming along? I can grab you one if they haven’t sold out. Speaker_1: That would be lovely, actually. A bit of live music is *exactly* what I need after this week. Yes, please do. You are a lifesaver. Speaker_2: No problem at all. I’ll check online now, just to be sure. Anything else on your mind? Exhausted from the supermarket wars? Speaker_1: Just… planning what meals I can cobble together *without* oat milk, mostly. And hoping the pasta doesn’t stick together. It’s the little things, you know? Speaker_2: Oh, absolutely. The small victories. Alright, let me sort the Jazz Collective ticket and then perhaps… we order a takeaway? My brain is officially fried too. Speaker_1: That sounds utterly perfect. Indian? Speaker_2: Indian it is. I'm already craving a vindaloo. Speaker_1: Excellent choice. You’re a wonder. Speaker_2: I try. Now, let's conquer this ticket situation.

Speaker_1: Right, onions are sizzling nicely. You’re sure you want chorizo *and* chicken in this paella? It feels… ambitious. Speaker_2: Ambitious is good! It’s Saturday night, we deserve ambitious. And honestly, the chorizo will give it a lovely smoky flavour. Trust me. How’s the beanbag coming along? Still attacking it with those needles? Speaker_1: Attacking is a strong word. Gently… persuading it to become a beanbag. It’s slow going. I’m on the fifth panel. This chunky yarn is lovely and soft, but it’s a beast to work with. I’m seriously considering using the smaller needles next time. Speaker_2: Fifth panel, that’s progress! You'll have a massive, cosy beanbag in no time. It'll look brilliant in the living room, especially when it's finally finished. Did you manage to sort out the shower curtain? I noticed the old one was looking a bit… tragic. Speaker_1: Oh, don’t even. I ordered a new one online. A lovely teal one. It should arrive tomorrow. But then I started looking at bathroom mats, and suddenly the whole bathroom wants redecorating. Speaker_2: (Chuckles) The ripple effect of a new shower curtain. It’s a dangerous game. What’s wrong with the current bathroom, anyway? It’s perfectly functional. Speaker_1: Functional, yes. Inspiring? Not so much. It’s just…beige. Everything is beige. I saw this gorgeous wallpaper online, with little birds on it. And I’m thinking pale grey tiles. Maybe even a new mirror. Speaker_2: Birds, huh? That's a bit…bold for you. I always thought you were more of a geometric pattern kind of person. Speaker_1: I am! But I’m feeling adventurous. And beige is just… depressing. Don’t get me wrong, I love a neutral, but this is just… flat. It needs life. Speaking of life, are you adding peppers to this paella? Speaker_2: Already done. Red and yellow, for colour. And a pinch of saffron, naturally. It wouldn't be paella without saffron. You know, while you're redecorating the bathroom, maybe we could finally tackle that wonky shelf in the hallway? Speaker_1: Oh, please no! One disaster at a time. I have enough on my plate with the beanbag and the potential bathroom overhaul. We’ll leave the wonky shelf for another day, shall we? It’s been wonky for years, it's practically a feature now. Speaker_2: A very… structurally questionable feature. Right, I think this needs another splash of wine. Just to deepen the flavour, of course. How's the yarn holding up? Still not tempting to just chuck it and watch TV? Speaker_1: Tempting, very tempting. But I’m determined. I will conquer this beanbag, even if it takes me until Christmas! And then… who knows? Maybe I'll take up pottery. Speaker_2: Pottery? Now *that* would be ambitious. Speaker_1: (Laughing) One step at a time! First, paella. Then, beanbag. Then...we'll see. Speaker_2: Sounds like a plan. Speaker_1: Right, pass me the paprika. Speaker_2: Coming right up. Speaker_1: And tell me again why you think chorizo and chicken is a good idea, while I check the rice… Speaker_2: Because life is too short for boring paella! Speaker_1: (Shaking her head, smiling) You’re incorrigible.

Speaker_1: Right then, finished that crossword. Took me ages, though. Seven across… “A small, flightless bird…” Had me stumped for a good ten minutes. Speaker_2: Oh, you and your crosswords, George. Always got your nose in one. What was the answer? Speaker_1: Kiwi. Of course, it was Kiwi! Should’ve twigged sooner. You’d have had it straight away, wouldn’t you, David? Speaker_3: (Chuckles) Probably. I used to enjoy a good crossword in my younger days. Though I’m more likely to be poring over the financial news these days, sadly. Bit more… pressing. Speaker_2: Financial news? You’re still worrying about the markets, even in retirement? Honestly, David, you need to relax. Speaker_3: It’s not so much *worrying* as… keeping an eye on things. One has responsibilities, you know. The portfolio needs tending to, even if I’m not actively working. Speaker_1: Well, I’m glad somebody’s keeping an eye on things. I couldn't tell a share from a shillelagh. Not my cup of tea, that. Give me a good mystery novel any day. Speaker_2: Speaking of mysteries, have you heard from Sarah lately? She said she was going to call after her holiday, but it’s been nearly a week. Speaker_3: No, I haven’t. I assumed she was just settling back in. Busy unpacking, doing laundry… the usual post-holiday rigmarole. Speaker_1: She usually rings straight away. She knows we like to hear how she’s getting on. That young man of hers… always asking about me, that’s good. Speaker_2: He’s a lovely boy, isn’t he? Very polite. Reminds me a bit of his grandfather, actually. Though a bit more…trendy, perhaps. Speaker_3: He’s a sensible lad. A good match for Sarah. Although, I still harbour a slight reservation about their decision to move so far north. Speaker_1: North? It's not *that* far north. It’s only York! Speaker_3: It's a long drive for us, George. A very long drive. And I worry about Sarah being so far from us, should anything happen. Speaker_2: She's a grown woman, David. She’s perfectly capable of looking after herself. Plus, she’s got him, and they’ve got a lovely little house there. She's happy. That's the main thing. Speaker_1: Exactly. If she’s happy, we should be happy for her. Though a phone call wouldn’t go amiss, mind. Speaker_3: I’ll give her a ring tomorrow, then. Just to check everything’s alright. Can’t hurt, can it? Speaker_2: Good idea. And while you're at it, ask her about those wildflowers she was sending us seeds for. I can’t remember what she called them... Something about attracting bees? Speaker_1: Oh, yeah, the bee bombs! She said they were good for the garden. Though I’m not much of a gardener, myself. Too much bending down. Speaker_3: (Smiling) You and bending down, George… a classic combination. Speaker_2: (Laughing) Absolutely. Well, I’m going to put the kettle on. Who wants a biscuit? I’ve got digestives and shortbread. Speaker_1: Oh, go on then. A digestive would be lovely. Speaker_3: I’ll take a shortbread, thank you. And perhaps we can discuss this impending doom of the financial markets over tea? Speaker_2: (Rolling her eyes good-naturedly) Oh, here we go again…

Speaker_1: Honestly, I’m absolutely shattered. That shift was *brutal*. Old Mrs. Henderson decided today was the day to try and escape again. Speaker_2: Oh, not again! She’s a character, isn’t she? Still, you’d think after the third time they’d increase her meds or something. Speaker_3: Sounds… eventful. Anything interesting happen on your commute home, Dad? Besides narrowly avoiding death on the M25, obviously. Speaker_2: (chuckles) Surprisingly peaceful, actually. Though I did see young Timmy from number 47 attempting to parallel park. It was a masterclass in… not being able to parallel park. Took him a good ten minutes and a lot of reversing. Speaker_4: Oh, Timmy! He’s hopeless. Remember when he tried to build that birdhouse? It looked like a wonky shed. Speaker_1: (laughing) Oh god, yes. It leaned so far, I was convinced it was going to topple over in a light breeze. Speaking of building things, have we finalised the Christmas dinner menu? I was thinking goose this year, instead of turkey. Speaker_3: Goose sounds amazing! A bit more… festive, somehow. Though, can we please have Brussels sprouts banished forever? They are the enemy. Speaker_2: Brussels sprouts are a tradition, darling. A slightly unpleasant tradition, but a tradition nonetheless. Speaker_4: I’m with Lily. No sprouts! We had them last year, and I swear, they haunted my dreams. Speaker_1: Alright, alright, no sprouts. Happy? We can have honey-glazed carrots instead. What about desserts? I was thinking Yule log, but I'm open to suggestions. Speaker_3: Ooh, a Yule log would be lovely. Maybe Mum could make her chocolate orange cheesecake too? That’s always a winner. Speaker_4: Yes! And we *have* to have mince pies. I’ve already been eyeing up the Fortnum & Mason ones. They’re extortionate, but so worth it. Speaker_2: Fortnum & Mason? Really? You and your fancy mince pies. I'm happy with the Sainsbury's basics, thank you very much. Although… I did see they had some nice Stollen. Perhaps a Stollen is in order. Speaker_1: Don’t start you two. It’ll be a full-blown shopping rivalry before you know it. We still need to figure out presents, too. I’ve got most of your gifts sorted, but I’m struggling to find something for Uncle George. He already *has* everything. Speaker_3: He loves those ridiculously expensive socks, doesn’t he? The cashmere ones? Another pair might be a safe bet. Speaker_4: Or a really good bottle of whisky? He’s always moaning about the price of a decent single malt. Speaker_2: Good idea, Sarah. A nice whisky. I'll have a look around. Have you booked the train tickets for visiting Amy in Bristol yet, Helen? Speaker_1: Not yet, I was planning on doing it tomorrow. Prices seem to be fluctuating wildly. I'm hoping to get a decent deal. It's a long way to go just for a weekend, but I promised her I'd be there for her graduation. Speaker_3: That's lovely. Bristol is nice though, isn’t it? Very… trendy. All the artists and students. Completely different vibe to Kent. Speaker_4: It is a bit different, isn't it? I went there with Ben a few years ago. It felt so… *free*. Everything felt possible. Speaker_1: Well, hopefully, it’ll be a nice weekend. I just need to survive this next shift first. And avoid any more escape attempts.

Speaker_1: This coffee is lovely, isn’t it? Much stronger than what I’m used to back home. Speaker_2: Aye, it’s good stuff. They don't mess about with it here. Real Turkish coffee. I’ve been coming here for… oh, must be fifteen years now, winter months mostly. Gets you through the grey. Speaker_1: Fifteen years! Wow. You must know the place like the back of your hand. I'm only just getting my bearings. It’s beautiful, of course, but… different. Speaker_2: Different is a good word. It takes some getting used to. Did you manage to get out and about much yesterday? Beyond the pool, that is. Speaker_1: Not a tremendous amount, no. Just a little wander around the harbour. It was *packed* with people. Mostly British, it seemed. And a lot of stag dos, actually. It felt a bit… Blackpool, to be honest. Speaker_2: (chuckles) Blackpool with sunshine, you mean. That’s Kyrenia for you. Saturday is always busy. All the day-trippers from the south come up. They get a good exchange rate, you see. Speaker_1: Oh, I didn’t realise that. Is it easy enough to cross the border? I was reading something about needing to show your passport and… well, I’m a bit cautious, I suppose. Speaker_2: Perfectly safe. A bit of a faff, admittedly. You just show your passport, they stamp it, and you’re through. It's mainly a formality. I’ve done it dozens of times. You can get a bus right into Nicosia – it’s a fascinating city, very divided, of course. Worth a visit, if you’re feeling adventurous. Speaker_1: That sounds intriguing, actually. I’d like to see a bit more of the ‘real’ Cyprus, not just the tourist areas. What about eating? Any recommendations? I had a kebab last night, but it wasn’t particularly… inspiring. Speaker_2: Kebab’s are hit and miss. Best bet is to get away from the harbour front. Go up into the old town, look for somewhere filled with locals. Ask for “meze”. That's a selection of small dishes. You’ll get everything from hummus and olives to grilled halloumi and lamb. It’s a feast. Speaker_1: Meze... right, I'll remember that. Any particular restaurants spring to mind? Speaker_2: There's a place called ‘The Lodge’ up near the castle. It's run by a lovely family, really authentic. And not overpriced, which is a bonus. Though, honestly, you can’t go far wrong stumbling into a little taverna. Speaker_1: That’s good to know. I tend to wander aimlessly until something catches my eye. It’s usually how I find the best places. Have you ever tried the local wine? I spotted a few bottles in the supermarket. Speaker_2: Oh, the Commandaria? It's a sweet dessert wine. Historically, it was the favoured drink of the Knights Templar. Very good, but very strong. A little goes a long way. I prefer the local dry white, though. It goes well with the meze. Speaker_1: Knights Templar, you say? That’s quite a history! This place is full of surprises. Speaker_2: It is. It really is. You just have to look beyond the sun loungers and the package holidays. Would you fancy coming with me to the market on Tuesday? It’s a proper local market, not one of those tourist traps. You can haggle for everything – spices, fruit, clothes… you name it. Speaker_1: That sounds wonderful, actually. I'd love to. I haven't haggled in years!

Speaker_1: Honestly, the students were dreadful today. Just absolutely dreadful. Didn’t read the assigned chapters, kept asking questions already covered in the lecture… it was relentless. Speaker_2: Oh, no. Really? Was it a specific class or just… a general bad day? Speaker_1: I think it was mostly the second years. They're starting to get that end-of-term ‘I can’t be bothered’ attitude already, and it’s only November! It makes me wonder if I’m doing something wrong, you know? Am I not engaging them enough? Speaker_2: Don’t beat yourself up about it, El. You’re a brilliant lecturer. They’re probably just overwhelmed with everything else going on. Exams looming, socials… the usual chaos. Remember how *we* were? Speaker_1: True, true. We were masters of procrastination. Still, it’s frustrating. I spent ages prepping that lecture, and to have them just… blankly stare back at me. It feels a bit pointless. Speaker_2: I had a similar thing with my postgrads, actually. One of them, Ben, was convinced his dissertation topic was brilliant, but when I probed him on the methodology… it just wasn’t there. Had to gently suggest he rethink things. Awkward. Speaker_1: Oh, those dissertation supervisions. The bane of our existence. Still, at least you were being constructive. I just wanted to yell at my second years. Speaker_2: (Chuckles) Controlled outbursts are sometimes necessary. Though perhaps not in front of undergraduates. Speaking of controlled… look at that smog! It's getting worse, isn't it? Speaker_1: It's awful. You can actually *taste* it. It was bad yesterday, but today it’s like breathing through wool. I saw Old Man Zhang coughing his lungs out by the market. Speaker_2: It's terrifying, to be honest. We should really invest in those air purifiers for the flat. I keep putting it off, thinking it'll improve, but it clearly isn't. Speaker_1: Definitely. And maybe start wearing masks again when we walk to work. Though it feels so… dystopian, doesn't it? Speaker_2: It does. But what choice do we have? It’s affecting our health. Speaking of health, did you hear back from Sarah about next weekend? She said she might be able to join us for that hike. Speaker_1: No, not yet. I texted her this morning, but she’s probably busy. She’s always busy with her kids and her pottery. Though she did mention something about a particularly disastrous kiln firing last time we spoke. Speaker_2: Oh dear. Pottery can be a cruel mistress. Well, hopefully, she can make it. It would be nice to catch up properly, away from marking and lectures and… air pollution. Speaker_1: Absolutely. It feels like ages since we’ve had a proper, relaxed weekend. Come on, let’s hurry up and get home – I need a cup of tea and to escape this haze. Speaker_2: Lead the way. Though honestly, a week in the Lake District is starting to sound *very* appealing. Speaker_1: (Smiling) Don’t tempt me. Don't. We discussed this. We have grants to write! Speaker_2: Priorities, priorities. Still… fresh air. And no smog. Just saying. Speaker_1: (Laughing) Just walk faster, then. Before I start applying for research funding for a portable oxygen tank. Speaker_2: Deal. Speaker_1: Right. Let’s go.

Speaker_1: (Chopping vegetables with a rhythmic thud) Right, so, anyone fancy a chilli tonight? I've got loads of peppers that need using up. Speaker_2: (Stirring something on the hob) Chilli sounds lovely, actually. A bit spicy? My stomach's been a bit…sensitive lately. Speaker_3: (Scrolling through her phone at the kitchen table) Oh yes, please make it spicy! I’m craving something with a kick. Look at this photo, though. Remember Auntie Maureen’s 60th? Speaker_3: (Laughing) Skegness! Classic Auntie Maureen. She’ll be bringing back stories for days. Right, I'm starving. What time are we aiming for lunch tomorrow? I was thinking maybe that little Italian place near the market? Speaker_1: Oh, that sounds nice! They do a lovely pasta salad. Around oneish? Gives me time to finish this report for work. It’s dragging on forever. Honestly, spreadsheets are the bane of my life. Speaker_2: One’s good. I need to chase up a few things with the contractors tomorrow morning. They're still having issues with the new ventilation system. It’s like talking to a brick wall sometimes. Speaker_3: Ugh, sounds stressful. I spent most of today battling with a client who wanted to completely change the tone of voice *after* we’d already signed off the copy. It’s infuriating when they don’t trust your expertise. Speaker_1: You’d think they’d hire someone if they weren't happy with your work, wouldn't you? Anyway, back to more important things… chilli. I’m thinking rice and some crusty bread on the side? Speaker_2: Perfect. Actually, did you see that new documentary about the Amazon rainforest on Channel 4 last night? It was absolutely heartbreaking. Speaker_3: I missed that! Was it the one with the indigenous tribes? I read an article about it, sounded really powerful. I’ve been hooked on ‘The Great British Bake Off’ though, it's just so wholesome. Speaker_1: Oh, I'm not a massive baking fan, but it *is* nice, isn’t it? A bit of light relief. (Tastes the sauce) Mmm, needs a bit more chilli powder, I think. How was your day, love? (Looking at Speaker_2) Apart from the ventilation system woes. Speaker_2: It was okay. Bit of a rush, as usual. Old Mrs. Higgins was a bit confused about her medication again. Spent a good twenty minutes trying to explain things to her. She's such a sweet lady, but her memory is… fading. Speaker_3: That must be hard. It's awful seeing people struggle like that. I volunteered at the care home for a while, it really puts things into perspective. Speaker_1: It does. You're a good egg, you know that? Right, chilli’s nearly ready! Let’s get the rice on. Anyone want a drink while I finish this off? Speaker_2: A glass of wine would be lovely, actually. A small one. Speaker_3: I'll have a sparkling water, please. Trying to be healthy, remember? (Winks)

Speaker_1: Honestly, this new bus route is a joke. It’s supposed to make getting to the science park easier, but it takes longer now! Speaker_2: Really? I hadn't even noticed a change. I cycle, mostly. Though I did see a bit of a kerfuffle at the bus stop on Trumpington Road yesterday. Speaker_1: Oh? What happened? Speaker_2: Some student was giving it large about… well, everything, really. Something about university fees and exploitative practices. Had a whole placard and everything. Blocked the bus for a good ten minutes. Speaker_1: (Scoffs) Sounds about right for Cambridge. Everyone's got an opinion and a placard. Did anyone try and actually *talk* to him? Speaker_2: A couple of people, but he was pretty entrenched. Very passionate, I’ll give him that. It reminded me a little of some of the stuff at Imperial, actually. More direct action though, usually. Speaker_1: Imperial? Right, that’s where you did your Masters, yeah? How did it compare to Cambridge, overall? I mean, beyond the protest styles. Speaker_2: Hugely different. Imperial was…focused. All engineering, all the time. Cambridge feels… broader. More historical, obviously. And a lot more emphasis on tradition. Speaker_1: Tradition meaning pointless formal dinners and having to wear a gown? Speaker_2: (Laughs) Amongst other things. At Imperial, if you needed a lab, you booked it and got on with it. Here, you have to apply for access, write a risk assessment, and possibly present it to a committee. Speaker_1: Oh, *brilliant*. Sounds utterly exhausting. Speaker_2: It can be. But it’s also… charming, in a frustrating way. It forces you to think through things, I suppose. It’s just… slower. And more expensive, when you factor in the gown hire. Speaker_1: Speaking of expensive, have you been to the Cambridge University Press bookshop lately? They’re charging an arm and a leg for everything. I needed a specific linguistics textbook for a project and nearly had a heart attack. Speaker_2: Yeah, it's ridiculous. I've started ordering everything online. It’s cheaper, even with the postage. They're relying on the tourist trade, I think. Everyone assumes anything with the Cambridge name on it must be gold-plated. Speaker_1: Exactly! It’s just… frustrating. You’d think a university town would have reasonably priced books. It feels like they’re actively trying to price students out of learning. Speaker_2: Well, they’re certainly not making it easy. Maybe this student protester had a point, even if his methods were a bit… disruptive. Speaker_1: Maybe. Though blocking the bus probably didn't win anyone over. Still, it's all a bit much, isn’t it? The buses, the book prices, the bureaucracy… sometimes I just want to run away back to Sunderland. Speaker_2: Back to the land of sensible bus routes and affordable textbooks? I can see the appeal. Though I doubt you’d find a decent engineering consultancy job there. Speaker_1: True. Trade-offs, I guess. Fancy a cuppa to commiserate about the perils of Cambridge life? Speaker_2: Sounds perfect. I’ll put the kettle on. And maybe we can brainstorm ways to circumvent the University Press’s pricing strategy. Speaker_1: Excellent plan. Operation: Affordable Learning is a go! Speaker_2: (Smiling) Right then. Let’s do it.

Speaker_2: Honestly, this cheese board is ridiculous. They’ve just… dumped a load of different things on it. Do you even *like* goat's cheese, Mary? Speaker_1: Oh, I do, actually. Not the really strong stuff, mind you. A little goes a long way. Though, I’m more interested in these olives. Are they stuffed? Speaker_3: They are, Mum. With pimento, I think. Honestly, this place is lovely though. A good find, Sarah. It's nice to get out of Birkenhead for a change. Speaker_2: Glad you think so, Chloe. I stumbled across it online. Needed somewhere halfway between our places, and Hunsonby seemed perfect. Beautiful countryside. Speaker_1: It is pretty. Reminds me a bit of County Clare, actually, though nothing quite matches Ireland, does it? Though I suppose you wouldn't remember County Clare, being a little babe when we last went. Speaker_3: I have vague memories, Mum. Mostly rain and sheep. And Grandma telling me horrifying stories about selkies. Speaker_2: (Laughing) Oh, brilliant! Your Grandma was a character. Speaking of characters, how’s Liam? Still causing mayhem? Speaker_1: He's a handful, that boy. Absolutely a handful. He tried to convince me the other day that square roots were a conspiracy theory. A conspiracy theory! Imagine, after thirty years teaching the blessed things. Honestly, where do they get it from? Speaker_3: Sounds like my nephew, Alfie. He’s currently convinced dinosaurs aren't real and the museums are all part of a massive hoax. Speaker_2: Oh, kids! They're amazing, aren’t they? Little sponges for nonsense. How is Daniel, by the way, Sarah? Are things... going well? Speaker_2: And are you still seeing him? Speaker_1: Oh, Daniel’s grand. He’s coming up next weekend, you know. Finally. Been ages. He’s bringing that friend of his, Mark, too. Apparently, Mark's a history buff. Hoping he doesn’t corner me with talk of the Wars of the Roses. I’ve enough trouble remembering fractions as it is. Speaker_3: Oh, good! That’s lovely, Mum. It’s good to have someone around. Do you think they'd mind if we all tagged along to that little market in Penrith on Saturday? Speaker_1: Oh, I don’t know, darling. I didn’t want to impose. Daniel and Mark have been looking forward to a quiet weekend. Speaker_2: I'm not sure I'd call a weekend with your mother quiet, honestly. But yes, you can tag along. As long as I get a chance to browse the vintage clothes. Speaker_3: (To Speaker_2) You and your vintage clothes! Honestly, you’d think you were living in the 1950s. Speaker_2: What’s wrong with the 1950s? Excellent fashion sense, good music… less obsession with social media. Speaking of which, I was trying to explain to my boss the other day the difference between ‘affect’ and ‘effect’. He truly thought they were interchangeable. It's appalling the state of the English language these days. Speaker_1: Oh, you’re telling me! My students used to drive me mad with their misuse of ‘there’, ‘their’, and ‘they’re’. It was a constant battle. And don't even get me started on the apostrophe. Speaker_3: It's just laziness, honestly. People can’t be bothered to think anymore. My job is full of people who can't write a coherent email. It’s frustrating.

Speaker_1: Honestly, it’s just… relentless, isn’t it? All this concrete. You wouldn’t think, would you, being right next to the river, that you’d see so much grey. Speaker_2: It is a bit grim, this stretch. Though, it does improve as you get closer to Greenwich. More greenery. And you can actually *see* across the river properly then. It’s just… Woolwich feels very… functional. Speaker_1: Functional is a polite word. It feels like someone just dumped a load of buildings here. And look at the O2. Still can’t believe they built that monstrosity. Think of the cost. Speaker_2: It’s alright, isn’t it? Not to my taste, but it’s become a landmark. The kids quite like going there for concerts. Though getting *to* it is a nightmare. We really need a car, don’t we? Speaker_1: Don’t even start. We’ve had this conversation a hundred times. Where would we *park*? And the cost! Insurance, petrol… it’s just not worth it. We manage perfectly well with public transport. It's just inconvenient sometimes, especially when we're all lugging stuff for a family holiday. Speaker_2: True. Remember that trip to Cornwall last year? Getting all the beach gear and the kids' stuff onto the train was… an experience. Though, at least we didn’t have to worry about traffic. Speaker_1: Exactly. And honestly, thinking about driving all that way, sitting in jams… it gives me anxiety just thinking about it. It’s less stressful, even if it takes a bit longer, to get the train. Speaker_2: I suppose. It's just... I was reading a recipe online the other day, an American one, and all the measurements were in cups! Cups! What is a cup? Is it a mug? Is it smaller? It’s infuriating. Speaker_1: Oh, don’t even get me started on American measurements. It’s all so imprecise. We have perfectly good metric system. It’s baffling why they haven’t adopted it. Speaker_2: It’s a whole different philosophy, isn’t it? Everything over there is… bigger. More dramatic. More… *cup-shaped*. It makes you wonder, doesn’t it, what’s the point of all this striving? All this building? All this… volume? Speaker_1: (laughs) You’re getting philosophical on me now. It’s a lovely day for it, I suppose. Though I think it’s more about distracting ourselves from the fact we’re walking past a sewage works. Speaker_2: Good point. Distraction is key. Perhaps the point *is* distraction. To keep us from thinking too much about the… the inherent meaninglessness of it all. Speaker_1: Oh, stop it. You’re going to give me a headache. Let’s just focus on getting to Greenwich and finding a nice pub. And maybe they’ll have proper pints measured in *millilitres*. Speaker_2: Now *that*’s a good idea. A proper pint sounds very appealing. Although… does a millilitre really matter, in the grand scheme of things? Speaker_1: (smiling) Don’t push it. Speaker_2: Just saying. Speaker_1: Come on, let's speed up before we get stuck behind another group of tourists. Speaker_2: Alright, alright. But I'm blaming you if my existential crisis flares up again. Speaker_1: Deal. Speaker_2: Do you think the Cutty Sark is open today?

Speaker_1: Honestly, this weather is *depressing*. It’s been raining non-stop for three days. I tried to go for a run this morning, but I was soaked through within five minutes. Speaker_2: Tell me about it! I'm already damp just thinking about my shift later. At least the residents at the home don’t mind the rain so much, keeps them reminiscing about summer holidays, bless 'em. Though it does mean more laundry, of course. Speaking of which, have you seen my phone? I swear I left it on the kitchen counter. Speaker_3: Probably under a mountain of stuff, Mum. It’s always the way. I think Leo was building a fort there earlier. Oh, and about the sports day… it’s next week, and the forecast is looking grim. Real grim. Speaker_1: Oh no! That's awful. Leo was so excited. He's been practicing his running like a little Olympian. All that effort for a soggy field. Speaker_3: I know! And Maisie’s been going on about the egg and spoon race for weeks. I’m thinking of getting them some waterproofs, but they'll just complain about being too hot and sweaty. Honestly, kids. Speaker_2: Remember when you two were little? We used to have that little inflatable pool in the garden, even in the rain. Your dad said we were mad, but you didn’t care! Gillingham summer rain is practically a rite of passage. Speaker_1: Oh God, yes! And we’d fill it with bubbles, even though it was freezing. Mum, you always let us get away with murder. Speaker_3: You were always braver than me, honestly. I’d be shivering, and you’d be splashing. Anyway, did you see what Emily got Lily for her birthday? Another build-a-bear. Seriously? That girl has a whole army of them. Speaker_1: Oh, Emily. Always overdoing it. Lily’s room is practically a teddy bear convention. I'm trying to get Leo interested in, like, building Lego or something. More practical. Speaker_2: It’s nice they have something to cuddle though, isn’t it? Little comfort blankets. Speaking of comfort, how’s Finn doing with the potty training? Still a work in progress? Speaker_3: Oh, don't even ask. It's a battlefield. One step forward, two steps back. We had a minor victory this morning, but then there was… an incident… this afternoon. I’m starting to think he’s deliberately doing it just to wind me up. Speaker_1: Oh, bless you. It’s the worst, isn’t it? It feels like it goes on forever. I remember trying to get Ben to swim properly, honestly, he was terrified of putting his face in the water. We took him to that swimming pool in Folkestone every week. Useless. Speaker_2: Folkestone pool is freezing! No wonder he didn’t like it. I took your dad there once, years ago. He nearly turned blue. We had to get him a hot chocolate and wrap him in a towel. Speaker_3: (laughing) Oh, Dad. He always complained about the cold. You know, I really need to get a new blender. The old one’s making the most awful noise. It sounds like it’s about to explode every time I use it. Speaker_1: I can take a look at it later, if you want. Maybe it just needs tightening up or something. I’m surprisingly good at fixing things, you know, for a humanities grad. Speaker_2: That’s lovely of you, dear. Anything to save a bit of money, right? Honestly, everything is so expensive these days.

Speaker_1: Right, so, genuinely, what’s the big picture looking like for you? Beyond just surviving term three. Speaker_2: (Sighs) Term three *is* the big picture right now, to be honest. But… you're right to ask. I’ve been doing a lot of thinking. The Head of Department keeps hinting about a potential Lead Practitioner role next year. It’s… tempting. More responsibility, more pay, but honestly, more paperwork. Speaker_1: Paperwork is the enemy of all good things. But Lead Practitioner could be good for your CV, right? Long game. You’ve always talked about wanting to potentially move into educational consultancy, eventually. Speaker_2: Exactly. It's that 'eventually' that feels so… distant. And frankly, after twenty years in the classroom, the thought of *more* meetings feels exhausting. Though, maybe it’s just the Australian sun frying my brain. Speaker_1: (Chuckles) Could be the sun. Or the sheer volume of spiders. But seriously, think about what would genuinely *fulfil* you. Not just what looks good. We’ve finally got the freedom to be a bit selfish with our aspirations, haven’t we? No mortgages, no kids demanding everything... Speaker_2: Don't remind me about the kid thing. My sister just sent me pictures of little Leo. It's adorable, meltingly so… and simultaneously makes me feel slightly guilty. Speaker_1: Guilt is unproductive. We’ve had this conversation a million times. We made a conscious decision, remember? To focus on experiences, travel, build something *ours*. Speaking of which, have you heard back from Sarah and Mark about joining us in Thailand next year? Speaker_2: Mark emailed. He's cautiously optimistic. Sarah’s still juggling work commitments, apparently. She’s angling for a sabbatical. Said she’s finally brave enough to ask. Speaker_1: Good for her! Thailand with them would be amazing. We could rent a little villa, do some diving, actually learn to cook Thai food properly… Speaker_2: Mmm, that sounds idyllic. I’ve been looking at some online TEFL courses, actually. Just… playing with the idea. If we were spending extended periods overseas, I could potentially pick up some freelance tutoring work. Keep the skills sharp, earn a bit of pocket money. Speaker_1: Now *that’s* a smart idea. You'd be brilliant at that. And it means we don’t solely rely on my fluctuating tech investments. Building a diversified income is key. I've been pitching that app idea to a couple of venture capitalists. Still early stages, but the feedback’s been positive. Speaker_2: That's fantastic, darling! You’ve been working on that for ages. I’m so proud of you for just going for it. Have you thought about what it would look like, if it *did* take off? Would we even come back to the UK? Speaker_1: Honestly? I'm starting to wonder if ‘home’ is becoming a feeling, not a place. We could base ourselves anywhere. New Zealand, maybe? It's been too long. Speaker_2: Oh… that’s… a big thought. My mum would have a field day. But yes. New Zealand does call to me. And we promised your dad we'd visit more… though he's probably more interested in assessing my gardening skills. Speaker_1: (Laughing) He is. Right. Okay. We've covered lead practitioner roles, potential Thai adventures, freelance tutoring, app ideas, and possible repatriation to the land of the long white cloud. I think we need another glass of wine to process all this.

Speaker_1: Honestly, I still can't believe you’ve never played Pokémon. Not even a little bit? Speaker_2: Nah, never got it. All that catching and battling… seemed a bit much, innit? Always preferred a good RPG with a story. Speaker_3: You're missing out, seriously. Pokémon was *life* growing up. Remember trading cards at primary school? Absolute chaos. Speaker_4: Oh god, the playground Pokémon card economy. It was wild. People were practically bartering their lunch money for a holographic Charizard. Speaker_5: My little brother was obsessed. Used to try and ‘evolve’ his actual pet hamster. Poor thing. Speaker_1: (Laughing) No way! What? Speaker_5: Yeah, he thought if he fed it enough weird stuff, it’d turn into something stronger. Mum nearly lost it. Speaker_2: Kids are mental. Speaking of mental, did you see old Mrs. Higgins at the bus stop earlier? Giving me proper side-eye 'cause I didn't hold the door open for her. Speaker_3: Oh, she’s a nightmare. Thinks everyone's out to get her. And she has a face like a slapped arse, doesn't she? Speaker_4: Rude but true. Manners are just…gone. No one has them anymore. Especially not on the roads. Speaker_1: Tell me about it. Someone nearly ran me off the road on the way here. I gave them a bit of a beep, though. Felt good. Speaker_2: You didn't, did you? You and your road rage. You’re like a coiled spring, ready to fight over a parking space. Speaker_1: It's not road *rage*, it’s assertive driving! And it’s just… sometimes you feel like you’re in fight or flight, you know? Everything’s just a bit *much*. Speaker_3: I get that. Everything's stressful at the uni library right now. It’s all deadlines and stressed-out faces. I just want to hide under a blanket with a box of After Eights. Speaker_4: After Eights are the ultimate comfort food. Remind me to get some for our camping trip next month. Speaker_5: Camping? Are we still doing that? Thought that was off after… well, after last year with the midges. I swear they tried to carry me away. Speaker_1: We are! We’re going to a different site this time. Hopefully, fewer bloodsucking insects. Plus, I've got a fancy new mosquito net. It's got fairy lights. Speaker_2: Fairy lights? What is this, a festival? Speaker_1: It makes it cosy! Anyway, right, someone needs to pop to the shop. I’m out of Malteasers. And Amy, you’re closest. Speaker_3: Oh, come *on*. I’m studying! Speaker_4: I nominated you! It’s your turn. Plus, I need a Red Bull. I practically live on them during exam season. Speaker_5: I could go, but my Fitbit says I’ve already done enough steps for one day. Gotta hit that 10,000, you know. Speaker_2: A Fitbit? Seriously? You're tracking your steps? It's a pub trip, not a marathon. Speaker_5: It's motivating! Keeps me accountable. Speaker_1: Okay, look, does anyone want to go to the shop or am I going to have to wrestle someone for the car keys? I swear, I remember when that Costa used to be a proper service station, with a shop that sold everything. Now it's all overpriced coffee and uncomfortable chairs. Speaker_3: I'll go. Fine. But you’re all owing me big time. And I want a Jaffa Cake as well, not just Malteasers.

Speaker_1: (Chewing thoughtfully) That gravy’s good, Elsie. Proper good. Not like that watery stuff you get at the pub these days. Speaker_2: (Smiling) Oh, thank you, Arthur. It’s just a bit of beef stock, thickened with flour, nothing fancy. Years of practice, that’s all. Speaker_3: It *is* lovely, Elsie. Seriously. And the roast potatoes are perfect – crispy on the outside, fluffy inside. You’ve outdone yourself. Speaker_4: Absolutely. I think I’ve officially eaten my weight in potatoes. Though, to be fair, I was pretty hungry after that lecture this afternoon. Student essays… honestly, some of them. Speaker_1: Essays, eh? What are they writing about now? Everything’s all ‘woke’ and political, isn’t it? Saw it on the telly last night. Blimey. Speaker_3: (Chuckles) It depends on the module, Grandad. I had one today on the socio-political impact of… well, it’s rather complicated. Let’s just say it involved a lot of critical race theory. Speaker_2: Critical what-now? Sounds dreadful. Give me a good gardening programme any day. Gardener’s World is a lifeline this time of year. Speaker_4: He’s got a point, Elsie. I’ve been binge-watching that football documentary on Netflix. About the 90s Premier League. Proper nostalgia. Speaker_1: Football! Now *there's* something I understand. Norwich were rubbish again, weren’t they? Saw the score online. Honestly, they’ll be relegated if they carry on like this. Speaker_3: They did put up a bit of a fight against Liverpool last weekend, though. Speaker_1: A bit of a fight? They got thrashed! Three-nil, wasn't it? It's a disgrace. Used to be a time when Norwich could hold their own. Speaker_2: Well, things change, Arthur. You can’t live in the past. Speaking of changes, are we still on for the garden party next month? I've started thinking about the decorations. Speaker_4: Sounds good to me! I can help with… um… logistical things. Making playlists, maybe? Speaker_3: I can do the cake! I've been experimenting with a new lemon drizzle recipe. It's rather impressive, if I do say so myself. Speaker_1: (Eyes lighting up) A lemon drizzle? Now you're talking. Elsie used to make a good lemon drizzle. Not as good as your mother’s, mind you. Beatrice could bake a cake that would raise the dead. Speaker_2: (Smiling fondly) Oh, Beatrice. She had a talent. And a mischievous streak. Speaker_3: Buttercup’s a sturdy lass, she'd have been alright. It just... slipped. That log’s a bit wonky. Speaker_2: (Grinning) Maybe it was trying to escape the pineapple pizza smells! Speaker_1: (Shakes her head, smiling) Oh, you two. Honestly. Now, let's put some music on. Something a bit more cheerful than the grumbling of Old Man

Speaker_1: Right, so milk first, or tea bag first? Honestly, it’s a fundamental life decision. Speaker_2: (Chuckles, stirring something on the hob) Tea bag first, always. Milk after. Although, I wouldn’t trust any action hero who willingly goes through that much cosmetic… enhancement. Speaker_1: Exactly. It's all a bit suspect. It's like, just…be normal. Eat your greens. Which, by the way, I haven't done nearly enough of lately. I need to start being less reliant on biscuits. Speaker_2: (Sniffing the air) You and me both. I haven’t seen a vegetable in approximately three days. All research, all the time. I did attempt to make a soup last week, but it ended up resembling wallpaper paste. Speaker_1: (Laughing) Wallpaper paste? Oh, dear. Maybe stick to the theoretical flavour profiles, then. And leave the actual cooking to me. I might even attempt a chip butty sometime this week, just for old times’ sake. Speaker_2: You are a lifesaver. Honestly. Cambridge needs you, and your chip butty expertise. Speaker_1: I’m just doing my civic duty. Now, here's your tea. Milk after, as per your scientifically-proven method. Speaker_2: Perfect. Thank you. You’re the best. Speaker_1: I know. Speaker_1: Right, okay, my turn! Ugh, this is a tough one… “Astronaut.” Oh dear. No describing sounds, no saying ‘space’… oh, this is going to be awful. Speaker_2: You’ve got this, Cariad! Speaker_3: (Groaning) Don't remind me. I thought I was going to end up tumbling down a mountainside. My knuckles are *still* white thinking about it. Speaker_1: Honestly, this is a lovely turnout for an Alumni Day, isn’t it? I wasn't sure what to expect. Speaker_2: It is, yeah. I think the free wine helps! Though it’s nice to see so many people still connected to the Faculty after all this time. Are you an alumnus yourself? Speaker_1: Just recently. Finished my Masters in Applied Linguistics last year. It’s amazing how much language can tell you about a culture, and history. Are you still involved with any research, Professor? Speaker_3: Oh, dabbling, dabbling. Mostly mentoring students now. Though I still try to keep my hand in with sociolinguistics. Spent a good portion of my career looking at dialectal variations across the country. My wife and I are Londoners originally, but we’ve lived in Cambridge for… well, too long to count. Speaker_2: London's changed so much! I haven't been back properly in ages. My family’s still there, though. Speaker_3: It has. Though some changes are positive, I suppose. Although I can't say I understand a word the youngsters are saying these days! It’s all… slang, isn’t it? Reminds me of when I visited Wales with a rugby team years ago. Couldn't decipher a single conversation. Speaker_1: (Smiling) Rugby? You played? Speaker_3: Briefly. Back in my youth. Wasn’t much good, truth be told. More a spectator these days. Though honestly, the rules are getting far too complicated. Used to be a much simpler game. You just had to run with the ball! Speaker_2: I’m a terrible sports fan, I confess. I tried to get into football, but it just… didn’t click. Speaker_1: Me neither. Though I do enjoy a good tennis match now and then. Wimbledon is a must, even if it’s just for the strawberries and cream. Speaker_3: Ah, Wimbledon! A British institution. Now *that*’s something worth preserving. Tell me, Chloe, what drew you to Applied Linguistics specifically?

Speaker_1: Honestly, it’s so weird being back here. Feels like ages since I’ve properly seen you both. Two years is… a long time, isn’t it? Speaker_2: It *is* a long time, Liam. Still wrestling with angry patients and dodgy teeth? Speaker_2: You have *no* idea. Mrs. Higgins decided to argue with me about the price of a scale and polish yesterday. Like I make up the prices! Remember Auntie Carol used to work in a warehouse? Speaker_1: Vaguely. Isn’t she still going on about the ice bucket challenge? She did like three videos. Speaker_2: (Groans) Don't even. She’s still sharing things on Facebook about how it ‘changed the world’. It was a moment, Carol, a moment! She forwarded me one yesterday, with a picture of her looking really proud. Speaker_3: Oh god, the Facebook. I had to unfriend Uncle David last month. He started posting conspiracy theories. It was exhausting. Seriously, what *is* it with our family and Facebook? Speaker_1: It’s a slippery slope. Remember when Grandma got addicted to FarmVille? She wouldn't talk about anything else at Christmas. Speaking of family, how are the kids, Chloe? Are they still driving you mad? Speaker_2: (Smiling) Constantly. Leo’s at that age where everything is a negotiation. Absolutely *everything*. And Maisie's started asking about adoption. She had a project at school about different families. It was sweet, but a bit…heavy. Speaker_3: Oh, wow. That's... mature of her to ask, isn't it? Did you explain everything okay? Speaker_2: We did our best. It opened up a really good conversation, actually. It's made me think we should maybe look into fostering at some point. Speaker_1: That’s amazing, Chloe. Really. I always thought you'd be a brilliant foster mum. Speaker_3: It suits you. You’re so patient. Unlike some people I know… (She glances pointedly at Liam). Remember when you tried to build that Lego Millennium Falcon and gave up halfway through? Speaker_1: Hey! That was a complex build! And it *looked* good for the first few hours. Anyway, I'm better at things that aren't requiring miniscule brick fitting. How’s Ben? Still doing long hours? Speaker_3: Exhausting. He’s been talking about a promotion, but it means more responsibility and even longer hours. I keep telling him his health is more important… He just brushes it off. He never really did proper exercise at school, just avoided the PE lessons. It's a shame. Speaker_2: Sounds familiar. My dad was the same. He insisted he was “too busy” to exercise, then complained about his knees. Mum was always telling him to get off his backside. It’s a Bedford thing, I reckon. We’re all a bit too fond of a sit-down and a biscuit. Speaker_1: Probably. You can’t beat a good Bedfordshire biscuit, though. Although, I’ve been trying to cut down on the sugar. Trying. Speaker_3: Good luck with that! Pass the crisps, would you

Speaker_1: Honestly, this coffee machine is driving me round the bend. It makes a lovely cup, when it *works*, but half the time it just gurgles and spits, and then refuses to froth the milk.
