Designed to fall apart after a year. It’s infuriating. Speaking of falling apart, have you two given any more thought to the storage costs? The removal people quoted me a fortune for keeping everything while we sort out the house. Speaker_1: A fortune is right. I nearly choked on my tea when I saw the estimate. Apparently, needing space for "sentimental items" incurs a premium. Sentimental items! It's just a load of boxes filled with old photographs and my grandmother’s china. Speaker_2: I did a bit of digging online, and there's a self-storage facility just outside Penrith that’s marginally cheaper. Not by much, but every little helps. Though even then, it's going to eat into the renovations budget, isn’t it? Speaker_3: It is. It's all eating into the renovations budget. Honestly, I'm starting to wonder if we should just sell everything and move into a bungalow. Less to worry about. Less to store. Speaker_1: Don't be ridiculous, Arthur. You spent years building up your collection of antique maps! You can’t just abandon that. Speaker_3: I know, I know. It’s just… frustrating. It’s not just the money, it’s the whole mess of everything. Then you turn on the news and it’s just…well, you know. Politics. Speaker_2: Don’t get me started. I was reading an article about the Labour leadership race this morning. It's all so…predictable. More infighting. More empty promises. Speaker_1: I’m losing faith in *all* of them, to be honest. It feels like no one is listening to the ordinary person anymore. They're all too busy jostling for position. Remember when people actually went into politics to *make a difference*? Speaker_3: Idealism. A dangerous thing, idealism. It gets crushed pretty quickly in that world. I used to be quite idealistic, you know. Thought I could change things, make a real impact in my field. Speaker_2: You did make an impact, Dad. You were a brilliant engineer. Everyone always said so. Speaker_3: That's kind of you, love. But it all feels a bit…pointless now. Building pipelines for an industry that’s destroying the planet. What was the point of all that? Speaker_1: Don't beat yourself up about the past, Arthur. You made a good living, provided for your family. You can’t be held responsible for the decisions of corporations. Although… that pipeline *was* awfully close to the Lake District. Speaker_2: Mum! Speaker_1: I'm just saying! And look, let's not ruin our morning coffee – even if the machine is being difficult – by dwelling on the state of the world. Shall we talk about something less depressing? Like…what colour to paint the spare room? Speaker_3: Oh, please no. Not colour charts again. I swear, Mary, you’ve been looking at paint samples for six months.

Speaker_1: Honestly, Mum, the thought of Christmas already fills me with dread. Not the *day* itself, necessarily, but the build-up. The frantic shopping, the endless cooking… It's just… a lot. Speaker_2: Oh, now, darling, don’t say that. Christmas is magical! Though, I do agree about the shopping. It's become so commercialised, hasn’t it? Remember when it was about making things, not *buying* things? Speaker_1: Vaguely. I was quite little. I remember Mum trying to get me to make paper chains, which ended up looking like mangled worms. It felt less magical and more… sticky. Speaker_2: (Laughing) Oh, you always were a creative one! No patience for neatness. So, have you started thinking about what to get anyone yet? Your father's birthday's barely been and gone. Speaker_1: No, not really. I was thinking maybe a weekend away for you and Dad? Somewhere quiet. You both deserve a break. You’re always working, aren't you? Still doing consultancy? Speaker_2: Still plugging away, yes. It keeps me busy, keeps the brain ticking over. It’s mostly online now, thankfully. Less travelling. Although, this last project… a company in Birmingham… honestly, the bureaucracy! It took me three days just to get access to their systems. Speaker_1: Oh, bless you. Sounds exhausting. Are you enjoying it though, generally? Is it fulfilling? Because you seemed a bit down last time we spoke. Speaker_2: It’s… alright. It pays the bills. I miss the teaching, I have to admit. The direct interaction with people, the feeling of actually *helping* someone learn. Consultancy is a bit… detached. Speaker_1: You were such a brilliant lecturer. You should go back to it. There’s a lot of demand for experienced people. Maybe a part-time position? Speaker_2: I’ve considered it. But the universities… they’re all so focused on research now, aren't they? Teaching is almost secondary. And the pension… I’m not sure I could afford to give up the security of my consultancy earnings. Speaker_1: That's fair. It’s a tricky one. What about the grandkids? Are you seeing them much? Leo's getting so big! Speaker_2: Not as much as I’d like. Sarah's always so busy with work and little Leo and everything’s so far away now you’re in Devon. We had him for a night last week, though. He absolutely adores building dens. We turned the entire living room into a fortress! It was chaotic, but wonderful. Speaker_1: Oh, that sounds lovely! I wish I could see him more often too. Maybe we could make a proper Christmas visit? Stay for a few days? Speaker_2: That would be fantastic, darling. Absolutely fantastic. And your brother, David? Is he coming down this year? Speaker_1: I think so. He said something about needing a break from London. He’s still going strong with the photography, isn't he? Seemed really happy last time I saw him. Speaker_2: He is a good boy, David. Always has been. Though a bit of a dreamer. He needs to get himself settled, find a nice girl. Speaker_1: Mum! You and your matchmaking! He's perfectly happy on his own. Let him be. Speaker_2: (Smiling) Just saying! A partner would do him good. Anyway, back to Christmas. Perhaps we can start brainstorming gift ideas now? Before the shops get even more manic.

Speaker_1: Honestly, I thought Gran was gonna kill Grandad last night. The snoring! It was like a foghorn. Speaker_2: (Chuckles) You’re telling me! I was half-expecting the ceiling to come down. He wasn't letting *anyone* get a wink of sleep. Did you hear that little snort he does right before a proper rumble starts? Speaker_3: Oh god, the snort. It's a warning sign. Like a tiny, congested trumpet. I actually shoved my pillow over my head, it was that bad. I swear, he practices it. Speaker_4: My dad snores a bit, but it’s nothing like that. It’s more of a gentle purr. Your Grandad sounds…intense. Speaker_5: Intense is an understatement. It’s a full-on orchestra. Remember when we stayed at their house for that football match and he kept waking himself up with it, then just…rolled over and started again? Speaker_1: Oh, brilliant memory! He didn't even register it happened! Completely oblivious. Speaking of oblivious, have you seen Sarah lately? She’s gone all quiet. Speaker_2: Quiet? Nah, I saw her in Waterfields yesterday. She was having a right good natter with Brenda behind the counter. She was moaning about her coursework, naturally. Speaker_3: Oh, Waterfields. I went this morning. Got a couple of those little sausage rolls. Honestly, they’re addictive. And Brenda slipped me an extra éclair. She’s a legend. Speaker_4: I need to go to Waterfields! I’ve been craving one of their jam doughnuts all week. And they do the best Richmond sausages, don’t they? Proper meaty. Speaker_5: Richmond sausages *are* top tier. Although, me Nan swears by the ones from the market. Says they’ve got more flavour. She's a bit of a sausage connoisseur. Speaker_1: Your Nan’s a woman after my own heart. My Grandad used to carry a handkerchief *specifically* for wiping his sausage roll fingers. A proper linen one! Speaker_2: That's… dedication. I’ve lost count of how many times I’ve wiped my hands on my jeans after a sausage roll. Speaker_3: You animal! You can’t just use your jeans! It’s a sacred food item! It requires respect. And a linen handkerchief, clearly. Speaker_4: (Laughing) You’re all mad! But I’m totally getting a linen handkerchief now. For sausage roll emergencies. Speaker_5: So, back to Sarah…Did she mention if she’s seeing Ben anytime soon? Haven’t heard anything about them for ages. Speaker_1: No, she just said she was focusing on her dissertation. Didn’t mention Ben at all. Which is weird, isn't it? They were inseparable last month. Speaker_2: Could be one of those temporary break things. You know, the dramatic student romances. They’ll be back together by next week, probably after a tearful reconciliation involving late-night kebabs. Speaker_3: Probably. They’re a bit of a whirlwind, those two. Honestly, I give them a month. But I'm happy to be proven wrong! The entertainment value alone is worth it. Speaker_4: Well, if they do break up, she knows she can always come here for a jam doughnut and a good moan. Waterfields cures everything. Speaker_5: True that. And we're always here for her, even if it means listening to endless stories about Ben and his questionable fashion choices.

Speaker_1: Honestly, that was the busiest weekend *ever*. I feel like I haven’t stopped moving since Friday afternoon. Speaker_2: Oh yeah? What were you up to? Aside from, you know, generally being brilliantly busy? Speaker_1: Well, Friday was Sarah’s birthday, which was lovely, but involved a *lot* of coordinating with everyone to get to the restaurant on time. Then Saturday was the volunteer day at the animal shelter – which was rewarding, don’t get me wrong, but covered in…well, everything. And then Sunday was supposed to be a chilled-out recovery day, but Mum decided it was the perfect time to redecorate the spare room. Speaker_2: Oh, bless her. Always finding a project. Sounds exhausting though. Did the redecorating at least *look* nice? Speaker_1: It will, eventually. Right now it just looks like a bomb’s hit it. She’s gone for a very…bold shade of teal. It’s like, staring into the ocean. Or a slightly aggressive swimming pool. Speaker_2: Teal, eh? A bit much, maybe. My Margaret would never. She’s all creams and beige these days. Says it’s calming. Speaker_1: Calming is good. I needed calming this weekend. How was yours? Did you manage to get out on the bike at all? Speaker_2: A little bit. Saturday was alright, did a decent run around the lanes. But Sunday… rained. Solid. Proper Midlands drizzle, you know? The kind that gets *inside* you. So I ended up spending the afternoon sorting through old invoices. Thrilling. Speaker_1: Oh, the glamour! Sounds…productive. At least you weren’t covered in animal by-products. Speaker_2: True enough. Though dealing with dodgy invoices can feel a bit like that sometimes. Listen, about next weekend… Margaret and I were thinking of driving over to Stratford. Might catch a performance at the RSC. Fancy joining us? Speaker_1: Oh, that sounds *really* nice, actually. Stratford is lovely. What are they doing at the moment? Speaker_2: Midsummer Night’s Dream. Thought you might enjoy that. It’s a bit of light relief after your hectic weekend. Speaker_1: That *does* sound perfect. I’d love to. Let me just check my work schedule tomorrow, but I'm pretty sure I'm free. Speaker_2: Excellent! Margaret will be pleased. She keeps saying you’re too busy to have any fun. Speaker_1: Tell her I'm making a concerted effort. Though she’s probably right. It's just…work’s been a bit crazy lately with the new project launching. It's all go, go, go. Speaker_2: Well, you deserve a break. And a bit of Shakespeare. It’ll do you good. We’ll sort out the details tomorrow, yeah? Speaker_1: Sounds good! Thanks so much for the invite. It's good to actually be *talking* about something other than spreadsheets and animal shelters for a change. Speaker_2: Anytime, love. That’s what family’s for. Now, are we nearly there? My legs are starting to seize up. Speaker_1: Almost. Just around this bend. We can grab a cuppa when we get in. Speaker_2: That sounds like heaven. Speaker_1: Mum’s probably still wrestling with the teal paint. Speaker_2: Oh dear. At least it'll be a conversation starter. Speaker_1: It definitely will be. Speaker_2: Right. Nearly there then…

Speaker_1: Honestly, the Year 10s are *exhausting* this year. They’ve got zero motivation. It’s like pulling teeth to get them to conjugate a simple verb. Speaker_2: Oh, tell me about it! My lot are the same. I think it’s the post-lockdown thing, isn’t it? They’ve just… lost the habit of learning. It’s a real struggle. What languages are you teaching at the moment? Speaker_1: French and a bit of German. Though, the German class is tiny. Five students, and honestly, two of them are only there because their parents made them. It's a bit demoralising, really. You? Speaker_2: Spanish and a very reluctant bunch of Year 7s attempting French. Spanish is alright, I enjoy it, but trying to get them excited about the past participle...it’s a battle. It makes me question everything, you know? Like, am I even doing a good job? Speaker_1: Oh, absolutely. I have those moments too. Especially when they ask, “When are we ever going to *use* this?” and you're scrambling for a relevant response beyond “university applications.” Speaker_2: Exactly! It’s hard to make subjunctive mood sound appealing in the real world. Though, I did take a group to Barcelona a few years ago and seeing them actually *use* the language… that was magical. Speaker_1: Oh, I'd love to do a language exchange trip. It's just getting the budget sorted that's the killer. Speaking of things that are killers… how are you coping with everything now Elsie’s here? Speaker_2: (laughs) Coping is a strong word! It’s… chaotic, lovely, utterly exhausting. She’s seven months now, and just starting to crawl, which is a whole new level of vigilance required. You realize how many things are actually within reach when you’re constantly retrieving them from her tiny hands. Speaker_1: Oh, I can imagine! My sister keeps sending me videos of her nephew, and it's just a constant stream of near-disasters. It’s terrifying and adorable all at once. Are you thinking about going back to work full-time? Speaker_2: That’s the million-dollar question, isn't it? I’m currently on maternity leave, and the thought of leaving her is… heartbreaking, honestly. But financially, we need to. My husband’s been amazing, taking on more childcare, but it’s not sustainable long-term. I'm thinking of going back three days a week to start. Speaker_1: That sounds sensible. A good compromise. I never really understood the pull of wanting a family until recently, but now I'm starting to feel… well, a bit broody, to be honest. It’s scary though, isn’t it? Changing everything. Speaker_2: It absolutely is. It’s the biggest change you’ll ever make, I think. But it’s also… incredible. Even the sleep deprivation and the constant worry. It’s worth it, you know? Speaker_1: I guess you’re right. Maybe I’ll just stick to trying to make my Year 10s conjugate verbs for now. That's challenging enough! Though, to change topics completely… have you been keeping up with your Italian Duolingo streak? Speaker_2: (groans) Don't remind me! It’s currently at 180 days, and I'm terrified I'm going to lose it. Elsie’s taken over my evenings, so finding the time is tough. I feel so guilty admitting I haven't even opened the app for three days. Speaker_1: Oh, don't feel bad! We all drop things sometimes. Maybe we can do a language exchange night? We can practice our French and Spanish, and you can grill me on my very rusty Italian. Speaker_2: That's a brilliant idea! Wine, languages, and complaining about teenagers… sounds like the perfect evening to me.

Speaker_1: Right then, lovely bit of Victoria sponge, wouldn’t you say, Margaret? Just the ticket with a cuppa this afternoon. Speaker_2: It is nice, Arthur. Though a bit sweet, even for me. You know I can’t have too much sugar these days. The doctor’s warnings and all that. Speaker_3: Oh, don't be silly, George, just enjoy it. A little bit of what you fancy does you good. Besides, Arthur makes a cracking sponge. Doesn’t he, Arthur? Speaker_1: Well, I do try. It’s all about the beating, really. Gotta get the air in there. Look at that robin, though. Building a nest again in the pyracantha. Bold as brass, that one. Speaker_2: They are, aren't they? Always the first to spot the new feeders, too. Filled them up this morning, did I. Seed and those little fat balls. Keeps ‘em going through the colder spells, even though it's getting milder. Speaker_3: Have you seen Mrs. Higgins’ garden? It’s completely overrun. Vines everywhere and weeds taller than I am. I swear, she’s given up entirely. Speaker_1: Poor soul. Getting on a bit now, isn’t she? It’s hard work, gardening. Especially when your knees aren’t what they used to be. Speaker_2: She always was a bit… eccentric. Remember those puppets she used to make? Horrible things. All felt and button eyes. Gave me the shivers, they did. Speaker_3: Oh, I remember! She used to put on shows for the grandchildren. They loved them, though, didn’t they? Little Timmy used to be fascinated. Speaker_1: He was a quiet lad, Timmy. Used to follow me around the garden when he was little, asking about the birds. Shame about his diabetes, though. Started so young. Speaker_2: It’s awful, isn't it? Seems to be more and more of it about these days. All that processed food, I reckon. And sugar in everything! Speaker_3: You've got a point there, George. Everything seems to be full of sugar. Even things you wouldn’t expect. It's a wonder any of us are still standing. Speaking of standing, look at old Mr. Peterson trying to prune those roses. He's wobbling all over the place! Speaker_1: He’s a stubborn one, that. Refuses to admit he needs a bit of help. It's all very well being independent, but there's a limit. You don’t want to end up falling and breaking a hip. Speaker_2: They don’t make ‘em like they used to, do they? These young ‘uns just don’t have the same resilience. Everything’s too easy for them. Speaker_3: Now, George, that's not fair. There are plenty of hard-working young people about. You can’t tar them all with the same brush. More tea, anyone? I think I saw a bumblebee trying to get into the honeysuckle. Must get a closer look. Speaker_1: Yes please Margaret, that would be lovely. And you're right, of course. Don’t want to sound like a grumpy old man. It’s just… things change, don’t they? Speaker_2: They do, Arthur. They do indeed. Though a good slice of cake and a bit of sunshine always makes things seem a little brighter. Speaker_3: Absolutely! Now, who wants another biscuit? I’ve got ginger nuts…

Speaker_1: Right, I think I'm going to go for the grilled halloumi with the salad. It smells amazing. Are you having the kebab again, David? Speaker_2: (Chuckles) You know me too well, Sarah. Can't resist a good kebab when in Cyprus. Though, I might try the sheftalia, if they have any left. Old Man Yiannis always sells out quickly. Speaking of Yiannis, did you see him having a right go at Mrs. Papadopoulos earlier? Speaker_1: Oh, no! What happened? She’s usually so meek. Speaker_2: Apparently, she tried to order the lamb chops and told him she wanted them well-done. Yiannis nearly exploded! Said it was a crime against lamb, a sacrilege! She just shrunk back, poor woman. He's got a passion for his cooking, that one. A bit loud sometimes, but a good heart. Speaker_1: (Laughing) Oh, Yiannis. He *is* a character. It reminds me of my Uncle George, utterly uncompromising about his roast potatoes. Must be crispy, must be Maris Pipers, no argument! He drove my Aunt mad. Speaker_2: Reminds me of my sister, actually. Remember how obsessed she was with her Persian cat, Mr. Bigglesworth? She’d practically serve him salmon on a silver platter. She always said he had a sensitive palate. Speaker_1: Oh, goodness, yes! The cat who thought he was royalty. How is she, by the way? It feels like ages since I’ve seen her. I know she wasn't doing well with her arthritis. Speaker_2: She's…managing. It's gotten worse, sadly. She's started seeing a specialist, trying these new injections. Says they help, but she’s still in a lot of pain. It’s heartbreaking, really. She’s always been so vibrant. It’s a harsh reminder, isn’t it? About how quickly things can change. My brother, as you know, he had that scare last year. Speaker_1: I remember. That was awful. You must have been so worried. Speaker_2: Terrified. Absolutely terrified. Made me think a lot about…well, everything. About what really matters. It's why I’m trying to enjoy these little things, you know? This sunshine, this food, a good chat with a friend. Speaker_1: Absolutely. We need to grab these moments when we can. It's wonderful being here in Northern Cyprus, isn't it? So peaceful. I've been trying to learn a bit of Turkish from Ali, the waiter. He’s very patient. Speaker_2: Good for you! I tried a few years ago, but it didn't stick. The numbers are tricky, aren’t they? I couldn't get past 'bir, iki, üç...' Speaker_1: It *is* tricky. I can manage 'bir, iki, üç, dört, beş' but then it all falls apart. Ali says I have a good accent though! He says all English people sound a bit grumpy when they try to speak Turkish. Speaker_2: (Laughing) That’s probably true! We’re not known for our melodic tones, are we? Speaking of tones, I really should get my hearing checked. I've been asking people to repeat themselves more and more. Think I need new hearing aids. Speaker_1: Don’t put it off, David. It makes such a difference, doesn't it? My grandfather was the same, wouldn’t admit he couldn’t hear a thing. Drove my grandmother crazy. Speaker_2: Sounds familiar! My mother was much the same. Stubborn to a fault. Still, I suppose that's family for you. A collection of quirks and stubbornness, all wrapped up in love.

Speaker_1: Honestly, Mum, the commute is killing me. An hour and a half each way. It's just… draining. I keep meaning to look at places closer to London, but everything is so tiny and expensive. Speaker_2: Oh, darling, I know. It’s dreadful. We were talking about that just yesterday, your Dad and I. It’s no life, spending all that time travelling. Have you seen that little development near Wimbledon? Might be worth a look. Though knowing London prices… Speaker_3: (Chuckles) Wimbledon? You’ll need a lottery win for Wimbledon. Still, good on her for looking. When *I* started commuting into Birmingham, it was a good forty-five minutes, and I thought *that* was bad. Nowadays, you young’uns are expected to live like this. Speaker_1: It's not just the time, Dad, it’s the cost! Trains are ridiculous. And then I feel guilty about using the car because of the environment. It's a whole thing. Speaker_2: Well, you’re doing a good job, love. Project Co-ordinator sounds very important. Are they giving you any real responsibility yet, or is it still mostly admin? Speaker_1: It’s getting there. I’m shadowing Sarah on the new campaign launch next week, which is exciting. Lots of meetings, lots of spreadsheets… but it’s a step up. Speaker_3: Good, good. You need to be getting your teeth into something. Sarah, is she still with that fella, the architect? Speaker_2: Yes, they're still going strong. They went to Italy last month, apparently. Sent us a lovely postcard. Speaking of which, are we doing a Secret Santa again this year? I’ve been trying to think of something for Sarah. Speaker_1: Oh, yes! I think Auntie Brenda suggested it. I’ve already got a few ideas. Maybe something for the house? You two keep talking about renovations. Speaker_2: We are, aren’t we? That downstairs bathroom… It’s been on the ‘to do’ list for five years now. Your Dad wants to rip the whole thing out, start from scratch. Speaker_3: It’s a disaster area! I’m telling you, it needs a complete overhaul. Plus, the plumbing is ancient. One day it’s going to burst and flood the whole house. Speaker_1: You two need to get organised! Maybe as a Christmas present to yourselves, you could book a consultation with a builder? Speaker_2: That’s not a bad idea, actually. We could. Your Grandad would have loved helping with that, you know. He was a dab hand with anything to do with houses. Speaker_3: He was, wasn’t he? Always tinkering, always fixing things. I miss the old fella. Remember when he tried to build that shed in the garden? It was leaning at a forty-five-degree angle. Speaker_1: (Laughing) Oh, God, yes! Mum kept threatening to call the council. Speaker_2: He was stubborn as an old mule, your Grandad. But he had a good heart. How’s Mark doing by the way? Have you seen him recently? Speaker_1: Not for ages. He's got a massive rugby match next weekend, apparently. He's been training like mad. I’m trying to get tickets, but it's a nightmare. They’re all gone. Speaker_3: Rugby? Pah. Give me a good game of cricket any day. Though, I have to admit, it’s good to see young people getting involved in something. Keeps them off the streets, eh? Speaker_2: Don't start, Arthur. It’s a perfectly respectable sport. Honestly, you and your cricket… I’ve got the shepherd’s pie in the oven, by the way. It’ll be ready in about half an hour. Would anyone like another cup of tea?

Speaker_1: Honestly, I was scrolling through TikTok last night, and you won’t BELIEVE the catfish I found. Proper wild. Speaker_2: Ooh, go on then! I love a good catfish story. Is it one of them where they've stolen photos off a model or somethin'? Speaker_1: Worse, I think. This one was pretending to be…an army veteran. Like, massively decorated, hero status. But then someone did a reverse image search and all the photos were of this bloke who runs a landscaping business in Florida! Speaker_3: No way! That's dedication to a lie, isn't it? What was the catfish trying to get out of it? Money? A date? Speaker_1: Both, apparently. Been chatting to this woman for months, all romantic, building her up…then started hinting at needing help with ‘medical bills’. It was a whole production. She nearly sent him a grand! Speaker_2: A grand?! Bless her. People are mental. It's like, how do you even *think* you can get away with that stuff? Speaker_3: It’s the confidence, innit? The sheer audacity. Reminds me of some of the people on Jeremy Kyle, honestly. Speaker_1: Oh god, don't even get me started on Jeremy Kyle. I was flicking through channels the other day and it came on. I forgot how…intense it was. Speaker_2: Intense is an understatement! It was a societal study in chaos, wasn't it? All the screaming and the lie detectors… Speaker_3: And the storylines! Every episode was like, "My fiancé is my brother!" or "She stole my best mate!" It was ridiculous, but I was hooked. Speaker_1: I know, right? So trashy, but you couldn't look away. I think it was the sheer desperation of some of the people on there. It was…sad, actually. Speaker_2: Yeah, you’re right. It wasn't just entertainment. There were some proper broken people on that show. But then they'd all be shouting at each other and I'd lose the thread of the actual sadness. Speaker_3: Remember that one with the bloke who thought his girlfriend was having an affair with his mum? Speaker_1: Oh my god, YES! And his mum was just sat there, completely unfazed! She was the coolest person on the whole show. Speaker_2: That was a legendary episode. Honestly, they should bring Jeremy Kyle back just for the drama, but like…with a therapist on stage to actually help people. Speaker_1: Now *that's* an idea. "Jeremy Kyle: Healing Edition." Speaker_3: I'd watch that. As long as it still had a lie detector, though. Just for the spectacle, y'know? Speaker_2: Definitely! It wouldn’t be the same without the dramatics. Speaking of dramatics, have you seen what Sarah posted on Instagram?… Speaker_1: Oh, no… what now? Speaker_3: Let me guess, another picture with Mark? . . . Speaker_2: Worse, a video of them 'couple dancing' to some cringe song while she’s wearing one of his shirts. Honestly, I'm living for the mess. . . . . Speaker_1: Oh, my days. She's really going for it then, isn't she? . . . . . Speaker_3: When is she gonna realise he’s useless? Poor lass. . . . .......

Speaker_1: Right, so I was thinking… Paris next summer? Properly thinking about it, not just dropping hints. Speaker_2: (Smiling, stirring her soup) Paris. That’s… ambitious, darling. Ambitious and lovely. What sparked this sudden burst of Parisian longing? It isn’t the pastries, is it? Though, admittedly, they *are* exceptional. Speaker_1: No, it’s… well, it’s a few things. Professor Dubois was talking about the Sorbonne’s library today, and it sounded incredible. All those original texts, metres and metres of Classics. And honestly, I just need a break from… everything here. Uni’s stressing me out, the city’s buzzing, I just want to *breathe* somewhere different. Speaker_2: I understand perfectly. London can be suffocating, even for those of us who’ve lived here decades. And the Sorbonne… ah, memories. I spent a very happy year there, after Vienna, before settling here, really. Though my French was… shall we say… enthusiastic rather than accurate. Speaker_1: Enthusiastic? That’s a polite way of putting it, knowing you. Didn’t you once accidentally order a plate of snails thinking they were mushrooms? Speaker_2: (Laughing) Don’t remind me! The waiter’s face! And my poor Father, he was mortified. He spoke fluent German and Italian, you know. Expecting a certain standard of continental sophistication. Being raised in Italy definitely gave him expectations. Speaker_1: Speaking of languages, I’m struggling with German. It’s just… so structured. All those cases. It feels completely alien compared to Latin, even. And I thought I was good at languages! Speaker_2: It *is* difficult. The declensions can be a nightmare. But think of it as a puzzle. A complex, infuriating puzzle. And it's a beautiful language, truly. My grandmother used to sing Lieder to me when I was little – Schubert, Schumann… Such emotion. Perhaps I could help you with it? Speaker_1: Seriously? That would be amazing! You're way better at it than anyone I've asked so far. Speaker_2: Of course, darling. Anything. Though, first… this computer. It’s being utterly obstinate again. I was trying to upload some photos from Tuscany – the bee pictures, remember? – and it just keeps freezing. It’s infuriating. It used to be so simple, just point and click. Speaker_1: (Sighs) Computers. Always the bane of your existence. Okay, let me have a look. Did you try restarting it? The usual first step. Speaker_2: Naturally! Do you think I’m a complete novice? I restarted it three times! It’s probably a driver issue. Honestly, these modern contraptions. They seem designed to deliberately make one’s life more complicated. Speaker_1: Maybe. Or maybe we’re just getting old. Speaker_2: (Raises an eyebrow) Old? I’ll have you know I just finished a new watercolour piece, inspired by the olive groves near Lucca. It's quite vibrant, actually. Perhaps we can visit Lucca one day. It’s wonderfully quiet, and the pasta is divine. Although not as exquisite as what your Nonna used to make. Speaker_1: You remembered Nonna! I haven't talked about her in ages. And yes, her pasta was legendary. Okay, Paris is contingent on fixing this infernal machine, then. And maybe a crash course in German from a Vienna-trained linguistic expert. Speaker_2: (Smiling warmly) A fair deal, I think. Now, let’s see if I can breathe some life back into this digital beast. And then perhaps we should decide what to do about dessert. I made a lemon tart. It’s very… Parisian.

Speaker_1: Honestly, Dad, you were practically tailgating that lorry! It’s making me nervous. Speaker_2: (Scoffs) Tailgating? I was maintaining a safe following distance. You young people exaggerate everything. Besides, they were going far too slow. Speaker_3: He does have a point, love. They *were* crawling. Though, a bit of space is always good, isn't it? Especially on a motorway. Speaker_1: Crawling is better than causing an accident! And you nearly swerved into the next lane when that car pulled out. Speaker_2: I reacted! That’s what drivers *do*. I’ve been driving for fifty years, I think I know what I’m doing. Speaker_3: Fifty years… goodness me. Remember that awful little Ford Anglia you learned in? The one that smelled of damp dog? Speaker_2: (Chuckles) Ah, Bessie. Now *that* was a car. None of this modern nonsense with all the electronic… whatchamacallits. Speaker_1: Speaking of modern nonsense, have you sorted out the MOT for the Rover yet, Dad? It’s due next week, isn’t it? Speaker_2: It is. I’m taking it to Old Man Hemmings. He’s a bit of a rogue, but he’ll always look after me. Won’t charge me the earth, unlike those big garages. Speaker_3: Hemmings… isn’t he the one who failed my Darren’s car because of a slightly dim brake light? Speaker_2: He’s thorough, is Hemmings. Safety first, eh? Anyway, this traffic's building up. Should’ve left earlier. Seems everyone’s heading to Dorset. Speaker_1: Tell me about it! I’ve got an essay to write on post-structuralism, and I was hoping to get some reading done in the car. Now I’m just watching the brake lights of the car in front. Speaker_3: Post-structuralism… sounds dreadful. What even *is* that? Something to do with buildings and… structures? Perhaps we should stick to the tennis tournament for now. Lions are a little too ambitious, don’t you think? Speaker_1: Right, who wants an apple? It’s a slightly less beige option than school dinner chicken. Speaker_2 & Speaker_3 (in unison): Me! Speaker_1: Okay, okay, one each. And then we need to think about what you’re wearing for the tournament. It might be chilly. Speaker_3: Can I wear my lion costume? Speaker_1: (Smiling) Leo… no. Speaker_3: But I want to tame the tennis balls! Speaker_1: (Chuckles) We'll find something a little more suitable, I promise. Something warm, and sporty. Speaker_2: Maybe my new purple hoodie? Speaker_1: That sounds perfect, Lily. That sounds perfect.

Speaker_1: Honestly, the special effects were incredible, but the plot…thin as a wafer. All flash and no substance, really. Speaker_2: (Chewing thoughtfully) Hmm. That sounds about right for most of these blockbusters these days, doesn't it? Give 'em something shiny to look at and they won't notice the story’s missing a few chapters. Reminds me of Parliament, actually. Speaker_3: (Chuckles) Dad, you always find a way to bring it back to politics. But you’re not wrong. It *was* very… visually arresting. I was thinking about that debate at Cambridge last week, actually, the one about historical teaching. Speaker_1: Oh, the one about narratives? I read a bit about it. A lot of contention, wasn’t there? Seems people are really divided on how much focus should be on, well, perspectives. Speaker_3: Exactly. It felt a bit performative, to be honest. A load of academics shouting at each other about ‘decolonising the curriculum’ while ignoring the practicalities of getting kids to actually *learn* dates and key events. Speaker_2: Decolonising… fancy word. When I was at school, history was about Kings and Queens, battles and empires. Simple. And we learned it all by rote. Probably did us more good than all this… nuanced approach. Speaker_1: But wasn’t that part of the problem, Dad? A very… specific narrative? I mean, my history teachers were brilliant, but it was very focused on British achievements. Very little about, say, the impact of colonialism on other cultures. Speaker_3: That’s the point, isn’t it? It’s not about erasing history, it’s about presenting a more complete picture. But it’s incredibly difficult to balance that with the constraints of the national curriculum. It’s already crammed full. Speaker_1: It is. And revised constantly! Honestly, the poor teachers are running to keep up. Remember when they changed the way they taught Maths? Utter chaos. Speaker_3: (Laughing) Oh God, yes. I remember my mum trying to help me with ‘new maths’ and ending up more confused than I was. She’d been taught completely differently. Speaker_2: I never understood all that new maths business. Numbers are numbers, aren’t they? Straightforward. When *I* was at school—which, admittedly, was a long time ago—we had a proper grounding. Latin, Greek… it taught you discipline. Speaker_1: It sounds… intense. I did Latin for a year, hated it. I was much more focused on English Lit. And Drama. Speaker_3: See, that’s the thing. The system needs to be more flexible. University degrees are so expensive now. They need to be *directly* linked to industry, with more opportunities for placements and real-world experience. My firm’s always complaining about graduates lacking practical skills. Speaker_1: Absolutely. I've noticed it with some of my students going on to university. They've got the academic knowledge, but they’re completely unprepared for the realities of the workplace. Perhaps a mandatory year in industry after the second year of a degree? Speaker_2: A year out? Sounds like a good idea. Give them a chance to see if all that book learning is actually worth anything. And maybe teach them a bit of common sense while they’re at it. Nowadays… honestly. Speaker_3: You’re brutal, Dad. Speaker_2: Just being honest, son, just being honest. Now, who’s for pudding? Speaker_1: Me! Chocolate cake, please! I deserve it after battling with Year 10 all day.

Speaker_1: Right proper chilly this morning, innit? Feels like October already, not August. Speaker_2: It does, doesn’t it? Lovely and sunny now, though. Makes a difference. I put the washing out. Hopefully it’ll dry. Everything’s been so damp lately. Speaker_3: Damp is an understatement, Margaret. We had a proper downpour yesterday afternoon. Nearly flooded the patio. Had to send young Thomas out with a mop. Speaker_4: (Chuckles) Sounds like you've got him working hard for his keep. Reminds me of when I was a lad. My old man always had me doing jobs around the house. Said it built character. Speaker_1: Character and blisters, more like. My dad weren't one for making me graft, no. He was always more interested in his pigeons. Spent his whole life with them birds. Daft, really, when you think about it. Speaker_2: Your father was a lovely man, Albert. He always had a kind word. And he did build that magnificent pigeon coop, didn’t he? A real craftsman. Speaker_3: He was. Reminds me… I was sorting through some old photos the other day, and came across one of your mum, Eileen, Albert. She was a beauty. And she always remembered everyone’s name. A proper lady. Speaker_1: Aye, she was. Always worried about everyone else. Always baking. Couldn’t get her to sit still, she couldn’t. Always on the go. Wonder what she’d make of all this, eh? All the trouble in the world. Speaker_4: She’d be heartbroken, I reckon. Reminds me of my grandmother. Lived through the war, she did. Lost her brother at Dunkirk. Never really spoke about it, but you could see it haunted her. These conflicts…they ripple down the generations, don’t they? Speaker_2: They do. It’s awful what’s happening over in Ukraine. Makes you feel so helpless. Brings it all back, doesn’t it? The stories you heard growing up… Speaker_3: Absolutely. And the way the police are dealing with these protests now. Seems a bit heavy-handed to me. Blocking roads, arresting people… Freedom of speech is going out the window. Speaker_4: It's a tricky one, isn't it? Striking a balance between allowing people to protest and maintaining order. But some of those tactics do seem a bit draconian. Still, better than what you see in some other countries. Speaker_1: Speaking of order, Doreen, remember that awful mahogany sideboard your parents had? The one that smelled of beeswax? Speaker_2: (Laughs) Oh, how could I forget? It dominated the whole room! Absolutely enormous. Your mother used to polish it every week, Albert. Said it was an heirloom. Speaker_3: It was. Came down through the family for generations, apparently. My great-great-grandfather brought it over from France. Or so the story goes. Speaker_4: Probably embellished a bit over the years. Still, a lovely piece of furniture. Pity it ended up in the auction. I'd have loved to have had it, but it wouldn’t have fitted in my flat. Speaker_1: It was a beast, alright. The kind of thing they don’t make anymore. Solid as a rock. You wouldn’t find anything like that at IKEA. Everything’s chipboard now. Speaker_2: True. They don't build things to last anymore, do they? Everything is disposable. Makes you appreciate the things that have survived, like that old photo album. It’s funny, isn't it, how a simple photograph can take you right back to another time.

Speaker_1: Right, so just to be clear, you’ve got the keys to the flat, Mum has a box of stuff for you – mostly photos, I suspect – and I’m just…processing the whole ‘last drive’ thing. Feels weird, doesn’t it? Speaker_2: Weird is an understatement, son. Absolutely strange. Thirty-odd years, dropping you kids off at school, picking you up, driving you to uni… and now it’s the last run from your mum’s. Feels like a chapter’s closed, that’s for sure. Though, to be honest, a lot of chapters feel closed recently. Speaker_1: Tell me about it. This whole house move feels like a massive upheaval. You sure you’re alright with all this, Dad? Really? Speaker_2: Of course I am. It’s… sensible. Downsizing. Makes perfect financial sense. Though, a part of me wishes your mother was still around to argue about it. She’d have a whole list of reasons *not* to move, you know. "Too much history," she'd say. "Where will I put the china?" Speaker_1: (chuckles) God, she would. Speaking of financial sense, how’s the mortgage looking on the new place? Everything sorted? Speaker_2: Nearly. The solicitor’s being a bit slow, to be honest. Keeps asking for the same documents again and again. Drives me mad. Standard, I suppose. But yes, the finances are… manageable. Though, don't mention the word 'interest rates' to me, I might have a little fit. Speaker_1: I hear you. They're scary. Listen, are you still feeling a bit rough? You sounded a bit congested on the phone yesterday. Speaker_2: Just a bit of a cold, I think. Old age creeping up on me, that’s all. Shouldn't have been outside helping your sister load the van on Saturday. Damp air did for me. Probably. Though Brenda from work swears it’s going around. She’s been brewing ginger and lemon tea all week. Speaker_1: You should get some of that. Mum always swore by ginger and lemon. Speaking of Brenda, how's work? Still dealing with complaints about broadband speed? Speaker_2: Oh, you have *no* idea. It's relentless. People yelling down the phone, blaming *me* for their internet not working. Honestly, some of them… you’d think I personally built the infrastructure. They’re lucky I'm relatively patient. It's good money, though. Keeps me ticking over. Speaker_1: You deserve a medal. Seriously. So, Auntie Carol, did you manage to speak to her about Christmas? She was asking if we were all going to be at yours this year. Speaker_2: Yes, I did. She’s already planning the menu, naturally. Turkey, stuffing, the works. Expect a full report next time we speak. Honestly, she treats Christmas like a military operation. Speaker_1: (laughing) She does, doesn’t she? Remember that time she tried to deep-fry the turkey? Speaker_2: (groans) Don’t remind me. The smoke alarm went off, we nearly set the kitchen on fire, and the turkey tasted like burnt oil. We ended up ordering pizza. Speaker_1: Good times. You know, I was thinking about… you used to take me to the cinema all the time when I was little. Do you remember that? *Toy Story* was the first film I ever saw. Speaker_2: Of course, I do. Used to get a big bucket of popcorn, didn't I? And you always insisted on sitting right at the front. Nearly gave me a crick in my neck trying to keep an eye on you. Speaker_1: Hey, the closer the better! It was amazing. It's funny, the things you remember. I'm going to miss these drives, Dad. Just… chatting. Speaker_2: I’ll miss them too, son. But it doesn’t mean it has to

Speaker_1: Right, so we’re agreed – roast beef then? Your Nan always loved a good roast, and it feels…fitting, doesn’t it? Speaker_2: Yeah, roast beef’s good. Though she did say last week she wasn’t keen on gravy anymore. Something about it being “too sludgy,” which, honestly, sounded a bit like her. Speaker_1: (Chuckles) Oh, she always had a way with words, didn’t she? Alright, no gravy. We can do horseradish sauce, and maybe a nice minted jelly. Now, the table. I was thinking I’d put Uncle George next to you. He’s been asking after you, and he’ll keep you entertained with his stories. Speaker_2: Oh, no. Please not George. He’ll spend the entire meal talking about his fishing trips and how he almost caught a cod the size of a small child. Can I maybe have Auntie Brenda instead? She’s much kinder. Speaker_1: Hmm. Alright, Auntie Brenda it is. But you owe me one. George will be devastated. And then…let’s see. Your cousin Liam is coming with his girlfriend, right? They can go on the end, near the window. Speaker_2: Yep, that sounds good. He said she’s really looking forward to meeting everyone. She’s a bit shy, apparently. Speaker_1: Oh, bless. We’ll make her feel welcome. Right, food mostly sorted. I’m going to pop down to Billingsgate tomorrow morning for the beef. They have the best quality, and I want it to be perfect. Speaker_2: Billingsgate? Wow, that’s a trek! Are you sure? Old Man Hemmings does a lovely bit of beef down at the market. Speaker_1: Hemmings is alright, but it’s not *Billingsgate* alright? It's her birthday, and I want everything to be special. Plus, I need to get some salmon for myself. Been craving it all week. Speaker_2: Speaking of craving… didn’t you say you were rearranging the kitchen cupboards? Are you still on for finding space for all those candles you bought? Speaker_1: Oh, don't even remind me. It's a disaster! I thought I had a brilliant system, but then I ended up with a mountain of Tupperware and nowhere to put the decorative things. And have you seen how many tins of tomatoes we have? It’s ridiculous. Speaker_2: (Laughing) You do love a bargain tin of tomatoes. I'll help you when I come round on Saturday. We can sort it all out. Speaker_1: That would be amazing, thank you. Oh, and I found some old photos while I was having a clear-out. Some lovely ones of her when she was younger. I’m going to put them on the mantelpiece. Speaker_2: That’s a lovely idea. She always loved looking at old photos. It sometimes…it sometimes brings her back, you know? Even just for a moment. With everything…you know...the dementia. Speaker_1: I know, darling. It’s heartbreaking. That’s why we need to make this birthday as happy and memorable as possible. I'm recording some of the Great British Bake Off tonight; she really likes Paul Hollywood. We can watch an episode after dinner. Speaker_2: Perfect. And I'll make sure I bring her favourite shortbread biscuits. The ones from that little bakery in Stamford, remember? Speaker_1: Oh, she loves those. You’re a star. Right, so beef, no gravy, Auntie Brenda next to you, Billingsgate trip, cupboard chaos, old photos, and Bake Off. Anything else? Speaker_2: Just… let's hope she has a good day. That’s all that really matters.

Speaker_1: Honestly, this pain is ridiculous. I’ve been popping paracetamol like sweets all day. Speaker_2: Still your wisdom teeth then? Are they actually *coming* through, or just… being generally awful? Speaker_1: A bit of both, I think. One's definitely poking, feels like it’s trying to bore a hole straight through my cheek. And the other… well, it just feels like someone’s constantly prodding it with a fork. It’s vile. Speaker_2: Oh god, that sounds grim. Have you managed to get an appointment with a dentist? Is it even possible here in France? Speaker_1: I’ve tried! They’re saying the earliest they can see me is…next Tuesday. Which feels like a lifetime away. Mum keeps saying I should’ve gone to a dentist before we came, but honestly, who thinks to plan dental work around a holiday? Speaker_2: Mum, always the planner. Mine would have just said, “Oh, you’ll be fine, a bit of pain never hurt anyone.” Remember when I broke my wrist and she tried to convince me it was just a sprain? Speaker_1: (laughs) Oh, your mum! Honestly. They're all the same aren't they? Just… dismissive of actual discomfort. Though, to be fair, yours *is* a bit of a tough cookie. Speaker_2: She is. Still, it’s nice being away from it all, even if you're suffering. Just… peaceful. Are you dreading going back to uni? Speaker_1: Oh, massively. I'm gonna have to start properly thinking about dissertations and everything, and I just haven't got the headspace for it right now. I’ve been deliberately avoiding it. And then there's the whole house move thing. Speaker_2: Oh yeah, your folks are still moving, aren’t they? Is it all going okay? Doncaster to…where again? Speaker_1: Lincoln. It’s taking forever. Apparently, the people buying our house are being really difficult. Mum's on the phone constantly, getting stressed. It's a nightmare. She's convinced they're trying to haggle the price down at the last minute because they found a… a hole in the garden shed. Speaker_2: A hole? In a shed? Really? That’s… pettiness on a whole new level. She needs to tell them to sort it themselves if it bothers them so much. Speaker_1: That’s what I said! But she's worried it'll fall through. Honestly, she's a nervous wreck. I’m trying to be supportive, but it's hard when it’s all just…shed-related drama. Speaker_2: Sounds exhausting. Do you think you’ll go home for a bit to help before going back to uni? Speaker_1: Probably. I feel bad leaving her to deal with it all on her own, but I also need to get back and actually…you know…do some work. I’m just putting it off, hoping the wisdom teeth pain will somehow justify my procrastination. Speaker_2: A good excuse, if I ever heard one. Listen, if you need anything, just let me know. I’m happy to distract you by forcing you to attempt to speak French or something. Speaker_1: (grinning) Oh, god, don't threaten me with that. My French is…alarmingly bad. But yeah, thanks. I appreciate it. Maybe we should just focus on enjoying the rest of the holiday, and I’ll deal with the pain, the houses, and the dissertations when I’m back on home soil.

Speaker_1: Right, so, Operation Random Acts of Kindness is a go. Any initial thoughts? Apart from leaving glitter bombs everywhere, which is absolutely off the table, Leo. Speaker_3: (Giggles) But it would be *funny*! Speaker_1: No. Absolutely not. We're aiming for nice, thoughtful, not sparkly chaos. Elsie, you first. What wonderful thing could you do for someone? Speaker_2: Hmm… I could make Mrs. Peterson a card. She always gives me stickers. Speaker_1: That’s lovely, Elsie! A really thoughtful idea. And you, Leo? Something beyond attempting to bedazzle the postman? Speaker_3: I could…help Dad wash the car? Speaker_1: (Raises an eyebrow) A valiant offer. Though I suspect he might suspect ulterior motives involving a favour later. But yes, good! It counts. We could also bake something. I was looking at lactose-free cake and cookie recipes. Your tummy hasn’t been entirely happy with dairy lately, Elsie. Speaker_2: Ooh, cookies! Chocolate chip? Speaker_1: Possibly. Or maybe something with orange… It's nearly Chinese New Year, isn’t it? We could make mooncakes, although those are…a bit more involved. Speaking of which, did you two know it’s the Year of the Dragon? Speaker_3: Dragons are cool! They breathe fire! Can we decorate the house with dragons? Speaker_1: We can definitely decorate. I’ve got some red paper and gold glitter – *responsible* glitter, not the bombing variety – and we can make paper chains. Maybe even try our hand at calligraphy, though my Chinese writing skills are…non-existent. Speaker_2: Mummy, can we have a Chinese takeaway? Speaker_1: We can *discuss* a Chinese takeaway. After acts of kindness, mind you. We don’t want bribery involved. Right, back to ideas. I was thinking about leaving little notes of encouragement in library books. Speaker_3: Or we could use the chess pieces as money! Like, if someone needs a pound, they can have a rook! Speaker_1: (Laughs) That’s…creative. And slightly illogical, but creative. Though I foresee arguments over the relative value of a knight versus a bishop. No, we're sticking to actual money for charitable donations, I think. I've been trying to think of things we can do that don't *cost* a lot. Speaker_2: We could give Grandma flowers! Speaker_1: That’s a brilliant idea, Elsie! We could pick some from the garden, or maybe buy a small bunch. Speaking of Grandma, did you know Auntie Carol is thinking about dying her hair purple? Speaker_3: Purple?! That’s awesome! Speaker_1: I know! She said she wants to “rebel against the grey.” I think she’s having a mid-life crisis, but a colourful one. I was toying with the idea of a subtle blue streak myself, actually. What do you think? Speaker_2: Blue is pretty! Like the ocean! Speaker_3: Can *I* dye my hair purple when I’m older? Speaker_1: (Smiling) We’ll discuss that when you're a bit older, Leo. Let’s focus on making the world a kinder place *before* we worry about vibrant hair hues. Okay, Elsie, card for Mrs. Peterson, Leo, helping Dad with the car – let’s schedule those for tomorrow afternoon. And we'll definitely bake cookies. Operation Random Acts of Kindness: Phase One, commence! Speaker_1:

Speaker_1: Mum, did you *see* Mrs. Henderson’s car this morning? It was… well, it wasn’t really a car anymore, was it? Speaker_2: (Sighs) Oh dear. No, I missed that. What happened? Another seagull incident? They're getting bolder, you know. Saw one try to steal a chip right out of old Mr. Davies’ hand yesterday. Speaker_1: No, way worse! Apparently, someone ran a red light on Queens Road and smashed right into her. She wasn’t in it, thank goodness, but the car… it was awful. All crunched up. Speaker_2: Oh, that’s terrible. Poor woman. Glad she wasn’t hurt. It makes you think, doesn’t it? How quickly things can change. It's a bit like Alice falling down the rabbit hole, isn’t it? One minute you're pottering along, the next… chaos. Speaker_1: Kind of, yeah. Though Alice’s chaos was a lot more… whimsical. Have you read *Alice in Wonderland* to Leo yet? Speaker_2: Not yet, darling. I keep meaning to. He’s been obsessed with dinosaurs lately. Roaring all day long! Such a little terror. Speaking of little terrors, did you notice that new scratch on your knee? How did *that* happen? Speaker_1: Oh, that? Just tripped over the cat in the garden. Felix was being a menace, weaving between my legs. It stings a bit. I think I'll have a scar. Speaker_2: You always were a bit clumsy, my love. It'll fade, don't worry. I have a *fantastic* scar story, actually. When I was about your age, I tried to build a stage for a puppet show in the garden… needless to say, it collapsed, and I ended up with a massive splinter in my hand. Had to go to A&E! Speaker_1: Ouch! Was it painful? Speaker_2: Oh, it was dreadful. But it was worth it for the puppet show! Speaking of shows, are you still practicing your song for the school play? Speaker_1: Yeah, I think so. It’s really hard… it’s that high note in the chorus. And Miss Davies wants me to *really* embody the character. She said I need to find the character’s inner life. Speaker_2: (Chuckles) Sounds intense. What song is it again? Speaker_1: It’s from *Wicked*. “Defying Gravity.” It's so good, but hard to sing. I've been looking at tutorials online, on YouTube, to get the high note right. Speaker_2: Good for you! Using the internet for good. Leo, on the other hand, just uses it to watch videos of people opening presents. He’s convinced that’s the entire point of Christmas. Speaker_1: (Laughing) Boys! What did Grandma send you for your birthday? I haven’t seen it yet. Speaker_2: A rather… interesting knitted tea cosy. Bright orange. With little seagulls on it. Speaker_1: (Bursting out laughing) Seriously?! Grandma and her seagulls! Speaker_2: Absolutely. She said it reminded her of Hastings. Honestly, sometimes I think she just enjoys making me laugh. Have you been doing much reading? I noticed you had that big book by Agatha Christie on your bedside table. Speaker_1: I’m about halfway through, it's really good! It is a bit difficult to get into though! It's mystery so you get stuck. It’s so twisty.

Speaker_1: Honestly, after last night, I feel utterly drained. Giving that advice to the solar panel lot… it's just reliving it all again, isn't it? Feels like Groundhog Day with pylons and turbines. Speaker_2: It *is* exhausting, isn’t it? You put so much into fighting the wind farm, then another one pops up, or now, fields covered in solar. It's relentless. Did they seem receptive to what you said? The solar group, I mean. Speaker_3: Receptive? Aye, they were. Colin, bless him, was scribbling notes faster than I’ve ever seen. They’re a bit…naive, though. Thinking a strongly worded letter to the council will do the trick. They haven't grasped the scale of it yet. Speaker_1: Exactly! It's not about convincing the Development Control Committee. It’s about understanding who *really* pulls the strings. And the money. Oh, the money involved. They need to dig, find out who’s funding the applications, who stands to benefit. Speaker_2: You were right about the planning appeal, though. That's where they nearly tripped themselves up. Not having a proper barrister, relying on a local solicitor who hadn't dealt with anything like it before… a complete disaster waiting to happen. We were lucky to get away with it, honestly. Speaker_3: Lucky and determined. Don’t undersell your work, Margaret. You practically lived in the library for months, chasing down precedents. And you were brilliant at getting the local press onside. That’s crucial. Public opinion can sway things, even with a biased council. Speaker_1: The press helped, certainly. Though I still think they sensationalized it a bit. ‘Save Our Skyline!’ rather dramatic, wouldn’t you say? Still, it got people talking. But honestly, it’s the council itself…they’re just so easily swayed. A few promises of ‘green jobs’ and they’re putty in the hands of these energy companies. Speaker_2: It’s not all their fault. They're under pressure from central government. Foot-dragging on truly sustainable energy solutions puts them in a difficult position. They’re supposed to meet these climate targets, and frankly, wind and solar are the easy answers, regardless of whether they're suitable for the local environment. Speaker_3: Easy and profitable for someone. That's the crux of it. And all this talk of ‘renewable energy’… where’s the investment in *storage*? We can generate all the power in the world, but if we can't store it when the wind isn't blowing or the sun isn’t shining… it’s pointless. Government pours money into subsidies for these projects, but a pittance goes towards serious research into battery technology or alternative storage solutions. It’s bonkers! Speaker_1: Precisely! We need a breakthrough in energy storage. Something beyond lithium-ion batteries. Maybe hydrogen, maybe something else entirely. But it needs serious funding. It's the same old story, isn't it? Line the pockets of the energy companies now and worry about the long-term consequences later. Speaker_2: It’s… frustrating. It makes you feel powerless. Speaking of long-term consequences, have you been following the Scottish referendum at all? Only two weeks now. Speaker_3: Aye. Keeping an eye on it. Looks like it’s going to be a close one. A bit worrying, if I’m honest. A split Britain… not a pretty thought. Speaker_1: I agree. It feels incredibly divisive. Though I do understand the arguments for independence. They feel overlooked and undervalued, don't they? It’s a complicated situation. Speaker_2: Definitely. It'll have repercussions for years to come, whichever way it goes. More political battles ahead, I suspect. Just what we need, after all this turbine nonsense.

Speaker_1: So, how’s the driving going, love? Any closer to passing that test? Speaker_2: It’s…progressing. Slowly. Had another lesson yesterday, and Mr. Henderson, bless him, is still saying my junctions are “ambitious.” Speaker_3: (Chuckles) Ambitious, is it? That's a polite way of saying you’re still shooting the gap! Your father was the same when he first learned, you know. Nearly took out Old Man Hemmings’ hedge on Woburn Road. Speaker_1: Now, Margaret, don't embellish! I didn’t *nearly* take it out. I just…misjudged the width of my father’s Austin A30. It was a narrow escape, admittedly. But it taught me a valuable lesson about spatial awareness. Speaker_2: Right. So, basically, I’m following in your footsteps, Dad. Except with a slightly more modern vehicle and hopefully fewer near-hedge experiences. The parallel parking is the worst. I just get flustered. Speaker_3: You just need to visualise it, dear. Think of it like… threading a needle. Slow and steady. And don’t look in the mirror *too* much – that’s what Derek always says. He gets right stressed watching people park. Speaker_1: Derek’s a backseat driver even when he’s not *in* the car. Speaking of cars, have you looked into insurance quotes yet? That can be a shock, you know. Especially for new drivers. Speaker_2: I’ve had a look, yeah. It's… eye-watering. Trying to add me as a named driver on Mum’s policy is the cheapest option, but even then it’s not exactly budget-friendly. Speaker_3: Well, it’s peace of mind, isn’t it? And you’ll be able to visit more often. Speaking of visits, are you still thinking about that little tour of France this summer? Speaker_2: I am! I’ve been looking at gites in Normandy. Nothing fancy, just a little cottage with a garden. I thought maybe a week or so, just to practice my French and…you know, relax. Speaker_1: Normandy’s lovely. We went there years ago, Margaret and I. The food was excellent. Though I must say, trying to order a simple cup of coffee was an ordeal. My schoolboy French wasn't up to much. Speaker_3: Oh, you’d manage, Arthur. You always charm your way through. What about you, love? Still on for dinner with Bethany and her husband on Wednesday? Speaker_2: Yes, definitely. I promised them ages ago. It’ll be good to catch up. She’s been really busy with a new project at work. Speaker_1: Good, good. Keep in touch with your cousins, that’s important. Family’s all you’ve got in the end. I spoke to your Auntie Sheila yesterday, she sends her love. She’s still complaining about the price of tomatoes. Speaker_3: Oh, Sheila. Always a drama with the tomatoes. Right, I'm off to finish prepping for court tomorrow. Another day, another dodgy defendant. Hopefully, it won’t be too lively. Speaker_2: Good luck, Mum. I signed up for classes though, that helps. Boxing, actually. Speaker_3: Boxing? Wow, that’s a change from spreadsheets and engineering diagrams! Speaker_1: Yeah, well, needed something to release some of this Cambridge traffic frustration. It’s good, genuinely. Though I’m pretty sure I’m perpetually bruised. Speaker_4: I’ve been trying to get back into running. It's just…the weather’s been so unpredictable. One minute it's sunshine, the next it's torrential rain. Speaker_2: Seriously! Speaker_1: Honestly, that was a dodgy call. Dodgy, man. Speaker_2: (Eyes glued to the TV) What? Oh, the offside? Yeah, a bit tight. Though, to be fair, he *was* leaning. Mental, isn’t it? All the timelines and stuff. Speaker_2: Absolutely bonkers, but brilliant. Michelle Yeoh is incredible. Bit of a commitment though, it’s a long one. Maybe having a professional do it next year would be a good shout. Save everyone a lot of stress. And potential back pain. Speaker_1: You're probably right. It's just…expensive. Plus, my Dad genuinely *likes* pottering about. It’s his ‘thing’. Though he does have a tendency to over-enthusiastically prune things into oblivion. Speaker_2: (Chuckles) Sounds about right. Right, look at that! Good tackle. Finally, some proper football. Speaker_1: About time. Though, honestly, they're all just running about like headless chickens. No finesse, no artistry. It's just brute force these days. Remember when Bergkamp used to play? *That* was football. Speaker_2: I’m too young to properly remember Bergkamp, you’re showing your age! Though, I've seen the highlights. He was class, no denying that. What are you planning for Easter besides dodging gardening duties? Speaker_1: Probably just chill, loads of chocolate, maybe a walk if the weather plays ball. We could go punting if it’s nice. You fancy that? Speaker_2: Punting sounds good. And essential chocolate consumption is definitely a priority. It wouldn’t *be* Easter without it. Speaker_1: Couldn’t agree more. (Both turn back to the TV, a brief silence descending as they watch the game.) Speaker_2: Honestly, the ref needs glasses. Speaker_1: Tell me about it. Speaker_2: Maybe he’s a West Ham fan? Speaker_1: (Laughs) Now *that* would explain everything. Speaker_2: Everything. Speaker_1: Alright, let's get another cuppa. Speaker_2: Good shout. Speaker_1: And maybe hide some chocolate from my dad. You never know. Speaker_2: Wise move. A very wise move. Speaker_1: Alright, back in a minute. Speaker_2: Right. Go easy.

Speaker_1: (Sighs contentedly, flipping through a photo album) Ah, look at this one. Young Master Leo, barely able to walk, covered head to toe in chocolate. Must have been… what, three years old? Speaker_2: (Peers over his shoulder) Wow! He looks… intense. Like a tiny, chocolate-covered warrior. Speaker_3: (Chuckles, joining them) Intense is a good word for it. He hadn’t quite mastered the concept of ‘sharing’ back then. Remember the birthday party, Margaret? The cake incident? Speaker_4: (From her armchair, knitting) Ach, how could I forget? Poor wee Sophie was devastated. Leo decided her entire slice was rightfully his. A greedy little monkey, he was. But a lovely one. Speaker_1: He’s grown into a lovely one, hasn’t he? It's hard to believe he’s nearly sixteen now. This photo book is a treasure. It reminds me of all the silly things, the little moments you forget. Speaker_2: He hasn’t changed *that* much, really. Still has that mischievous glint in his eye. Seen some of his TikToks, pretty funny stuff. Speaker_3: TikToks? Oh dear. I don’t understand any of this new technology. Is that the one with all the dancing? Speaker_1: It’s a bit more than dancing, love. But he’s a good lad. Honestly, I'm very proud. He’s doing well in school, too. Did you hear he's trying out for the cross-country team? Speaker_4: Cross-country? That's a good, healthy thing. Reminds me of the London Marathon. I watched it every year for decades when I lived in London. The atmosphere was electric. Speaker_3: Oh, yes! I remember you telling stories about volunteering at the water stations. Standing there cheering everyone on. You were always so enthusiastic. Speaker_4: Well, someone had to keep their spirits up! It's a gruelling race, that. Though nothing like… well, nothing like a proper hike in Iceland. Have you seen the pictures from your trip, Sean? Speaker_1: I showed them to Leo actually. He was fascinated by the glaciers. Said it looked like another planet. We are hoping to go back soon. Speaker_2: Iceland looks awesome. You said it was freezing though? Speaker_1: It was crisp, let's say. But the scenery more than makes up for it. The Northern Lights, the waterfalls… incredible. Much more exciting than being cooped up watching films. Though we did go to the cinema last week, didn’t we, Eleanor? Speaker_3: We did. Saw that new superhero one. It was… loud. A bit much for me, to be honest. I preferred it when we went to the funfair a couple of weeks ago. Remember the dodgems? Speaker_2: (Grinning) Oh man, those were great! You were really going for it, Mum! Nearly crashed into Mrs. Higgins. Speaker_3: (Laughing) She deserved it! She was hogging all the good cars. Speaker_4: Funfairs… they’re a bit much for my old bones these days. Although, I used to love taking the children to the one in Glasgow. Such happy memories. It's almost Leo's birthday soon, isn't it? What are you getting him? Speaker_1: We’re still debating. He wants a new gaming headset, but I'm thinking something a little more… practical. Maybe a contribution towards his driving lessons? Speaker_3: Good thinking! Driving lessons are a sensible gift. Although, knowing Leo, he'll probably just spend the money on more TikToks.

Speaker_1: Honestly, Mum, that crumble was incredible. Seriously, you’ve not lost your touch. It tasted exactly like the ones you used to make when I was little. Speaker_3: Oh, it's just a simple recipe, dear. Apples, a bit of butter, flour, sugar… nothing fancy. Though, finding good cooking apples these days is a challenge. They just don’t *taste* like they used to. Speaker_2: They don't. Everything tastes… engineered, doesn’t it? Like it’s been bred for appearance rather than flavour. Always with a Werther’s Original stuck to his cardigan. He used to call me “Little Blossom”. Honestly, the things I forgot until you start talking, Mum. Speaker_2: It *is* a small world, isn't it? We’d spend our pocket money on ‘aggies’ – those glass marbles – trying to win each other’s best ones. Speaker_2: I remember marbles! I was terrible at them. Always losing mine.
