It’s awful and wonderful. Speaker_3: eBooks? What are those? Is that one of those things with a glowing screen? I much prefer a proper book. The smell of the paper, the feel of it in your hands… Speaker_2: It's different, Mum. It's convenient. You can carry a whole library around with you. Though I do agree, there's something special about a physical book. I’ve started crocheting again, trying to rediscover a hobby. It’s very therapeutic, but I’m really rubbish at it. My scarves always end up looking… wonky. Speaker_1: Wonky scarves are charming! I tried knitting once. A disaster. I ended up with a tangled mess of wool and a lot of frustration. You’re much more patient than me. Although, I watched a documentary last night about textile art… it was fascinating. It made me feel guilty about my abandoned knitting project. Speaker_3: Well, it's good to have hobbies. Keeps the mind active. I’ve been re-watching ‘Call the Midwife’. It’s lovely, though it does remind me of… well, never mind. It's a good programme for a quiet evening.

Speaker_1: Right then, lovely bit of cheddar this, isn't it? Not like that plastic stuff you get nowadays. Proper matured. Speaker_2: Mm, very nice. Though I do favour a Red Leicester, personally. A bit of sweetness to it. You wouldn't catch me with a bit of Edam though. Always a bit…bland, don’t you think? Speaker_1: Bland’s a good word for it, Eileen. Like drinking water with a hint of cheese. Remember old Mrs. Higgins used to swear by Edam? Said it agreed with her tummy. Speaker_2: Oh, bless her. She did have a delicate constitution, didn’t she? Always complaining about a draft. Even in July! I swear she thought the sun was trying to give her a cold. She was a dear, though. Always a kind word. Speaker_1: She was. Used to bring us a pot of her plum jam every year. A bit tart, mind you. Always needed a good dollop of cream with it. But you couldn’t refuse, could you? Speaker_2: Of course not. It was the thought that counted. Though I always felt a bit guilty, secretly adding the cream. She’d have had my hide if she knew! Still, a good bit of jam is a good bit of jam. Have you seen young Timothy next door lately? He’s grown another foot, I swear. Speaker_1: Can’t say I have. Haven't been out much this week. Knees are playing up again. Damp weather, I reckon. It'll be raining cats and dogs before you know it. Speaker_2: Oh, dear. You should get those knee pads I saw advertised on the telly. The ones the footballers wear, but for everyday use. Apparently, they’re marvellous. Speaker_1: Knee pads? Me? I’d look a right fool, wouldn’t I? Walking around like RoboCop. No, thank you very much. A bit of liniment will have to do. And avoiding the garden, mostly. Speaker_2: Suit yourself. Though you do miss out on the roses. They're coming on beautifully this year. That new variety I got… the ‘Peace’ one… it’s just spectacular. Speaker_1: Roses are all well and good, but give me a nice vegetable patch any day. Something you can *eat* at the end of it. That's proper satisfaction. Remember your dad's tomatoes? Best you ever tasted. Speaker_2: Oh, Harold's tomatoes *were* good. He used to fuss over them something dreadful. Spent more time talking to them than he did to me sometimes, I swear! Said they needed encouragement. Speaker_1: He did. Said the sun had to know which ones he liked best. A funny old bird, your Harold. A very funny old bird. Still, he knew his tomatoes. And he knew how to make a proper cup of tea. Speaker_2: He certainly did. None of this wishy-washy stuff. Strong enough to stand a spoon up in it. Just like you like it, love. Now, are you going to finish that crust? I don’t want it to go to waste. Speaker_1: Alright, alright. Don't nag. Although it's a very good crust, has to be said. A good crust makes the sandwich. Speaker_2: That it does. That it does. Speaker_1: Right. Where were we then? Oh yes, Mrs. Higgins and her Edam... Speaker_2: …and her delicate constitution! Speaker_1: And the plum jam! A right old character, she was.

Speaker_1: Honestly, this latte is *saving* my life. Week six of Year Two is hitting different, you know? Little Timmy decided to paint himself with glitter glue today. Glitter. Glue. Everywhere. Speaker_2: (Laughing) Oh, bless him. Sounds… festive. I had a similar situation with Leo and the Play-Doh. Luckily, it wasn't glitter, just a vaguely alarming shade of purple stuck in his hair. How’s your mum doing, by the way? I haven’t spoken to her in ages. Speaker_1: She’s well, thanks. Still obsessed with cross-stitch. Last time I spoke to her she was going on about a new pattern involving badgers. Badgers! Apparently, it’s very intricate. She was also subtly enquiring about when I’m going to give her grandchildren. The usual. Speaker_3: (Smiling) Oh, the badger obsession sounds… very Mum. Mine’s currently convinced she can renovate an entire Victorian house single-handedly. She found a “bargain” on Rightmove. It needs, like, *everything* done. Speaker_2: Oh god, that's ambitious. My dad tried a similar thing. He ended up with a shed that leaned at a forty-five-degree angle and a very strained relationship with a bricklayer. Speaking of bargains, anyone got any gift ideas for Ben’s birthday? I'm completely stumped. He says he doesn’t *want* anything. Speaker_1: Ugh, the worst! Men are so difficult. What about an experience? Like, that axe-throwing place we talked about? Or maybe a brewery tour? He loves a good craft beer. Speaker_3: Ooh, brewery tour is good! Or… and hear me out… a language course? He’s always saying he wants to learn Italian. Imagine him trying to order a cappuccino in fluent Italian! Speaker_2: (Chuckles) That *would* be amazing. Although, knowing Ben, he'd probably end up accidentally ordering a live octopus. He’s got that effect on people, apparently. Remember that time he tried to explain cricket to a group of Americans and just… confused everyone into silence? Speaker_1: Oh my god, YES! They were just staring at him, completely baffled. He was using all these terms like silly mid-on and leg before wicket… it was glorious. He’s hopeless. Speaker_3: He genuinely thinks everyone understands cricket. It's adorable. How’s work, actually? Still battling with the endless copy edits? Speaker_1: It's relentless. This week it's all about organic dog biscuits. Apparently, there’s a huge market for artisanal treats for pampered pooches. Honestly, the lengths people go to for their pets. Speaker_2: Tell me about it. My neighbour, Brenda, dresses her pug in tiny outfits. Actual outfits. Like, little cardigans and hats. It's… a choice. Anyway, I've got to dash. Got a parent-teacher meeting this afternoon. Wish me luck. Speaker_1: Good luck! Prepare for a barrage of questions about phonics and handwriting. Speaker_3: And arguments about screen time, inevitably. Right, I’m off to wrestle with structural surveys and the terrifying reality of Victorian plumbing. See you both soon! Does this fit what you were looking for? I can continue the conversation or adjust it as needed. Speaker_1: Oh! Quick update actually, my car’s making a really weird noise. I think it might be the exhaust. It sounds like a strangled walrus. Speaker_2: A strangled walrus?! Oh, no. That sounds expensive. Speaker_3: Definitely sounds expensive. You need to get that checked out before it completely disintegrates. Definitely.

Speaker_1: Right, so I was chatting to Old Man Hemmings over the fence this morning, you know, the one who’s always complaining about the bins? Speaker_2: Oh, God, yeah. What was he on about *this* time? Honestly, that man could find fault with sunshine. Speaker_1: Apparently, young Jamie next door reversed his mum’s car a bit too enthusiastically and nudged his rose bush. A *single* rose bush. He was making it sound like a national tragedy. Speaker_3: (Sighs) Sounds about right for around here. It’s always something with him. Though, a rose bush…bit dramatic, innit? Speaker_4: (Eyes glued to a book) Dad, can we talk about Harry Potter later? I’m right at the good bit. Speaker_1: In a minute, lad. It’s just…it's the constant negativity, you know? I try to be friendly, but it drains you. Reminds me a bit of some of the students, always looking for something to dissect and complain about. Speaker_2: Well, you’re a lecturer, you’re used to complaints! Though, I get my fair share at the school. Little terrors, some of them. But at least they're usually about something legitimate, like the dinner lady giving them too much gravy. Speaker_3: Speaking of school, I had a right nightmare with a customer at reception today. Kept going on about how the council is letting the area go to rack and ruin. Said it’s attracting…well, let’s just say people with bad intentions. Speaker_1: Oh, don’t even start me on that. I saw something on the news last night. Horrific stuff, that ISIS business. It makes you feel helpless, doesn’t it? And then you worry about bringing that closer to home, even if it's just through scaremongering. Speaker_2: It’s frightening. My sister’s husband’s cousin, bless him, he’s out in Iraq with the army. I try not to ask too many questions, but it’s always at the back of your mind. Speaker_4: (Looks up, briefly) Is ISIS like Voldemort? Really evil? Speaker_1: (Hesitates) That’s…a complicated question, son. Let’s just say they're people who do terrible things, and try to scare other people. Much, *much* worse than anything Voldemort did. Speaker_3: Honestly, sometimes I just want to escape all of it. That’s why I love reading. Getting lost in a good story. I've been rereading 'Pride and Prejudice' actually. So relaxing. Speaker_2: (Chuckles) Austen is a good shout. I’m more of a thriller person myself. Something to take my mind off cleaning toilets and dealing with sticky fingerprints! Honestly, my back is killing me today. I’ve been scrubbing floors since seven this morning. Speaker_1: You work so hard, love. You really do. I wish I could help more, but you know how demanding the university is. Marking essays is a never-ending battle, and honestly, the quality is getting worse. They can’t even write a coherent paragraph anymore! Speaker_4: Can I go back to Harry Potter now? Please? Speaker_1: Alright, alright. Just finish your juice first. It’s just…I was thinking about maybe getting the back garden sorted. That fence needs repairing, and the paving slabs are all wonky. The house feels…tired, doesn’t it? Speaker_2: Tired? It's practically antique! But yeah, it needs a little TLC. We’ve lived here long enough, haven’t we? It’s home, though. Despite Old Man Hemmings. Speaker_3: It is a nice house, actually. And the location is brilliant. Close to everything, but still quiet enough. And you've always made it feel really welcoming.

Speaker_1: Honestly, the thought of all the paperwork for Nepal is giving me a headache already. Visas, vaccinations… it’s not like popping to France anymore, is it? Speaker_2: No, it's a whole operation. I remember when we went to Thailand, you needed a yellow fever certificate if you’d even *looked* at Africa. It was ridiculous. Still, Nepal… magnificent. I’ve always wanted to trek there. Are you thinking of the Everest region? Speaker_3: Oh, Everest is a bit… ambitious for me, I think. More the foothills, gentle hiking. Though Geoffrey keeps saying he wants to ‘conquer’ something. Honestly, at our age! Speaker_1: Geoffrey! He barely conquers the garden these days. Speaking of conquering, did you see that bike race went right through the village yesterday? The Tour of Britain? Utter chaos, but quite a spectacle. Speaker_2: I did! Absolutely rammed. Old Mrs. Higgins nearly got taken out by a cyclist trying to get a good view. She was waving a Union Jack and everything. Speaker_3: My daughter, Sarah, she’s training for an Iron Man. Can you imagine? Swimming, cycling, then a marathon! She’s incredibly dedicated. She was out on her bike all morning, probably training for it. It’s inspiring, really. Speaker_1: Good for her! Though, all that lycra... I don’t think I could manage it. It's a far cry from my cycling days when I was a girl, just a sensible skirt and sensible shoes. We used to cycle all the way to Bristol, you know, for a treat. Speaker_2: Sensible skirts! That's the spirit. Speaking of treats, I popped into the Village Shop yesterday. They’ve finally got decent sausages. Not those watery things they used to sell. Speaker_3: Oh, good. The Village Shop is a lifeline, isn’t it? Though, I still prefer the Farm Shop for fruit and veg. Everything’s so much fresher. And they do a fabulous gluten-free bread. Speaker_1: Gluten-free, there’s always someone needing gluten-free these days. Though, honestly, when I was a teacher, dealing with allergies was a nightmare. One little boy couldn’t even *look* at peanuts. It’s all changed with the free school meals now, hasn't it? Speaker_2: It has. Apparently, it's all very strict about what constitutes a packed lunch now, too. No sweets, no chocolate biscuits. My colleague's daughter is furious, she's a bit of a lunchbox queen. Speaker_3: It's a good thing, really, isn’t it? Encouraging healthier eating habits. Though, I remember during the war, my mother-in-law… well, she was evacuated from Siberia, can you imagine? Ended up in Africa! They were eating whatever they could get their hands on. Root vegetables, mostly. Nothing fancy. Speaker_1: Incredible. My mother used to talk about rationing, how they used to make soup out of everything. Turnips, parsnips, even potato peelings! It sounds dreadful now, but they didn’t know any different. Speaker_2: It makes you think, doesn’t it? About how much we waste these days. Speaking of wasting, my husband, Arthur, has become quite the chef in his retirement. He makes the most amazing curries. Really takes pride in it. Speaker_3: How lovely! My Geoffrey… well, he's good at making toast. That’s about the extent of it. He’ll help with washing up, mind. Speaker_1: That's a bonus! I used to be hopeless at washing up. It always felt like such a waste of perfectly good hands. Though, it's interesting, I was talking to Margaret, you know, from the school – she's retired now but used to be the display co-ordinator – and she was saying how much the job has changed. All digital displays now, instead of painstakingly cutting out letters. Speaker_2: Oh, I can

Speaker_1: Honestly, this week at work has been *mental*. You wouldn’t believe the requests I’ve had. Like, someone wanted a falconry display… *inside* the conference hall. Speaker_2: (Laughing) No way! A falconry display? Seriously? Cambridge isn’t exactly lacking in green space, is it? Speaker_3: That’s… ambitious. Did you manage to politely explain why that wasn't feasible? Speaker_1: Politeness went out the window after the third phone call demanding I source ethically sourced, miniature Shetland ponies for a themed team-building exercise. Miniature! Shetland! Ponies! I just… I said it wasn’t possible due to health and safety. Speaker_2: Oof. Sounds stressful. My job's thankfully a bit more grounded, but the deadlines are brutal at the moment. We’re launching the new production line next month and everything feels a bit last minute. Speaker_3: Tell me about it. I’m drowning in admin at the moment. Old Mr. Henderson decided he needs *everything* in triplicate, handwritten, and delivered to his office by 3pm. Every. Single. Day. Speaker_1: Oh my god, that sounds like a nightmare. Is he… okay? Seriously. Is he a bit of a dinosaur? Speaker_3: A dinosaur is being generous. He’s actively resisting all attempts at digitalising anything. He thinks email is ‘a fad’. Speaker_2: (Shaking her head) Some people. It’s good to vent though, isn’t it? It's just... It feels like everyone expects you to just *manage*, you know? Like, manage the impossible, manage the ridiculous, and still manage to smile. Speaker_1: Exactly! And then when things inevitably go wrong, it’s *always* your fault. I had a delegate complain the coffee wasn’t hot enough. Apparently, that ruined their entire conference experience. Speaker_2: Oh, dear god. The coffee! It's always the coffee. Remember Sarah at uni? She had a meltdown because the uni canteen ran out of oat milk. Speaker_3: (Smiling) Oh, Sarah! She was… a lot. I miss those days though, don’t you? Less responsibility, more questionable life choices. Speaker_1: Definitely. Though, even then, we managed to create chaos. Remember the time we tried to ‘borrow’ those traffic cones for a themed party? Speaker_2: (Bursting into laughter) Oh, don’t remind me! We almost got arrested! And the party was… underwhelming to say the least. Speaker_3: It was truly awful. But fun! We need to do something fun soon, properly. Not just complaining about work over tea (though that’s also good, admittedly). Are you both free next Saturday? There’s that new jazz club opened in town, I was thinking we could check it out? Speaker_1: Ooh, yeah! I’m in. I need a night where I don’t have to think about miniature Shetland ponies. Speaker_2: Sounds perfect. Count me in too. Maybe we can even plan a proper weekend away sometime? I've been needing a break. Speaker_3: Ooh yes! That’s a fantastic idea. We haven’t done a proper girls’ trip in ages. We could go to the coast? Or maybe even… Brighton? Speaker_1: Brighton! Yes! We could be really terrible tourists. Speaker_2: (Smiling) I’m already looking at train tickets. Let's aim for a weekend in, oh, November? Before the Christmas chaos descends. Speaker_1: Perfect! I'll start mentally preparing my terrible tourist outfit.

Speaker_1: Honestly, the council are unbelievable. Demolishing the library? It’s just… short-sighted. Speaker_2: Tell me about it. I saw the plans online - luxury flats, naturally. They’ve got no interest in community spaces, do they? Just maximising profit. Speaker_1: Exactly! And they call it ‘regeneration’. It's destroying everything that *makes* Plumstead, Plumstead. I'm properly fuming. I was thinking we should start a petition. Speaker_2: A petition is a good shout. We could get it going online, change.org or something? Easy enough for people to sign. I’d definitely sign it. Speaker_1: I was thinking that. And we should get the local paper involved, see if they’ll run a story. It feels like nobody’s listening otherwise. Speaker_2: Good plan. Though, knowing the *Plumstead Penny Pincher*, they’ll probably just run a tiny piece buried on page seven. Still, it’s better than nothing. How’s the transcription work going, by the way? Still loads of legal stuff? Speaker_1: Ugh, yes. Endless depositions about car accidents and neighbour disputes. It’s soul-destroying, honestly. I’m starting to feel like I know more about fender benders than anyone should. It’s good money, though. And flexible, which is essential with everything else going on. Speaker_2: That's the main thing, isn’t it? Flexibility. My shifts are a nightmare at the moment. They've put me on late turns three times this week. It completely messes with my sleep. Speaker_1: Oh, that's rubbish! You need your sleep. Are you at least getting extra for working lates? Speaker_2: A measly twenty quid a shift. It’s not worth the exhaustion. And then Brenda, you know Brenda from accounts, keeps complaining about how *she’s* the one doing all the work while I’m at home ‘having a lie-in’. Speaker_1: Brenda sounds… delightful. Lumosity, isn't it? Do they actually work? Or are they just another way to part people from their money? Speaker_1: That's what I'm wondering. Speaker_2: Ooh, good idea. What did you come up with? Speaker_1: Okay, don't laugh. “Lazy Lions Don’t Eat Pickles.” Lumosity, Lazy, Lions, Don’t, Eat, Pickles. Gran-level memory tricks. I’m embracing my inner granny. Seriously though, if we don’t do something about this library, it'll be a real loss for everyone. We need to get that petition circulating ASAP. Speaker_2: Agreed. Let’s do it. And maybe, after we’ve saved the library, we can take a brain training class… taught by lazy lions eating pickles. Speaker_1: (Smiling) It’s a deal. Speaker_2: Right, more noodles? I’m starving. Speaker_1: Definitely. Fuel for fighting the council!

Speaker_1: Right, well, that was a lovely bit of quiche, wasn’t it? Marjorie, you really do make a good quiche. Speaker_2: Aye, it were good. Though a bit rich for me, these days. Gets right to me, it does. Still, can’t complain, can you? Speaker_3: Oh, don't be silly, George. A little richness never hurt anyone. You had a good portion, didn’t you? More than either of us, actually. Speaker_2: Had to keep me strength up! Been dealing with them Jehovah’s Witnesses again this morning. They’re persistent, I’ll give ‘em that. Speaker_1: Oh, not again? They’ve been round here a couple of times themselves. Always polite enough, but… persistent is the word, yes. What did you tell ‘em this time, George? Speaker_2: Told ‘em what I tell ‘em every time. “Not interested, thank you very much.” Though this young lad, he kept going on about the end of the world. Said it’s just around the corner. Speaker_3: Oh, they always say that, don't they? Been saying that for decades. Bit of a sales tactic, I reckon. Gets people worried. Speaking of worried, did young Daniel ever sort out that parking ticket he got at Cromer? Speaker_1: I believe so. He mentioned it at the weekend. Apparently, it wasn't too bad, a reduced rate because he’d parked on a yellow line briefly. He was trying to drop the children off quickly, you see. Dreadful parking situation down there, isn't it? Especially in the summer. Speaker_2: You try finding a spot near the pier! It’s a nightmare. Used to take us half an hour just to drive around and around. Back in the day, of course. Speaker_3: It's always been bad. Though it’s even worse now with all the holiday lets. Every house is a car, it feels like. Makes a person not want to bother, honestly. Speaker_1: Reminds me, did you two see old Mrs. Higgins down at the village fete last week? She was trying to win that coconut shy. Swung so hard, nearly took out poor Mr. Peterson! Speaker_2: (Chuckles) Oh, I did see that! Nearly sent him flying. Mrs. Higgins is a character, she is. Always stirring something up. Speaker_3: She’s got spirit, that's for sure. Though I'm still trying to figure out why she's so fiercely opposed to the new bins the council's putting in. Says they're an eyesore. Speaker_1: She's probably just got a lot of stuff she needs to…store, shall we say? It’s the same with Arthur down the road. His garden is overflowing with…well, everything. Old tyres, broken furniture... Speaker_2: Clutter, you mean? That’s what it is. People hold onto everything these days. Can't bear to part with a thing. Taxing us all for the refuse collection, they are! It's a disgrace. Speaker_3: It is a bit steep, isn’t it? And then they wonder why nobody bothers to vote. Honestly, it's all a mess. I've been meaning to call the dentist, too. My tooth's been giving me gyp for weeks. Speaker_1: Oh dear. You need to get that sorted, Marjorie. Can't mess about with teeth. Difficult getting an appointment these days, though, isn't it? Seems they're all booked up months in advance. Speaker_2: You’re lucky if you can even *get* an NHS appointment. They're all pushing for private treatment. It’s a scandal, it is. Speaking of scandals, I saw a robin in the garden this morning. A bit early for a robin, isn't it? Speaker_3: Oh, they come earlier every year, George. Climate change, you know. Everything's changing. Now

Speaker_1: Honestly, Mum, the logs are just… pathetic. Honestly, you’d think for the price they charge now, they’d be decent seasoned wood. It’s all damp and smoky, just awful for the burner. Speaker_2: You’d think so, wouldn’t you? Though I suppose demand is up. Everyone’s at it with the log burners these days, trying to save on the heating bill. Speaker_3: (Chuckles) Saving on the heating bill. A quaint notion. Though I do remember a time when a good fire was the only heat you *had*. Not this central heating nonsense. Do you recall old Mr. Henderson, next door in Edinburgh? He'd boast about never putting the heating on, even in January. Just layer upon layer of woollens. Speaker_4: Henderson, yes. Stubborn man. His wife, poor soul, was permanently chilled. Though he did have a lovely cat. A ginger tom, very independent. Much like himself. Speaker_1: Speaking of animals, have you seen Mrs. Higgins’ new poodle? It’s… a creature. All fluff and no substance. And she dresses it in little outfits! Speaker_2: Oh dear. Sounds about right for Mrs. Higgins. She’s always been a bit… eccentric. Did you hear about that new Italian restaurant opening on the High Street? Apparently, it’s rather good. Speaker_3: Is it? We tried that dreadful tapas place last week. Overpriced and underwhelming. The patatas bravas were… an insult to potatoes. Speaker_4: (Sighing) The standards these days. It’s all style over substance. Much like the state of education, to be frank. These academy schools… utterly dreadful. Speaker_1: It's all about the budget, isn't it? Cutting corners everywhere. I was transcribing some interviews the other day about outsourcing customer service to India. Apparently, it's saving companies a fortune, but the quality... well, it's not great. Speaker_2: It’s the same everywhere, isn’t it? Chasing the cheapest option. I had a meeting today about streamlining processes at work. Which basically means doing more with less. It’s exhausting. Speaker_3: Exhausting for you, perhaps. Imagine what it’s like being a headmistress dealing with all of *that*. The paperwork alone! Though I always said a good mashed potato could solve most problems. Speaker_4: (Smiling) Your mashed potato *was* legendary, my dear. Smooth as silk. No lumps whatsoever. Unlike some I’ve encountered. Remember young Timothy, at the school fête? Insisted on adding gravy to his mashed potato *and* custard. Speaker_1: Oh, don't even get me started on school fetes! The sheer chaos. Have you been to that new antique shop just outside of town? They seem to have a lot of interesting bits and bobs. I was thinking of getting a new cushion for the sofa, something a bit more… substantial. The current one needs reupholstering. Speaker_2: I saw a rather nice chair in there last week. A wingback, I think. A bit pricey, but… tempting. Speaker_3: Reupholstering is a good idea. It’s far more sustainable than buying new. Though finding a good upholsterer is a challenge. They seem to be a dying breed. Speaker_4: And don’t forget the fudge! You brought some lovely fudge last time, didn’t you, dear? The lavender and honey one. Simply divine. Speaker_1: Oh, yes, I’ll have to get some more. I was thinking of going to that little shop in York next month. My sister’s been asking about going too, she was just telling me about her travels from Tokyo. Said it’s completely different to anything she’s ever experienced. Speaker_3: Tokyo! My goodness. A long way to go for a holiday. Is your niece enjoying herself?

Speaker_1: Honestly, the council tax this year… it’s gone up again. Seems they think we’re all suddenly rolling in it. Speaker_2: Tell me about it, Arthur. Mine’s crept up too. Not as much as yours, I expect, living in that nice little bungalow. More room means more rateable value, they say. Speaker_3: It's daylight robbery, the lot of it. They promise improvements, better services, but what do we actually get? More potholes and bin collections that seem to miss a week more often than not. Speaker_1: Exactly, Margaret! And they wonder why people get so fed up with politics. Speaking of which, did you see that interview with that chap from the Labour party? Sounded like he hadn't a clue about the real world. Speaker_2: Oh, don't get me started on politics. They're all the same, aren't they? Promises promises… I remember when they were talking about building more affordable houses. Still waiting. Speaker_3: Affordable for who, Norman? Certainly not for young people starting out these days. My granddaughter, Sarah, she’s been looking for a place in Norwich. The prices are scandalous. Speaker_1: Hemmings was a good sort. Used to help me with the garden when my back was playing up. Still, Spain… that sounds nice. I did a bit of travelling in my younger days, mostly for work, but saw some lovely remote places. Up in Scotland, particularly. Proper wilderness. Speaker_2: Remote places, eh? I’m not one for all that. Give me a nice cup of tea and the telly any day. Speaking of which, have you managed to get one of those smart TVs, Arthur? Speaker_1: I have, Norman. My daughter set it up for me. It's… complicated. All these streaming services and apps. Makes my head spin. I mostly just watch the news and the gardening programmes. Speaker_3: I've got one too, but I'm still getting the hang of it. My grandson tries to explain it to me, but it goes in one ear and out the other. I prefer a good paperback, myself. Less fuss. Speaker_2: I'm the same, Margaret. Though I do enjoy a good detective show. Now, did anyone understand what happened in *Vera* last night? That plot was a tangled mess. Speaker_1: I missed *Vera* actually. Was busy trying to figure out the Sat Nav. Taking me down lanes barely wider than my car! The thing’s got a mind of its own, I swear. Speaker_3: Oh, those Sat Navs. They're a blessing and a curse, aren't they? My sister followed hers straight into a river once. Well, almost. Had to be towed out by a farmer. Speaker_2: Goodness gracious! That’s a story! Makes you appreciate a good old-fashioned map, doesn’t it? Although, I suppose nobody uses those anymore. Speaker_1: No, they don't. It's all technology these days. Still, I suppose we have to move with the times, don’t we? Even if I don't always understand where they're moving *to*.

Speaker_1: Right, so the lad from Dell was absolutely useless, wasn’t he? Said the warranty was up. Up! It’s barely a year old. Speaker_2: (Mouth full) Mmmhmm. Coulda just fixed it, though, couldn't he? Sounds like a simple graphics card thing. Speaker_3: Honestly, tech support these days… they read from a script. It's infuriating. Didn't *you* used to fix computers for a living, darling? You could probably do it blindfolded. Speaker_1: I could, alright. But time, you see? Time's the killer. Between work and… (Gestures towards Speaker_4, who is attempting to build a tower of peas) …keeping this one from dismantling the dining room, there’s not much left. It’s dinner. And Dad’s complaining about computers again. Speaker_1: I’m not complaining, I’m stating a fact. It's a perfectly good machine! And it's a pain not having it for streaming the rugby on Saturday. Speaker_3: Speaking of Saturday, has anyone finalised plans? Are we still going to Ciaran’s for the match, or are we having people here? Speaker_2: Ciaran's is good. More space for… you know… enthusiastic shouts when Ireland scores. Speaker_1: Agreed. Less chance of breaking anything *here*. Though, I'm making the fajitas, so someone needs to run to the shops for extra sauce. We always run out. That medium one just doesn't cut it. Speaker_3: I can go after Leo’s bath. Don’t want him covered in sauce and running wild. He'd look like a tiny, spicy monster. Speaker_4: (Grinning) Monster! Roar! Speaker_1: A very accurate description. And while you're at the shops, could you see if they have those ear-plugs for swimming? I said I'd take young Master Leo to the pool on Sunday, but I'm dreading the water in his ears. Those little ears stick *right* out! Speaker_2: He's got cute ears, Dad. Speaker_1: He does. But they’re prime targets for water retention. It’s a personal trauma from my own childhood, I tell you. Spent half my life shaking my head like a dog. Speaker_3: (Chuckles) You did have a talent for waterlogged ears, yes. Alright, sauce, ear-plugs, and then I’ll try to wrestle Leo into the bath. What about after the rugby on Saturday? Fancy a quiet night in, or shall we brave the town? Speaker_2: Town, definitely. Haven’t been out in ages. Maybe catch a film? Speaker_1: Rest my feet after a hard-fought afternoon cheering on the boys. Town sounds good. Just… promise me no impromptu karaoke. Please. For the sake of everyone’s ears. Especially mine. Speaker_4: (Slurping peas loudly) Karaoke! Speaker_3: (Sighs) We'll see, darling. We’ll see… Speaker_2: Oh, and Dad? You should just try fixing the computer yourself. Seriously. It'll be quicker than arguing with Dell. Speaker_1: Hmm. Maybe you’re right. Maybe I will. After the fajitas, of course. And a lie-down.

Speaker_1: Right, pizza’s almost ready! Who’s excited? Speaker_2: (Squeals) Me! Pizza! With pineapple? Speaker_3: No pineapple! Pineapple doesn’t *belong* on pizza! It’s…it's wrong! Speaker_1: We’ll have a bit with and a bit without, okay? Everyone gets a happy pizza. Now, while it’s cooking, let's talk about something else. I was trying to explain to Grandma on the phone how you two communicate with each other... it’s a secret language, isn’t it? Speaker_2: It’s not a secret! It’s just… faster. Speaker_3: Yeah! And grown-ups don't *get* it. It's all about faces. Speaker_1: Faces? Like, pulling funny faces? Speaker_2: And wiggles! And knowing what the other one is thinking before they say it! Speaker_1: Wow, that *is* impressive. Almost telepathic. Speaking of things people don’t believe in…did anyone want to talk about the Loch Ness Monster? Speaker_3: Nessie IS real! I saw a picture! Speaker_1: Oh really? What did the picture show? Speaker_3: A long neck! And a bumpy back! And it was swimming in the water! Speaker_2: My friend Leo says Nessie is just a really long eel. Speaker_1: A really long eel, huh? That’s a good theory. Maybe. So, back to pizza. If I have three slices, and you have two, and then I have another one... how many slices do I have? Speaker_3: Er… four! Speaker_1: Good job! See, maths *is* useful. Especially when it comes to pizza allocation. Now, after pizza, what are we doing? Still thinking about that fairy garden? Speaker_2: Yes! We need sparkly things! And tiny houses! Speaker_3: And a little pond! With a frog! Speaker_1: A pond and a frog it is. Oh, and remember we need to pick out outfits for Auntie Carol’s party on Saturday? Any ideas what you want to wear? Speaker_2: I want to wear my princess dress! The sparkly one! Speaker_3: I want to be a superhero! With a cape! Speaker_1: Sparkly princess and superhero… excellent choices. We’ll have to see if we can find capes. Honestly, sometimes I wish I could just do a handstand whenever things get too complicated. That always seems to clear my head. Speaker_2: (Attempts a wobbly handstand, falling onto a cushion) It's hard! Speaker_3: I can almost do a handstand! But I need to practice! Speaker_1: You both need cushions! And maybe we can practice *after* the pizza, okay? Speaking of which… it’s ready! Let's eat! If I had five pizzas...and we ate two...how many pizzas would we have left? Speaker_3: Three! Speaker_1: You’re brilliant! Now, eat up before Nessie comes and steals it. Speaker_2: Nessie likes pineapple, right? Speaker_1: (Sighs) We'll avoid that philosophical debate for now. Just eat your pizza. Speaker_3: And no talking with your mouth full! Speaker_1: You're a little teacher, aren't you? Speaker_3: Yes! Speaker_2: Mmm. Pizza! Speaker_1: Perfect. A happy pizza-eating family. That's all a person could ask for.

Speaker_1: Honestly, this Peka is incredible. I’ve never tasted lamb so tender. It's completely falling off the bone. Speaker_2: (Chuckles) Told you! Croatian cooking is something special. It’s all about slow cooking and fresh ingredients. This region, Istria, they call it the ‘Tuscany of Croatia’ for a reason. Everything just *tastes* better here. Though you might want to save some room for dessert, I hear the *fritule* are divine. Little fried dough balls, apparently. Speaker_1: Ooh, definitely. I'm already planning the dessert strategy. Though I miss chips. Speaker_4: (Smiling) A man of simple pleasures. Speaking of places, we should definitely explore Rovinj tomorrow. I read it’s a stunning little town, built on a peninsula. Apparently, the sunsets are something else. Speaker_1: Yes! I already looked at pictures. It looks gorgeous. We should get some proper photos, although my phone camera isn't great. Maybe we can convince someone to bring a proper camera. Speaker_2: Your Dad has his fancy one, hasn’t he? Always taking pictures of everything. Honestly, sometimes it's a bit much. Speaker_3: He took a photo of a lizard by the pool today. A really close-up one. It looked kinda scary. Speaker_4: Lizards are harmless, son. Actually, they’re rather beneficial, keeping down the insect population. Reminds me of a story… back in Nigeria, we had geckos in the house – tiny things, chirping away all night. Thought they were annoying at first, then found out they were eating all the mosquitoes. Speaker_1: Nigeria? Wow. You’ve been everywhere, haven't you? It’s a bit of a jump from Croatia! Speaker_4: It is! A long story for another time. Although, no place feels quite as…relaxed as this. It’s nice to get away from everything. Even the news. Remember all that fuss about Ebola a few years back? Crazy times. Speaker_2: Don't remind me! I was working in the city then, all the airports were on high alert. Those immigration officers were particularly prickly. Always felt like they were looking for something. Speaker_1: Speaking of travelling, where do you want to go next, Dad? You always have a list. Speaker_4: Oh, a long list! Japan is top right now. And Patagonia. Somewhere completely different, you know? Though with everything going on in the world…and those ridiculously long queues at airport security… sometimes it feels easier to just stay put. Speaker_3: Did you hear about that new robot they made at school? It can build things! Mr. Henderson showed us a video. Speaker_1: Really? What kind of things? Is it like something Steve Jobs would've made? Speaker_3: He didn't say. But it was really clever. It could put bricks together without anyone telling it to. Speaker_2: Imagine that. Things are moving so quickly, aren't they? It's amazing what they're doing with technology. Though, sometimes I think people rely on it too much. Remember when you used to get tics, Liam, when you were little and really stressed? Just needed a cuddle and a distraction. No technology needed. Speaker_4: (To Speaker_2) You always had a knack for calming him down. Still do.

Speaker_1: Right, well that was a good lunch, wasn’t it? Always a good spread when you lot come round. Though I swear, Margaret, you’re getting better at making that potato salad every time. Speaker_2: Oh, shush now, Arthur. Just enjoying myself. Though I did find a slightly better recipe online, used a bit of crème fraîche instead of mayo, makes all the difference. They say it’s a reclaiming thing, but really? At my age? Speaker_4: Happens to everyone, doesn’t it, David? They just buy the lists, hoping someone will bite. Just tell them you’ve already dealt with it, or hang up. Don’t give them any information. Speaker_1: Exactly! My cousin Bertie, bless him, fell for that a few years back. Gave ‘em his bank details. Nearly lost everything. Had to get his grandson to sort it out with a computer and all that. Still won’t touch one, Bertie. Says they're the devil's work. Speaker_2: (Chuckles) He’s not wrong, is he? Though I do rely on mine for recipes, and keeping up with the grandchildren. Little Emily sent me a picture of her sunflower today, practically taller than her! Speaking of, I was looking at seed catalogues this morning. Thinking about getting some sweet peas. Speaker_3: Good idea, Margaret. Though you'll need to get them in pretty soon. The weather's been so changeable. I saw a programme on the telly last night about a rather spectacular display at Abbey Gardens, Bury St Edmunds. They’ve got a whole section dedicated to climbing sweet peas. Speaker_4: Oh, yes, I remember that garden. Wonderful place. Though I’m not a huge fan of all the fuss they make over gardens on TV these days. It’s all so… staged. Give me a bit of wild countryside any day. Speaker_1: Now, you two are always on about gardens and flowers! I was watching that documentary on the war last night. Fascinating. Reminded me of old man Hemmings down the road. He used to sing hymns in the church *and* the abbey, he had a voice like an angel, he did. Though couldn't hold a tune when he was having a pint at the pub, mind. Speaker_2: (Laughing) Oh, Arthur! You always have a story to tell. Though I prefer a bit of music on the radio, or even a good drama. I'm missing 'Call the Midwife' terribly. Speaker_3: I'm trying to get back into reading. Picked up a magazine, *Country Life*, actually. Had an interesting article about the restoration of a stately home in Norfolk. Seemed a lot like the one near Costessey, Arthur, the one you used to talk about as a boy. Speaker_1: Oh, did I? Well, Norfolk's a fine county. Used to love driving around there, before they made all the roads so complicated. Couldn’t navigate for toffee anymore. Always got lost near King’s Lynn. Speaker_4: Speaking of driving, David, are you still planning on going to the party at the Golf Club on Saturday? I can give you a lift if you like. Don’t want you getting stuck. Speaker_3: That’s very kind of you, Richard. I think I might, actually. It’ll be good to get out. Though if the weather turns, I might just stay in and watch a bit of telly. Perhaps that programme about Abbey Gardens. Speaker_2: Definitely take Richard up on that offer, David. And Arthur, remind me to show you the pictures of Emily’s sunflower later. It’s a whopper! Now, anyone fancy another cup of tea?

Speaker_1: Honestly, that was a *day*. Three domestic disputes, a shoplifting, and then that lad with the… well, let’s just say a very creative explanation for being caught with a suspiciously large quantity of fireworks. What was he planning, a personal display for Valentine’s Day? Speaker_1: Something like that, apparently. He claimed he was “testing them for safety.” The magistrate didn’t look convinced. I sometimes wonder about the whole system, though. Does it actually *help* anyone, or are we just… processing people? I mean, short sentences, fines they can’t pay… does it really change anything? If folk had a bit more to go around, maybe they wouldn’t be driven to… well, to shoplifting or whatever else they’re up to. Speaker_1: Exactly! And it’s not even about being *rich*, just having enough to feel secure. Speaking of money, did you see the price of petrol this morning? Absolutely ridiculous. I’m starting to consider cycling everywhere. Speaker_2: Don’t go doing that! Solihull’s hills will have you regretting it before you reach the first one. I take the bus, myself. They’re fantastic kids, but getting them to grasp the gendered nouns is like banging my head against a brick wall. “La table” versus “le livre” – it just doesn’t click. Speaker_2: Oh, languages! My granddaughter’s learning German at university. Says it’s fiendishly complicated. She's hoping to go travelling afterwards, backpacking around Europe. Speaker_1: That sounds amazing. I always wanted to backpack around, but then life happened. Mortgage, job… you know how it is. Maybe one day. Did you ever manage to get up to Scotland this year? You mentioned wanting to visit your sister. Speaker_2: Not yet, no. The train fares are extortionate! And honestly, the thought of the journey… It's a long haul for an old woman. We’re hoping to do it next spring, though. My sister’s been promising to show me her new garden. She’s taken up gardening, can you imagine? After years of living in a flat in Aberdeen! Speaker_1: That's lovely! That sounds really nice. Perhaps she could give me some tips. My attempts at growing herbs usually end in a wilted mess. Speaker_2: (laughing) Oh, I’m sure she'd be happy to. She’s got a real knack for it, apparently. Right, well, I best be off. Bus leaves in five minutes. It was lovely chatting to you, dear. Speaker_1: You too! Stay warm, and hopefully, next week will be a little less… eventful. Speaker_2:

Speaker_1: Right, so we were talking about what makes people happy, weren’t we? What makes *you* happy, Lily? Speaker_2: Um… ponies! And chocolate! And… and when you read me stories! Speaker_1: Lovely! Those are all brilliant things. And what about you, Leo? What makes *you* feel happy? Speaker_3: Dinosaurs! Roar! And building really tall Lego towers that don’t fall down. Speaker_1: Oh, excellent choices. Very important things. It's good to have things you enjoy, isn’t it? Sometimes people think happiness comes from having lots of money… Speaker_2: Lots and lots of money? Like a million pounds? Speaker_1: Even more than a million! Imagine a huge pile of money. Would that make you happy, do you think? Speaker_3: I could buy ALL the dinosaurs! Every single one! Even the really, really big ones. Speaker_1: You could, couldn't you? But would having all the dinosaurs *make* you happy, or would it just be… nice to have them? Speaker_2: I’d buy a pony! A sparkly pink pony! And a chocolate fountain! Speaker_1: A chocolate fountain sounds amazing! But think about it – if you had all that money and no one to share the pony or the chocolate with… would it feel as good? Speaker_3: I’d share with you! And Lily! We could have a dinosaur park and a pony riding club! Speaker_1: That’s a very kind thought, Leo. See, that’s part of happiness too, sharing things with people you love. It’s lovely to have nice things, but feeling good inside, that’s the most important thing. What about lunch? Speaker_1: There’s a nice little Italian place near the South Kensington station. We could grab a bite there. Or we could pack a picnic and eat it in Hyde Park, if the weather’s nice. Speaker_2: Picnic’s good. Assuming it doesn’t rain. And we remember to bring a blanket. And you remember the sandwiches… you always forget the sandwiches. Speaker_1: I do *not* always forget the sandwiches! And I'll make a list, alright? A detailed list, covering everything. Now, are you finally happy about our Sunday adventure? Speaker_2: (grumbling) Happy enough. As long as there's a cup of tea waiting for me when we get back. And you don’t make me wear that ridiculous hat.

Speaker_1: Right, so Christmas dinner. Operation Festive Feast, as it were. We need a plan, eh? Last year was… chaotic. Mostly because of Aunt Carol and the gravy. Speaker_2: Chaotic is putting it mildly. I think I’m *still* finding cranberry sauce in unexpected places. And yes, the gravy incident. Good lord. We need a designated gravy monitor this year, I reckon. I volunteer… to *not* be it. Speaker_1: (Laughing) Fair enough. No, seriously, we need to divide and conquer. I’m happy to do the turkey, I think. I’ve perfected my roasting technique since last year’s slightly… pale attempt. Speaker_2: You have? That’s good. Because the pallor of last year’s bird was a major talking point. I can handle the stuffing, no problem. And maybe the roast potatoes? I’ve been experimenting with goose fat. Speaker_1: Goose fat? You’re a dangerous man, you are. That sounds incredible. Okay, stuffing and potatoes are yours. I’ll tackle the vegetables - Brussels sprouts, obviously, to appease Mum. Although I’m still petitioning for them to be banned. Speaker_2: Never going to happen. Brussels sprouts are a Christmas tradition. Like arguing with relatives and terrible Christmas cracker jokes. Speaking of which, have you seen what’s on at the cinema around Christmas? Any contenders for a pre-dinner movie? Speaker_1: I was looking, actually. There's that new sci-fi thing, “Echo Bloom”, getting good reviews. Or we could go for something more festive? There's always a terrible rom-com somewhere. Speaker_2: Let’s avoid the terrible rom-com. They’re a national embarrassment. “Echo Bloom” sounds good. Slightly escapist. What about everyone else? Have you spoken to Sarah and Mark? Are they coming up from Shanghai? Speaker_1: I texted Sarah this morning. They’re tentatively in. Mark’s got a conference, but he’s trying to reschedule. They said to say hello, by the way. They’re missing proper English pubs. Apparently, the ‘Irish Pub’ in Shanghai isn’t quite the same. Speaker_2: An Irish pub in Shanghai… that’s the definition of irony, isn’t it? It probably serves Tsingtao with a shamrock on top. Bless them. We should try and get Ben and Chloe over too. Haven't seen them in ages. Speaker_1: Good idea. They’re usually pretty reliable. I’ll give Ben a call tomorrow. He’s probably busy prepping for his exams. How’s his Mandarin coming along? Speaker_2: It’s improving. He’s starting to get cheeky with the taxi drivers, apparently. That’s when you know you’re making progress. He said the tones are still killing him though. He keeps accidentally ordering live chickens instead of tea. Speaker_1: (Roaring with laughter) No way! Live chickens? That’s brilliant. He'll be a true local in no time. Right, back to the dinner. Apart from the potential poultry pallor and the gravy crisis, what could possibly go wrong...? Speaker_2: Don’t jinx it! Honestly, the last thing we need is Uncle Barry attempting to carve the turkey with a breadknife again. Or your Mum insisting on singing Christmas carols at the top of her lungs throughout the entire meal. Speaker_1: Oh god, don't remind me. Though, to be fair, her rendition of ‘O Holy Night’ is… something else. Alright, Operation Festive Feast is officially underway. And this year, we're prepared. Mostly. Speaker_2: Mostly is good enough for me. Now, another beer? It’s thirsty work, planning Christmas.

Speaker_1: Honestly, Twitter is a cesspit tonight. Just… endless takes on absolutely nothing. I swear, people *need* drama. Speaker_2: Tell me about it. I was scrolling earlier and saw someone having a full-blown meltdown because their oat latte wasn’t frothy enough. Like, seriously? Speaker_3: Oh, the oat latte brigade are the worst. I had a woman yesterday practically accuse me of personal sabotage because we’d run out of oat milk at 2pm. Two. PM. Like I *planned* that. Speaker_1: Right? The entitlement is… something else. It's the same people who leave one-star reviews saying “staff were rude because they asked me to wear a mask.” Speaker_2: Ugh, the reviews. Don't even get me started. I got one today saying my sourdough was “too chewy.” Too chewy! It’s *sourdough*, it’s supposed to be chewy! Speaker_3: You get those, I get them. Someone left a review saying my cafe was "pretentious" because I had actual artwork on the walls, not just prints from IKEA. Pretentious! It's a local artist, supporting the community! Speaker_1: People just want to be outraged. It’s a hobby now. Speaking of outrage, have you seen that new bistro that opened up on Deptford High Street? Speaker_2: Vaguely. The one with the… aggressively minimalist décor? Speaker_1: Aggressively is a good word. It's like they designed it to actively repel humans. Just concrete and uncomfortable looking chairs. Speaker_3: Sounds charming. They charging, like, twenty-five quid for a plate of three olives? Speaker_1: Worse. Twenty-eight. And it’s described on the menu as “deconstructed Mediterranean vibrancy.” *Deconstructed*. Like what, they just threw the olives at the plate? Speaker_2: (Laughing) Oh, dear god. Honestly, some of these places. I’m trying to figure out a new colour scheme for the bakery, though. Thinking maybe a slightly warmer tone, less… sterile. Speaker_3: That's a good shout. Yours is lovely and bright, but maybe something a bit cosier for autumn? I’ve been sketching some ideas for a little revamp of the café too. Thinking about getting a new coffee machine. The current one's starting to sound like a dying walrus. Speaker_1: A dying walrus? That’s… vivid. You’re braver than me, starting a whole business revamp. I'm just trying to finish this dissertation. It's on the semiotics of internet memes, unsurprisingly. Speaker_2: Oh my god, that sounds… niche. Speaker_1: It is. It really, *really* is. But it pays the bills, sort of. Have either of you been to Margate recently? I’m thinking of taking a day trip next week. Speaker_3: Not for ages. Heard it's properly buzzing now, all trendy shops and vintage places. Speaker_2: Yeah, it’s had a bit of a renaissance. A friend of mine opened a little jewellery shop down there. Apparently, it’s doing really well. Speaker_1: That’s good to hear. I could do with some sea air and avoiding Twitter for a few hours. Maybe we should all go sometime? Speaker_3: Ooh, yeah, that’d be nice. A proper girls and a guy – a day trip to Margate, sounds perfect. Speaker_2: Definitely. Though I’ll bring earplugs, just in case we encounter any disgruntled oat latte enthusiasts. Speaker_1: Good thinking. Right, I should probably attempt to string a few coherent sentences together about Doge before my brain completely implodes. Night, you two. Speaker_3: Night! Sleep well. Speaker_2: Good night. And try not to dream in memes.

Speaker_1: Honestly, the state of that garden is appalling. I really must get out there tomorrow. It's just completely overrun. Speaker_2: (Mouth full) Can I have more peas, please? Speaker_1: Of course, darling. Just don't fill your mouth so much, it's not very polite. Oisin, are you eating your carrots? Speaker_3: They’re alright, Mum. Not as good as chips, though. Speaker_1: Well, we can’t have chips every night, can we? Carrots are good for your eyes. You want to be able to see when you’re biking with your friends, don't you? Speaker_4: Speaking of biking, I saw Mrs. Henderson out on her new electric bike today. She was going *fast*! Nearly took out poor Mr. Davies’ geraniums. Speaker_3: Serves him right, he’s always complaining about kids playing football near his house. Speaker_1: Now, now, let’s not encourage negativity. He just loves his flowers. Did anyone see those blue tits building a nest in the apple tree? Speaker_2: I saw! They were carrying bits of fluff and string. Speaker_1: Lovely! I wonder if they'll lay eggs. We’ll have to keep a close watch. It’s so exciting. Speaker_4: It is nice, isn’t it? Though I’m slightly terrified of getting dive-bombed. Remember last year with those swallows? Speaker_1: (Chuckles) Oh, don’t remind me! They were relentless. Anyway, Oisin, are you finished? You barely touched your roast chicken. Speaker_3: I'm not *that* hungry. Can I have some raspberries for dessert? Speaker_1: Of course, you can. But you need to eat some more of your dinner first. It's important to eat your vegetables. You’ve got that history exam coming up, don't you? You need all your brainpower! Speaker_3: I know, I know… It's just… dates and kings. It’s so boring. Speaker_4: Oh, history’s fascinating! It’s just about finding a way to make it interesting. Perhaps think of it like a story? Speaker_3: A really, really long and dull story. Speaker_1: Nonsense! Now, have a few more mouthfuls of chicken, and *then* we’ll discuss raspberries and perhaps even a small scoop of chocolate ice cream. Speaker_2: Ice cream! YAY! Chocolate! Speaker_4: (Smiling) You’re easily pleased, aren't you? Oh, I remember when Leo was this age. Everything revolved around food, and chocolate. He used to hide chocolate biscuits under his bed. Speaker_1: Children! They are little hoarders. Remember when Amelia tried to keep a gerbil in her doll’s house? Speaker_3: (Laughing) She named it Mr. Bigglesworth, didn't she? Speaker_1: She did! It was utter chaos. Honestly, sometimes I wonder where the years go. One minute they’re small enough to fit in your arms, the next they’re talking about history exams and complaining about carrots. Speaker_4: It’s true. It goes by in a flash. But look at them now; two lovely, healthy children. That’s what matters. And they’re both eating their dinner… eventually. Speaker_2: Can I have ice cream now? Please? Speaker_1: Almost, darling. Almost. Just a few more bites of those lovely peas. Then, dessert will be served!

Speaker_1: Honestly, Mum, the supermarket was a nightmare this morning. Absolute chaos. Everyone seemed to be panic buying again. Speaker_2: Oh, really? What were they grabbing this time? Toilet roll, like last time? Speaker_1: Worse. Pickles. Seriously, pickles. The pickle aisle was completely cleared out. I needed gherkins for the potato salad, and there wasn't a single jar left. Speaker_3: Pickles? Well, I never! What’s the world coming to? I used to make my own pickles, you know. Lovely and crisp, they were. None of this vinegary nonsense you get now. Speaker_1: I bet they were, Gran. You were always brilliant in the kitchen. I just ended up getting some capers instead. Hopefully, they’ll do. Speaker_2: Capers are nice. A bit different. You alright for bread, though? I know you were saying you wanted to make sandwiches for your lunch next week. Speaker_1: I got bread, thankfully. And cheese. Everything else just seemed… frantic. It’s like people are preparing for the apocalypse, one jar of pickles at a time. Speaker_3: It's this television, you know. Scaremongering. They put it all in your head. Speaking of heads, did you manage to get an appointment with Sharon for your eyebrows, dear? They were looking a bit… wild last time I saw you. Speaker_1: (Laughing) Oh, Mum! They’re not *that* wild. But yes, I booked in for next Tuesday. She’s fully booked for weeks after that, so I feel lucky. Speaker_2: Good thinking. It makes such a difference, having your eyebrows done. Makes you look so much more… put together. I keep meaning to go, but I just haven’t got around to it. Speaker_1: You should, love. Treat yourself. And speaking of treatments, you need a haircut! It’s getting a bit long, isn’t it? Speaker_2: I know, I know. It’s just… finding the time. And honestly, I don’t really like going to the hairdressers. They always try to upsell me something I don’t need. Speaker_3: I used to go to Mrs. Higgins down the road. Lovely woman. She’d always have a good gossip while she cut your hair. Those were the days. Though she did have a terrible habit of smoking while she was doing it! The smell would cling to your hair for days. Speaker_1: Oh, goodness! That's awful. They're not allowed to do that now, are they? Speaker_2: Definitely not! It’s been years since you could smoke indoors, thankfully. Gran, you really shouldn’t have had that cigarette earlier. It’s not good for you. Speaker_3: Oh, don’t fuss, dear. It was just the one. A little treat. I’ve earned it at my age. Speaker_1: Still, Mum. Honestly. Right, let's change the subject. I was thinking, we should all go out for a meal next week. Just the three of us. Somewhere nice. Speaker_2: Oh, that sounds lovely! Where were you thinking? That Italian place we went to last time was nice. Speaker_1: Yeah, or maybe… I don't know. Somewhere different. Somewhere with a bit of atmosphere. We could try that new tapas place on Bridge Street. Speaker_3: Tapas? What’s tapas? Is it foreign? I don’t really like foreign food. Speaker_1: It’s Spanish, Gran. Little plates of lots of different things. You can choose what you want. They do lovely seafood. Speaker_2: Sounds good to me. Let's do it. Tuesday, maybe? After your eyebrows, dear? Speaker_1: Perfect. Tuesday it is. Let me book a table. And then we can properly discuss the pickle situation. It’s a national crisis, I tell you!

Speaker_1: Honestly, this weaning thing is… a performance. He just looks at the spoon like I’ve offered him something deeply offensive. Speaker_2: (Chuckles, bouncing the baby gently) Oh, they all do that at first, Mum. It's a texture thing, mostly. He's used to smooth milk, and suddenly you’re presenting him with… mashed carrot. It's a shock to the system. Speaker_1: A shock is an understatement. It’s like a tiny, silent protest. And the mess! I spent twenty minutes cleaning carrot puree off the highchair *and* his eyelashes. Speaker_2: (Laughing) Oh, the eyelashes are the worst. My class were learning about facial features this week and I was telling them about babies, and even *they* all knew about the eyelash puree situation. Speaker_1: Right? It's a universal truth of motherhood. So, what’s happening this week then? Anything exciting planned with school? Speaker_2: Not particularly exciting, lesson planning mostly. Year Two are still horrifyingly obsessed with dinosaurs. I’ve lost count of how many ‘T-Rex facts’ I’ve had to listen to. Though, I’m starting a new block on communication next week, so we’re going to look at different ways of expressing ourselves. Speaker_1: Oh, that sounds lovely. Are you going to do any sign language with them? Speaker_2: That’s the plan! I've been doing a little online course, just a basic introduction. It's amazing how even simple signs can help them express what they need before they can really verbalise it. I thought it would be especially good for the quieter ones. Speaker_1: That’s a brilliant idea! Remember how frustrated little Leo used to get when he was tiny, before he could talk? Sign language would have been a lifesaver. Speaker_2: Exactly! And it's supposed to help with language development generally too. I'm a bit nervous about teaching it, though. I don't want to mess it up and give them all the wrong signs. Speaker_1: You’ll be fine. You're a natural teacher. What about catching up with family this week? Are you still going to your Auntie Maureen’s on Wednesday? Speaker_2: Yes, I promised. Although, Auntie Maureen’s definition of ‘a quick cup of tea’ is usually a three-hour interrogation about my life choices. Speaker_1: (Smiling knowingly) Oh, she’s a force of nature, isn’t she? You’ll need to take reinforcements. Perhaps your cousin, Sarah? Speaker_2: Good thinking! I'll give her a ring. And what about you? Are you and Dad meeting anyone? Speaker_1: We were thinking of going to see your Uncle George on Friday. He’s been a bit lonely since Auntie Brenda passed away, so we’re trying to pop in more often. Speaker_2: That’s really sweet of you. He does miss her terribly. Oh, and I almost forgot – Liam’s mum asked if we’d be free for dinner next Saturday. She’s making a roast. Speaker_1: Wonderful! We haven’t seen Liam in ages. Although, knowing him, he'll spend the whole time glued to his phone. Speaker_2: Teenagers, eh? A complete mystery. Hopefully, the roast will lure him away from the screen for at least ten minutes. Speaker_1: Let's hope so. Right, where’s that spoon… time for round two with the offensive carrot. Speaker_2: Good luck! I’ll be here, offering moral support… and wipes.

Speaker_1: It’s funny isn't it? How even a tiny incline feels like a proper hill after being in London for so long. Everything’s so…flat there. Speaker_2: (Chuckles) You get used to it. Although, I do think Londoners overestimate what counts as a hill. A slightly raised pavement is practically Mont Blanc to some of them. Speaker_1: Exactly! And look at this view though. You can actually *see* for miles. Not just across the road to another Pret. Speaker_2: It’s lovely. Proper Norfolk countryside. It's amazing how quickly you feel calmer just being amongst it all. Though, I’m still slightly nervous about getting completely lost. This network of footpaths is…extensive. Speaker_1: Don't worry, I’ve got the map on my phone. And honestly, even if we did get a bit lost, it wouldn’t be the worst thing. We’d stumble across a quaint little village, probably with a pub. Speaker_2: You’re always optimistic about finding a pub. Speaker_1: Well, it's a reasonable assumption in Norfolk, isn’t it? Every village seems to have at least one. Look, there's Wighton ahead – do you fancy heading that way? It’s supposed to be really pretty. Speaker_2: Wighton sounds good. Is it one of those villages where all the houses are made of flint? Speaker_1: Some of them, yes. A lot of them round here are. It gives them a really unique look, doesn't it? It’s amazing how they managed to build everything with that stuff. Must have been back-breaking work. Speaker_2: It is impressive. And it blends in so well with the landscape. It’s a world away from the brick and glass of the city. Do people actually *live* in these villages full time, or are they mostly second homes now? Speaker_1: A bit of both, I think. It’s changing, sadly. More and more places are becoming weekend retreats for people from London and Cambridge. Still a good community spirit in most of them though, thankfully. It's good to see. Speaker_2: That’s good to hear. It would be a shame if they just became ghost towns out of season. It’s the people that make a place, really. Speaker_1: Definitely. And the pubs, let's not forget the pubs! (laughs) Come on then, Wighton awaits. It's not a huge climb, I promise. Only a metaphorical mountain compared to London. Speaker_2: (Smiling) Alright, alright. Lead the way, mountain guide. Speaker_1: (Starts walking) Just don’t complain when my calves are aching tomorrow. Speaker_2: No promises! Although, I might offer to rub them. Speaker_1: Now you’re talking. Speaker_2: You’ve got me trained well. Speaker_1: It's a skill. Speaker_2: It is. A very useful skill. Speaker_1: Honestly, though... Isn't it nice just to be outside, walking, chatting, and not thinking about marking papers for a few hours? Speaker_2: It really is. It's precisely what we needed. Speaker_1: Exactly. A little bit of Norfolk magic. Speaker_2: I’ll raise a glass to that at the pub later. Speaker_1: Good plan. Speaker_2: Good plan indeed. Speaker_1: When we get there! Speaker_2: When we get there. And hopefully get a seat. Speaker_1: Always the pessimist.

Speaker_1: …and honestly, the CGI was just *awful*. Like, genuinely distracting. It ruined the whole thing. Speaker_2: Really? I thought it looked alright. Not groundbreaking, but passable for a superhero flick. What film were you on about again? Speaker_1: ‘Chronos’! The new one. Everyone was raving about it, saying it was the best one yet, and I was just…underwhelmed. Especially after the trailer. The trailer made it look amazing. Speaker_2: Oh yeah, that one. I haven’t seen it yet. I’m more looking forward to the new Nolan film. Apparently it’s properly mind-bending. Speaker_1: Ooh, that sounds good. I like Nolan. Not always *understand* him, mind, but I like him. Speaking of mind-bending, how’s Liam’s new job going? Still completely lost in jargon? Speaker_2: (chuckles) Oh, spectacularly. He tried to explain it to me last night. Something about ‘dynamic load modelling’ and ‘finite element analysis’. I just nodded and pretended to understand. Honestly, it sounded like he was making it up as he went along. Speaker_1: Classic Liam. So, still happy though? Is he actually enjoying it, or is it just a good paycheque? Speaker_2: He seems genuinely challenged, which is good. He was getting bored in his old role, said it was all a bit…routine. This is definitely pushing him, though. He’s working late most nights. Speaker_1: That’s a shame. He needs to have a life, the poor lad. You need to drag him out for a proper night, remind him what fun is. Speaker_2: I keep trying! He’s just…focused at the moment. And stressed. Which brings me to another point… the cyclists. Speaker_1: (groans) Oh, don't even get me started on the cyclists. Speaker_2: Honestly! I was driving into town earlier, and this bloke just swerved right out in front of me, no signaling, nothing. I had to slam the brakes on. Speaker_1: They're mental. Absolutely mental. They think they own the road. I swear they actively try to annoy drivers. Speaker_2: It’s like they’re invisible until they’re directly in your path. And they never look! I’m all for cycling, good for the environment and all that, but they need to be more aware. Speaker_1: Exactly! It’s not a personal challenge to see how close you can get to a car before they brake. It’s just…dangerous. I nearly took one out last week, purely by accident, thankfully. Speaker_2: See! It's only a matter of time before someone gets seriously hurt. It’s just…frustrating. Speaker_1: Tell me about it. They need a proper cycling test, with hazard perception and everything. Just like drivers. Speaker_2: That's a brilliant idea! They could learn some road etiquette then, maybe? Though I doubt it...

Speaker_1: Honestly, this is exactly what I needed. Fresh air, no emails… just fields. And look at those poppies! They’re everywhere. Speaker_2: They *are* stunning, aren’t they? Makes you wonder about the economics of it, though. All this land… what’s the most profitable thing to grow around here these days? It can't all be barley, can it? Speaker_1: Barley, oilseed rape, sugar beet mostly, I think. Old Man Hemmings down the lane does a roaring trade in lavender. Apparently, essential oils are huge. He’s got a whole distillery set up. Speaker_2: Lavender, huh? Sounds… less brutal than a monoculture of beet. I was reading a paper the other day, actually, about the long-term economic impact of prioritising short-term cash crops. Depletes the soil, reduces biodiversity… it’s a real issue. Speaker_1: Sounds like something you’d be writing yourself, to be fair. You and your sustainable development papers. Though, I imagine convincing a farmer to switch to a less profitable, but more sustainable, approach is… challenging. Speaker_2: Very. It’s about incentivising them, showing them the long-term benefits. And honestly, getting consumers to pay a little bit more for ethically sourced produce. It’s a whole systems thing. It's frustrating, though, when you see the data so clearly. Speaker_1: Tell me about it. Trying to get undergrads to understand basic economic principles is a similar struggle. It’s like talking to a wall sometimes. Did you hear about Sarah’s proposal finally getting approved? Speaker_2: No! Really? The one on language acquisition in bilingual children? That’s brilliant. I knew she’d get there. She’s so dedicated. Speaker_1: She is. She was practically bouncing when she told me this morning. Said the funding’s secured for three years. It means she can actually hire a research assistant. Speaker_2: Fantastic. She deserves it. It reminds me I need to chase up my own grant application. It’s just…finding the time. Feels like every spare minute is spent marking essays. Speaker_1: It does, doesn’t it? It’s ridiculous. I’m seriously considering just banning personal pronouns from essays. It would save me hours of correcting “I think” and “in my opinion”. Speaker_2: (laughs) You wouldn't! Though, honestly, the temptation is strong. Speaking of distractions, did you see the football last night? Chelsea absolutely demolished Spurs. Speaker_1: Oh, please don't. I'm trying to enjoy the peace and quiet. You know I support Arsenal. Don't rub it in. Speaker_2: Sorry, sorry! Just pointing out a minor detail. They were awful, Spurs. Utterly toothless. Speaker_1: They had a bad night. Everyone has a bad night. Though, I will admit, the way Saka played was… impressive. Even I can appreciate a good winger. Speaker_2: See? There *is* hope for you yet. Though, honestly, this walk is far nicer than thinking about football. Look at that meadow. It’s just… bliss. Speaker_1: It really is. And look, bluebells! We haven’t seen these for ages. Speaker_2: It's amazing, isn't it? Sometimes you just need to escape the city and remember what it’s all *for*. Speaker_1: Exactly. Emails, essays, economic models… it’s all just noise, really. Speaker_2: Quite. Though, I suppose the economic models *might* help us protect places like this in the long run. Speaker_1: (smiling) You always come back to it, don’t you? Speaker_2: It’s a curse. Now, let’s just walk and enjoy the flowers. Before I start lecturing you about the externalities of agricultural land use.

Speaker_1: Right, so if we're leaving here now, we'll get to Durham about… half past? Assuming the A1 doesn’t decide to be a car park again. Speaker_2: Yeah, sounds about right. It was horrendous last weekend, wasn't it? Proper stop-start all the way past Scotch Corner. I swear, people forget how to merge. Speaker_1: Honestly! It's like everyone suddenly forgets they passed their driving test. Speaking of driving, yours is looking extra shiny today. New wash? Speaker_2: Haha, yeah. Gave it a proper clean yesterday. Felt it needed it after that M62 debacle. Bit of bird poo, bit of…everything, really. It’s a magnet for grime, this car. Speaker_1: You say that like it’s a personality trait. Mine just collects dust and old takeaway wrappers, basically. Are you excited for the football tonight? Speaker_2: I am, actually! Bit nervous though, considering their form lately. They need to pull something out of the bag. You watching? Speaker_1: Definitely. My dad’s already booked the living room. It's a sacred space on match nights. He has all his rituals and everything. Bit mad, really. Speaker_2: Sounds familiar. My grandad was the same with cricket. He’d have the radio on, even if the TV was showing it, just in case the commentator said something important the TV coverage missed. Speaker_1: Oh, bless him. It’s good to have those little traditions, isn't it? So, back to Durham, are we meeting Liam and Sarah at that new Italian place? Speaker_2: Yeah, "Bella Notte", I think it’s called. I had a look at the menu online. Seems decent. Parking’s supposed to be a nightmare though, apparently. Speaker_1: Fantastic. That’s just what we need. Another parking saga. Reminds me of trying to get into that tennis tournament in London last year. Ended up parking about a mile away and walking. Speaker_2: Oh, the Queen’s Club? I've heard stories. It’s always chaos around those events. Speaker_1: Absolute chaos. Anyway, Durham shouldn't be *that* bad. We just need a plan. Maybe drive around a few times, stalk people leaving… Speaker_2: Stalking is a strong word. "Observing parking opportunities" is much more polite. Speaker_1: (Laughing) Fine, observing. Honestly, it's a good job places like the Angel of the North exist, just to give us something pretty to look at while we're stuck in traffic. Speaker_2: That’s true. It's quite a landmark, isn’t it? Always surprises people when they see it for the first time. Makes you realise how big it actually is. Speaker_1: And how much of a statement it is, even just driving past. Makes you feel a bit...Northern, somehow. Speaker_2: Definitely. Speaking of statements, have you been looking at flats in town at all? You mentioned wanting to move? Speaker_1: Just browsing, really. Nothing serious yet. It’s just…everything feels a bit cramped at the moment. And the parking situation where I am is legendary for its awful-ness. Speaker_2: Yeah, parking is a nightmare everywhere these days. Apparently they're building a new multi-storey near the station. Hopefully, that will ease things a bit. Speaker_1: I'll believe it when I see it. Still, a girl can dream, can’t she? Durham first though, Italian food and hopefully, minimal parking-related stress.

Speaker_1: Honestly, this Rebekah Vardy trial… it’s just *fascinating*, isn’t it? I mean, the things that come out. It’s all so… petty, really, isn't it? Speaker_2: Oh, I’ve seen a bit of it on the news. Sounds a right mess, that. All over a story in the paper, is it? Seems a lot of fuss. Speaker_3: (Chuckles softly) Fuss is what young people *make*, dear. Back in my day, we didn’t have all this… celebrity nonsense. Though, I do enjoy a good scandal now and then. Keeps things interesting. Speaker_1: It does, doesn’t it? It’s just the level of detail, the screenshots… it feels a bit intrusive, somehow. Anyway, enough about that. Have you noticed how many geese are around lately, Doreen? They're gathering in fields near my office. Speaker_2: Oh, *loads* of them! Down by the river, it’s absolutely covered. They’re proper noisy, aren’t they? Honking all day long. My Colin says they're getting ready to head off soon. Speaker_3: They know when it’s time, those birds. Been doing it for centuries. Used to watch them fly over Peterborough in massive V-shapes. Always gave me a feeling of… well, of something bigger, you know? Something moving with the seasons. Speaker_1: Yes, it’s incredible when you think about their migration. Thousands of miles, guided by instinct. It’s amazing. I read an article about how they navigate using the earth’s magnetic field. Speaker_2: Magnetic field? Blimey! That’s clever. I just thought they followed the sun, or something. Speaker_3: They were always said to follow the lead goose. A strong one, knows the way. And the others just… follow. Simple as that. Though, sometimes a young one would get left behind, poor thing. Always a sad sight. Speaker_1: I saw a heron down by the pond in the village yesterday. A really big one. It just stood there, absolutely motionless, then *swoop* – caught a fish! It was so quick. Speaker_2: Herons are lovely. We had one visit our garden once. Scared the life out of my cat! It thought it was a monster. Speaker_3: They’re beautiful, but they can be a bit of a nuisance, you know. They’ll take the goldfish right out of your pond if you're not careful. Mrs. Higgins lost a whole school of them that way, years ago. Speaker_1: Oh dear! That’s awful. It’s a delicate balance, isn't it? Trying to enjoy the wildlife without them causing chaos. It's funny how the seasons change everything, isn’t it? One minute it’s swifts and swallows, then the geese arrive, and then… winter. Speaker_2: It is, it is. Keeps life interesting. Though I could do with a bit less mud being tracked through the house by muddy wellies! Speaker_3: (Smiling) Oh, well, a little mud never hurt anyone, dear. It’s a sign of a life lived outdoors, isn’t it? And that’s a good thing. Speaker_1: You’re absolutely right, of course. More coffee, anyone? Speaker_2: Yes, please! Speaker_3: Just a little, dear. Wouldn't want to be too lively at my age! Speaker_1: (laughing) Never too lively for a good chat, though.

Speaker_1: Honestly, this quiche is amazing. Did you make it? Speaker_2: Thanks! Yeah, it’s a Jamie Oliver recipe. Ridiculously easy, honestly. Though I did nearly set the kitchen on fire trying to blind-bake the pastry. Speaker_1: (laughs) Oh no! You and blind-baking. It seems a universal struggle. I always end up with soggy bottoms. Speaker_2: Me too! It’s the bane of my life. Anyway, how’s the job hunt going? Last I heard you had that interview at the sixth form college. Speaker_1: Ugh. Don’t even ask. It was…an experience. They kept asking me about differentiation, and I just felt like they wanted me to say all the buzzwords. Like, yes, I differentiate, obviously, but I want to tailor lessons to the students, not just tick boxes. Speaker_2: Oh, the joys of education bureaucracy. They often forget the actual *people* involved, don't they? Was it a terrible panel then? Speaker_1: One of them kept interrupting me, and another just had this… intense stare. It was unnerving. And then they asked me about my experience with ‘challenging behaviour’ and I accidentally launched into a story about a Year 7 who tried to eat his pencil. Speaker_2: (bursts out laughing) Oh, bless him! No! Speaker_1: I know, right? It just *came* out! It wasn’t even a relevant example! I think it pretty much sealed my fate. I haven’t heard back, so I’m assuming it was a disaster. Speaker_2: Oh, no, that’s rotten. Don’t give up though. Something will come up. You’re a brilliant teacher. Remember that observation last year? They were raving about your rapport with the students. Speaker_1: Thanks, that’s kind of you to say. It just feels a bit hopeless at the moment. Especially seeing everyone else settling into their new roles. How’s work been for you? Still wrangling teenagers? Speaker_2: Still wrangling! It's…fine. A bit hectic, but fine.
