We’ve got a new head of department, though. Very enthusiastic. Possibly *too* enthusiastic. She wants us all to embrace ‘dynamic learning spaces’ which translates to moving desks around every five minutes. Speaker_1: Oh, God. No. The chaos. Speaker_2: Exactly! And she keeps talking about ‘growth mindset’ like it's a religion. It is important, but honestly, sometimes I just want to teach Shakespeare without having to justify it with six bullet points about resilience. Speaking of things that require a lot of patience… how's little Leo? Is he sleeping through the night yet? Speaker_1: (groans) Don’t even go there. He’s decided that 4am is playtime. My husband and I are running on fumes. I swear I haven’t had a full night’s sleep since he was born. Speaker_2: Oh, honey, that’s rough. It does get better, they say. Though I suspect ‘they’ haven’t actually been woken up by a tiny human demanding a feed at ungodly hours. Speaker_1: Precisely! I’m starting to hallucinate bedtime stories. Honestly, I'm considering a career change…maybe professional quiche-maker. You could be my pastry consultant! Speaker_2: (laughs) Deal! As long as you promise not to set the kitchen on fire. And seriously, don't beat yourself up about the interview. You’ll find something amazing.

Speaker_1: Honestly, I’m starting to freak out a little bit about… everything. Like, the future. It feels really… amorphous, doesn’t it? Speaker_2: Amorphous? That’s a good word for it. I’ve been feeling it too. It’s not like when we finished our masters and it was, ‘right, get a grad scheme, climb the ladder.’ It’s… what *is* the ladder now? Speaker_1: Exactly! Like, I’m happy enough at work, don’t get me wrong. Production Controller isn’t exactly glamorous, but it pays the bills. But is this *it*? Fifteen years of spreadsheets and chasing suppliers? Speaker_2: God, no. And that's the thing, isn't it? I thought I wanted to be a PA, a really efficient, organized PA. And I am! But it feels…limiting. Like I’m facilitating *other* people’s dreams. Speaker_1: Oh, I know that feeling. My mum keeps saying I should just be grateful I have a job, especially after… you know, everything. And I *am* grateful, truly. But grateful and content aren’t the same thing. Speaker_2: No, they really aren't. Remember Sarah from uni? The one who always knew she was going to be a documentary filmmaker? Speaker_1: Vaguely… didn’t she end up working in marketing for a toilet roll company? Speaker_2: (Laughs) That's the one! She was so heartbroken, but then she said… she said it freed her up. She started making little films in her spare time, completely independently. Said the pressure was off. Speaker_1: That’s… actually quite inspiring. I’ve been thinking about taking that pottery class at the community centre, purely for fun. Just to do *something* that isn't work or adulting. Speaker_2: Do it! Honestly, we need more ‘just for fun’ things. I’ve been looking into volunteering at the animal shelter. It’s a massive commitment, I know, but the thought of cuddly puppies… Speaker_1: Ooh, puppies! See, that's good. Although, my flatmate's cat is already trying to adopt me. She follows me everywhere. Speaker_2: (Chuckles) You're a cat magnet. Seriously though, maybe we should have a proper 'future planning' session? Like, actually sit down with a glass of wine and brainstorm? Not pressure, just… think out loud. Speaker_1: Actually, that’s a brilliant idea. We could do it next week? I’m free on Wednesday evening. We could order a takeaway and completely fail to come up with a five-year plan. Speaker_2: Perfect! Wednesday it is. And we can definitely fail. Failing together is much more fun. Maybe we should both write down three things we’d do if money wasn’t a factor, just as a starting point. Speaker_1: Oh, that’s good! Right. Let me think… travel, learn to play the piano, and… buy a ridiculously impractical vintage car. Speaker_2: (Laughing) A vintage car? You? That’s amazing! Okay, mine are: open a little bookshop-cafe, take a year off to volunteer abroad, and take singing lessons… despite being tone deaf. Speaker_1: Oh my god, that sounds wonderful. Okay, future planning session is officially on. And maybe we should avoid discussing worms at all costs. Speaker_2: Definitely avoid the worms. Wednesday, takeaway, and no existential crises induced by invertebrates. Sorted.

Speaker_1: Honestly, I’m starting to think Liam’s just… a bit of a knob, you know? Speaker_2: Oh, go on then. What’s he done *this* time? It was bad enough last week with the whole forgetting our cinema plans thing. Speaker_1: It's not one big thing, it's just… everything. He keeps texting Sarah, like, constantly. And it’s never anything important! Just, "Haha, that's funny" or "How was work?". It's so pathetic. Speaker_3: Sarah from uni? The one with the bright pink hair? Speaker_1: Yeah, that’s the one. I asked him about it casually and he just went all defensive, saying they're just being friendly. But *why* is he being so friendly with her when he's supposed to be with me? Speaker_2: Ugh, boys. Always something. I swear, they thrive on the drama. Is it like, proper flirting though? Or just… attention seeking on his part? Speaker_1: I honestly don’t know. That’s what’s driving me mad! It feels like he *wants* me to be jealous. Like he's fishing for compliments or something. Speaker_3: That is a bit manipulative, isn’t it? My ex, Tom, used to do that. He'd mention chatting to other girls just to see if I'd get all clingy. It was exhausting. Speaker_2: See! It's a tactic! You’re not imagining things. It's really annoying when they play games. Speaking of annoying, have you heard from Chloe lately? She's been so distant since we told her about Ben and I getting more serious. Speaker_1: Oh God, yeah. It’s awful. She hasn’t replied to any of my texts. I tried to call her yesterday, went straight to voicemail. I'm genuinely worried she's properly upset. Speaker_3: She always did have a bit of a thing for Ben, didn’t she? Even before you two officially got together. Speaker_1: Yeah, but I thought she was over it. We’ve all been friends for ages! I just don't understand why she can’t be happy for us. It's not like we stole him from her. Speaker_2: It’s that whole feeling of being left out, I reckon. Like, everyone else is pairing off and she’s still single. It's rubbish, but it explains her moodiness. She’s always been a bit sensitive. Speaker_3: It's hard, though. You don’t want to tiptoe around her forever. But you also don’t want to lose a friend. Speaker_1: Exactly! I just don’t want this to ruin our whole group. We’ve had so many good times together. Maybe I should just give her some space for now. Speaker_2: That’s probably a good idea. Let her process things. Honestly, dealing with other people’s feelings is exhausting. Which is why I'm so grateful Ben’s just… normal. Mostly. Speaker_1: *Mostly* being the operative word, obviously. It’s always something with the boys, isn’t it? The constant drama… Honestly, sometimes I think being single is easier. Speaker_3: Don’t say that! You and Liam *seem* good together. You just need to have a proper chat with him about Sarah. Lay down the law, you know? Speaker_1: I think you’re right. I’m just… scared of what he’ll say. And scared of potentially ruining things if it’s nothing. Speaker_2: Well, you deserve to feel secure in your relationship. You deserve someone who isn't texting other girls all day! You go for it, girl. You deserve a knob-free life.

Speaker_1: (Sighs contentedly) Right, this shepherd’s pie is *exactly* what I needed after the day I’ve had. Honestly, proofreading legal documents all day… it’s enough to make your eyes cross. Speaker_2: (Mouth full) It's good, Mum. Really good. Can I have some more gravy? Speaker_1: Of course, darling. Just a little though, you've already had a generous portion. So, Leo, how was hockey practice? Did you manage to score? Speaker_2: It was alright. Mr. Davies was being really strict today, making us do loads of drills. I didn’t score, but I did a good assist to Finn. He’s getting really confident now. Speaker_3: That’s good to hear. It's important to have those supportive teammates, isn't it? You learn just as much from them as you do from the coaches. Speaker_4: (Looking up from his phone) Yeah, Finn's a good player. He nearly scored a hat-trick last week. Speaker_1: Oh, that’s fantastic! You two seem to be really enjoying hockey this season. It's lovely to see you both so enthusiastic about something. Remember when you both insisted on learning the ukulele? That lasted all of five minutes! Speaker_2: (Groans) Don’t remind me! My fingers hurt just thinking about it. Speaker_3: (Chuckles) It was… a valiant attempt. So, Sarah, any progress on figuring out that trip to Cornwall? The kids have been asking about it non-stop. Speaker_1: I’ve been looking at cottages, actually. Found a few that are reasonably priced and close to the beach. It's just working out the dates with work. I’ve got that big marketing campaign launching in July, so it’ll have to be August, I think. Speaker_4: August is good! That’s after my geography fieldwork. Speaker_2: Can we go to Newquay? I want to try surfing again. I was terrible last time, but it was still fun. Speaker_1: We can definitely go to Newquay. We could even take a surfing lesson this time, get you both properly taught. I’m less keen on *me* attempting it, though. I'm more of a sandcastle builder, frankly. Speaker_3: (Smiling) I'm happy to supervise the sandcastle construction, if needed. It sounds like a lovely plan, that. We could explore some of the coastal paths too. Have you looked at Tintagel Castle? They say it’s spectacular. Speaker_1: I have! It’s on the list. Also, Mrs. Henderson at school mentioned a really good wildlife centre nearby. She said they rescue seals. Leo would *love* that. Speaker_2: Seals?! Seriously? That would be amazing! Can we feed them? Speaker_1: I don’t know if you’re allowed to feed them, darling. We'll have to check. But we can definitely go and see them. Right, who wants dessert? I made a crumble earlier. Speaker_4: Crumble! Yes, please. Chocolate ice cream with it? Speaker_1: Of course, chocolate ice cream. Although, I might sneak a bit of clotted cream in there too. When in Cornwall… you have to have clotted cream! Speaker_3: (Winks at Leo and speaker_4) You’re spoiling them, you know. Speaker_1: Only a little bit. They’re good boys, and they deserve a treat. And honestly, after a day of legal jargon and hearing about hockey drills, *I* deserve a treat too.

Speaker_1: Honestly, the scale of these trees is just… humbling, isn’t it? Makes you feel incredibly small. And a bit silly worrying about things like… what Brenda said at the party. Speaker_2: (Laughs) Oh, Brenda. She's a menace, that one. What did she say *this* time? Was it about Mark’s beard again? Speaker_1: Worse, actually. She cornered poor Aunt Carol and started giving her ‘advice’ on her gardening. Apparently, Carol’s roses are “tragically uninspired.” Can you *believe* the cheek? Carol’s roses are legendary! Speaker_2: No way! Brenda doesn't even *have* a garden! She lives in a flat with a balcony the size of a postage stamp. She’s all talk. It's just… a need to feel superior, I reckon. Speaker_1: Exactly! And Aunt Carol, bless her, just stood there taking it. She's too polite to tell Brenda to shove her ‘advice’ where the sun doesn’t shine. I wanted to intervene, honestly. Speaker_2: I would have! You're better at that sort of thing than me. I just clam up. Reminds me of what happened with Sarah and Liam at Christmas. Speaker_1: Oh god, don’t start. What fresh hell did they unleash? I thought things were finally calming down after the… incident with the cranberry sauce. Speaker_2: It's Liam's mother. She’s been subtly - and not so subtly - hinting to Sarah that she’s not “ambitious enough.” Apparently, being a primary school teacher isn’t a ‘proper’ career. Speaker_1: Oh, *wow*. That's… spectacularly rude. And so unfair. Sarah is brilliant with those kids. She’s making a real difference. Speaker_2: Tell me about it. Sarah was properly upset. Liam tried to defend her, but his mum just steamrollered him with all this talk about "potential" and “wasted talent.” It was awful. It took Sarah weeks to get over it. Speaker_1: Honestly, some people! They just don't understand that happiness isn’t measured in paychecks or prestige. It's just… exhausting dealing with that sort of negativity. Sometimes I think I need a permanent holiday just to recover from family gatherings. Speaker_2: Me too. Although a holiday in a redwood forest is a pretty good start, wouldn't you say? It puts everything into perspective. Brenda and Liam’s mum feel a million miles away here. Speaker_1: Absolutely. These trees have seen everything, haven't they? They've probably witnessed far worse family dramas than ours. Makes you think, doesn't it? Speaker_2: It does. Do you think… do you think we’ll ever be at that stage? Offering unsolicited advice on our nieces’ and nephews’ life choices? Speaker_1: (Grimaces) Oh, please no. Let's promise each other right now: no unsolicited advice. Ever. Unless specifically requested, obviously. Speaker_2: Deal. Absolutely. Now, are we stopping for lunch soon? I'm starting to think about… well, not roses, but definitely sandwiches. Does this meet your expectations? Would you like me to continue the conversation, or change anything?

Speaker_1: Right, so the Kievs are in. Nearly burnt my fingers getting them out of the freezer, they're *solid*. Honestly, you'd think they were designed to withstand a nuclear blast. Speaker_2: Cool! Are they the really cheesy ones? 'Cause the cheesy ones are the best. Speaker_3: They’re the ones with the garlic butter, dear, not just cheese. Though honestly, I’m still not convinced they’re as good as they used to be. They seem… smaller. And less garlicky. Speaker_1: Smaller, definitely. It's shrinkage, I tell ya. Everything’s shrinking. Speaking of shrinkage, did you see that England game yesterday? Utter collapse. Speaker_2: Wales were brilliant! Proper smashed ‘em. I was shouting at the TV the whole time. Mum didn’t like it. She said I was being a bit… loud. Speaker_3: (Sighs) Loud is a diplomatic way of putting it, darling. You were practically conducting the orchestra with your yelling. And calling the England players… *wallies*. Speaker_2: Well, they *were* wallies! Missing tackles, dropping the ball… it was embarrassing. Speaker_1: Ah, you’ve got your Grandad’s vocabulary already, haven’t ye? Wallies. He’d be proud. Though he’d probably have a more… colorful description. Speaker_3: Please, let’s not delve into your father’s colorful descriptions. Anyway, are we still on for Granny next weekend? She was asking about you, Leo. Speaker_2: Yeah, I guess. Can I bring my game console? There's nothing to do at Granny's except look at old photos. Speaker_1: You can bring it, but you’re not glued to it all weekend, understood? Granny wants to *talk* to you, not watch you stare at a screen. And no backchat, young man. Speaker_2: I don’t *always* give backchat. Speaker_3: Oh, really? Remind me of last Tuesday when I asked you to put your shoes away… Speaker_1: (Chuckles) See? This is what I mean. Alright, alright. Enough family history. I was meaning to ask, have you managed to upload those photos from the holiday to Dropbox? I can’t seem to find them. Speaker_3: I thought I did. Or maybe Flickr? I always get confused. I started a whole album, but I can’t remember which platform. Honestly, it's all so complicated. Speaker_1: Flickr.Definitely Flickr. You said you liked the filters better there. Look, I’ll have a poke around later. My head’s pounding, though. Probably need a biscuit. Speaker_2: Biscuits would be good! Can I have one? Speaker_3: You can have one *after* your dinner, Leo. And don’t even think about asking for one of those chocolate ones. Speaker_1: Speaking of things outside, did you see that hedgehog in the garden this morning? Little fella was rooting around under the bushes. Speaker_3: I did! It was lovely. I really hope it doesn’t get hurt. The foxes are around here a lot lately. Speaker_2: Hedgehogs are cool. They look like spiky potatoes. Can we get one as a pet? Speaker_1: (Laughing) Absolutely not. They're wild animals, Leo. And they need a lot of space. Now, eat your Kiev before it gets colder. And no wallies at the dinner table, alright? Speaker_2: Fine. But Wales are still the best.

Speaker_1: Right, so I’ve chopped all the onions, you can start on the peppers if you like? It’ll just save a bit of time. Speaker_2: Sounds good. Though honestly, I'm still full from that ridiculous cheese and pickle sandwich I had at lunch. Proper doorstep it was. Speaker_1: Oh, you and your sandwiches! You'd eat a sandwich for breakfast if you could get away with it. Speaking of getting things, have those cups arrived yet? The ones I won on eBay? Speaker_2: Oh, the vintage ones? Yes! They arrived this morning. Parcel was left by the back door. I’ve put them in the display cabinet in the dining room. They're *gorgeous*, honestly. Really delicate. You’ve got a good eye for these things. Speaker_1: Oh good! I was worried they'd be chipped or something. Sometimes the pictures are…optimistic, shall we say? I’m hoping to use them when my sister comes down next week. Speaker_2: That’s a lovely idea. She’ll appreciate that. Are you making that lemon drizzle cake again? She’s obsessed with it. Speaker_1: Naturally! It’s practically a requirement for her visits now. Although… I’m thinking of trying a new recipe. I saw one with poppy seeds. Speaker_2: Ooh, poppy seeds sound nice. You’re very domestic all of a sudden. Speaking of domestic, I got some of that buckwheat bread from the market today. Speaker_1: Oh lovely! Is it the one from that new baker? The Polish lady? Speaker_2: That’s the one! It smelled amazing. Apparently, she only does it on Saturdays, so I had to get there early. She had a queue already forming. Speaker_1: That market is getting really popular, isn’t it? It's good to see. Better than another betting shop, anyway. Speaker_2: Absolutely. It's bringing a bit of life back to the area. So, about Friday…are we still going to The Black Swan for my leaving do? Speaker_1: Of course! Wouldn’t miss it. Though I still think it’s ridiculous you’re leaving after ten years. Speaker_2: Tell me about it. It’s just…time for a change. And frankly, I need less paperwork in my life! I’m hoping some of my colleagues will actually turn up. Old man Hemmings swore he would, but knowing him… Speaker_1: He’s all bluster, Hemmings. He'll be there. And even if he isn’t, we'll make sure you have a good time. We'll commandeer a table and everything. Do you want me to text Sarah and Mark to remind them? Speaker_2: That would be brilliant, actually. They’re terrible at remembering these things. Honestly, I spend half my life reminding them about their own birthdays. Speaker_1: Women. We have to keep everything organised, don’t we? Now, hand me those peppers. And tell me more about this amazing bread… Is it really as good as it smells? Speaker_2: It is. It's a little bit nutty, really dense...you'll love it with soup. Honestly, you need to try it toasted with some avocado. Speaker_1: Avocado, you say? Right, that’s going on the shopping list for tomorrow. Speaker_2: Good thinking. And maybe another slice for me? Just in case. Speaker_1: (laughing) Always! You’re incorrigible. Speaker_2: It's a gift! Now, about those peppers…

Speaker_1: Honestly, the paperwork is just… relentless. I’m drowning in it for this placement. It’s not even *interesting* paperwork, it’s just compliance stuff. Speaker_2: Compliance is the bane of everyone’s existence, isn't it? Especially now. Everything’s under scrutiny. You know, dealing with smaller businesses, you see how easily things can… slip through the net. It’s scary. Speaker_3: Slip through the net? You mean like, people not declaring everything? Speaker_4: (Chuckles) Oh, lad, you have *no* idea. I was talking to a bloke down the pub last week – runs a little building firm – and he was moaning about a client wanting to pay half in cash. Said it was “easier”. I nearly choked on my pint. Speaker_1: Oh, God. That's… blatant. Did he take it? Speaker_4: He said he politely declined. Said he’d rather deal with traceable transactions. Good for him. But it happens. A lot. It's tempting, especially when you’re starting out. Speaker_2: Tempting, yes. But the fines now are eye-watering. Not even worth the risk, even for a small amount. I had a client a while back who thought he could just… shuffle some money around accounts. Thought he was being clever. HMRC caught him within a month. Nearly lost his business. Speaker_3: Sounds stressful. I wouldn’t know where to even begin with all that. I'm still figuring out what I’m doing with me life, let alone dodgy accounting! Speaker_1: Tell me about it. Uni’s clever and all, but it doesn’t exactly prepare you for real-world… stuff. Like working out your taxes, or understanding why everything needs to be documented three ways to Sunday. Speaker_2: Well, you’re lucky to have us, aren't you? I can always give you a crash course. Honestly, it's not as scary as it seems. Understanding the basic principles is key. It’s all about the paper trail. No trail, big trouble. Speaker_4: That's right. And it’s not just the fines either, it's the reputation. Word gets around in Doncaster, you know. A dodgy reputation can ruin you. Speaking of reputations… how are the little ‘uns doing? Are they behaving themselves? Speaker_1: They are… a handful. Little Jack is convinced he can fly. Keeps jumping off things. Honestly, it's terrifying. And Lily is currently obsessed with glitter. *Everything* is covered in glitter. Speaker_2: (Laughs) Oh, glitter. The herpes of the craft world. It gets *everywhere*. You’ll be finding it for years. Speaker_3: Sounds lively! I haven’t seen them properly since Christmas. They were running around like mad things then. Speaker_4: They grow up fast, don’t they? Seems like yesterday they were toddlers. Now they’re demanding iPads and arguing over who gets the last biscuit. What about you, lad? Still thinking about that apprenticeship you were talking about? Speaker_3: Yeah, I’m still looking. It’s harder than I thought, finding something that actually interests me. Most of it seems a bit… well, boring. Speaker_2: It's important to find something you enjoy. You're going to be spending a lot of time doing it! Don’t settle just because it’s easy. Have you looked at anything outside of Doncaster? Maybe something in Leeds or Sheffield? Speaker_1: Or even further afield? There’s a whole world out there! You could… I don’t know, learn a trade? Go travelling? It’s your time to figure it out. Speaker_4: Aye, she’s right. Don’t put too much pressure on yourself, but don't drift either. A bit of ambition never hurt anyone. Now, who wants another glass of wine? This French stuff is rather good, you know.

Speaker_1: Honestly, this weather is doing my head in. One minute it’s sunshine, the next it’s threatening to pour down. Makes planning anything impossible. Speaker_2: Tell me about it. I had a garden fete to organise for the hospice, and I was sweating buckets all day, stressing about whether everyone would get soaked. Thankfully, it held off, but it was a close call. Did alright though, raised nearly £800. Speaker_3: That’s brilliant, Dad! You’re amazing at those things. I’m just trying to survive a week of Year 6s hyped up on sugar and impending freedom. Honestly, the energy is…something else. Speaker_4: Sounds chaotic! I had a woman trying to return a dress yesterday, saying it didn’t fit anymore. It was clearly worn, tag was off, everything. Some people, honestly! You just can’t win. Speaker_1: Oh, the joys of retail! Still, at least you're not wrangling thirty nine seven-year-olds. How’s the sign language class going, love? Are you still enjoying it? Speaker_3: I am, actually. It’s harder than I thought, remembering all the different signs, but really rewarding. I’ve been practicing with some of the kids at school who have hearing impairments, and they absolutely love it. It’s lovely to be able to communicate with them on their level. Speaker_2: That’s fantastic, sweetheart. Always good to learn a new skill, especially one so helpful. Speaker_4: It sounds really worthwhile. I wouldn't have a clue where to start, though. My brain just doesn’t work like that. Speaker_1: We were thinking… well, I had a scan appointment today. Speaker_2: Oh? And…? Don’t leave us hanging! Speaker_1: Everything looks good. We’re having a little girl! *(A chorus of excited sounds and congratulations erupts)* Speaker_3: Oh my gosh, that’s amazing! Congratulations! I’m so happy for you both! A little niece! Speaker_4: That’s wonderful news! I'm already picturing all the cute outfits. Seriously, I might have to start saving now. Speaker_2: Brilliant! Absolutely brilliant! A granddaughter! I’m over the moon. We’ll have to start planning a little shopping trip, won’t we? Though, your mother will probably have a list as long as my arm already. Speaker_1: You have no idea. She’s already sent me links to twenty different prams. Twenty! I told her it's only the first scan! Speaker_3: (Laughing) Oh, grandmothers. They’re a force of nature. But it's lovely she’s so excited. Speaker_4: Definitely. It’s nice to know you’ve got that support. So, when are you due, if you don’t mind me asking? Speaker_1: End of February. Which means… a winter baby. Probably a lot of snuggles and hot chocolate. Speaker_2: And a very exhausted Mum and Dad! We need to get organised. We should think about getting the spare room ready. It’s been a bit of a dumping ground, hasn't it? Speaker_3: I’m happy to help paint, if you like? I’ve got a weekend free next month. Speaker_4: And I can definitely do some shopping for little girl things. I'm a professional shopper, remember? It's in my job description, basically. Speaker_1: That would be amazing, both of you. Honestly, I feel so much better just talking about it. It feels…real now.

Speaker_1: Honestly, this canteen food is…consistent. Consistently bland. But it’s quick, I suppose. Speaker_2: Tell me about it. I swear they season everything with the same grey powder. At least the salad bar is okay. Did anyone actually manage to get a decent coffee out of that machine though? Mine tasted vaguely of metal. Speaker_3: No, mine was awful. I think I’ll just stick to tea for the rest of the week. So, how’s everyone’s week been? Aside from canteen-related grievances, of course. I feel like I’ve just been drowning in proofs. Honestly, the amount of commas people misuse… Speaker_4: Oh, don’t even *start* on the commas. I think my brain is actively rejecting the sight of them after formatting that manuscript yesterday. It was a historical fiction, which is lovely, but the author had a… unique approach to punctuation. It felt like a personal challenge. Speaker_1: Right? I’m currently looking at transcriptions for a dialect study, and sometimes I just stare at the page and wonder what language people are even speaking. It’s fascinating, but also incredibly exhausting trying to decode everything. Speaker_2: Oh, that sounds *intense*. What dialect are you researching? Speaker_1: I’m focusing on variations in East Anglian English, specifically around Aylesbury. It's surprisingly diverse, even within a relatively small area. Lots of subtle shifts in pronunciation and vocabulary. Speaker_3: That’s really cool! I mean, terrifying for transcription, probably, but cool. It's amazing how much regional variation there still is. Publishing can kind of iron all that out, though, doesn't it? Everything has to be ‘standard’ English. Speaker_4: It does. It's a bit sad, actually. You lose so much flavour. I grew up in Sweden, and we have a lot more acceptance of different linguistic variations. It feels much more… natural. Speaker_2: That's a really good point. I’ve been doing some proofreading for a children’s book and the author deliberately included some colloquialisms, and the editor was *obsessed* with trying to remove them. Said they weren’t “accessible” to a national audience. Speaker_1: Accessible… it’s such a buzzword. Sometimes I wonder if it just means ‘sanitized’. I had a supervisor once who insisted I remove any slang from my interview recordings. Said it wasn’t ‘academic’. Like, people actually *talk* like that! Speaker_3: Exactly! It feels like we’re constantly being told to erase the way people truly speak. It’s… frustrating. I was thinking about that actually, with the amount of non-fiction we do, especially on historical topics. Shouldn't we be trying to *preserve* different linguistic styles, not smooth them all out? Speaker_4: Definitely. Especially when you're dealing with historical texts. It’s part of the authenticity. It’s like stripping the character out of something. Are any of you going to the launch event next week? For the new poetry collection? Speaker_2: I think so! I've heard good things about the poet. It’s a good excuse to get out of the office, anyway. And maybe there'll be less grey powder involved. Speaker_1: Good idea. I'm in. After a week of deciphering accents, some actual poetry sounds rather lovely. Speaker_3: Count me in too. Though I may need to mentally prepare myself for more comma debates afterwards. Speaker_4: Sounds like a plan. And maybe we can collectively complain about the coffee. It's a bonding experience, really.

Speaker_1: Right, so the visa application… absolute state, innit? They want a *photocopy* of the original photocopy of my passport. Who even *does* that anymore? Speaker_2: Seriously! It’s like they’re deliberately trying to make it difficult. I spent ages last night filling out the forms, and then realised I needed a different pen colour for section four. A different *colour*, mate. Speaker_1: You’re joking! What colour did they want? Lilac? Speaker_2: (laughs) Nah, blue, but I’d already done it in black. Had to start again. It’s a nightmare. And the passport photos… mine look like I’ve been mugged. Speaker_1: I know! I went to that booth in the market, thinking it’d be quick. It just… highlighted every single flaw. I look like a criminal. We need to re-do them, definitely. Speaker_2: Yeah, we do. Think your mum’s got that decent camera she used for your graduation? We could try and get a passable shot in her garden. Better than those booth things. Speaker_1: Good shout. I'll ask her. We need to get this sorted, though. Deadline’s looming. Speaking of sorting, how’s the donations looking? Have you had much on the JustGiving page? Speaker_2: Slow, to be honest. A few quid from family, a couple from mates… not exactly setting the world alight. I was thinking… what about Gumtree? We could put an ad on there, explaining what we’re doing and asking for sponsorship. Speaker_1: Gumtree? That’s… clever actually. Bit random, but it could reach a different audience. I’ll knock something up tonight. “Two lads, one ridiculous car, driving to Mongolia for charity! Sponsor us!” Keep it simple. Speaker_2: Perfect! And we need to sort out the car stuff proper. Have you booked that mechanic to give it a once-over? Speaker_1: Yeah, booked him for Saturday morning. He said he'll check the fluids, tyres, brakes… the usual. He reckons with a bit of luck, she’ll hold out. She's a brave little Fiesta. Speaker_2: Brave indeed. Remember that time you tried to drive her through that field after the festival? Speaker_1: (groans) Don't remind me. She was stuck for hours. Had to get Farmer Giles and his tractor to pull us out. That was a low point. Hopefully, Mongolia won't involve any fields. Speaker_2: Let's hope not. We’re going to need all the car’s strength for the actual roads, never mind any impromptu off-roading adventures. Have you thought about what we're taking for tools and spare parts? It’s going to be a long way with limited resources. Speaker_1: I’ve started a list. Jack, spare tyre, oil, water… the basics. Your dad said he's got some old gaffer tape that's practically indestructible. Apparently, it held his garden shed together during the storms last year. Speaker_2: (laughing) Perfect! Gaffer tape is the answer to everything. Right, let’s crack on with this Gumtree ad then. And I'll text my mum about the passport photo situation. This rally is gonna be… an experience, to say the least. speaker_1: Definitely an experience. A potentially disastrous, incredibly muddy experience. But for charity, yeah? We're doing it for the kids! speaker_2: Exactly! And pictures of us looking like absolute idiots will be good for donations, right? speaker_1: It's a solid plan. A solid, slightly insane plan.

Speaker_1: Honestly, I still feel dreadful. Like, absolutely knackered. Did *anyone* actually sleep last night? Speaker_2: Sleep? Girl, I barely blinked. Sat with you in A&E for hours, then had to walk all the way back up here. My feet are killin’ me. How’s the arm, actually? Still throbbing? Speaker_3: (Yawning) It’s a miracle I’m functioning at all. I had a lecture at nine. *Nine*. After all that. And yes, arm, still looks like a balloon. Honestly, you scared the life out of us crashing into that table, Liv. Speaker_1: I know, I know. I keep replaying it. One minute I’m reaching for a biscuit, the next…snap! And the pain! It was awful. They said it’s just badly sprained, thankfully, no break. But the doctor kept going on about needing to rule things out. Ruled out what?! I felt like a science experiment. Speaker_2: They always say that, don't they? "Rule things out." It's just their way of covering themselves. Still, good they checked it out. Did they give you anything stronger than paracetamol? Speaker_1: Just paracetamol. And a sling. A very fashionable sling. I look like I’m auditioning for a period drama. Speaker_3: You do, actually. Very ‘damsel in distress’. Speaking of distress, did you see Ben texting you last night while we were at the hospital? Speaker_1: Ben? Oh god. I didn’t even look at my phone. Was he being…Ben? Speaker_2: Understatement of the century. Basically, he was super concerned but simultaneously managing to make it all about how *he* was worried. Like, “I was so scared for *you*, it’s been a really hard week for *me*…” Honestly, the man’s a walking drama fest. Speaker_1: (Groans) Ugh. He’s exhausting. I really thought…well, never mind. I need coffee. Strong coffee. Anyone with me? Speaker_3: Lead the way. I think I’ve still got remnants of sleep clinging to my brain. Maybe a biscuit too. You know, for medicinal purposes. (They move to the kitchen. The sound of a kettle boiling and cupboard doors opening) Speaker_2: So, are you gonna tell me about this ‘thought’ you had about Ben? C’mon, spill. We're your flatmates, we're built for this. Speaker_1: It's nothing. Just…I was thinking maybe he’s not actually serious about wanting a future. He keeps talking about ‘taking things slow’ and I’m starting to think ‘slow’ means ‘never’. Speaker_3: Ooh, red flag city. My cousin went through that with her boyfriend. "Slow" turned into "radio silence." Speaker_1: Exactly! It just feels like I’m putting in all the effort. And then he pulls the sympathy card every time I try to…you know...talk about it. Speaker_2: He sounds like a right pain. Honestly, you deserve someone who doesn’t need you to feel sorry for them every five minutes. There are plenty of fish in the sea, Liv. Or in Lancaster, I suppose. (They return to the bedroom, coffee mugs in hand.) Speaker_3: Speaking of Lancaster, how’s Uni life generally? Settling in okay? Besides almost breaking your arm, of course. Speaker_1: It’s…a lot. The work is harder than I expected, and I miss home. And the people are…nice, but it’s hard to really *connect*, you know? Speaker_2: Yeah, it takes time. It’s different being away, isn’t it? Feels like you're constantly having to re-introduce yourself. Speaker_3: Absolutely. I still haven't found my 'people’ yet. Which is worrying, because it's nearly December!

Speaker_1: So, lad, did you have a good time at Auntie Brenda’s anniversary do on Saturday? Honestly, it was a bit of a whirlwind, wasn’t it? Speaker_2: Yeah, it was alright. A bit crowded though, wasn't it? Couldn't really move without bumping into someone. And loads of people I didn't even know. Speaker_1: Oh, aye, Brenda always invites everyone and their dog! She’s got a huge family, you know. Cousin Margaret brought three of her husband’s sisters this time, and I swear I’d never clapped eyes on them before. Did you manage to speak to young Thomas? He's grown a foot since I last saw him! Speaker_2: Not really. He was just messing about with his phone the whole time. I said 'Hi' but he didn't really look up. It was more interesting watching Grandad try and work the photo booth. Speaker_1: (Chuckles) Oh, bless him! He’s hopeless with technology, isn’t he? He kept asking me how to get his picture ‘on the telly’. Took me a good ten minutes to explain it just went to a screen! Did you see him nearly knock over the cake? Speaker_2: Yeah! That was funny. Mum had to grab it just in time. He was going on about wanting a bigger slice afterwards too, even though he’d already had two! Speaker_1: He’s always been a greedy one, your Grandad. Remember when he ate all the Quality Streets at Christmas when you were little, and then blamed it on the dog? Speaker_2: (Laughs) Oh yeah! I remember that! He said Buster had a secret sweet tooth. Speaker_1: He did! And your Auntie Carol was on form, wasn’t she? Telling everyone about her new pottery class. For a good hour, solid. Speaker_2: She's always got a hobby, hasn't she? Last time it was bird watching. She made us go out with her at dawn, even though it was freezing. Speaker_1: Aye, she's enthusiastic, I'll give her that. But honestly, all those floral dresses… she looks like a walking garden! Did anyone ask about your exams? I felt like I was being grilled by everyone about your A-levels. Speaker_2: Yeah, a few people. Mostly Grandma. She kept saying I need to get good grades so I can ‘get a proper job’. Like being a game designer isn't a proper job. Speaker_1: Oh, don't pay her any mind. She's from a different generation. She thinks anything not involving a suit and a briefcase isn't worthwhile. But you've always been good with computers, haven't you? You've got a real talent for it. It’s just…she worries. Speaker_2: I know, I know. It wasn’t *too* bad though. I got to chat with Uncle Richard for a bit. He was asking about the robotics club at school. He actually seemed interested. Speaker_1: Good. He’s a good lad, your Uncle Richard. Always supportive. Well, all in all, it was a nice day, wasn't it? A bit chaotic, but nice. It's good to see everyone together. Speaker_2: Yeah, it was. Though I think I need a lie-down now. All that family time is exhausting! Speaker_1: (Smiling) You and me both, love. You and me both. Now, how about a cup of tea, then? Speaker_2: Sounds good. Speaker_1: Right then, I'll put the kettle on.

Speaker_1: Honestly, Dad, are you *sure* you packed enough water? I’ve already finished half mine and we’ve barely left Manchester. Speaker_2: (Chuckles) Drama queen. Yes, I packed plenty. There’s a whole case in the boot, remember? Along with about seven different types of biscuit. And relax, we're not crossing the Sahara. Speaker_1: It’s just… I get really thirsty. And I need a pen. I wanted to start that holiday journal Gran got me, but I can’t find one anywhere. Speaker_2: Check under your seat. I think I saw one rolling around earlier. Honestly, you lose more pens than I do money. Speaking of which… how are your A-Levels looking now that results are out? Are you still firm on York? Speaker_1: Yeah, York’s still the one. I’m terrified, obviously. Everyone says Latin’s a killer exam. Mrs. Davies warned us the examiners are *brutal*. Speaker_2: Latin, eh? Fancy that. I barely scraped through French. Still, you’re a bright spark. You’ll be fine. What about lunch? Fancy stopping somewhere around Birmingham? I saw a decent-looking services on the motorway map. They might even have a Holland & Barrett if you’re craving one of those vitamin gummy things. Speaker_1: Ugh, don’t remind me about vitamins. They taste like sadness. And Birmingham’s ages away! Can’t we just skip lunch and aim for a proper dinner in Cornwall? I’m craving a pasty. Speaker_2: A pasty it is, then. But we'll need petrol soon, and I wouldn't mind a cuppa. My IBS has been acting up a bit, so maybe a peppermint tea. Speaker_1: Oh, not the IBS talk again. You and your stomach. It’s like a whole other person. Speaker_2: (Sighs) It feels like it sometimes. Speaking of feeling unsettled, I still can’t believe how much hassle it was moving all our stuff. All those boxes… it took me a week just to unpack the DVDs. Did I ever tell you about the time I tried to assemble that flat-pack furniture? Disaster. Speaker_1: Only about a million times. You ended up using duct tape and swearing a lot. Speaker_2: A slight exaggeration. But it got the job done. Though now the washing machine’s making a funny noise... I suspect another delivery and another afternoon battling IKEA instructions. Speaker_1: Sounds… fun. Are we going through Gloucestershire? I always forget which counties we go through. It's such a long drive. Speaker_2: We will be. It's a bit of a trek, this journey, isn’t it? Reminds me of that time we drove to Norway to try and see the Northern Lights. That was amazing. Though freezing. Speaker_1: I remember! Mum kept saying we were wasting our time, but the lights *were* incredible. It smelled so different there, too. Not like everything smells of exhaust fumes here. Speaker_2: See? Worth it. Though honestly, I'd rather face a Norwegian winter than another Amazon delivery driver who can't find our house. It’s a miracle they ever deliver anything! Speaker_1: Seriously! They always say they've ‘tried’. Have you seen that new Jurassic Park film? It looks amazing. We could watch it on the way if I bring the DVD. Speaker_2: Ooh, good shout. Though I'm a bit of a moomins man myself, very sensible. Right, traffic’s starting to build up. Should be alright. My mate Terry reckons he saw someone trying to install a cat flap on a moving car the other day. Said it was a disaster. Speaker_1: (Laughing) You’re making that up! Speaker_2: Swear on my life. Apparently the cat wasn’t impressed either. You know, Egyptians used to worship cats. Imagine if all our pets had their own temples. Speaker_1: That’d be

Speaker_1: Honestly, the state of the garden is appalling. I keep meaning to get out there, but… well, you know. Life just gets in the way. Speaker_2: Tell me about it. I spent the weekend battling spreadsheets. Thought I'd finally get on top of things, ended up further behind. At least you *have* a garden to neglect. My balcony is currently sporting a single, rather sad-looking geranium. Speaker_3: (A slight chuckle) Neglect is a strong word, dear. It simply requires…strategic management. A garden, like a school, demands consistent attention. You can’t just leave things to run wild, expecting a pleasing outcome. Speaker_4: Aye, that's true enough. It’s a bit like wood, innit? Leave it untreated and it’ll rot. Needs a bit of oil, a bit of care. Though I’m more used to dealing with oak than roses, mind you. Speaker_1: Strategic management sounds lovely, but I’m picturing a small jungle out there. It's just overgrown. I really need to tackle the rose bushes, they’re getting completely swallowed by bindweed. Speaker_2: Bindweed is the devil’s work. It’s insidious. You pull it, it just comes back stronger. Like a particularly persistent office memo. Speaker_3: It’s about getting to the root of the problem, isn’t it? With both the bindweed *and* the memos, Archibald. You must be firm and unrelenting. Don't allow it to gain a foothold. Speaker_4: (Laughing) Firm and unrelenting, eh? Good advice for life in general, that. Reminds me o’ me old boss. Relentless he was. Drove us all mad, but got the job done. Speaker_1: I wish I could be relentless with the garden, but I’m more of a ‘procrastinate until it’s almost too late’ kind of person. It's embarrassing, really. I used to have such a lovely garden. Speaker_2: Don’t beat yourself up about it. We all have our priorities. Besides, a bit of wildness is good for the bees, isn’t it? Speaker_3: While I appreciate the sentiment, it’s essential to maintain a sense of order. A neglected space reflects a neglected mind, I always say. Speaker_4: Now hold on a minute, Eilidh. Just 'cause someone's garden's a bit wild doesn't mean their mind's away with the fairies. Sometimes folk just got other things on their plate. I've got three kitchens to finish this month, that takes some attention, you know? Speaker_1: Oh, three kitchens! That sounds…busy. What sort of kitchens are they? Modern? Country cottage style? Speaker_4: A real mix, actually. One’s a very sleek, minimalist thing, all handleless cabinets and stainless steel. Another’s proper farmhouse, big aga, lots of painted wood. And the third... well, the third’s a bit of a disaster, frankly. The client keeps changing their mind. It’s a nightmare. Speaker_2: Sounds stressful. At least spreadsheets don’t demand constant redesigns. Though they *do* demand a surprising amount of coffee. Speaker_3: The key, Archibald, is to anticipate the changes. A good administrator… or a good headmistress… is always one step ahead. Speaker_1: I think I’m several steps behind on everything at the moment. Maybe I should just move into a flat with a balcony, then I’d only have one geranium to worry about. Speaker_4: Don't do that. A garden's good for the soul. Even a messy one. You just need to carve out a bit of time, that's all. I'll give you a hand with those roses if you like. I'm pretty good with a pair of secateurs.

Speaker_1: Right, Operation Mother’s Day is a go! What do you two think? We need a plan. Gran’s expecting a visit, of course, but what else can we do to make it special? Speaker_2: (Small voice) Can we make her a card? With glitter? Speaker_3: And draw a picture of a dinosaur! A really, *really* big one! Gran likes dinosaurs, doesn’t she? Speaker_1: She does! A glittery dinosaur card sounds amazing. Excellent ideas, both of you. We can definitely do that. I was also thinking, maybe we could bake her something? Cookies? Brownies? Speaker_2: Cookies! With sprinkles! Pink sprinkles! Speaker_3: No, chocolate sprinkles! They're better. Chocolate is the best. Speaker_1: (Chuckles) Okay, okay, we can compromise. Half pink, half chocolate sprinkles. Deal? Both Speakers 2 & 3: Deal! Speaker_1: Good. Now, I was also wondering if Gran would like to come to Forest School with us next week? It’s a bit muddy, but you two *love* it. Speaker_3: Forest School is awesome! I found a really cool stick last time. It’s a magic wand! Speaker_2: I made a fairy house! It was covered in leaves and moss. Speaker_1: See? Gran would love that. Although, she might need wellies. And maybe a change of clothes. Speaker_3: She’s a bit like a stick in the mud sometimes, isn't she? Speaker_1: (Raises an eyebrow, trying not to laugh) Oh, are you now? Where did *you* hear that? Speaker_2: Daddy said it! Speaker_1: (Sighs) Right. Well, it’s an idiom, darling. It means she can be a bit stubborn. It doesn’t mean she *is* a stick! Speaker_3: What’s an idiom? Speaker_1: Oh, good question. It’s like… a saying that doesn’t mean exactly what it says. Like if I said “it’s raining cats and dogs,” it doesn't *actually* mean cats and dogs are falling from the sky, does it? Speaker_2: No! That would be silly! Speaker_1: Exactly. It just means it’s raining very hard. Speaker_3: So if I said you’re “pulling my leg” you’re not actually pulling my leg? Speaker_1: (Laughing) No, you’re not! You're surprisingly quick on the uptake for someone who just learned what an idiom is. Speaker_2: Can we go back to the cookies now? I want to start planning the sprinkles! Speaker_1: Yes, absolutely. Sprinkles are very important. But first, let’s write Gran a little note and tell her about our Mother’s Day plans, and ask her about Forest School. What do you say? Speaker_3: Okay! And we can write “Happy Mother’s Day, best Gran ever!” Speaker_2: And lots of hearts! And glitter! Speaker_1: Perfect. Let’s get started then. Operation Mother's Day is officially in full swing!

Speaker_1: Honestly, I’m still reeling from Auntie Maureen’s funeral. It just…doesn't feel real, you know? She was always *there*. Speaker_2: I know, it’s awful. I keep expecting her to ring, complaining about the price of tomatoes or something. She was a force of nature, wasn’t she? Speaker_1: A total force. And she fought that cancer for so long. Years, didn’t she? It feels almost… selfish to be relieved it’s over, but the pain she was in towards the end… Speaker_2: You're not being selfish at all. It’s natural to feel a sense of peace when someone you love is finally at rest. It’s the watching them suffer that’s the truly unbearable part. My Nan was the same. Held on for so long, but the last few months… just watching her fade. Speaker_1: It’s horrible. And it makes you think, doesn’t it? About your own mortality, your family. I’ve been feeling so anxious lately, constantly checking myself for lumps and bumps. Ridiculous, I know. Speaker_2: Not ridiculous at all. It’s a completely normal reaction. It’s fear, pure and simple. Are you talking to anyone about it? You’ve always been so good at bottling things up. Speaker_1: I’m trying to be better about that. I booked a session with that counsellor, Sarah, you recommended. Haven’t had it yet, but just booking it felt…lighter. And I’m trying to talk to Ben more, but he just keeps saying "You’re fine, you're worrying too much.” Men, honestly. Speaker_2: They mean well, but they just don’t *get* it, do they? Honestly, Sarah’s brilliant. She really helped me when I was struggling after my mum’s diagnosis. Just having someone to vent to, without judgement, made such a difference. Speaker_1: That’s what I’m hoping for. It’s just… everything feels so fragile all of a sudden. And then Leo's been having such a tough time at school. Speaker_2: Oh no, what’s happening with him? Is it still that bullying situation? Speaker_1: It's… evolved. It started with the teasing, but now it’s more subtle. Exclusion. He’s saying they won’t let him play football at breaktime, that they whisper when he walks past. He’s so quiet about it, which worries me even more. He’s normally so boisterous. Speaker_2: That’s awful. He's such a sweet boy. Have you spoken to the school? Speaker_1: I have, but they’re being frustratingly vague. “We’re monitoring the situation.” "Encouraging positive behaviour.” It feels like they’re just hoping it’ll go away. I’m thinking of going in again, demanding a proper meeting with the head. Speaker_2: You absolutely should. Don't let them brush it under the carpet. And make sure Leo knows you believe him. That’s the most important thing. My Liam went through something similar in year five, and it took ages to get it sorted. It really knocked his confidence. Speaker_1: It’s just… I feel like I'm failing at everything at the moment. Work is stressful, Auntie Maureen’s gone, Leo’s unhappy, and I’m a mess of anxiety. Speaker_2: Hey, stop that. You’re not failing at anything. You’re a brilliant mum, a fantastic friend, and you’re dealing with a lot right now. It’s okay to not be okay. We all have those moments. Remember what we were saying about Nan? She always said, "This too shall pass." Cliché, I know, but sometimes clichés are true. Now, let's have another cuppa and you tell me about this work stress. What’s your latest client doing to drive you insane?

Speaker_1: Right, so I think I’ve finally cracked the code with this week’s lesson plan. It's all about conditional sentences, which… honestly, feels like teaching a particularly frustrating magic trick. Speaker_2: (Chuckles) Oh god, conditionals. They’re the bane of every language learner’s existence, aren’t they? Especially the mixed ones. I remember struggling with those for ages when I was learning French. Speaker_1: Exactly! It’s like, “If I *had* studied, I *would* be…” and their brains just short-circuit. Speaking of brains short-circuiting, how did your linguistics seminar go yesterday? Anything interesting? Speaker_2: It was alright. Professor Davies went on a tangent about the history of the definite article in Old English. Fascinating, obviously, but a bit…much for a Tuesday morning. I basically spent the hour doodling little speech bubbles. Speaker_1: (Laughing) Sounds about right. Davies *does* have a tendency to get lost in the weeds. Did he mention his trip to South Korea again? He’s obsessed with it. Speaker_2: Oh, you know he did. Apparently, he wants to do a comparative study on honorifics in English and Korean. He was saying how incredibly different the roles of men and women are, linguistically, over there. It’s all about showing respect, but it’s so gendered. Speaker_1: Yeah, he's mentioned that before. It's a tricky topic, isn't it? I read an article once that pointed out how much subconscious politeness structures our language here, even if it’s not explicitly gendered like in Korean. Speaker_2: True. Thinking about politeness… I’m starving. And I completely forgot to pack a lunch. Speaker_1: Seriously? You, the queen of meal prep? What happened? Speaker_2: I was rushing this morning, trying to finish that essay on Chomsky's theories – which, by the way, still feel utterly incomprehensible – and just…forgot. Speaker_1: Okay, okay. Don't worry. I was thinking we could order something. Fancy a veggie Thai? There’s that place on St. George's Road that does a decent Pad See Ew. Speaker_2: Ooh, yes! That sounds amazing. Although… maybe we should actually *cook* something at some point? We've been living off takeaway for a week. Speaker_1: You’re right. We should. I was thinking of trying that lentil shepherd’s pie recipe I found. It's pretty simple, even for me. Speaker_2: That sounds… healthier, at least. Though honestly, I'm always a bit skeptical of vegetarian shepherd's pie. Feels a bit blasphemous, doesn’t it? Speaker_1: Blasphemous? That’s a strong word. It’s just lentils and vegetables! Speaker_2: I know, I know. It’s just… my grandma always made the *real* thing, with proper lamb. And she was very firm in her opinions about vegetarianism. Said it was “unnatural.” Speaker_1: Ah, the grandmothers. Always the gatekeepers of tradition. Speaking of tradition, I saw your brother posted pictures from that lantern festival in China. Looks incredible. Speaker_2: Oh, yeah! He’s having the time of his life. He said the street food is insane, though he’s refusing to try anything with – and I quote – “wiggly bits”. Speaker_1: (Laughing) Classic Mark. He's such a picky eater. Anyway, I was browsing online last night, and I found someone selling a retro gaming console. It’s an old Game Boy Advance, in pretty good condition. Speaker_2: Ooh, no way! I loved that thing. I used to spend hours playing Pokemon Ruby. Are you thinking of getting it? Speaker_1: Maybe. It’s a bit pricey, but… nostalgia, you know? It would be nice to have something a bit more… tangible

Speaker_1: Honestly, this pizza is saving my life. I swear, that physics problem set nearly broke me. It was genuinely offensive. Speaker_2: Tell me about it. I’m still reeling from the module assessment feedback. Mr. Davies just…eviscerated my essay. Said it “lacked intellectual rigour.” Intellectual *rigour*? It was a 2000-word analysis of TikTok trends! Speaker_3: (Mouth full of pizza) Davies is just a wind-up merchant. Remember when he tried to convince us that Schrödinger’s cat was a metaphor for Brexit? Speaker_4: (Laughing) Oh my god, yes! And then he got genuinely offended when someone pointed out the logical flaws. Speaking of flaws, has anyone seen my sports kit top? I swear I left it in the living room. Speaker_1: Didn't you wear it to Sugarhouse last week? You were doing that weird dance with Ben to Charlie Simpson. Speaker_2: Oh, *that* dance. I have photographic evidence somewhere. It’s horrifying. Speaker_3: You looked like a malfunctioning robot, honestly. Though, Sugarhouse was good. Remember when we all tried to sneak in flavoured vodka? Speaker_4: And Liam got caught by security? Classic. He acted like he’d committed a federal crime. Speaker_1: Honestly, Liam's dramatic flair is a gift. Reminds me of Jack Whitehall. Speaking of, is anyone watching *The Big Fat Quiz* on Boxing Day? We *have* to. Speaker_2: Definitely. It's tradition! Though, last year was a bit ropey. They kept referencing stuff I hadn't even been born when it happened. Speaker_3: I’m more of a *University Challenge* person, to be fair. I love feeling smugly superior about random facts. Speaker_4: You *always* feel smugly superior, love. Anyway, anyone playing Articulate tonight? I've been practicing my describing skills. Speaker_1: Ooh, yes! We need to put a ban on anyone using overly complicated descriptions again, though. Remember when you tried to explain ‘Vampire Diaries’ last time? It took ten minutes and involved explaining the entire mythology of supernatural creatures. Speaker_2: In my defence, it *is* a complicated show. And it’s vastly underrated, might I add. It has more emotional depth than *Twilight*, definitely. Speaker_3: (Grimaces) Don’t even mention *Twilight*. Honestly, it's a cultural stain. I still have nightmares about Edward Sparkles. Speaker_4: Ok, ok, no *Twilight* talk. Has anyone read anything good lately? I’m in the mood for a thriller. Preferably one with a ridiculously convoluted plot. Speaker_1: I just finished *Cloud Atlas*. It's a bit of a mind-bender, but worth it. Or if you want something lighter, the *Chaos Walking* trilogy is good fun, despite being a bit… cheesy. Speaker_2: I’m halfway through a book about a woman who fakes her own death. It’s brilliant. Lots of twists and turns. Speaking of twists and turns, remember that time we tried to camp in the Lake District and it absolutely poured down? Speaker_3: Oh god, the flooding in Lancaster that year was awful. We were genuinely worried about the house getting submerged. Speaker_4: And then we discovered the leaky roof in the kitchen? That was a fun surprise. I swear, this house is a death trap. Speaker_1: It’s character building! Though, if anyone’s thinking about going to Africa next summer, I’m in. I want to see actual wildlife, not just England's finest pigeons. Speaker_2: I'm tempted. Although, airport security terrifies me. They always flag me for extra checks. I think it’s because I crack my knuckles so much. Speaker_3: You *do* crack your knuckles a lot. It’s genuinely unsettling. Makes me think you're about to start a fight. Speaker_4

Speaker_1: Aye, honestly, the traffic’s been mental since we left Durham. I thought getting out of the city would be the worst of it, but it's just…constant. Speaker_2: Yeah, it’s pretty grim. I wasn't expecting this on a Tuesday afternoon. Thought everyone would be at work. Maybe there’s something on down the A1? Speaker_1: Dunno. Maybe. Though, it’s not just the A1, even the little back roads were packed. I was thinking, right, someone’s probably had a right shunt somewhere, causing a knock-on. Speaker_2: That’s always a possibility. Makes you wonder if it’s worth the hassle sometimes, doesn’t it? Just to visit your mam for a couple of hours. Speaker_1: Don’t say that! She’ll be gutted if I only stay for a couple of hours. She’s been making a massive effort with the garden, she wants to show it off. Says she's got a new rose bush that smells "divine." Speaker_2: (chuckles) Divine, eh? Sounds like your mam. Still, it's good of you to go. I barely see my folks, and they live closer than yours. Guilt, mostly. Speaker_1: I get that. It’s easy to let weeks slip by. I was telling Sarah about this lass at work, she booked a holiday to Turkey and then her cat got ill and now she's cancelling and losing all the money. Speaker_2: Oh, no! That’s awful. Poor lass. Cats are expensive enough without having to cancel a whole holiday because of them. Speaker_1: Tell me about it. They're little fluffy money pits. She was saying she feels awful about leaving him with someone else, but also, she's proper stressed about the financial side of it. Ended up having a right cry during lunch. Speaker_2: That's rough. You'd think travel insurance would cover something like that, wouldn't you? Speaker_1: You'd think! But apparently, it's a pre-existing condition. The cat's always been a bit… delicate, she said. Apparently, it's a clause in the small print. It's always the small print, isn’t it? Speaker_2: Always. Reminds me of when I tried to claim on my car insurance after that little scrape last year. The list of things *not* covered was longer than the list of things that were. Speaker_1: Oh god, what happened with that? I remember you mentioning something... Speaker_2: Some idiot pulled out on me at a roundabout. Minor damage, but still. They tried to wriggle out of it, said it was my fault. Had to get a solicitor involved. It was a nightmare. Waste of time and money. Speaker_1: See, that’s the worst. It’s not even the damage, it’s the stress of dealing with them. I'd rather just pay for it myself sometimes. Speaker_2: Exactly! Honestly, it's more trouble than it's worth. Though, I suppose that’s why they make it so difficult. Speaker_1: Speaking of trouble, did you ever manage to sort out that problem with your washing machine? You were saying the spin cycle was making a noise like a jet engine taking off? Speaker_2: (groans) Don’t even get me started. It's still happening. I think the bearings have gone. I've been putting off calling someone to look at it. I'm dreading the bill. Speaker_1: Maybe there's a YouTube tutorial or something? My dad fixed our dishwasher with one of those once. It was amazing. Speaker_2: I’ve thought about it, but I'm not exactly mechanically inclined. I’m more likely to make things worse. Plus, getting under the thing…no thanks.

Speaker_1: This weather, eh? Proper miserable. Feels like November already. Speaker_2: It does, doesn’t it? I swear my joints are aching more with this damp. It gets right into your bones. Speaker_3: Gran, you said you had a doctor’s appointment yesterday? How did it go? Speaker_2: Oh, it was the usual. He poked and prodded, told me to lose weight, and prescribed more of those pills. Honestly, I think I’m rattling with the amount of medication I take now. Speaker_4: That’s frustrating. Do you feel they’re actually *helping* though, with the pain? Speaker_2: A little, maybe. Hard to tell. It’s just… everything feels a bit achy these days. And I’m tired. Always tired. Speaker_1: Tired’s right. Can’t even face watching the football properly. Norwich were dreadful again last night. Absolutely dreadful. Speaker_3: Oh dear. Dad, you get so worked up about their games! It can’t be good for your blood pressure. Speaker_1: What else is there to get worked up about, eh? The weather? My knees? It’s the football, keeps me going. Though I tell you what, the commentator was a right pain. Kept going on about tactics, nobody cares about tactics when they're losing 3-0! Speaker_4: (Chuckles) Sounds about right. I tried to explain blockchain to my students today. Similar level of glazed expressions, I think. Speaker_3: (To Speaker_2) Mum, have you managed to get that new telly set up? The one you ordered online? Speaker_2: Oh, don't even *start* me on that telly. That’s been a disaster! First, the delivery man left it in the garden in the rain. Then, trying to connect it to the internet… honestly, it might as well be written in ancient Egyptian for all the sense it makes. Speaker_1: You need young Alex to come round. He's good with all that techy stuff. He sorted out my tablet when I couldn't even find the on switch. Speaker_2: I did ask him, but he's so busy with work. Said he'd try to pop over next week. Honestly, it’s just a waste of money. I might as well have stuck with my old one. At least I understood that! Speaker_3: It’ll be worth it once it's set up, Mum. You’ll have all those streaming services, and you can finally watch ‘Great British Bake Off’ in proper HD. Speaker_2: Hmm. That is tempting. But honestly, the stress of getting it working… it's giving me a headache. And then *this* weather! Makes you just want to curl up with a hot water bottle and a good book. Speaker_4: A hot water bottle and a good book sounds lovely, actually. Perhaps that’s what I need to do this evening, escape the marking. Speaker_1: Hot water bottle, eh? Good idea. My feet are like blocks of ice. I think I’ll join you in a bit of misery watching re-runs of ‘Dad’s Army’. That's something to look forward to. Speaker_3: Alright, you two. Don't let the weather get you down too much. And Mum, don’t worry about the telly, we’ll sort it out. Maybe I can come round tomorrow and give it a go? Speaker_2: Oh, that would be lovely, dear. Thank you. Just promise you won’t get frustrated with me if I can’t understand a thing. Speaker_3: No promises! But I’ll try my best.

Speaker_1: Honestly, the wedding planning is… consuming my life. I spent three hours last night comparing ribbon colours. *Ribbon* colours! Speaker_2: (Laughing) Oh, you’re already lost in the details! It’s good though, right? Means you’re excited. How’s Mark coping? He doesn’t seem the ribbon-choosing type. Speaker_3: He’s mostly just nodding and saying “Sounds lovely, babe.” I think he’s secretly terrified. He did try to suggest brown tape once. Brown *tape* for wedding decorations. Speaker_4: (Gasps dramatically) The audacity! Did you… did you veto that immediately? Speaker_1: Vetoed is an understatement. I think I may have shrieked. He quickly backtracked saying it was a joke. A *very* bad joke. Speaker_2: Men. Honestly. Speaking of men… how’s Liam? Still refusing to discuss anything remotely resembling the future? Speaker_3: Ugh, don’t even get me started. He just avoids the topic. Like, if I even mention the word ‘commitment’ he suddenly remembers he needs to… check the football scores. Or feed the goldfish. Speaker_4: The goldfish?! Does he even *have* a goldfish? Speaker_3: It’s a metaphor, obviously! It’s just... frustrating. I want to know if we’re on the same page. I’m not asking for a ring, just a conversation! Speaker_1: I feel you. It’s awful when they shut down like that. It makes you question everything. Speaker_2: Well, maybe you need to stage an intervention. Get all the girls together, corner him with a nice dinner and a carefully worded list of questions. Speaker_4: Ooh, I’m in! We could make it a themed intervention. Like, ‘Operation: Future Talk.’ We'd need code names. Speaker_1: (Giggles) This is getting out of hand. But honestly, it’s tempting. Although, I’m trying to avoid inflicting my wedding stress on everyone else. Speaking of dinner… I was thinking we could all go to that new Italian place on Friday? I need a night away from swatches and seating plans. Speaker_3: Yes! Absolutely. That sounds amazing. I haven't had proper pasta in weeks. Speaker_4: Count me in. I need carbs and gossip. And maybe we can brainstorm Operation: Future Talk while we’re there. For, you know, research purposes. Speaker_2: Perfect. It's a date then. Though, honestly, sometimes I think I’d rather spend a quiet night in. Sarah keeps going on about how she and Ben are ‘thinking about’ kids. Speaker_1: No way! Sarah? The one who swore she’d never change a nappy? Speaker_2: The very same. She’s completely gone off the deep end with baby names. I heard her suggesting ‘Peregrine’ the other day. *Peregrine*! Speaker_3: (Bursts out laughing) Oh my god. That's… intense. Speaker_4: I’m starting to think marriage and kids are just a collective delusion. A beautifully decorated, extremely expensive delusion. Speaker_1: Don't say that! It’ll put me off the ribbons all over again. But yeah, it’s all a bit… overwhelming, isn't it? Especially seeing everyone else move forward. Speaker_2: It is. But, hey, at least we have each other to complain to, right? And copious amounts of pasta. Speaker_3: And maybe, just maybe, we can save Liam from a goldfish-filled future. Speaker_4: To pasta, friendship, and Operation: Future Talk!

Speaker_1: Honestly, this new telly… it’s got more buttons than a blasted spaceship. And half of 'em I haven’t a clue what they *do*. Doreen, you were saying your grandson, young Thomas, is good with these things? Speaker_2: Oh, he is, Arthur. A whizz, that boy. Spends all his time on that computer, mind you, but he understands all this streaming and on-demand malarkey. He sorted my tablet out when it froze last month. Said I was trying to run too many things at once. Honestly, I was just looking at pictures of the great-grandchildren! Speaker_3: (Chuckles) It’s the same at school, honestly. Trying to get the little ones to focus when they’ve all got a phone in their pockets. It’s a constant battle. Though, I have to say, some of the educational apps are brilliant. We're using one at the moment for phonics that's genuinely engaging. Speaker_1: Phonics, eh? Funny how things change. Back in my day, it was just chalk and talk, and a good whack on the knuckles if you weren’t paying attention. Times were different, I suppose. Not necessarily better, mind you. Speaker_2: Oh, definitely not better, Arthur. We’ve come a long way. Though it does worry me, all this screen time. I used to take the children out riding, you know? Old Maggie, the pony, she was a saint. Little Emily practically lived in the saddle. Speaker_3: That sounds lovely, Doreen. My daughter’s been talking about getting the kids into horse riding. Says it's good for discipline and builds confidence. I'm a bit wary, though – it's an expensive hobby, isn’t it? Speaker_1: That it is, lad. That it is. Everything’s getting more expensive. I’m dreading the winter, I am. Heating bills are going through the roof. And my pension…well, let's just say it doesn't stretch as far as it used to. Speaker_2: Tell me about it, Arthur. I’m just thankful I managed to save a little something when I was working. Though it dwindles, doesn't it? Seems like it just disappears. Still, we manage. A cup of tea and a good chat always makes things feel a bit better. Speaker_3: Absolutely. And look, Arthur, if you're really struggling with the heating bills, there are schemes available. I was reading about one the other day, a warm home discount. I can send you the link if you like? Speaker_1: Oh, would you, lad? That’d be very kind of you. I'm a bit proud, you see. Don't like asking for help. But a body has to swallow their pride sometimes, I suppose. Speaker_2: Nonsense, Arthur. There’s no shame in it. We all need a hand from time to time. Remember when I broke my wrist last year? You were the one fetching and carrying, making sure I was alright. Speaker_3: And speaking of fetching and carrying, I promised my lot I’d pick up a new board game on the way home. They’ve been asking for ‘Ticket to Ride’ for ages. Apparently, it’s all about building railways and collecting sets. Sounds complicated. Speaker_1: Railways? Now *that* I understand. Used to spend hours down at the station as a boy, watching the steam trains come and go. Wonderful machines, they were. Not like these electric things now, all silent and soulless. Speaker_2: Everything changes, Arthur. Everything changes. But thankfully, some things stay the same. Like good company and a nice cup of tea.

Speaker_1: …and honestly, the teenagers I’m teaching at the moment, their grammar is appalling. Absolutely appalling. You wouldn’t believe it, coming out of secondary school. Speaker_2: (Chuckles, stirring his tea) Ah, well, things change, don’t they? When I left school, we were all expected to write properly, beautifully even. Penmanship was a thing! Now it’s all thumbs and screens. Speaker_1: Exactly! It’s the screens. They’re texting each other in abbreviations, and then they try to write an essay…it’s a disaster. Still, it keeps me employed, I suppose. Though sometimes I wonder if I’m just fighting a losing battle. Speaker_2: Don't say that! You're a good teacher, I know you are. It’s a valuable skill, knowing another language. Makes you see the world differently, doesn’t it? Remember that trip we took to Italy, a few years back? You were ordering for us in fluent Italian, and I felt like a right buffoon! Speaker_1: (Laughing) Oh, don’t be silly! You managed perfectly well. Though I do enjoy being able to use it. So, how was your weekend? Did Margaret enjoy the garden centre? Speaker_2: Oh, she absolutely loved it. Spent a small fortune, naturally. Hydrangeas mostly. She's convinced she can get them to bloom blue, despite the soil being resolutely pink. It's a running battle, really. I just help carry things. Speaker_1: Sounds…domestic. It’s good she has a hobby though. Keeps her busy. I think I’ll finally tackle the garden this weekend. It’s become completely overgrown. Though I’m not nearly as green-fingered as your Margaret. Speaker_2: You’ll be alright. Just a bit of weeding and hacking, that’s all. Speaking of keeping busy, how’s your brother, David? Haven't seen him in ages. Speaker_1: He's good, actually. He’s finally started that pottery course he was talking about. He’s really into it, apparently. Making all sorts of…interesting creations. He sent me a photo of a rather wonky-looking vase. Speaker_2: (Smiling) Good for him. Always good to have something to occupy you in retirement, isn’t it? I’ve been tinkering with my stamp collection. Found a rather rare Penny Black the other day. Speaker_1: Oh, really? That's impressive! You've had that collection for years, haven't you? Your father started it, didn’t he? Speaker_2: That's right. Passed it down to me. It's a good link to him, I suppose. He used to take me to stamp fairs when I was a boy. Happy memories. We were thinking of going to Stratford-upon-Avon next week, Margaret and I. Fancy a theatre trip? Speaker_1: Oh, that sounds lovely! I haven’t been to the theatre in ages. What’s on? Speaker_2: They’re doing ‘As You Like It’. Margaret’s a big Shakespeare fan. I mostly just enjoy the atmosphere, to be honest. And a nice pre-theatre dinner. Speaker_1: That sounds perfect. I might just take you up on that. Let me check my schedule and I’ll let you know for sure tomorrow. Speaker_2: Splendid. Always a pleasure to have your company. Now, shall I refill your cup? Speaker_1: Please. And thank you, George. This really is lovely.

Speaker_1: Honestly, that was the most… underwhelming Valentine’s Day ever. Like, seriously. Speaker_2: Oh no! What happened? Don’t tell me Liam didn’t even *attempt* romantic gestures? Speaker_1: Attempt is a strong word. He remembered it was Valentine’s Day, which is a start, I guess. But it was… a Tesco meal deal and watching football. Speaker_2: (Laughing) Oh, bless him. He’s… practical. Speaker_1: Practical bordering on completely oblivious! I mean, I didn’t expect roses and a fancy restaurant, but a *little* effort? I saw Chloe’s boyfriend got her a weekend away to Brighton! Brighton! Speaker_2: Ooh, fancy! Is Brighton nice? I’ve never actually been. My mum always said it was full of stag dos and… well, just a bit much. Speaker_1: It can be, yeah. But it's cute! They went to this little cinema on the pier, apparently. Old-school vibes. We should go sometime, proper girls’ trip. Speaker_2: Ooh, I'd be up for that. Anything’s better than another night in watching terrible reality TV. Speaking of which, I spent my evening trying to decipher what my flatmate was ordering in this new Vietnamese place. Speaker_1: Oh, the one near the library? I’ve walked past, it smells amazing. Speaker_2: It *is* amazing! But the menu… it’s all in Vietnamese, mostly. And she was speaking to the waiter in Vietnamese, and I just sat there looking bewildered while trying to point at a picture of noodles. Speaker_1: Haha! That’s hilarious. You need a translator! I’m going to try and learn some basic Italian before my trip to Rome next year, just so I don’t end up in a similar situation. Speaker_2: Good idea. Though, honestly, even ordering a coffee can be stressful when you're trying to remember all the phrases. I went to that fancy Italian place near the market last week and completely butchered my pronunciation. The waiter definitely judged me. Speaker_1: They always do! It’s like they're actively listening for you to mess up. I’m terrible with accents anyway. I can never tell the difference between someone from Birmingham and someone from… well, anywhere else in the Midlands! Speaker_2: (Laughing) Oh, you're so London! We get that all the time. People always lump everyone from the Midlands into one big accent. It’s frustrating! My cousin gets so annoyed. She’s from Nottingham, and people just assume she’s from… I don't know, somewhere near Manchester. Speaker_1: I’m so sorry! That’s awful. I genuinely can’t tell! My ears just aren’t trained. I can pick up a slight Scouse accent though, probably because of all the Liverpool fans around here. Speaker_2: Fair enough. You do get a lot of football fans. So, back to Valentine’s… did you at least get a nice dessert with your Tesco meal deal? Speaker_1: (Sighs) A discounted box of chocolates. That were already half-eaten. Speaker_2: Oh dear lord. Right, we’re going for cocktails later, my treat. You deserve a proper Valentine’s do-over. Speaker_1: You are an angel. Definitely in. And maybe we can strategically position ourselves near the Vietnamese place – for research, obviously. Speaker_2: Excellent plan. Operation: Noodle Deciphering is a go! Speaker_1: I'm in.

Speaker_1: Honestly, the sheer audacity of him to say that on Question Time… it wasn’t even a *dog whistle*, it was a full-blown foghorn of racism. Speaker_2: (Slurping noodles) Mmhmm. Classic. Honestly, I switched off after the first ten minutes. It’s just exhausting, you know? Constantly having to dissect every syllable for coded bigotry. This Dan Dan noodles are *incredible* though, seriously. You have to try some of mine. Speaker_1: I will, I will. I just… it feels like we’re going backwards. Like all the progress everyone fought for is just… eroding. And he’s got a platform to say that stuff! Speaker_2: It’s because the platforms are broken, isn’t it? Algorithmically amplified outrage. And the media loves a good controversy. Keeps the clicks coming. It’s all just… a game to them. Though, realistically, it affects real people. Speaking of affecting people, Mrs. Henderson from the office is at it again. Speaker_1: Oh, *not* her. What is it this time? Is she still trying to take credit for my designs? Speaker_2: Worse. She spent the entire morning complaining about “woke” housing policies. Apparently, building affordable flats near her leafy suburban paradise is a personal affront. Said it would “ruin the character of the area.” Speaker_1: (Scoffs) Oh, for goodness sake. The ‘character’ being exclusively for people who already own property and can afford extortionate council tax? Speaker_2: Exactly! It’s amazing how quickly ‘community spirit’ evaporates when it’s threatened by, you know, *people*. I tried to gently point out the housing crisis and systemic inequalities, but she just glazed over. Honestly, sometimes I wonder why I bother.
