Speaker_1: It’s the same argument all the time, isn’t it? ‘Protecting property values’ is just a euphemism for ‘keeping out anyone who isn’t already privileged.’ It’s all tied together, isn’t it? The racism, the classism, the whole system. Speaker_2: Totally. It's all branches of the same rotten tree. Capitalism incentivises that kind of thinking. Competition for limited resources. Scarcity mindset. Makes people… unpleasant. Speaker_1: And the housing situation just *fuels* it. It's designed to be a system where owning property is the ultimate goal, the ultimate marker of success. And then they’re outraged when someone suggests maybe, just maybe, everyone deserves a safe and decent place to live. Speaker_2: It’s mad. I've been looking again, you know, trying to figure out if I can actually get on the ladder, or even just a slightly less precarious rental. Everything in Zone 3 is still ridiculously priced. I saw a studio flat in Finsbury Park the other day… smaller than my bedroom in university, and still £1600 a month. Speaker_1: That’s insane! And you’re a working journalist! It's just… it feels impossible sometimes. I’m lucky, I guess. My parents helped with a deposit, but even then, it took years of saving. Speaker_2: You’re lucky, yeah. But even with your salary, it's still a struggle, right? Knowing you're just feeding the beast, essentially. Paying off someone else’s mortgage… Speaker_1: Precisely. It’s a system designed to keep us all scrambling. And then, politicians like that bloke on Question Time come along and blame *us* for the problems, rather than the system itself. Speaker_2: Right? Anyway. More noodles? We need energy to fight the good fight, or at least commiserate effectively. Speaker_1: Definitely more noodles. And maybe a large pot of tea, just to brace myself for the next news cycle.

Speaker_1: Honestly, I’m dreading Tuesday. Just…dreading it. Speaker_2: Nursery drop-off? It’ll be alright, Mum. He’ll probably be fine, and you’ll feel awful for the first hour then better. Honestly. Speaker_1: That's what everyone says. It's not *him* I’m worried about, you know? He’s a little social butterfly, always wanting to be with other kids. It’s *me*. It’s the thought of leaving him, that’s all. Suddenly I’m back at work and… well, it feels selfish really. Speaker_2: It’s not selfish! You need to work, you want to work. And little Leo will have a brilliant time, learning and playing. Think of all the new things he’ll experience. Speaker_1: I know, I know. It’s just… it’s a big change. And then trying to balance everything. Work, picking him up, dinner, bedtime… I feel like I’m already exhausted just thinking about it. Speaker_2: You’ll get into a routine. It’ll be hectic for a bit, but you will. And Dad’s helping, right? Speaker_1: He is, he is. Though he keeps suggesting we watch that awful police procedural on Tuesday nights. Says it’ll ‘take my mind off things’. Honestly, half the time I’m too tired to even *see* the television. Speaker_2: Ugh, no way. That show is so predictable. We should have a proper girls’ night when you’re settled back in. Maybe a film? Or we could finally try that new Italian place. Speaker_1: Oh, that sounds lovely. It feels like ages since we’ve just… hung out. What are you thinking for your summer holiday then? Any plans? Speaker_2: Still up in the air, to be honest. I was thinking maybe Interrail again? Last time was amazing, but a bit rushed. Or maybe something a bit more… chilled? Somewhere with a beach. Speaker_1: A beach sounds wonderful. Maybe Spain? We could all go. Leo would love building sandcastles. Although, realistically, it might be a bit ambitious for this year… Speaker_2: We could look into it. No promises, but no harm in browsing, is there? Speaking of Leo, how's the weaning going? He’s been having purees for ages, hasn't he? Speaker_1: That’s the other thing stressing me out! He is, and he’s getting a bit bored of it now. I tried him with some mashed sweet potato yesterday, and he just… spat it out. Made such a mess. Speaker_2: Oh dear. They can be so dramatic. Have you tried finger foods? Little bits of steamed carrot or broccoli? Speaker_1: I have, but he just gums them and then throws them on the floor. It’s a complete waste of food! And honestly, it's a right mess. Speaker_2: It's a phase. He’ll get the hang of it. You just keep offering him different things, and eventually something will stick. Don’t stress too much. It's all part of the fun... well, not the throwing on the floor part! Speaker_1: Easy for you to say, you're not the one cleaning it up! And honestly… it just feels like everything is changing all the time. One minute he’s a tiny baby, the next he's potentially joining the workforce at nursery! Speaker_2: (Laughs) You’re such a worrier. He’ll be fine. And *you*’ll be fine. Now, finish your sandwich. You need your energy for Tuesday.

Speaker_1: Honestly, the day just… vanished. I feel like I achieved absolutely nothing. Just endless emails and pointless meetings. How was your day, David? Speaker_2: Much the same, actually. Spent most of it on the phone, chasing donations. It's getting harder and harder, you know? People are tightening their belts. Though, I did manage to get a commitment from old Mr. Henderson for the garden revamp. Small victory. Speaker_3: Mine was… eventful. Had a right nightmare with a delivery driver refusing to bring a stock order all the way to the back of the shop. Said it wasn’t his job. Honestly! Spent a good half hour arguing with him. Speaker_1: Honestly, Moodle is driving me up the wall. I spent three hours last night trying to get the Turnitin integration to *actually* work for the essay submissions. Speaker_2: Three hours? Ugh. And you can tell me more about what’s happening with your cousin’s family. Maybe we can brainstorm some ideas. Speaker_2: That would be brilliant, thank you. Speaker_1: (Chuckles) Aye, that sounds like Ben. He’s all about the cookin’. Remember that time he tried to make paella at that party in second year? Speaker_2: Oh god, the paella incident. That was a disaster. The rice was still crunchy and it smelled vaguely of burnt plastic. Speaker_4: And he insisted it was “authentic”. Honestly… Speaker_3: He’s a good lad, though. Despite his questionable culinary skills. It’ll be weird if he actually moves out. Feels like we’ve all been stuck in Whitehaven forever. Speaker_1: Tell me about it. I swear, if I have to see another grey sky and hear another seagull squawkin’, I’ll lose it. Speaker_2: Don't threaten us with a good time, Liam! Speaker_3: (Eyes wide) Falling in love? In a game? Wow! Speaker_1: It's all very complicated. Anyway, I also grabbed that book about space. The one with all the sparkly planets. Remember asking for that? Speaker_2: Ooh, yes! The one with the black holes! Are black holes scary? Speaker_1: They're a bit mysterious, aren't they? They suck everything in. But they're also really far away, so we don’t need to worry about being sucked into a black hole anytime soon. Speaker_3: Good. I don’t want to be sucked into a black hole. I want to eat a monster biscuit! Speaker_1: Me too, actually. Let's get this biscuit-making started, then. And then Bartholomew gets his very important half-birthday celebration. Speaker_2: Yay! Sprinkles! Speaker_3: And blue icing! For the monster! Speaker_1: Okay, okay, sprinkles *and* blue icing. Let’s do this. Where’s the flour…? Oh dear. I hope we have enough. Speaker_2: I'll look! Speaker_1: Honestly, the state of Facebook these days. It's just… relentless. Every single person I knew from primary school is suddenly a life coach or selling protein powder. Speaker_2: (Chuckles, taking a sip of his beer) You've hit the nail on the head. It’s become a marketplace of aspiration, isn’t it? Everyone's presenting this hyper-curated version of their lives. I swear, if I see one more "manifest your dreams" post, I’m muting someone. Speaker_1: It’s exhausting! And the arguments… remember when it was just for sharing photos of cats? Now it's full-blown political warfare in the comments. Speaker_2: Dark days. I mostly use it now to keep an eye on Mum, to be honest. She's discovered groups dedicated to vintage china and spends hours debating the merits of different floral patterns. It's… endearing. Speaker_1: Oh, that sounds perfectly Mum. Mine’s currently convinced she’s found a long-lost relative through one of those ancestry things. She's already planning a trip to Ireland. Speaker_2: Oh, lovely! That's actually a good use of it, isn’t it? Connecting with family. Speaking of connections… did you see Old Man Hemmings’ car yesterday? Down by the bakery? Speaker_1: Hemmings? The one with the ridiculously bright orange Rover? No! What was he doing with it? Still driving that thing, is he? Speaker_2: Apparently. It was parked halfway up the pavement, hazard lights flashing. He was arguing with Mrs. Gable about having blocked her driveway. It was a glorious mess. The Rover looked… even more orange in the afternoon sun. Speaker_1: (Laughing) Oh, that’s classic Hemmings. That car is a hazard to society. I genuinely thought he’d finally traded it in for something a bit more sensible. Maybe electric? Speaker_2: Sensible and Hemmings don't really go hand in hand, do they? He reckons it’s a classic. Apparently, it’s appreciated in value. He showed me some online forum or other where people were offering him a fortune for it. Speaker_1: Online forums? Oh dear. I bet those were the same people selling protein powder on Facebook. You can't trust anything you read on the internet, you know. It's all algorithms and bots and… Speaker_2: …and orange Rovers. Don’t forget the orange Rovers. Honestly, sometimes I feel like we’re living in a simulation. Everything is just… heightened. Speaker_1: Tell me about it. I spent an hour this morning trying to explain to a student why citing Wikipedia isn't acceptable academic practice. You’d think it was common knowledge. Speaker_2: It’s the age of information overload, isn't it? Everyone thinks they're an expert. It’s hard to sift through the noise. Speaker_1: Exactly! And then there’s the endless cycle of outrage… it’s draining. I need another drink. Do you want another one? Speaker_2: Yes, please. And maybe we can actively *not* talk about the internet for the next round. Speaker_1: (Smiling) Deal. Let's reminisce about the good old days… when the biggest problem was deciding which Spice Girl was your favourite. Speaker_2: Ah, simpler times. Baby Spice for me, always. Speaker_1: Predictable. Speaker_2: Hey! She was the sweet one! Speaker_1: That’s… a take. Speaker_2: (Grinning) I stand by it.

Speaker_1: Right, honestly, the day was *brutal*. Old Mrs. Higgins was back, complaining about the price of the biscuits *again*. Like, it’s printed on the packet! Speaker_2: (Eyes glued to the TV, where a giant meatball is plummeting towards a town) Ooooh! That was a big one! Do you think everyone's okay? Speaker_1: (Sighs) Probably not, darling. It’s a cartoon. They bounce. Honestly, it’s the complaining that gets me. You’d think people had nothing better to worry about than 5p on a pack of Digestives. Speaker_2: But she probably really likes Digestives. And 5p is like…a whole sweet! Speaker_1: True, true. Speaking of which, are you actually eating those crisps or just… arranging them? You’ve barely touched them. Speaker_2: I’m saving the ready salted for the end. These are cheese and onion. I’m building a city. See? This one’s the library, that one’s the…meatball factory. Speaker_1: (Chuckles) Brilliant. You've got a knack for that. Right, can you pass me the remote? I can’t reach it from here. Think I’ll flick through and see if there’s anything… less catastrophic on. Speaker_2: Which button? There’s loads. Speaker_1: The red one. No, the other red one. Top right. No, wait… the *silver* one, then red. It’s a nightmare this remote. Honestly, everything’s over-complicated these days. Speaker_2: Got it! But I like it when it rains meatballs. It's so funny. Do you think the scientist should have stopped making them, though? Even if everyone liked them? Speaker_1: That's… a really good question, actually. It's kind of like, what's more important, making people happy or being responsible? It’s a surprisingly deep film, for something about flying food. Speaker_2: Is that what grown-ups talk about when they watch films? Like, the deep stuff? Speaker_1: Sometimes. Although usually it's just… moaning about work. Which brings me back to Mrs. Higgins and the biscuits. And my boss breathing down my neck about sales targets. It's exhausting. She called me lazy... can you believe it? Speaker_2: Lazy! That’s not fair! You work really hard. You’re studying *and* working. Speaker_1: Thanks. It's just… draining. And I feel like I’m constantly having to justify myself. It’s like, if I don’t match some ideal of ‘productive’ then I’m worthless. Speaker_2: That’s what Bethany was saying in feminism society. About how girls have to be seen as, like, always trying to achieve something, whereas boys can just *be*. It’s rubbish. Speaker_1: Right? It's completely rubbish. It’s funny isn’t it, how even watching a silly film about meatballs brings us back to all that? Speaker_2: (Pointing at the screen) Look! They’re using the spaghetti as bungee cords! Speaker_1: Amazing. You know, when we were kids, we used to have these conversations all the time. Just bouncing ideas off each other, not really worrying about sounding smart or… politically correct. Feels like everything’s got so much heavier, hasn't it? Speaker_2: Maybe. Or maybe we’re just noticing things more now. Like, about the scientist being a bit selfish. And about Mrs. Higgins being a bit… extra. Speaker_1: (Smiling) You're a good kid. You really are. I just hope you don’t end up having to argue about biscuit prices for a living. Speaker_2: I'm going to be an artist. And artists don't work in shops. They make important things. Like pictures of raining meatballs.

Speaker_1: So, another weekend gone, eh? Did you catch the match? Everton were… well, Everton. Speaker_2: Catch it? Lad, I *live* for the match. Though living out here in Finland means a lot of dodgy streams and getting up at ungodly hours. They were shocking, weren’t they? Absolutely shocking. Looked like they hadn't bothered turning up in the first half. Speaker_1: A recurring theme, sadly. Though, given the state of things generally, it hardly feels surprising to see a bit of listlessness, does it? I mean, look at the political landscape back home. Utter chaos. Speaker_2: Chaos is an understatement, mate. It’s a right mess. Remember when Blair came in? Everyone was saying ‘New Labour, new hope!’ Real change, they promised. Look at it now. Seems like every politician's only in it for themselves. Speaker_1: Exactly! And the hypocrisy is astounding. All that talk about the working class and then…well, look at the state of the country. The widening gap, the cuts... It’s disheartening, to say the least. Studied it for years, written papers on the rhetoric of New Labour, but even *I* underestimated how quickly it would all unravel. Speaker_2: I remember voting for him, y’know. Thought he was the answer. He sounded alright, did Tony. Proper smooth talker. But then you see the wars, the dodgy dossiers… Started to smell a bit fishy, didn’t it? Speaker_1: Incredibly fishy. And the way they spun it all! The language was masterful, deliberately ambiguous. Trying to appeal to everyone, meaning they appealed to no one effectively. It’s a fascinating subject for analysis, actually, that kind of political rhetoric. But as a citizen? It’s infuriating. Speaker_2: Infuriating’s a good word for it. Makes you wonder what’s the point, y’know? I spend my days driving people around, listening to their gripes. Everyone’s feeling squeezed. The government’s obsessed with these… these ‘stakeholder’ initiatives. What even *is* a stakeholder? Sounds like something out of Dracula. Speaker_1: (laughs) A rather apt analogy, actually. It’s a buzzword designed to obscure accountability. It’s about shifting responsibility, distributing blame. "Oh, we consulted with all stakeholders." Meaning, they listened to everyone and did exactly what they wanted anyway. It's linguistic trickery. Speaker_2: Trickery’s right. It's all trickery. And then they wonder why no one trusts them. They've lost touch with real people, the ones struggling to make ends meet. All these politicians in their fancy suits, talking about abstract concepts… They don't know a day in my life, driving around Liverpool in the rain. Speaker_1: Precisely. And that disconnect is only growing. It’s easier to grandstand with empty promises than address the systemic issues. It's ironic, isn't it? I lecture on the power of language, and then watch politicians systematically abuse it to manipulate public opinion. Speaker_2: It's enough to make you give up on the whole lot of 'em. Still… gotta have hope, eh? Maybe Everton will pull it together next week. That’s something to aim for, at least. Speaker_1: (Smiling) A noble sentiment. And perhaps a more achievable goal than political reform at this juncture. Speaker_2: You got that right. Now, speaking of hope… fancy a coffee? This Finnish stuff’s surprisingly good. Speaker_1: I would like that very much.

Speaker_1: Honestly, wading through those BNC recordings for the new project is *killing* me. It's just… so much beige. Like, conversation after conversation about the weather and what they had for tea. Speaker_2: Oof, sounds grim. Still, at least you're getting paid to listen to people chat, right? Beats my Sunday, which is mostly staring at a Word document and aggressively editing semicolons. Speaker_1: True, true. Though sometimes I fantasize about just chucking it all and becoming a professional dog walker. Specifically, pug walker. Imagine being surrounded by little wrinkly faces all day. Speaker_3: (Chuckles) You and your pugs! You’re obsessed. Speaker_1: They're just so *comical*. Anyway, have you updated your LinkedIn recently? I keep getting those "people you may know" suggestions, and half of them are people I actively avoided at uni. Speaker_2: Briefly. Mostly to ignore the recruiters desperate for 'Content Creators' who apparently require a PhD in English Literature. It’s insulting, honestly. Social media just feels… exhausting these days. Everyone curating this perfect life. Speaker_1: Tell me about it. I saw Amelia’s photos from the Maldives. Seriously? Turquoise water and cocktails at sunrise? Makes my rainy East London flat look particularly bleak. Speaker_3: Oh, the Maldives. I was supposed to go there with… well, never mind. It’s a long story. But the thought of being on a tiny island surrounded by ocean just makes me panic. Speaker_2: You and flying, eh? Still haven’t cracked that one? Speaker_3: Nope. The idea of being suspended thousands of feet in the air in a metal tube… It’s my biggest fear. Honestly, I’d rather swim to Spain. Speaker_1: (Laughing) That’s… ambitious. Though, if anyone could do it, it’d be you. You spent half your childhood swimming in the Welsh rivers, didn't you? Speaker_2: She did! It’s true. Grew up practically amphibious. Speaking of Wales, are you still planning to visit your family soon? Speaker_3: Next weekend, hopefully. Mum’s been going on about needing help with the garden. Which basically translates to 'sit and watch me prune roses while I complain about the neighbours.’ Speaker_1: Sounds idyllic. I miss having a garden. Living in London, you forget what actual green spaces are like. Though, I’m thinking of trying to squeeze in a trip to Barcelona in the autumn. Speaker_2: Oh, nice! Have you been before? Speaker_1: No, never. Always wanted to go. A friend of mine lives there now, said it’s amazing. He’s trying to convince me to move. Speaker_3: Barcelona’s lovely. Though, be warned, the pickpockets are legendary. Keep your belongings close! Speaker_1: Noted! Maybe I’ll just stick to looking at pug pictures instead. Safer that way. Speaker_2: Honestly, you probably would be. Hey, anyone fancy another coffee? This conversation is turning into a lovely chaotic mess. Speaker_3: Yes please! And maybe we can look at adopting a pug. Just to discuss the logistics, of course. Speaker_1: (Smiling) Oh, you’re enabling me. Fine. Pug research begins now. Speaker_2: Excellent. The most important research of our lives. Speaker_3: Definitely. And we can all complain about LinkedIn later. Speaker_1: Deal.

Speaker_1: Right, so I was thinking, maybe a fragrant rice with that? It’ll soak up all the sauce nicely. You’re chopping onions like a pro, by the way. Much faster than me. I had a breakthrough on Tuesday, though. Might actually finish the chapter by the end of the week. Speaker_2: Excellent! See? You just need occasional breakthroughs. Speaking of breaks, have you thought any further about that tattoo? The one with the… constellations? Speaker_1: Yeah, I did some more sketching. Speaker_2: Oh, Ben from the pub? Good. Don't go to one of those dodgy places with questionable hygiene. Seriously. Remember what happened to poor old Derek? Speaker_1: (Grimaces) Don’t remind me. Floral infection is *not* a good look. I’ve checked this guy’s portfolio, it’s solid. Anyway, what about you? Any news from the literary world? Still battling with interns who think ‘proofreading’ means running spellcheck? Speaker_2: (Laughs) You know me too well. Honestly, the things I find. One of them suggested changing ‘metaphor’ to ‘similie’ because it "sounded more modern." I nearly had a stroke. *A door opens and another voice enters* Speaker_3: Hello! Am I interrupting culinary artistry? Smells amazing in here. Speaker_1: Liam! No, not at all. Just prepping dinner. Come on in, have a seat. Speaker_2 is telling me horror stories about her interns. Speaker_3: Oh, the intern saga continues then. Classic. Honestly, you'd think universities taught basic grammar these days. Listen, I just wanted to quickly say hi, I’ve been completely swamped with Christmas lists. The publishers are demanding everything to be finalized by next week, it’s madness! Speaker_2: Christmas already? It feels like October was five minutes ago. Are you surviving the festive push, Liam? Speaker_3: Barely. Everyone's panicking about getting their books positioned for the Christmas market. It’s all “must-have gifts” and “perfect stocking fillers.” Honestly, sometimes I think I'm selling scented candles, not literature. Speaker_1: Sounds stressful. We were chatting about plans for Christmas, actually. I was thinking of going home to Mum and Dad this year. Are you doing anything special? Speaker_3: Probably the usual. Family, far too much food, and attempting to navigate my aunt’s political opinions. It’s a tradition. What about you, Speaker_2? Any grand plans? Speaker_2: I'm honestly thinking of just staying put. Maybe a quiet one with a good book and a roaring fire. I might finally tackle the spare room renovation. It’s been on the ‘to-do’ list for approximately five years now. Speaker_1: You and that spare room. It’s become a legend. I offered to help, remember? I'm surprisingly handy, despite what you think. Speaker_2: (Smiling) I haven't forgotten. Perhaps I’ll take you up on that offer. After I’ve dealt with the onslaught of Christmas book proposals, of course. Right, back to the chaos. But thank you for the escape, both of you. I needed that.

Speaker_1: Right, so I think this needs a *bit* more chilli powder, don’t you? It's looking a little…pale. Speaker_2: Mmm, yeah, definitely. Not enough kick. And maybe a squeeze of lime? It'll brighten the flavours up. Oh, and have you seen my new trainers? Speaker_1: (Stirring the pot) Lime, good shout. And *no*, I haven't seen your trainers. Are they the bright orange ones you were eyeing up online? Speaker_2: The very same. They arrived this morning. I wore them to pilates. Honestly, they’re a game changer. Speaker_2: She said it was fine, she went with a small group tour, which she’d recommend. Apparently, the markets are insane – like, a total sensory overload, but in the best way. Speaker_2: Oh no! It’s a tricky one. You need to really let it simmer, don't you? Low and slow. I’ve got a recipe from my auntie, she used to live in Marrakech for a year. I could send it over? Speaker_2: I know the feeling. I'm stuck in a rut with pasta. It's just…easy. But I'm trying to be better. That’s why I signed up for the cookery class. Speaker_1: Oh, how is that going? Speaker_2: It’s fun! Last week we made sushi, which was…challenging. I'm pretty sure mine looked like a small, ricey explosion. But the instructor was really patient. It’s a good way to force yourself to learn new skills. Speaker_1: Absolutely. You're always so good at picking up new things. I admire that. Right, I think this chilli is pretty much there. Time for the rice, then? Speaker_2: Sounds good. Oh! And I almost forgot – I nominated you for the book club’s ‘most likely to travel the world’ award. Speaker_1: (Smiling) You did *what*?! Oh, you are terrible! But…kind of sweet. Though, realistically, travelling the world feels a million miles away right now. Although... maybe next year? I’ve been saving… Speaker_2: See? You *are* a potential world traveller! It’s just a matter of time. Now, about those trainers… Do you think orange is too much? Speaker_1: Never too much orange, my friend. Never. Speaker_2: Good. That’s what I thought.

Speaker_1: Honestly, the student feedback this year is… something else. I’m getting a real mixed bag. Some of them are genuinely engaging, asking insightful questions, and then you get the ones who clearly haven’t read a single assigned reading. Speaker_2: Tell me about it. I had one student email me last week, asking for a summary of the entire module… two weeks before the exam. Two weeks! It's just… the entitlement, sometimes. Do you think it's a generational thing? Speaker_1: Maybe. Or maybe it’s just the pressure they’re under. Everyone’s so focused on getting the ‘right’ qualifications to get the ‘right’ job. It’s all very… transactional. Remember when we were at uni, it felt a bit more about actually *learning*? Speaker_2: Nostalgia’s a powerful thing, isn’t it? Though I do recall a lot of all-nighters fuelled by instant noodles and questionable life choices. Still, you're right. It feels different now. Speaking of different… did you see Sarah’s photos from her trip to Bali? Speaker_1: Oh, yes! Absolutely stunning. She looks so relaxed. She really needed that break. She was completely frazzled after dealing with… well, everything. How *is* Mark, actually? She didn’t say much in her messages, just that things were ‘complicated’. Speaker_2: Complicated is putting it mildly. Apparently, he's decided he needs to “find himself” which, as far as I can tell, involves learning to surf and documenting it all on Instagram. It’s… a bit much. She’s trying to be supportive, but I think she’s secretly furious. Speaker_1: Oh, that’s dreadful. Poor Sarah. He always struck me as a bit… flighty. Remember that time he tried to start a kombucha business and then gave up after two weeks because “it smelled funny”? Speaker_2: (Laughing) Oh god, yes! The Kombucha King. He’s brilliant at starting things, absolutely hopeless at finishing them. It’s exhausting just *being* around him. I feel terrible for Sarah. She deserves someone a bit more… grounded. Speaker_1: Absolutely. And she's such a rock for everyone else. It's not fair. Oh! I nearly forgot. I ended up having to cut Amelia’s toenails for her yesterday. She’d bent over backwards trying to do them herself and couldn't reach! Speaker_2: (grimaces) Oh, *no*. That sounds… uncomfortable for everyone involved. Is she okay? Speaker_1: Perfectly fine. She's surprisingly ticklish. It was a whole operation involving a magnifying glass and me pretending to be a professional podiatrist. She’s a good sport, though. It’s just… sometimes I feel like I’m constantly solving everyone else’s little crises. Speaker_2: That’s just you being a good friend, love. It’s what you *do*. And honestly, after a day of battling student feedback and existential crises, a bit of toenail trimming probably feels… grounding. Speaker_1: You've got a point. Maybe I *am* a secret podiatrist at heart. Speaker_2: Maybe you are. Right, shall we grab some dumplings for dinner? I'm starving. Speaker_1: Definitely. And we can continue dissecting the lives of our friends over spicy noodles. It’s a tradition, after all. Speaker_2: A very important tradition, indeed. Speaker_1: Look, is that Old Man Li’s stall? Quick, before all the good ones are gone!

Speaker_1: Honestly, I’m shattered. That spin class nearly killed me. I feel like my legs are going to fall off. Speaker_2: (Chuckles, sipping his coffee) You and me both. I thought I was fitter than I am. Old age creeping up, you know? Though, to be fair, I haven’t done a proper spin class in… well, ages. Speaker_1: It's brutal. But good brutal, right? Clears the head. Speaking of clearing heads, did you catch that documentary about… well, it was a bit out there, but about the simulation theory? Speaker_2: Oh, *that* one. My brother was going on about it for weeks. Something about us all living in a computer program? Sounds a bit… dramatic, doesn’t it? Speaker_1: Dramatic, yes. But fascinating! He made some really interesting points about glitches in reality. Like, have you ever had that feeling of déjà vu, so strong it feels… wrong? Speaker_2: Right, yeah, I have. But I just put that down to a lack of sleep or too much coffee. My wife, Sarah, thinks it’s all nonsense. She's much more grounded. She was watching one of those royal documentaries last night – the one about Charles and Diana. That was a drama of a different kind. Speaker_1: Oh, I saw trailers for that. It looks intense. Sarah’s your wife… how’s the planning going for the anniversary? Is the big party still on? Speaker_2: It’s… complicated. We were thinking a big bash, you know, invite everyone. But then Sarah started worrying it would be too much fuss, too stressful. She's rather low-key, my wife. I’m trying to convince her a small gathering with close friends and family is a good compromise. It's twenty years, you know? Should be celebrated. Speaker_1: Definitely. Twenty years is a milestone. You’ve got to do something. You’re good together, though. I always think you two are really solid. Which is amazing, considering how hectic your job is. How's work going, anyway? Speaker_1: It’s on the socio-linguistics of online gaming communities. Basically, how people use language to build identity and signal belonging. It *sounds* cool, but translating that into a coherent, 12,000-word argument… Speaker_2: That actually sounds fascinating! A bit niche, maybe? But good niche. Is the data collection side going well? Speaker_1: It’s…ongoing. I’m mostly doing forum analysis and some interviews. People are surprisingly willing to talk about their online personas. Though, a lot of it is just teenagers, which feels a bit limiting. Speaker_2: Well, that’s your demographic, isn’t it? Still, good to get a range. Lancaster is going to be a nice change of scenery though, right? Not just staring at a screen all day. Speaker_1: Absolutely. And seeing your family! I’m really looking forward to meeting your mum and dad properly. I feel like I’ve only met them briefly at Christmas and things. Speaker_2: They're really excited to meet you. Mum’s already planning all sorts of things. Potentially a trip to the coast? If the weather holds up. Speaker_1: Oh, that would be amazing! I haven’t been to the coast in ages. Not since… well, since that disastrous cockle-picking trip with my cousin. Speaker_2: *Laughs* Oh god, don’t remind me. I’d almost forgotten about that. You ended up with sand *everywhere*. Speaker_1: Everywhere! And feeling incredibly guilty about potentially illegally harvesting cockles. Honestly, a really bleak day. We definitely earned our fish and chips after that. Speaker_2: Speaking of earning things, have you thought any more about what you want to do after the Masters? Any career ideas? Speaker_1: Honestly? Not really. I'm kind of hoping something will magically fall into place. I like the research side of things, obviously, but the academic job market is…grim. Maybe something in lexicography? Or content strategy? I’m throwing darts at a board. Speaker_2: I get that. I’m toying with the idea of going into teaching, but it feels like a huge commitment. And the workload… Speaker_1: Yeah, my aunt’s a secondary school teacher and she’s perpetually exhausted. Although she loves it, apparently. It’s just…a lot. Speaker_2: My dad was talking about potential redundancies at his work the other day. It’s just a constant worry, isn’t it? Even with a degree, you’re not necessarily secure. Speaker_1: It’s terrifying. My brother was threatened with redundancy a few months ago, which was awful. Luckily, he managed to avoid it, but the stress was insane. How's your brother, by the way? Still living in York? Speaker_2: Yeah, he’s still there. He's really settled, actually. He’s got a little flat and everything. Mum fusses over him constantly, making sure he’s eating properly. It's a classic mum thing. Speaker_1: Haha! My mum’s the same. Always sending care packages full of biscuits and homemade soup. It’s endearing, but a bit…suffocating sometimes. Speaker_2: Definitely. It's good to get away, isn’t it? And Lancaster should be a good escape for both of us. Are we visiting the university campus at all? Speaker_1: I think so. Your aunt said she’d arrange something. It’ll be interesting to see what it’s like. I was looking at postgraduate courses there briefly, actually.

Speaker_1: Right, so then Liam proper tripped over, didn't he? Right in front of everyone at the gig. Speaker_2: (Laughing) No way! Liam? Seriously? He’s always going on about how coordinated he is. Speaker_1: I know, right? Total showman. He went flying. Landed right near the speaker. Thought for a minute he’d broken something. Speaker_2: Oh dear. Was the band any good at least? Who were they again? The… Static Waves? Speaker_1: Yeah, Static Waves. They were alright. Not amazing, a bit loud, really. But the atmosphere was decent. Loads of people were there, mostly sixth formers though, predictable. Speaker_2: Yeah, that’s the problem with gigs in Doncaster, isn’t it? Always a younger crowd. I’m starting to feel ancient at 22. Speaker_1: Don’t be daft. You’re not ancient. Though, thinking about it, it feels like ages since we were all cramming into the back of Mrs. Higgins’ car to get to a band practice. Speaker_2: (Smiling) Oh god, those were the days. The smell of damp dog and cheap air freshener. And the absolute terror of her driving. Speaker_1: She was a menace. A lovely menace, but a menace nonetheless. Remember when she nearly took out a lamppost on Frenchgate? Speaker_2: (Chuckles) How could I forget? Everyone screamed. Anyway, what have *you* been up to? Apart from witnessing Liam’s spectacular fall? Still painting miniatures? Speaker_1: Yeah, still at it. I’m working on a whole squad of Space Marines at the moment. It’s… therapeutic, actually. Gets me away from revision. What about you? Still obsessed with that guitar? Speaker_2: Absolutely. Been trying to learn this new riff by IDLES. It's driving me mad, though. My fingers are killing me. It’s way harder than it sounds. Speaker_1: IDLES are wicked. You’ll get there. You always do. Remember when you first started and couldn’t even hold a chord? Speaker_2: (Groans) Don't remind me. It was brutal. My housemates were threatening to evict me. Said it sounded like a dying cat. Speaker_1: (Laughing) They weren’t far off, to be fair. Have you been practicing with Ben and Chloe lately? Are they still trying to form a band? Speaker_2: They are. Actually, they’re sounding pretty good. Ben’s got some decent songwriting skills. Chloe’s drumming is…enthusiastic. Speaker_1: Enthusiastic is a polite way of putting it. She hits those drums like she’s personally offended them. Speaker_2: Exactly! But that’s Chloe. Speaking of bands, have you heard anything from The Northern Lights since they went to uni in Newcastle? Speaker_1: Not much. I saw something on Facebook, they played a gig at some student union thing. Seemed to go down well. I miss their gigs, though. They were always a good night. Speaker_2: Yeah, they were. Proper local legends. It's strange, isn't it? Thinking about everyone going their separate ways now. Uni, jobs… everything’s changing. Speaker_1: It is. Still, we’ve got each other, haven’t we? And Mrs. Higgins’ dodgy driving stories to reminisce about. Speaker_2: That’s true. Cheers to that. (Raises his glass) Speaker_1: (Clinks glasses with him) Cheers! To dodgy driving and Space Marines.

Speaker_1: Right, okay, so I’m going to use my researcher to fly to Atlanta. And then… oh no, wait. The eradication counter is at two! We are *so* close to curing blue. Speaker_2: (Chuckles, a thick Welsh lilt) Hold your horses, Sarah! Don’t get ahead of yourself. You need the three cubes to even *start* eradicating. You’ve got two in Atlanta, that’s it. Speaker_3: (From across the table, stirring his tea) Aye, and don’t forget about the outbreak in Santiago. That’s looking nasty. Honestly, this game is stressful. I’m a chef, not a global pandemic manager. Speaker_4: (Quietly) I think it’s brilliant. Properly tense. Though I’m still trying to figure out this Operations Expert role… what exactly does ‘share knowledge’ *mean* in practice? Speaker_5: (Leaning forward, a mischievous glint in his eye) It means you get to be a bit of a busybody, Rhys! You go around telling everyone what to do, pretending you’re terribly clever. It’s the Welsh way. Speaker_6: (Laughing) Oh, Glyn, you’re awful! But he’s not wrong, Rhys. You can give Sarah a card from your hand if it helps her research. Think of it as… strategic interference. Speaker_1: Yes, please Rhys! Honestly, I'm flailing. I had a whole plan for tackling blue, thinking I was about to win, and then *bam* – another outbreak in Cairo. Speaker_2: Okay, okay. Rhys, give Sarah the blue card. I'm going to build a research station in Essen. We need somewhere central for Europe. And keep an eye on that black disease, it’s creeping across Russia. Speaker_3: Russia? Seriously? This is just like real life, isn’t it? Always something going on in Russia. Reminds me of the time I tried to cater a wedding for a Russian diplomat… Speaker_4: (Interrupting gently) Oh, do tell! Was it chaotic? Speaker_3: Chaotic doesn’t even *begin* to cover it. They wanted caviar fountains, a live bear… I’m not joking! A *bear*! Luckily, health and safety intervened. Speaker_5: (Roaring with laughter) A bear! I can just picture it, Huw. You looking horrified, trying to explain to a Russian dignitary why a bear isn’t conducive to a pleasant wedding reception. Speaker_6: You always have the best stories, Huw. It truly is a gift. Speaker_1: Okay, focus people! Bear stories later. Rhys, did you give me the card? I need to research… right. Atlanta, then hopefully eradicate. Speaker_2: Given! Now, the problem with this game is the relentless pace. It feels like a proper sprint. Anyone fancy a cuppa? I’ll put the kettle on. Speaker_4: Yes, please. Strong and sweet, if you don’t mind. And maybe someone could explain this ‘forecasting’ thing again? I feel utterly lost when it comes to predicting outbreaks. Speaker_5: Forecasting is just fancy guesswork, love. You look at where the cubes are building up and make an educated…or not so educated…stab in the dark. Speaker_6: Don’t listen to Glyn. It’s about probability, really. And a lot of luck. This last time we played, we lost because of a rogue outbreak in Algiers. Speaker_1: Oh, don't even mention Algiers. That city is cursed in Pandemic. Right, Atlanta research… dice roll… please be good to me! Oh… yes! Success! One step closer to curing blue!

Speaker_1: Right, so, the CBeebies panto is booked! Tickets secured for Saturday afternoon. Are you both excited? Speaker_2: (Excitedly) Yes! Is Mr. Tumble going to be there? Speaker_3: I hope so! Will there be a dragon? I *love* dragons. Speaker_1: I think there's a very silly dragon involved, yes. And Mr. Tumble is definitely making an appearance. It's all about getting into the Christmas spirit early, isn’t it? Though, it feels a bit strange booking Christmas things in November. Speaker_2: It’s not Christmas yet! My birthday is *before* Christmas! Speaker_1: You are absolutely right. We mustn’t skip over your birthday! We’re still figuring out what we're doing for that, aren’t we? Any more brilliant ideas than the zoo? Speaker_3: Can we have a massive cake? With dinosaurs on it? Speaker_1: A massive dinosaur cake is a *very* good suggestion. We can definitely do that. I was thinking maybe a small party too, just a few friends from school? Speaker_2: I want Lily and Thomas to come! And Chloe! Speaker_1: Okay, Lily, Thomas, and Chloe. Noted. We’ll have to check with their parents. It’s going to be a summer birthday, so hopefully, we can do something outdoors if the weather is nice. Maybe a picnic and games in the park? Speaker_3: Can we have a bouncy castle? Speaker_1: (Laughing) A bouncy castle is a bit ambitious for the park, darling. Maybe for a bigger birthday? Speaking of things outdoors, I saw on CBeebies this morning they were doing a story about a little robin who was lost. It was very sweet, but it made me think about winter already. Speaker_2: I like ‘Bluey’ the best! Bluey is so funny! Speaker_1: Bluey is brilliant, isn’t she? That show is so clever. It’s lovely seeing them try and teach kids about family life and emotions in such a fun way. Do you remember what Nana said last week? “Happy as Larry” she was, because we were all having a good time. Speaker_3: What does ‘Happy as Larry’ *mean*? Speaker_1: It’s an old saying, sweetie. It just means very, very happy. Really content. Nana uses lots of old sayings. Speaker_2: Like when she said, ‘Don’t count your chickens before they hatch!’ That was weird. Speaker_1: (Smiling) That’s another one! It means don’t assume something good will happen until it actually *does*. It's a bit of a warning. Anyway, back to important things! World Book Day is coming up soon, too. Have you started thinking about costumes? Speaker_3: I want to be a pirate! With a proper sword! Speaker_1: A pirate sounds brilliant! We can definitely work on that. And then there’s Mother’s Day… oh goodness, it’s all happening so fast. I need to start planning something special for Nana. Speaker_2: I'm making her a card! With glitter! Speaker_1: Oh, that’s lovely! She will absolutely adore that. You two are so thoughtful. Okay, CBeebies panto, dinosaur birthday cake, World Book Day costumes, and Mother’s Day… we’re officially in planning mode! Is this conversation helpful? Would you like me to continue it or make any changes? Speaker_1: Right, so, the CBeebies panto is booked! Tickets secured for Saturday afternoon. Are you both excited? Speaker_2: (Excitedly) Yes! Is Mr. Tumble going to be there? Speaker_3: I hope so! Will there be a dragon? I *love* dragons. Speaker_1: I think there's a very silly dragon involved, yes. And Mr. Tumble is definitely making an appearance. It's all

Speaker_1: Right, this sourdough is genuinely amazing. Where did you get it, Chloe? Not the usual place, is it? Speaker_2: No, actually. Old mate Dave from down the road is doing a ‘micro-bakery’ thing from his kitchen. Apparently, he’s a retired chemist, which explains the obsession with hydration percentages and gluten development. Speaker_3: A retired chemist making sourdough? That’s… oddly perfect. Sounds very ‘Great British Bake Off’ contestant backstory. Speaker_1: Ha! It is good though. Seriously. So, any progress on the flat hunt, Sarah? Still looking at places in Bristol? Speaker_2: Bit of a disaster, actually. Saw a place yesterday that looked amazing online – modern, city centre, all that jazz. Turned up and it smelled… damp. Like, properly damp. And the landlord kept referring to the ‘character’ of the mould. Speaker_3: Oh, *no*. "Character" is code for “structural issues and potential respiratory problems”. You deserve better than a mouldy character flat. Speaker_1: Definitely. Bristol’s a nightmare for that, isn’t it? All those old buildings… Still, gotta stay positive. You’ll find something. Are you still keen on being closer to Liam? Is that driving the Bristol search? Speaker_2: It’s part of it. It’s just… he seems so settled there. Proper Bristolian now, complaining about the tourists and the students. And I miss him, obviously. It feels a bit silly, commuting up to Manchester every other weekend. Speaker_3: It *is* a long commute. But if it’s worth it, it’s worth it, right? Though, I can see how it would be nice to just… be there, without the travel. Have you considered the compromises? Maybe somewhere halfway? Speaker_1: Yeah, a halfway point could work. Though then you’re not really close to *anyone*. It's a tough one. Speaking of tough, how’s the teaching going, Amy? Any particularly… spirited students lately? Speaker_3: Oh, you know. A mixed bag. I’ve got one lad who genuinely believes Shakespeare was a collective of AI robots from the future. Trying to argue linguistics with him is… an experience. Speaker_2: (laughing) Oh my god. That's amazing. And terrifying. Speaker_1: AI robots! That’s a new one. I had a student once who insisted the Second World War was a hoax perpetrated by the pigeon fanciers’ association. Speaker_3: Pigeon fanciers?! Seriously? Speaker_1: Swore blind. Said they controlled the flow of information. Apparently, they needed to boost the market for homing pigeons. It's a long story. I’ve learned not to question it. It’s less stressful. Speaker_2: Wise move. Have you been on any of those dating apps, Sarah? Anything beyond mouldy landlords and Bristolian Liam? Speaker_2: Ugh, don’t even ask. It’s a wasteland. Either incredibly bland profiles saying they ‘enjoy long walks and good food’ – which, frankly, *everyone* does – or…well, honestly, the other end of the spectrum. I swear half the blokes on there just use pictures of themselves holding fish. Speaker_3: The fish thing is real, isn't it? It's… a baffling trend. Like, are you trying to demonstrate your provider skills? Speaker_1: Maybe it's a subtle dominance display. “Look at me, I conquered this fish!” Speaker_2: (groaning) I need to delete the apps. They’re actively making me less hopeful about humanity.

Speaker_1: Honestly, this lemon drizzle is the best I’ve made. I think I finally got the balance right between the zest and the juice. It's a bit crumbly though, isn't it? Speaker_2: It’s lovely, honestly, Sarah. Seriously good. And crumbly’s good! Gives it a rustic feel. Speaking of good, did anyone else spend their childhood trying to build a perfect tower with those wooden building blocks? The ones painted in really garish colours? Speaker_3: Oh my god, yes! I had a set. Spent *hours* meticulously stacking them. They always fell down, though. It was incredibly frustrating. I think I was trying to engineer something structurally sound before I even knew what engineering *was*. Speaker_1: (Laughing) I remember those! Mine were mostly used as furniture for my Sindy dolls. Never really got the tower thing. Though I *did* have a very impressive collection of miniature teacups. My Nan bought them for me. She collected them herself. Speaker_2: My Nan collected porcelain dolls. Absolutely terrifying things. They’d just… stare. I used to hide them in the airing cupboard. My mum had this weird phase where she tried to get me to learn French. Little cassette tapes, everything. Utterly useless. I can still remember a few phrases, mostly involving farm animals. Speaker_3: Oh, I did French in school! Managed to scrape a C. I think I was more interested in dissecting the teacher's accent. Miss Dubois was from Normandy, and she’d get *so* frustrated with our pronunciation. It was almost a hobby of mine, subtly mimicking her. Speaker_1: (Smiling) Naughty! I did German. Even worse. It feels like I’ve completely purged all knowledge of it from my brain. Though, funnily enough, I find I pick up bits and pieces of languages when I travel. Little phrases, just enough to be polite. It's odd. Speaker_2: You’ve done a lot more travelling than us, haven't you? That account management role must keep you busy. How’s it going with the new client, the engineering firm? Speaker_1: It's...challenging. They're very detail-oriented, naturally. And quite resistant to anything that deviates from their established processes. It's a lot of explaining, a lot of justifications. It requires a lot of patience, let me tell you. It reminds me a bit of dealing with my brother actually. Always had to have things his way. Speaker_3: Sounds familiar. I had a similar issue with a supplier recently. Trying to convince them that their invoice was, shall we say, *optimistic*. It took a week of emails and a very firm phone call. Speaker_2: Oh, dealing with finances. That’s my world! It’s always interesting what people try to get away with. I had someone try to claim for a 'team building event’ which involved a trip to the races. Seriously! I had to explain that wasn't acceptable. Speaker_1: Oh, that's brilliant! You’ve got to admire the audacity. Sometimes I think people just assume HR will rubber-stamp anything. Speaker_3: It’s the same with expenses. "Business lunch" that conveniently coincides with a football match. I’ve seen it all. Honestly, you'd think adults would have more imagination when it comes to fibbing. Speaker_2: Absolutely. It’s exhausting! Still, it’s a job, isn’t it? Pass the lemon drizzle, would you? It’s a necessary sugar boost after all that talk of dodgy expense claims.

Speaker_1: So, how was it then? Honestly, spill the beans. Did you have a good time? Speaker_2: Yeah, seriously! You two have been gone a week, practically radio silence. We needed updates! Was the hotel decent? Speaker_3: Oh, it was lovely, honestly. A little… older than the pictures suggested, mind you. Bit of chintz, if you know what I mean. Floral wallpaper everywhere. But clean as a whistle, and the staff were absolutely wonderful. Speaker_4: Aye, that’s the main thing, isn’t it? Staff. We had a cracking young lad on reception, name of Ben. Kept us right with directions and recommendations. He told us the best pub for a proper Sunday roast. Speaker_1: A proper Sunday roast? Standards are high, Dad. Speaker_4: And it *delivered*, lass. It delivered. Yorkshire puddings the size of your head, proper gravy… I had two helpings. Nearly burst. Speaker_2: Good to know your priorities haven’t changed, Dad. Mum, what about you? What did *you* think? Speaker_3: Oh, I enjoyed it. The scenery was breathtaking, honestly. We did a lovely coastal walk, though my knees were complaining by the end of it. And the little villages were just gorgeous, all quaint and colourful. We bought a few bits and bobs in a little craft shop. Speaker_1: Oh, nice! Anything good? Speaker_3: Just little things. A knitted tea cosy, because why not? And a couple of little ceramic hedgehogs for the garden. Speaker_2: Hedgehogs? Really? Speaker_4: She’s got a thing for hedgehogs, lad. Always has. Remember that time she rescued that one with the tangled foot? Speaker_1: Oh, yeah! The one you named Prickles? Speaker_3: Don’t remind me! That was a whole ordeal. We had it in a box in the spare room for days. It kept trying to escape. Speaker_2: Sounds chaotic. Did you manage to do any proper sightseeing? Besides the pub crawl, Dad? Speaker_4: We went to that castle, Scarborough Castle, it was. Bit windy up there, nearly lost my hat. But the views were smashing. You can see for miles. And we went to Whitby, of course. Had to get some fish and chips. Speaker_1: Whitby! Did you go to the Abbey? That’s supposed to be amazing. Speaker_3: We did! It was beautiful, very atmospheric. Though a lot of steps, I'll tell you that. My legs were aching for days. And it was packed with tourists. Speaker_2: Sounds busy. Did you take many photos? We want to see *everything*. Speaker_4: Oh, aye. Loads. I'll have to sort them out. They’re mostly of the scenery, and me with a pint in various pubs. Speaker_1: Of course they are. Mum, did you miss Winston and Maisie? Speaker_3: Terribly! I kept expecting to feel a little nose nudging my hand, or a furry head resting on my lap. I even dreamt about Winston trying to steal my breakfast. Speaker_2: They definitely missed you too. Winston was a bit mopey when you left. Maisie… well, Maisie just wanted more snacks as usual. Speaker_4: Right, speaking of snacks, is there any of that cake left? The one your sister brought round? Speaker_1: There might be a slice or two… Let me check. It's in the kitchen! Would anyone like a cuppa as well?

Speaker_1: (Stirring a mug, slightly grumpy) Morning, you two. Anyone else smell burnt toast? Pretty sure it wasn’t me. Speaker_2: (Cheerfully chopping fruit) Morning, Mark! And yes, that was absolutely me. Tried a new rye bread, forgot it wasn’t white. It’s…rustic. Speaker_3: (Reading a newspaper at the kitchen table) Rustic is a polite word for carbonized, Sarah. You nearly set off the smoke alarm. Did you at least scrape off the worst of it? Speaker_2: Of course! Though honestly, a little char adds flavour, doesn’t it? Anyway, how was your run, Mark? You were out early. Speaker_1: Bracing. Absolutely freezing. The canal path was slick with ice in places. Almost lost my footing a couple of times. Thinking I might stick to the treadmill for a bit now, honestly. My knees aren’t getting any younger. Speaker_3: Sensible. Though, risking life and limb for a Saturday morning run is very…you. Speaking of risking things, have you seen this article about that actor, what’s his name…the one from *Bridgerton*? Apparently, he’s investing heavily in crypto. Speaker_2: Oh, Luke Newton? No, but that sounds spectacularly ill-advised. Celebrities and crypto, it’s a disaster waiting to happen. They get told what to do by…well, anyone. Speaker_1: It’s the same principle as dodgy investments, really. People thinking they can get rich quick. It's all just applied engineering, really – leveraging risk and reward. Only in this case, the engineers are charlatans. Speaker_3: (Chuckles) You manage to bring everything back to engineering, don’t you? It’s admirable. Although, I suspect understanding stress tolerances in bridge design is slightly more useful than understanding meme coins. Speaker_2: Absolutely. Anyway, are we still on for that pottery class next weekend? I booked us in, thought it would be a laugh. Speaker_1: Pottery? Seriously? Last time you did anything remotely arts and crafts related, you ended up covered head to toe in glitter. Speaker_2: It was a Christmas card making session! And it was…festive. Besides, it’ll be good to try something different. It's not like you’re swimming in exciting hobbies at the moment. Besides, I need a birthday present for my mum. Speaker_3: It sounds wonderfully awful, actually. I’m in. I’m picturing a chaotic scene of flying clay and passive-aggressive shaping. Speaker_1: (Sighs) Fine. But I’m warning you, if I end up with clay in my beard, I’m blaming both of you. Do you want me to pick up some pastries on the way back from work later? There’s that new bakery down the high street. Speaker_2: Oh, yes please! Those almond croissants looked amazing. Speaker_3: Anything with chocolate will do for me. I’m battling a serious news fatigue this morning. Honestly, it's just one depressing story after another. Even my phone is relentlessly pushing bad news at me. Speaker_1: Turn off the notifications, then. Honestly, it’s good to disconnect sometimes. I tried to explain to my Uncle Brian the other day how algorithms work and he just…looked at me like I was speaking Martian. Speaker_2: Bless him. He’s a lovely man, but technology isn't his forte, is it? He still thinks the internet is a series of tubes. Speaker_3: (Laughing) A series of tubes! That's brilliant. Well, I’m off to wrestle with a deadline. Enjoy your treadmills and rustic toast, you two.

Speaker_1: Honestly, Reg, you're going to miss us all terribly when you’re out in Saudi. It’s not just leaving Peterborough, it’s leaving *us*. Speaker_2: She’s right, you know. It won't be the same without you winding up Dad at Christmas. Or generally just…being here. Speaker_3: Yeah, who am I gonna moan to about work now? You always understood the state of things down at the yard. Speaker_4: (Chuckles, taking a long sip of his beer) Don’t you lot start gettin’ all sentimental on me now. I've seen lads shipped off to worse places than Saudi. At least you’ll be earnin’ proper money, eh? Not like some of the…jobs around here. Speaker_1: It's a good opportunity, obviously. And the money is amazing. But it just feels…weird. You’ve lived here your whole life. Speaker_2: Remember when you got absolutely lost trying to drive to Stamford? Even with the Sat Nav? Speaker_3: (Laughing) Oh, God. That was a mess. You ended up in some farmer’s field, convinced you’d discovered a new shortcut. Google Maps was laughing at you too, wasn't it? Speaker_4: Google Maps! Pah! Give me a proper map and a compass any day. These youngsters rely too much on their little screens. Couldn’t find their way out of a paper bag without one. Speaker_1: That’s a bit harsh, Dad. It's just…convenient. Although, in Reg’s case, even the Sat Nav couldn't save him. Speaker_2: He swore the Sat Nav was deliberately misleading him. Said it had a personal vendetta. Speaker_4: I’ll tell you what’s misleading – estate agents. Your Mum and I were thinkin’ about down-sizing, a bit of decorating, and the fella tries to tell us a three-bedroom semi is 'charming and full of potential'. Potential for what? Collapse? Speaker_3: You need my mate, Liam. He's a builder, does a good job, doesn’t rip you off. Speaker_1: Actually, speaking of jobs… I think I might apply for that assistant manager role at the library. It’s a pay rise, and it's… quiet. Speaker_2: Quiet? You? The woman who once accidentally set off the fire alarm during a book display competition? Speaker_1: (Smiling sheepishly) It was a rogue glitter cannon! And it was for charity. Honestly, I need less excitement in my life. Speaker_4: Good on ya, lass. Sometimes a bit of peace and quiet is just what you need. It's easy to get caught up in all the madness. It’s just…I’ll miss havin’ you all close. Remember Sarah? From the pub quiz? She’s movin’ to Australia next month, can you believe it? Speaker_3: Everyone’s leavin’. It feels like. Speaker_2: We’re not going anywhere, mate. Unless Reg offers to pay for us all to come and visit in his new palace. Speaker_4: (Waving his hand dismissively) Don’t hold your breath. But look, I’m gonna make the most of these last few days. How about we all go bowling on Friday? Or maybe a curry? Speaker_1: Bowling sounds good. And we definitely need a proper leaving do, Dad. No more of this quietly sneaking out while everyone’s distracted. Speaker_2: Yeah, we need to give you a send-off you won’t forget. Even if it means subjecting Reg to one last round of Dad jokes. Speaker_3: And I’m bringing the competitive spirit. Prepare to lose, Reg. Prepare to lose badly.

Speaker_1: Honestly, this air is doing wonders for my sinuses. Back in London, it feels like I'm constantly battling something. You two feeling alright? Any London-lung clinging on? Speaker_2: I'm surprisingly good, actually. I think getting away from the… children… for a few days is medicinal in itself. Though, my feet are killing me. These shoes were a terrible idea for all this walking. Speaker_3: Tell me about it! I’m regretting the stylish-over-practical choice intensely. Speaker_1: Right, so, the bunting… I’m thinking lilac and white? For the Christening, obviously. Do you think that’s a bit… much? Speaker_2: (Small voice, fiddling with a toy) Pink! Pink and sparkly! Speaker_1: Honestly, this weather is dreadful, isn’t it? Rain, rain, rain. Makes you just want to curl up with a book all weekend. Speaker_2: Tell me about it! Speaker_1: Right, so basically, this whole pile… it’s all for the methodology chapter. And honestly, it feels like it’s multiplying overnight. Speaker_2: Methodology? Blimey. That sounds… intense. They might have notice boards where you could advertise. Speaker_1: Yeah, that's on the list. I've also emailed the Salford council to see if they have any mailing lists for residents. No joy so far, though. Speaker_2: Keep badgering them. Bureaucracy, eh? It's relentless. Look, why don't you just map out the different options? Like, a flowchart. What are the pros and cons of each, the resources needed, the potential problems? Sometimes just *visualising* it helps. Speaker_1: Actually, that’s… a really good idea. I’ve been so bogged down in the details, I haven’t stepped back and looked at the bigger picture. I think I’ll do that now. Cheers, mate. You’ve saved my sanity, or at least postponed the breakdown for another few hours. Speaker_2: No worries, mate. That's what friends – and fellow sufferers of postgraduate stress – are for. Now, fancy a tea? And then, perhaps, we could avoid the methodology chapter altogether and talk about something completely mindless? Like, the Premier League? Speaker_1: Absolutely. Tea sounds amazing. And yes, please, let’s talk football. This paperwork can wait… for at least five minutes.

Speaker_1: Honestly, I had the strangest dream last night. I was presenting a sales pitch… to a room full of badgers. Speaker_2: (Chuckles) Badgers? Seriously? What were you selling them? A big, fluffy golden retriever. It was running around the garden, and the kids were just… beaming. Speaker_1: Oh. See, that’s nice. A dog… We’ve talked about it. Speaker_2: I know. I just… It felt so right in the dream. So cozy. It’s just finding the time, isn’t it? And the right breed. And generally being responsible adults. Speaker_1: Tell me about it. It’s a big commitment. Although, if I won the lottery… Speaker_4: If *I* won the lottery, I would buy a dinosaur! A real one! Speaker_1: (Smiling) A real dinosaur, huh? That's ambitious. I’d get a gardener. And a dog. Definitely a dog. And maybe a really sophisticated badger-proof presentation case. Just in case. Speaker_2: You and your badgers! But seriously, the lottery… What would *you* do? All the things that could be easier with a bit of luck. Though, sometimes the best things are the ones you work for… even if they don’t involve inflatable dinosaurs. Do you want me to continue the conversation or explore a different angle? (Edited- formatting) Edited to include both children’s dialogue, and more detail about lottery discussion.

Speaker_1: Honestly, the state of it. Absolute chaos. Speaker_2: What? What’s happened now? You sound…stressed. Speaker_1: A&E. I had to go to A&E last night. Speaker_2: Woah, hold on. What for? Are you alright? What happened? Speaker_1: I tripped. Over…nothing, basically. Just completely lost my footing coming down the stairs at Mum’s. Speaker_2: Seriously? You okay? Did you break anything? You’ll be hobbling around for weeks. Speaker_1: I know! And I have that conference next week in Bristol. How am I supposed to get around? I was hoping to do some sightseeing too. Speaker_2: Oh, that’s a pain. Maybe you could hire one of those mobility scooters? Be a bit dramatic, but practical. Speaker_1: (Laughs weakly) You’re not wrong. Just… momentarily gravity-challenged. Seriously though, look after yourself. Don’t try to be a hero. Rest it up, ice it, and let it heal. And ditch the stairs for a bit, yeah? And maybe some of those fancy ankle support things? Speaker_1: Oh, that would be amazing, actually. You're a lifesaver. Speaker_2: No problem. Consider it payback for… well, for being you. And for letting me mooch off your snacks whenever I’m here. Speaker_1: (Laughing) Deal!

Speaker_1: Honestly, the state of things… did you see that report on the BBC last night about the unrest in France? Absolute chaos. Speaker_2: Did a bit, yes. Flicked through it while having my tea. Speaker_2: Appreciate that, Arthur. I might just take you up on that. It's just...a big change. It’ll be a lot less stressful than dealing with demanding customers and broken seaside trinkets, I reckon. Speaker_1: I can imagine. Just promise me you won’t start dressing up in period costume. Don't want to see you in breeches and a powdered wig! Speaker_2: (laughing) No promises! Though it might attract the tourists, eh? Speaker_1: Probably. But for my sake, please refrain. Now, let's talk about young David...heard he's been promoted again. Speaker_2: Oh really? That's good news. Clever lad. Always was a bright spark. Speaker_1: He certainly is. Makes a fella proud, doesn't it? Though I still wish he’d settle down and give me some grandchildren…

Speaker_1: Right, so are we thinking pub grub, or shall we head somewhere else afterwards for something proper? I'm suddenly quite craving a curry. Though, he was a brilliant lecturer. Speaker_1: He was. Right, I’m going to brave the bar. Do you want another pint? I’m getting a diet coke, trying to be good. Though maybe a little morose for a Friday night. Speaker_1: Morose, but classic. Makes me want to go and mope in a corner thinking about lost loves. Speaker_2: Don’t do that! You'll scare the locals. Speaker_1: Right mess of a day, the weather’s been. Bucketing it down since I left the house. Nearly lost my favourite beanie! Speaker_2: Aye, a proper dreich one.
