Might be a good shout, aye. Let me check the diary. Although if it’s anything like this weather, I’ll be needing a full waterproof suit. Speaker_1: Definitely. And maybe a midge net. Just in case. Speaker_2: Don’t remind me. Right, another pint? I’m needing to warm up. This dreich weather’s getting to me. Speaker_1: Aye, go on. You’ve earned it after battling the midges. One pint coming up.

Speaker_1: Right, so, the week ahead. Utter chaos, I foresee. You alright with picking Leo up from football on Tuesday? I’ve got that meeting with Mrs. Henderson about… well, you know. The funding. Speaker_2: Tuesday’s good. Though honestly, football practice seems to be consuming his life. It’s every other night! Is he even enjoying it, or is it just… pressure? Speaker_1: He loves it, honestly. He really does. It’s the social side as much as anything, I think. All those little boys running around, causing mayhem. Keeps him out of trouble, doesn’t it? Speaker_2: True. Though I’m pretty sure the mayhem *is* the trouble. What about Wednesday? Is Dad still doing the supermarket run? Speaker_1: He said he would. Though knowing your father, he'll probably forget the milk again. Honestly, it’s like pulling teeth getting him to remember a shopping list. Speaker_2: (Laughing) You’re telling me. It’s been like that since I was little. Remember the time he came back with three tubs of pineapple chunks instead of peaches for my birthday crumble? Speaker_1: Oh, *don't* remind me. The crumble was… interesting. Speaking of which, how’s planning for the nursery going? Have you had any luck with viewings? Speaker_2: It’s a nightmare. Everything’s either booked up for months, or outrageously expensive. I went to see one yesterday, it was tiny! And smelled faintly of disinfectant and despair. Speaker_1: Oh, bless. That doesn’t sound promising. You’re right to be picky though. It’s where little Noah will be spending a lot of time. You want somewhere happy and safe. Speaker_2: Exactly! And somewhere they don’t just shove all the kids in front of Peppa Pig all day. I swear, some nurseries rely on television as a babysitter. Speaker_1: Ugh, don’t even get me started on kids’ TV these days. It’s all flashing lights and relentless noise. Whatever happened to good old-fashioned storytelling? Speaker_2: I know! I tried to watch something with my class today and it was just… overwhelming. Honestly, I need a cup of tea and a lie-down after five minutes of some of that stuff. Speaker_1: I completely understand. Have you seen that new drama everyone’s talking about, ‘The Crimson Tide’? Apparently, it’s brilliant. Speaker_2: Oh, I’ve heard of it! Sophie was going on about it at work. Said it's a bit slow-paced, but the acting is incredible. I might have to give it a go. I need *something* to watch. Everything else seems… rubbish. Speaker_1: It is good. Really good. And you deserve a bit of escapism. You work so hard, and trying to navigate the nursery situation on top of everything else... It’s exhausting just listening to you. Speaker_2: Thanks, Mum. It’s just… a lot. I feel like I’m constantly juggling a million things. And trying to be a good teacher, a good mum, a good… everything. Speaker_1: You *are* good at everything, darling. Don’t forget that. And if you need anything at all, anything at all, you know you can always ask. We’re here for you. Speaker_2: I know. Thanks. Maybe… maybe you could come with me to another nursery viewing next week? Just for moral support? And an extra pair of eyes? Speaker_1: Absolutely! Consider it done. And maybe afterwards, we can go for a nice piece of cake. Definitely *not* pineapple crumble, though.

Speaker_2: This pasta’s proper good, actually. You’ve outdone yourself, ANON. Speaker_1: Aye, well, me nan always said a good ragu solves everything. Though, truth be told, I just followed a recipe I found online. Don’t want you thinkin’ I’m some culinary genius. Speaker_3: (Chuckles) Don't undersell yourself! It’s a vast improvement on my usual dinner of microwave meals. Honestly, work’s been *mental* lately. I barely have time to boil an egg, let alone cook a whole feast. Speaker_2: Tell me about it. Been graftin’ twelve hour shifts on that building site, rain or shine. Back aching somethin’ fierce. The gaffer's been on me case all week too, says I’m not shiftin’ enough bricks. Like it's a competition! Speaker_1: Oh, that’s rubbish! Some bosses just love a power trip, don’t they? I had a nightmare at work last week. This conference… absolute chaos. VIPs turnin’ up late, AV equipment malfunctionin’, the catering messed up the dietary requirements… It was a full-on disaster. Speaker_3: Oof, sounds stressful. What kind of conference was it? Speaker_1: Biotech. Loads of scientists and investors. All very important and very… particular. I swear, one woman nearly had a meltdown because her sparkling water wasn’t chilled *enough*. Speaker_2: (Laughing) Seriously? People are weird. I’d be more bothered if I had no water at all, sparklin’ or not! Speaker_3: You're a man of simple pleasures, aren't you? I'm dealing with budget cuts at work, that’s my ‘sparkling water’ equivalent. They want me to streamline everything, basically do the job of two people for the same money. Speaker_1: That’s awful! You should push back on that, shouldn't you? Speaker_3: Easier said than done. Corporate life, innit? Everyone’s just tryin’ to survive. Speaking of surviving… how’s things with Liam? You two still… okay? Speaker_1: (Sighs) It's… complicated. We had a bit of a row last weekend. Over clothes, of all things. Speaker_2: Clothes? What, he doesn’t like your style? Speaker_1: It's not that! It’s just… he’s always commentin’ on what I wear. Says I wear too much black, that I need to ‘brighten up’. Like me mood depends on the colour of my jumper! I like black! It’s practical. And comfortable. Speaker_3: Men, honestly. Always thinkin’ they can redesign your entire personality. It’s control, isn’t it? Subtly tryin’ to change you. Speaker_1: Maybe... I don’t know. It just feels like he doesn’t really *get* me, y’know? I’m happy wearin’ me boots and jeans and a leather jacket. I don't want to be all frilly dresses and heels just to please someone else. Speaker_2: You tell him that! Don’t let him dim your shine. You look awesome as you are. Speaker_3: Absolutely. And look, if you need to vent or just have a proper girl’s night, you know we’re here. We can order pizza and watch terrible reality TV – a far better use of your time than arguin’ about clothes. Speaker_1: (Smiling slightly) Appreciate that, both of you. Maybe we should. Actually… are you both free next Saturday? There’s a new pub quiz at The Eagle, supposed to be good. Speaker_2: I’m in! Need to test my general knowledge. Speaker_3: Count me in too. A pub quiz sounds perfect. And maybe we can avoid discussing anything remotely work-related.

Speaker_1: Right then, this tea's brewed nicely, hasn’t it? Bit strong, maybe, but I like it like that. Reminds me of my Nan’s. She'd make a cuppa that could stand a spoon up in it. Speaker_2: Oh, don’t I know that feeling! My mother was the same. Always said a proper brew needed to have some… backbone. None of this wishy-washy stuff. Though, honestly, sometimes it felt like drinking paint stripper. Speaker_3: (Chuckles) You two and your strong tea! I prefer mine a little gentler, myself. Years of marking essays, I suppose. Needed something soothing. Though, the staff room brew was legendary for its potency. Kept us all going through parents' evening. Speaker_4: Speaking of potent brews, does anyone remember old Mrs. Higgins down the road? She used to add a pinch of salt to her tea. Said it brought out the flavour. I tried it once, out of politeness, and it was… an experience. Speaker_1: Salt in tea! Good heavens! That’s a new one on me. Sounds like something a sailor would drink. Though, I did have a friend who swore by a drop of brandy in his tea when he had a cold. Said it cured everything. Speaker_2: Brandy now, that’s more like it. A little tipple can certainly warm you up on a chilly day. Though, I draw the line at salt. Honestly! What will they think of next? Speaker_3: It’s all these fancy teas, isn’t it? Earl Grey, Darjeeling, Jasmine… Give me a good strong builders’ tea any day. Tetley’s or PG Tips, you can’t go wrong. Speaker_4: I rather like a bit of chamomile sometimes, especially before bed. Helps me relax. Though, you’re right, there’s something very comforting about a classic cuppa. It's the ritual, I think. The kettle boiling, the tea brewing, the quiet moment to yourself. Speaker_1: That’s right. It's a good excuse for a sit down and a natter. Can't beat a good natter with friends. And a strong cuppa, naturally. More biscuits anyone? I’ve got digestives and ginger nuts. Speaker_2: Oh, go on then, a digestive would be lovely. Though I'm trying to watch my weight, you know. Retirement doesn't mean you can eat everything in sight! Speaker_3: Nonsense! You’ve earned it. After all those years looking after little ones, you deserve a biscuit or two. I’ll have a ginger nut, if you don’t mind. Keeps the cold at bay. Speaker_4: I’ll join you both. A digestive sounds perfect. It’s amazing how a simple cup of tea and a biscuit can make everything seem a little bit better. Does this fulfill your request? Would you like me to adjust or expand on it in any way? Let me know if you'd like me to continue the conversation or change anything. Speaker_1: Now, where did I put the sugar…? Ah, here it is. You take sugar, don’t you, Margaret? Speaker_2: Just the one, thank you, Arthur. Don’t want to overdo it. Speaker_3: None for me, please. I find it spoils the flavour. Speaker_4: One, for me as well. A little sweetness is always welcome. Speaker_1: There we are. All sorted. Now, is anyone else noticing how dark it gets these evenings? Seems like only yesterday we were enjoying long summer days…

Speaker_1: Honestly, this roast is amazing, Mum. You’ve really outdone yourself. Speaker_2: It’s lovely, isn’t it? Though, I think I’ve had about three Yorkshire puddings already. No self-control. Speaker_3: (Mouth full) These potatoes are *chefs kiss*. Seriously, best roast I’ve had in ages. Though, to be fair, my cooking skills peak at beans on toast. Speaker_4: You say that, but your curry last month was phenomenal, Rhys. Don’t undersell yourself. Speaker_3: That was a lucky accident, powered by a pre-made paste and sheer desperation. Speaker_1: Speaking of desperation, did you manage to book that hotel in London for the exhibition, Ben? Speaker_4: Yeah, got a decent deal actually. Small place near Shoreditch, but it has good reviews. I was worried everything would be booked solid with… well, everything going on. Speaker_2: Everything going on? You mean the protests? I saw snippets on the news. Sounded a bit chaotic. Speaker_4: Chaotic is an understatement. Apparently, it's been building for weeks. The tube was completely disrupted last Tuesday. Speaker_3: London always has something going on. Remember that time we ended up walking miles because of a tube strike? Felt like a proper adventure. Speaker_1: An adventure involving blistered feet and a very expensive emergency kebab. Don't romanticize it, Rhys. Speaker_2: Oh god, the kebab! I completely forgot about that. It cost a fortune. Speaker_3: Worth it though. Saved our lives. Speaking of saved lives – are you still volunteering at the youth centre, Sarah? Speaker_1: I am, yeah. It’s… rewarding. Although, the CRB check process was a nightmare. Endless forms and waiting. It’s just a lot of responsibility, you know? Especially with everything you hear. Speaker_4: It’s the world we live in sadly. You’ve got to be careful. Speaker_2: It’s awful. Mum, remember when Uncle Geoff was talking about… well, you know… about little Timmy and… Speaker_1: (Interrupting quickly) Oh, let’s *not* go there, please. Honestly, that conversation gives me the creeps. The whole thing about circumcision is just… so sensitive. I can’t. Speaker_3: Fair enough. Awkward topic. More gravy, anyone? Speaker_4: Please. This gravy is a gift from the gods. Speaker_2: Did you see old Mrs. Higgins at the pub last week? She was going on about the price of a pint again. Said it’s daylight robbery. Speaker_1: She always says that. It’s her default setting. Though, she’s right, isn’t she? It’s getting ridiculous. Speaker_3: It’s just corporate greed, plain and simple. They're rinsing us. I'm sticking to driving, I think. Less expensive. Even with the petrol prices. Speaker_4: That’s a good shout. Though, I'm honestly terrified of driving in London. Carnage. Speaker_2: You get used to it. It's a different kind of driving. More… assertive. Speaker_1: Assertive is a polite way of putting it. It’s just aggressive. You need to develop a thick skin and a ruthless streak. And a good lawyer. Speaker_3: I'll stick to the train, thanks. Or walking. Or being carried, if someone's offering. Speaker_4: I saw a really interesting exhibition at the Tate Modern last month. All these massive abstract paintings. Completely baffling, but strangely compelling. Speaker_1: Oh, I love the Tate Modern. It’s just… a lot. Sometimes I need to sit down and process it all afterwards. Speaker_2: It's good for a rainy day. Or when you need to feel sophisticated. Speaker_3: Can we talk about the pudding yet?

Speaker_1: Right, spill. Holiday debrief. How was Greece? Honestly, don’t hold back. Was it as Instagrammable as it looked? Speaker_2: (Entering kitchen, grabbing a glass) Oh my god, it was… exhausting, actually. Beautiful, obviously, the photos don't lie, but *exhausting*. Constant sunshine, constant crowds. I needed a holiday *from* the holiday when I got back. You wouldn’t believe the queues for breakfast. Speaker_1: No way! I thought you were all about that relaxed vibe. Did you actually manage to, like, relax? Speaker_2: Briefly. On a boat trip, for about half an hour. Then someone’s kid threw up over the side and I spent the rest of the time trying not to breathe through my mouth. Speaking of which, how was your weekend at your parents’? Did your mum make you eat three roast dinners? Speaker_1: (Laughing) Almost. Two and a half. She was determined I needed “putting back together” after a stressful week at work. It was actually really nice though, honestly. Dad’s been getting really into gardening, and it’s… surprisingly captivating. Speaker_2: Aww, that’s sweet. He's always been a bit of a hidden talent, your dad. So, work’s stressful then? Still dealing with the chaos of the Henderson project? Speaker_1: You have *no* idea. Henderson is driving me insane. He changes his mind every five minutes. I swear, I spent half of Monday re-doing a presentation he’d already approved. It’s like talking to a brick wall. How are things with you? Still battling the world of mental health? Speaker_2: Always. It's been a tough week, actually. We had a patient sectioned, really sad case. It always hits me hard, you know? It’s just… draining. I’m glad I had the holiday, even if it was chaotic, just to recharge a bit. Speaker_1: I can imagine. You’re amazing at what you do, though. Seriously. It takes a special kind of person. Did you hear anything from… Liam while you were away? Speaker_2: (Rolls eyes) Oh god, don't even. He messaged me, naturally. Some rambling apology about “not being ready” and then proceeded to tag himself at a festival with some other girl. The audacity! Speaker_1: Ugh, the absolute *nerve*. I still can’t believe you dated him. He was… a choice, let's say. Speaker_2: I know, I know. I was young and easily swayed by a six-pack and a vaguely artistic personality. Lesson learned. Anyway, enough about him. Are you free next Saturday? A few of us are going to that new Italian place on Elm Street, "Bella Notte." Speaker_1: Ooh, Bella Notte! I’ve heard good things. Is Chloe coming? Speaker_2: Yeah, and Ben, and hopefully Amy if she can get a babysitter. It would be good to catch up properly. We haven’t all been together in ages. Speaker_1: Sounds perfect! I’m in. I need a proper girls’ night. And maybe a pasta mountain. Oh, and by the way, I’ve been trying to find a new housemate for the spare room. Have you mentioned it to anyone at work? Speaker_2: Actually, yeah, Sarah mentioned her friend is looking. She’s a teacher, apparently, really quiet and sensible, which… could be a good contrast to us. I’ll send you her number later? Speaker_1: That would be amazing! Fingers crossed she’s not a serial killer. Or a Liam in disguise. Speaker_2: (Laughing) Don't even joke! I've had my fill of questionable life choices for one lifetime. Let's just stick to pasta and gossip next Saturday, okay?

Speaker_1: Honestly, I’m still reeling from seeing Sarah yesterday. She looked… smaller. And just so tired. Speaker_2: It’s brutal, isn’t it? The chemo must be really knocking her about. She put on a brave face, as always, but you could see it in her eyes. Speaker_1: Exactly. She kept trying to talk about normal things, the kids, work… but then she’d drift off, talking about appointments and scans. It just makes you feel so helpless. Did she mention if they’ve decided on the next round of treatment yet? Speaker_2: She said they’re reviewing the scans next week. Apparently, it’s not responding as well as they’d hoped. She wasn’t giving much away, but… well, you could read between the lines. It sounded pretty grim. Speaker_1: Oh, that’s awful. I wish there was something, *anything* we could do. We need to make sure we keep checking in, even when she’s pushing us away. You know how she gets. Speaker_2: Definitely. A regular phone call, a quick visit when she’s up to it. Even just knowing someone’s thinking of her will help. Right, changing the subject slightly – have you had a proper look at those houses on Rightmove again? The one on Willow Lane? Speaker_1: I have, briefly. It’s… nice. Very chocolate-box village. But the garden's tiny, and the photos make it look a bit dark inside. Speaker_2: True, the garden isn’t huge, but it gets the sun for most of the day. And think of the commute! We could walk the kids to school. Remember how stressed we were about that in Norwich? The traffic was insane. Speaker_1: That’s true, the school run here is a dream. But I’m still worried about space. We'd need a dedicated office each, wouldn’t we? And what about a playroom for Leo? This house is just… cosy. Speaker_2: We could convert the loft. I saw a company online that does really good loft conversions. It would add loads of space, and a decent view. Plus, it wouldn't eat into the garden. Speaker_1: Loft conversions are expensive though, aren’t they? And disruptive. Remember Uncle George and his loft debacle? Took him six months and half his savings. Speaker_2: (Chuckles) Okay, point taken. But this company seemed reputable. Plus, you’d have to factor in the cost of getting the current house up to scratch anyway. The kitchen’s dated, the bathroom needs a complete overhaul… Speaker_1: It does. And the planning permission for an extension would be a nightmare, I bet. Everyone wants to expand outwards. It's all a bit overwhelming, isn’t it? Speaker_2: It is, but imagine it. A proper garden, a quiet village, walking distance to school… It’s worth considering properly, at least. I really think it would be good for all of us. Just a change of pace, you know? Speaker_1: I do. And honestly, just thinking about it is a nice distraction from everything else going on. Let’s go and view it, shall we? Just to get a real feel for the place. Speaker_2: Absolutely. I'll call the estate agent tomorrow. And maybe we can pop into The Crown afterwards for a pint? A celebratory "looking at houses" pint. Speaker_1: Perfect. And then, we should definitely get together with Sarah and Mark next week, once we know what’s happening with her treatment. Just to be there for them. Speaker_2: Agreed. That’s the most important thing right now. Everything else can wait.

Speaker_1: Right, I’ve had enough. Honestly, I’m starting a list. A proper, documented list of things I do not like about this job. Speaker_2: Oh, go on then. I’m already halfway through my own mental one, so I’m happy to contribute. What’s number one? Don’t tell me it’s the fire alarms again. Speaker_1: It’s *related* to the fire alarms, actually. It’s the students treating them like a game. Seriously, leaving toast burning just to set them off? It’s a waste of everyone's time. And mine especially when I’m halfway through a cuppa. Speaker_2: Ugh, tell me about it. Last week, someone microwaved metal. Metal, Mark! I had to evacuate a whole floor because of someone’s apparent inability to operate a microwave. Speaker_1: See! It’s just…thoughtless. They don’t think about the consequences. They don’t think about me having to stand outside in the freezing cold making sure nobody sneaks back in to grab their phones. Speaker_2: And then apologize to everyone for the inconvenience. It’s always “sorry, didn’t mean to” as if burning toast is an accidental occurrence worthy of a Nobel Prize! Speaker_1: Exactly! It’s not rocket science. Okay, number two on my list: the constant streams of lost keys. Honestly, five pairs a week. Where do they put them? Do they just…fling them into the ether? Speaker_2: It's like they've never encountered a keyring before. I swear, half of them look at me like *I'm* the crazy one when I suggest they attach something to their keys so they don’t lose them. Speaker_1: It’s just…basic life skills, isn’t it? And then they expect us to magically produce a spare. “Can you just let me in? It’s really important!” Important for what? Another Netflix binge? Speaker_2: Don’t even get me started on the noise complaints. 3am drum solos, impromptu parties… I’ve had to knock on doors more times this month than I have in the last six combined. Speaker_1: Oh yeah, the noise. That’s definitely going on the list. And the passive-aggressive notes left on reception complaining about…well, everything! “The bins were slightly overflowing.” Slightly! It was two extra bottles, Carol! Speaker_2: They’re adults, Mark! Actual adults! Why can't they just talk to someone directly instead of writing a strongly-worded essay about the state of the recycling? Speaker_1: It’s the anonymity of it, I think. They can hide behind a piece of paper and be all judgy without having to face anyone. It’s cowardly. Speaker_2: Definitely cowardly. Oh! And the state of the kitchens! Honestly, it’s like a biohazard zone in there sometimes. Speaker_1: Don't even. I actively avoid going in the kitchens now. Restricting it to Health and Safety spot checks only. I've seen things, Sarah, things I can’t unsee. Mould, questionable stains… Speaker_2: You’re starting to sound like a war veteran recounting battlefield horrors. We need hazard pay for this job, I swear. Speaker_1: I fully agree. Hazard pay *and* a therapist. Right, next on the list… the constant requests to reset their passwords. Speaker_2: Oh, lord, yes. That’s a classic. It’s the never-ending cycle of “I forgot my password again.”

Speaker_1: Honestly, seeing Mr. Henderson at that little tapas place in Malaga was *wild*. Of all the places… didn’t realise he holidayed over there. He didn't recognise me at first, bless him. Speaker_2: Malaga, eh? Fancy. Still, you get ‘em everywhere, don’t you? Used to work with a bloke who swore he saw his neighbour in bloody Buenos Aires. Probably just someone who looked like him. Speaker_3: It’s the package tours, isn’t it? Makes it almost inevitable. Brenda and Derek went to Prague last year, said it was overrun with people from Basildon. Speaker_1: (Laughing) Oh, the Essex contingent taking over Europe! Mum, you’d have loved the Christmas markets in Malaga though. They had all sorts of German sausages and glühwein… not quite the same as Germany, obviously. Speaker_2: German sausages… reminds me of Antwerp. Went there with Margaret, years ago. Absolute nightmare getting around, traffic was horrendous. Tiny little streets, built for horse and cart, not these modern monstrosities. Speaker_3: I’ve always wanted to go to Antwerp. Is it nice? Apart from the traffic, naturally. Speaker_2: The city itself is beautiful, proper old buildings, lovely squares. But honestly, getting anywhere felt like a military operation. And everyone speaking Dutch… I tried a bit of French, didn’t get me very far. Speaker_1: Honestly, I'm trying to pick up some Spanish on Duolingo. It's going…slowly. It's mainly just useful for ordering tapas, at this rate. Speaker_3: Good for you, love. Always useful to have another language under your belt. Though I’ve never had the patience. Elsie at work’s doing an evening class. Says it’s exhausting! Speaker_1: Speaking of exhausting, I’m dreading Christmas shopping. Herne Bay’s getting worse and worse. It was rammed last weekend. Speaker_3: Tell me about it. I took little Tommy there on Saturday, trying to get him a new football. Chaos. Everyone pushing and shoving and the parking… don’t even get me started. Speaker_2: Herne Bay… used to be a lovely little place. Used to take the boys down there when they were little. Built sandcastles, ate fish and chips. Simpler times. Speaker_1: Remember when Leo got stung by a jellyfish on Brighton seafront? He screamed the place down! Speaker_3: Oh, that was awful! Poor little man. He was convinced he was going to lose his arm. Leo’s birthday is coming up fast, isn't it? Speaker_1: It is. He wants a puppy. A proper, fluffy one. I'm trying to explain the responsibility… Speaker_2: Puppies are wonderful. But a lot of work. Reminds me of when our David brought a Labrador home from university. Shedded everywhere, chewed all the furniture. Still, the boys loved it. Speaker_3: They grow up so fast, don’t they? Seems like yesterday they were little terrors. I keep thinking about my mum, you know? This time of year always hits me. She loved Christmas. Speaker_1: (Softly) I know, Mum. It does. Thinking of Grandad too, especially now you're retired, Dad… I mean, you always used to have a Christmas project going, fixing something or building something. Speaker_2: Ah, well. That’s life, isn’t it? Gotta keep busy. I’m thinking of trying that caravanning thing. Saw a nice site down in Dorset, near the coast. Speaker_3: Oh, lovely! You and Margaret would enjoy that. It’s a good way to see the country. Just watch out for the midges! Speaker_1: You two are already planning your escape! Right, another scoop of rocky road, anyone? And Dad, you’ll have to tell us your latest rhyming slang. You always have a good one up your sleeve.

Speaker_1: So, did you see about the equality vote in Ireland? Like, the one about expanding the definition of family? Speaker_2: Oh yeah, I skimmed an article. Something about carers and… more than just traditional families, right? Honestly, it all feels a bit complicated. Speaker_1: Complicated? It’s just about making things fairer, isn't it? Like, why should it *only* be a mum and dad? My mate Liam has two dads, and he’s totally normal. It's weird judging people just because their family isn’t… textbook. Speaker_2: I’m not *judging*, darling. It’s just… it's a big change. And sometimes these things have unintended consequences. I read a comment online saying it could mess up inheritance laws. Speaker_1: Ugh, online comments. Don't even start. Everyone’s an expert all of a sudden. Inheritance laws sound boring anyway. It's about people being able to, like, legally recognise the people who actually care for them. Speaker_2: True, true. Though, you know your Nana, she'd have a field day. She's still trying to figure out why people even *want* to get married these days. “Back in my day…” she’d start. Speaker_1: (Laughing) Oh god, yeah. She thinks marriage is the only way to be proper. She keeps asking when I'm going to settle down, even though I'm fifteen! She’d probably faint if she heard about all this. Speaker_2: Honestly. She’d probably blame it on the youth of today. Which, let’s be honest, she often does. Speaking of settling down… did Uncle Mark finally propose to Fiona? She was hinting rather heavily at your birthday. Speaker_1: He did! He proposed at the bowling alley! It was SO embarrassing. She nearly knocked over a rack of shoes she was so excited. Then she started crying, and he didn’t know what to do. He just kept offering her a handkerchief. Speaker_2: (Chuckles) Oh, Fiona. She’s a drama queen. But sweet. That's lovely. So, a good birthday then? Speaker_1: Yeah, it was good. A bit chaotic. Mum tried to make a fancy cake, and it… didn’t go well. It kind of collapsed. It looked like something exploded. She tried to blame the oven. Speaker_2: (Smiling) Your mum and her oven. That’s a classic. Remember when she tried to bake biscuits for Christmas and they were basically charcoal? Speaker_1: Oh my *god*, yes! And she tried to pass them off as ‘rustic’! No one ate them. It's a good job we had the chocolate oranges. Speaker_2: She’s… unique. Bless her. Sometimes I think she actively tries to be embarrassing. Honestly, the stories she told about *me* at your cousins’ wedding… Speaker_1: (Grinning) Oh yeah! The one about you and the karaoke machine? Speaker_2: Don’t remind me. I thought I'd buried that! I was 18 and thought I was Beyoncé. It was a disaster. Speaker_1: (Laughing) It was brilliant! But seriously, about the vote…it’s just nice to see Ireland trying to do the right thing, you know? It feels…progressive. Speaker_2: I agree. It does. Though I still worry about the fine print. Still, I suppose it's a step in the right direction. Speaker_1: Definitely. Now, are you going to help me with my history homework, or are you too busy reliving your karaoke shame? Speaker_2: (Sighs playfully) Fine, fine. But you're listening to my embarrassing stories later. Consider it payment.

Speaker_1: Honestly, the state of things… did you see that story about the cat who accidentally ordered things online with its paws? Speaker_2: (Chuckles) No, I missed that! Though, likely not before we’re all pushing daisies. Speaker_2: Let’s not talk about daisies, shall we? It’s too depressing. I've been trying to get my head around this new update on the work system. It feels like virtue signalling. They introduced it, then got rid of it, now they’re bringing it back. Speaker_3: It’s simply another way for them to generate revenue, dear. Don't be naive. Give me a moment... backward glance… could it be ‘retrospect’? Speaker_1: Oh! That’s brilliant! You’re amazing at those, aren't you? Speaker_3: Indeed. A very clever solution, David. Now, shall we get dinner on? I’m absolutely famished. Perhaps some salmon? Speaker_1: That sounds lovely, Mum. Speaker_2: Perfect. Salmon it is. Speaker_1: Right, okay. Lego Ninjago’s packed away. That was a *very* intense battle. Honestly, it felt like a war zone in here for a minute. Speaker_2: (Sighs dramatically) But Mum! Speaker_2 & Speaker_3: (Grumbling slightly) Okay… Speaker_1: That’s the spirit! Now, let's find some adventures between the pages. Speaker_2: Can I read the one about the ninja again? Speaker_1: Honestly, it’s so lovely to have you both here. It feels like ages since we’ve all just sat and had a proper chat. How was the drive down, Chloe? Speaker_2: It was alright, Mum. Speaker_2: That sounds lovely, Mum. I'm happy with that. I need to buy a birthday present for Auntie Carol, anyway. Speaker_3: Yeah, that sounds good. I could do with a break from staring at textbooks. Maybe we can find a nice little café? I’m desperate for a proper cake. Speaker_1: Absolutely! We’ll find the perfect cake. And then, perhaps, we can come back here and I can bore you both with photo albums from your childhoods? Speaker_2: (groaning playfully) Oh, Mum, please no! Not the baby photos again! Speaker_1: (laughing) Oh, come on! They're adorable! And… educational. It shows you how far you've come! Right, first things first, coffee and cinnamon rolls. And then we can start planning the rest of our day. Does this conversation fit the parameters you set out? Would you like me to continue it, or perhaps adjust any aspects?

Speaker_1: This sandwich is… underwhelming. Seriously, they call this chicken and bacon? It’s mostly lettuce. Speaker_2: Tell me about it. Mine’s supposed to be tuna mayo, and it tastes suspiciously like just mayo. They really skimp on the filling here, don’t they? Speaker_3: You guys are complaining about sandwiches? I had chips for lunch, and they were soggy. Soggy! It’s a culinary crime. Speaker_1: At least chips *can* be good. A bad sandwich is just…sad. So, anyone actually do anything interesting over the weekend? Apart from suffer through mediocre lunchtime cuisine? I was planning on binging it tonight. Heard it gets pretty intense. Speaker_2: I started it last night. It’s good, really good. Luz is amazing. Though, I’m still trying to figure out what’s going on with that Belos guy… he's creepy. Speaker_3: Oh, you haven't gotten to the really creepy bits then. Trust me. It gets wild. You know, my mum was telling me about this thing she read online about… well, it’s complicated, something about political tensions between France and Algeria. Apparently, history is repeating itself. Speaker_1: Wow, that’s… a massive jump from soggy chips and cartoons. Speaker_2: Definitely. My dad was moaning about the same thing this morning on the news. Everyone needs to just get over themselves. It's 2024, seriously. Speaker_2: Yeah, it's ridiculous. Anyway, anyone up for another round of cards? I’m determined to beat you both this time. Even if I have to resort to discarding all your lands.

Speaker_1: Honestly, Mr. Davies is the *worst*. He just… doesn’t explain anything. Like, he’ll write equations on the board and just expect us to *know* what’s happening. Speaker_2: Tell me about it! He's so smug too, isn’t he? Like he thinks we’re all just, naturally gifted in physics. I swear, half the class is just pretending to understand. Speaker_1: Exactly! She’ll make my life a misery! I hate reading in front of everyone. Speaker_1: I know, right? She’s so determined to turn us all into the next Shakespeare. Honestly, I'd rather do another physics lesson with Mr. Davies. And that's saying something. Speaker_2: Totally. It's just… awkward. Especially when it’s, like, really flowery romantic poetry. Everyone just giggles. Speaker_1: Remember when Liam had to read that bit from ‘Romeo and Juliet’ and he went bright red? Speaker_2: (Laughing) Oh my gosh, yes! He completely stumbled over the words and then just started mumbling. Poor Liam. Speaker_1: He’s such a sweetheart. Speaking of people, have you noticed how quiet Chloe’s been lately? Speaker_2: Yeah, it’s weird. She usually has something to say about *everything*. I saw her in the library yesterday, looking really down. I wonder what's up. Speaker_1: Maybe something happened with Ben? They were arguing in the corridor last week, but she wouldn’t tell me what it was about. Speaker_2: Ooh, good point. That was a proper shouting match. They’re so up and down, aren’t they? One minute they’re all loved up, the next they’re trying to kill each other with words. Speaker_1: Drama central! Anyway, did you see that trailer for ‘17 Again’? It looks hilarious! Speaker_2: Oh my *god*, yes! I want to see that so bad! Imagine being a teenager again, but knowing everything you know now. You’d just ace everything. Speaker_1: Seriously! I’d definitely avoid talking to certain people and maybe… focus a bit more on my homework. Speaker_2: Me too! And I’d definitely tell myself not to wear those awful jeans I wore in year seven. The ones with the flower embroidery… Speaker_1: (Laughing) Oh no! Don’t remind me! We all made some questionable fashion choices back then. It's a good job there’s no photographic evidence… Or is there? Speaker_2: Oh no… don’t say that. My mum definitely has photo albums full of embarrassing pictures. This is a nightmare. Speaker_1: Maybe if we’re lucky, they’ll stay hidden forever… Right, I should probably get started on my English homework. Even though I’d rather be watching ‘17 Again’. Speaker_2: Same. But we both know Miss Harding will be, like, *super* strict about it. Better to just get it done. Speaker_1: Ugh. Fine. Wish me luck then. Speaker_2: Good luck! Speaker_1: Honestly, the thought of Monday… it’s actively making my Sunday worse. Like, just *knowing* it’s coming. Speaker_2: Tell me about it. Though at least I have the bakery to look forward to. Speaker_3: I'm hoping to get a few weekends away in the van. Maybe the New Forest. Somewhere I can take the dog. I’ve been slaving away at the café all spring, need some time to recharge. You know what we say back home? “No worries.” Just… everything’s sorted, everything’s good. Speaker_3: (Smiling) “No worries.” I like that. Sounds…relaxing. I could use some of that. It feels like it’s all been a bit… divisive, yes? A good cup of coffee makes everything a little better, though. More sugar for you, dear? Speaker_3: Aye, go on then. Just a half spoonful. Besides, I need to save up for a bigger sunglasses budget, clearly. Speaker_2: (Chuckles) Alright, alright. No pressure, darling. But you know, a lovely garden wedding… with fruit trees and maybe… a few chickens?

Speaker_1: Honestly, the state of Mrs. Higgins’ garden. You’d think someone was actively *trying* to grow weeds. It’s a jungle out there. I was thinking maybe a book? He’s been on about wanting to learn more about…German history, I think? Speaker_1: Oh clever! He did mention something about the Holy Roman Empire last time I saw him. He’s got a bit of a fascination with that period. Remember that trip we took to Germany with Gran? Speaker_2: Vaguely! I was about ten? All I remember is eating an awful lot of sausages and being incredibly bored in castles. Speaker_1: (Laughing) That sounds about right. Gran loved all those old places. She was convinced she was a princess in a past life. Anyway, how's work? Still drowning in copy? Speaker_2: Pretty much. It's manic right now. Everyone wants everything *yesterday*. I'm working on a campaign for a new nail varnish range at the moment. Honestly, the amount of money people spend on their nails... Speaker_1: It’s mad, isn’t it? That’d be lovely! Then we can properly plan your birthday. Are you still going to Berlin with Ben? Speaker_2: Yeah! We booked the flights last week. He's really excited. He wants to go to all the museums and I just want to eat currywurst and wander around. Speaker_1: Perfect balance! He seems like a really nice lad, Ben. You deserve to be happy. Speaker_2: He is. And I am. It's just... everything feels a bit hectic at the moment. Work, Christmas, planning the trip… Speaker_1: That’s life, love. It always feels hectic. Just remember to take some time for yourself, okay? A hot bath, a good book, Winston on your lap… whatever helps you unwind. I'm here if you need to vent too, you know that.

Speaker_1: Right, so… officially residents! Feels a bit weird, doesn’t it? Still smells very… new. And faintly of paint. Speaker_2: It does! It's lovely though, isn't it? And we should definitely buy some plants. Brighten the place up a bit. Speaker_1: Absolutely. Although… I'm slightly worried about the nursery next door. It's very… enthusiastic. I can already hear tiny voices. Speaker_2: (Laughing) Oh, bless! It'll be good. A bit of life, a bit of noise. Beats the sound of traffic, anyway. Although, I did notice a few smokers hanging around the entrance to the nursery during pick-up. Hopefully, it won’t be too bad. Speaker_1: Yeah, that’s a bit grim. I’m trying to cut down, anyway. Good excuse, I suppose. Right, back to food. I was thinking of attempting a proper meal tonight. Not just potatoes and pickles. Speaker_2: Oh, really? What were you thinking? I’m happy to help, but honestly, my cooking skills peaked at toast. Speaker_1: I was scrolling through recipes and found a really simple pasta dish with courgette and cherry tomatoes. It's quick, easy, and uses up some of the few things we have. Speaker_2: That sounds amazing. I'm on sauce duty then? Stirring and tasting… my specialities. Speaker_1: Perfect! You are officially sauce master. And after that, we collapse onto the sofa and admire our new kingdom. Speaker_2: Sounds like a plan. Oh, and I saw a really cute little cafe down the high street. We should check it out tomorrow afternoon? They do really good coffee, apparently. Speaker_1: Definitely. We need to scout out the local caffeine options. Right. Operation ‘New Flat’ is officially underway.

Speaker_1: Honestly, this burger is *amazing*. I’ve been craving a proper one all week. How’s your halloumi and roasted vegetable thing? Speaker_2: It's good! Really tasty, actually. A bit healthier than what I initially wanted, seeing as I skipped breakfast, but good. It’s so nice to actually sit down and properly *chat* though, isn’t it? It feels like ages since uni. Speaker_2: (Laughing) Oh my god, yes! That was insane. I think we genuinely thought we could just find a sheltered spot and be okay. And then the rain came. A lot more corporate than I expected, if that makes sense? Everyone’s really nice, but it’s very much ‘meetings about meetings’ kind of vibe. I’m mostly doing admin and social media scheduling at the moment, which is fine, but I was hoping for something a bit more creative. Speaker_1: That’s a bit frustrating. Is there scope to get involved in more of the campaign stuff? Speaker_2: I’m trying to. I volunteered to help with the new product launch, hoping to get some copy-writing in, but they’ve got a dedicated agency doing that. They said they’ll keep me in the loop, but… yeah. It’s okay. What about you? How's project coordinating treating you? Still wrangling spreadsheets? Speaker_1: (rolling her eyes) You know it. Spreadsheets are my nemesis. It’s actually pretty good though. It’s a small team, so I get to be involved in lots of different things, which is good for learning. It's just… demanding. Long hours sometimes. I’m seriously considering a holiday. Somewhere far away. Speaker_2: Ooh, where were you thinking? I’ve been daydreaming about Thailand. Beaches, cheap food... pure bliss. Speaker_1: Thailand sounds amazing! I’ve always wanted to go. I was thinking maybe Italy? Easier to get to, and I've been trying to practice my Italian on Duolingo. Pathetic, I know. Speaker_2: No, that’s cool! Italy would be lovely. My aunt went last year and raved about Florence. We should look into it together, actually. Maybe next summer? Speaker_1: That's a brilliant idea! Seriously, let’s. Okay, this is a proper catch-up. We need to do this more often. How are your parents? I haven’t spoken to them in ages. Speaker_2: They’re good, they're good. Mum’s taken up gardening, which is… a whole thing. She’s got every tool imaginable. Dad's still obsessed with cricket. They were asking about you last time I spoke to them. They remember you raiding their biscuit tin during uni visits. Speaker_1: (laughing) Oh god, I’m so sorry about that. I had a serious biscuit addiction back then. I probably owe them a lifetime supply. Anyway, how’s your brother? Still living in Manchester?

Speaker_1: Honestly, this pint is *exactly* what I needed. That commute from London was brutal. Speaker_2: Tell me about it. Even getting *into* Cambridge feels like a commute sometimes. You get a bit detached here in the Cambridge bubble, surrounded by… well, privilege, let’s be honest. Reminds me why I keep going back to Birmingham. Family, yeah, but also just… reality. What’s the data saying specifically about the North East? Speaker_1: Oh, it’s predictably awful. Sunderland’s right down there, unsurprisingly. It’s just… the systemic barriers are *so* entrenched. My mum still says there’s no opportunities up there for young people unless you leave. Bit depressing, really. She always wanted me to stay closer to home, but she also wanted me to have a better life. It’s a contradiction. Speaker_2: That’s… rough. My dad always drilled into me the importance of education, specifically because he grew up in a really working-class area of Birmingham. He wanted to break that cycle. It’s good you’re looking into it, though. Actually making a difference. Speaker_1: Trying to! It feels small sometimes, staring at spreadsheets. Speaking of small things, did you see what Sarah was wearing to that seminar yesterday? Speaker_2: Oh, *that* dress? The floral one? Speaker_1: Yes! It was… a choice. Honestly, it looked like something my gran would wear to a garden party. And she has *good* taste, but it just wasn’t right for a post-structuralist theory seminar. Speaker_2: (laughing) You are savage. She does have a… unique sense of style. Bless her. I think she gets most of her clothes from vintage shops. Speaker_1: That explains it then. It’s brave, I'll give her that! It’s a lot more adventurous than my wardrobe of various shades of grey. I haven’t bought anything new in months. Speaker_2: You always look good though. Simple and classic. I’m more of a t-shirt and jeans kind of guy myself. Functionality over fashion. Though, did you catch Fontaines D.C. at the weekend? Grian Chatten's style is… something else. All black, perpetually looking like he’s about to start a fight. Speaker_1: Ooh, yes! They were amazing. I’ve been obsessed with them since I first heard ‘Boys in the Better Land’. And you’re right, his whole vibe is just… cool. It’s deliberately understated, isn’t it? Like he doesn’t even *try* to look good, and that’s what makes him look good. Speaker_2: Exactly! It's authentic. Which is what I appreciate. Speaking of music, are you still going to that indie night at the Junction next week? Speaker_1: Definitely. I need a proper night out. Work is draining the life out of me. Plus, I heard this new band, The Beths, are playing. They’re from New Zealand, apparently, but they sound amazing. Very power-pop, a bit like early Blondie.

Speaker_1: Gran, did you see what happened in Parliament today? Proper chaos, like. Speaker_2: (Sighs) Oh, lad, don't get me started on Parliament. It’s always chaos. Always has been, always will be. Used to be proper gentlemen, you know, arguing with respect. Now it's just…shouting. Speaker_1: But this was different. They were practically at each other's throats! Over, like, a new law about… something to do with the environment, I think? Mr. Henderson at school was explaining it, but it went right over my head. Speaker_2: Environment, eh? They’re all talkin' about the environment now, aren’t they? Fancy that, after all these years, suddenly worryin' about the planet. It's all for show, you mark my words. Just tryin' to get votes. Speaker_1: But isn’t it important to look after the planet? Everyone says it is, and with the weather being all weird lately… Speaker_2: Aye, important it is. But they wouldn't be worryin’ if it didn’t get ‘em re-elected, would they? Back in my day, we didn’t have all this fuss. We just got on with things. Mind you, things *were* different. Less plastic, for a start. Everything came in glass bottles. Speaker_1: Dad said you used to get milk delivered in glass bottles? That sounds cool. Speaker_2: Cool? It was normal! Every mornin’, the milkman would leave ‘em on the doorstep. And proper cream on top, you could scoop it off with a spoon! Not like this watery stuff you get now. And the bottles were washed and used again, not thrown away like everything else. Speaker_1: That’s a good idea. Maybe they should bring that back. Do you think… do you think politicians even *care* about stuff like that? Speaker_2: (Chuckles dryly) Care? They care about power, lad. That’s all they care about. And money, of course. Don't you ever think they’re normal folk like you and me. They're a different breed altogether. Remember old Mr. Bailey down the street? He stood for Parliament once, a long time ago. Said he wanted to make a difference. Lasted about six months before he said it was all a load of…well, I won't repeat it. Speaker_1: What did he say? Speaker_2: (Waving her hand dismissively) Oh, never you mind. It wasn't very polite. Just that he realised they were more interested in lining their own pockets than helping people. He went back to fixin' clocks, which he was much better at, anyway. Speaker_1: So, you don't think anything will actually *change* with all this talk about the environment and stuff? Speaker_2: Change? Slow change, maybe. But a real, proper change? I doubt it. They’ll make promises, they’ll hold meetings, they’ll write reports… and nothing much will actually happen. It's always the same story, lad. Always the same. Now, how about a biscuit? I've got some nice ginger nuts. That'll cheer you up more than listenin' to me grumble about politics. Speaker_1: Alright, yeah, a biscuit sounds good. But… it just feels like they don’t listen, you know? Like, we’re all worried about things, and they’re just… arguing. Speaker_2: That’s because they don’t *want* to listen, lad. Easier to argue. Keeps them in the headlines, see? Now, stop frettin’ about it. You’re too young to be botherin’ your head with all this. Focus on your schoolwork, and leave the politics to them… even though they’re making a right mess of it. And have a biscuit.

Speaker_1: (Chewing thoughtfully) Now, that was a fine stew, Mary. A *very* fine stew. Though, young master Leo here seemed to be… excavating for treasure with his spoon, rather than *eating* the stew. Speaker_2: (Muttering, eyes fixed on his plate) It’s just…the potatoes are kinda sticking to the roof of my mouth. Speaker_3: Leo! Honestly. You're practically making a noise like a tractor. Remember what we talked about? Small bites, chewing with your mouth closed. It’s not a race. Speaker_4: (Chuckles softly) Oh, the manners of the young these days! Back in my day, a boy would be sent to bed without supper for that kind of behaviour. A good, firm telling-off was all that was needed. Speaker_1: Now, now, Margaret. No need for tales of the old days to frighten the lad. He’s just enjoying his food. A vigorous enjoyment, admittedly. Speaker_2: It’s just… good stew, Dad. Loads of it. Speaker_3: That doesn't excuse shovelling it in, darling. It's disrespectful to Mary who spent ages making it. Speaker_1: Speaking of ages, did you see that blood moon last night, Margaret? A right spectacle it was. All reddish and looming. Speaker_4: I did indeed. Went out onto the back step with a wee cup of tea. Gave me the shivers, it did. Reminded me of old stories - bad omens and all that nonsense. Still, a beautiful sight. Speaker_3: It was beautiful. Leo and I watched it from the window. He was asking all sorts of questions about space and why it was red. Little scientist in the making. Speaker_2: It was cool. Kinda spooky though, right? Speaker_1: Spooky is good. Keeps the imagination working. So, are we all agreed on a family outing this weekend? I was thinking Fitzgerald’s Park. We could feed the ducks, maybe get an ice cream… Speaker_3: That sounds lovely. A nice, easy day out. Though, Leo will want to go on the swings for hours. Speaker_2: (Brightening up) Swings are awesome! And the slide! Speaker_4: Fitzgerald's Park is a grand spot. I took a whole class of wee ones there for years. Always a bit of a scramble trying to keep them all together. Speaker_1: (Smiling) We’ll keep a close eye on this one. Say, Margaret, would you be able to… possibly babysit Leo for a few hours next week? Mary and I have that dinner with the McAllisters, and we don’t really want to drag him along. Speaker_4: (Without hesitation) Of course, I would. I adore that boy. He’s a right wee charmer. Always asking questions, just like his Granny was. Speaker_3: Oh, that would be amazing, Mum. You’re a lifesaver. We’re still trying to get a regular babysitter sorted, it’s proving difficult. Speaker_1: It is. Difficult to find someone you trust, isn’t it? Especially with a little hurricane like Leo. Speaker_2: Hey! I'm not a hurricane! Speaker_3: (Chuckling) A very *energetic* little boy, then. That's what you are. Now, finish your stew, please. Small bites, remember? Speaker_1: Good eating is a civilised thing you know. Speaker_4: Oh! It is important. Speaker_3: Yes, it is!

Speaker_1: Honestly, the whole Scottish referendum thing… still can’t quite believe it went the way it did. Thought it’d be a lot closer, you know? Speaker_2: Did you? I always thought ‘No’ would win, but I confess, I underestimated the momentum. Proper nail-biter though, wasn’t it? Remember staying up all night watching the results come in? Speaker_1: Vaguely. You seemed a bit apprehensive about it last week. Speaker_1: It was… alright. Not spectacular. A lot of the usual questions, ‘where do you see yourself in five years?’ ‘What are your leadership qualities?’ The whole rigmarole. There was a particularly trying colleague on the panel – Brenda Higgins. You remember her, always a bit… frosty. Speaker_2: Brenda Higgins. Oh, *her*. Yes, I remember. Thought she’d retire years ago. Still causing trouble, is she? Speaker_1: Still causing trouble. Kept interrupting, challenging everything I said. I think she fancies the job herself, probably. Made me feel like I was back in school, being grilled by the headmaster. Speaker_2: Sounds awful. They can be right pains, some of those people. Don’t let it get you down, though. You’re a damn good teacher, Arthur. They’d be fools to pass you over. Speaker_1: Thanks, Roger. I appreciate that. Trying not to dwell on it, really. Distracting myself. Speaking of distractions… how’s Sarah? Still enjoying university? Speaker_2: She's doing well, thank you. Keeps herself busy. Just finished her first term, absolutely exhausted. She's thinking about doing a year abroad, possibly in Spain. Always loved the language. Speaker_1: Spain, eh? Good for her. Getting out there, experiencing a different culture. That’s what it’s all about. My own daughter, Emily… well, she's settling into her new job. A bit of a whirlwind, this last year for her. Speaker_2: Still with Mark? Speaker_1: Still with Mark, yes. They’re talking about moving in together. It's… a big step. A bit nerve-wracking as a parent, you know? Want them to be happy, but also worry about the practicalities. Speaker_2: Tell me about it. It feels like only yesterday I was trying to figure out how to get Sarah to eat her vegetables. Now she’s talking about Erasmus programs and gap years. Time flies, doesn’t it? Speaker_1: It does indeed. It really does. As for me… well, things are ticking along. Bit quiet since Margaret passed, obviously. Still getting used to the silence, if you know what I mean. Speaker_2: I do, Arthur. I truly do. It's a big adjustment. Just remember, you’re not alone. We’re here for you, you know that, right? Speaker_1: I do. And I appreciate it, Roger. Truly. It’s good to have friends like you. So, enough about my woes. How’s the business? Still keeping busy? Speaker_2: Busy is an understatement. Had a couple of really difficult clients lately. You get all sorts, don’t you? One wanted me to build him a miniature replica of the Eiffel Tower out of matchsticks! Speaker_1: (laughing) You’re joking! Speaker_2: I wish I were! Said it was for his grandson. Honestly, people. Still, keeps things interesting, I suppose.

Speaker_1: Right, so, are we actually heading to Mum’s now, or are we doing another supermarket sweep first? I’m starving. Speaker_2: We said Mum’s, didn’t we, darling? I’ve got that potato salad to drop off, you know, the one with the dill? She loves it. Speaker_3: Dill, really? Seems a bit… much. I’m with Aaron, though. Lunch is a serious priority right now. This journey’s taking ages. Speaker_4: Aye, it is a bit of a trek. But it's good to get out of the house, innit? Least I think so. Been cooped up enough lately. Still, this sat nav is sending us round the houses. Honestly, you’d think it would know St Neots by now. Speaker_1: Seriously! It's like it's actively *avoiding* the quickest route. And the voice…it's so condescending. "In 200 meters, prepare to turn left." Like I haven’t driven before! Speaker_2: Oh, you're just like your father, always complaining about the technology. Remember when he refused to get a mobile phone for years? Said it was the devil’s work. Speaker_4: I did not! I just…preferred a good map. And knowing where I was going without a robot telling me. Though, I have to admit, that new telly with the built-in streaming is pretty handy. Speaker_3: Speaking of handy, has anyone looked into those student loan repayment plans properly? It’s a complete mess, honestly. I feel like I’m paying off a mortgage, not a degree. Speaker_1: Don’t even get me started. I’m still trying to figure out if consolidating makes any sense. It’s a nightmare. All this financial stuff… I wish I’d just learned to become a master board game player. Heard someone broke a world record for the longest continuous Monopoly game recently. Speaker_2: Monopoly? Oh, that game ends families, it does. My sister and I haven’t spoken properly since the Great Monopoly Incident of ‘87. Speaker_4: (Chuckles) '87, eh? Those were the days. I remember when a tenner could get you a decent shopping trip. Now? It barely covers the milk and bread. Speaker_1: Tell me about it! I went to Tesco yesterday, and I practically needed a loan to buy a few bits for dinner. It's outrageous. Speaker_3: I was thinking about trying to make pasta from scratch. It seems therapeutic, and probably cheaper in the long run. Although, my kitchen skills are… questionable. Speaker_2: Oh, I'm a dab hand at pasta making! Your grandmother taught me, bless her. It’s not as hard as it looks. Though, you need a good strong pair of arms. Speaker_4: Speaking of strong arms, have you heard from old Mr Henderson? The one who used to deliver our groceries? Apparently, he’s taken up competitive weightlifting. At his age! Speaker_1: No way! That’s amazing! Bet he’s got a good pension, though. Unlike a lot of us, stuck in these customer service jobs. Speaker_2: Well, we all have to start somewhere, darling. And it's a secure job, isn't it? That’s something these days. Right, I think I can see Mum’s house coming up. Are you boys alright for snacks in the car? I might have a biscuit or two… . . . . . . .......

Speaker_1: Honestly, this road is mental. I didn’t realise quite *how* countryside-y we were getting. It’s like…single track at points. Speaker_2: (Chuckles) Aye, well, you’re in proper farming country now, lass. Used to be even worse, mind. And Gran said the farm shop is worth the detour. Proper local produce and everything. Speaker_2: Worth it, aye. Old Man Hemmings has some cracking sausages. Proper pork, not that processed muck you get in the supermarkets. And his eggs…best you’ll ever taste. Free range, you see. The hens roam all over. Speaker_3: Free range, excellent. I’m trying to cut down on…well, everything, really. Eating better, more exercise. It’s all a bit overwhelming. Speaker_1: Tell me about it. I’ve started trying to meal prep, and it’s a disaster. I end up just ordering a takeaway anyway. Speaker_2: Meal prep? What’s that, some sort of fancy cookery? Back in my day, you just *cooked*. And you cooked what was in season. Didn’t have a choice, mind. No flying in mangoes in December then! Speaker_3: It's basically just cooking a load of food on Sunday so you have lunches for the week. Theoretically. Speaker_1: Exactly! Sounds good in theory. Look! Sheep! Loads of them. Speaker_3: Wow, there really are. They’re just…everywhere. Speaker_2: Those’ll be Hemmings’ sheep. He breeds them, sells the lambs. Good quality stock, he has. Proper North Country Cheviots, tough as old boots. Speaker_1: They’re all staring at the car. It’s a bit unnerving. Speaker_3: Probably wondering what these city slickers are doing invading their space. Speaker_2: They’re used to it. They see tractors and lorries all day. Oh, and has anyone been sneaking into the Easter chocolate? I swear the bunny’s getting smaller... Speaker_3: (Whistles innocently, avoiding eye contact) Nope. Not me. Definitely not me. I was busy building a Batmobile, remember? Speaker_1: (Raises an eyebrow) Right. And I suppose the chocolate fairy visited? Speaker_2: (Giggles) Maybe! I only had a tiny bit. It was yummy. It was a purple egg! Speaker_1: A purple egg, was it? Hmmm. Well, as long as you’re both helping with the Lego, I won’t say anything… for now. Right, back to sorting. Let's find those grey bricks, super-speed Batmobile builder! Speaker_3: Yes! Finding grey bricks! It’s my superpower!

Speaker_1: Oh my god, you are back! How was Greece? Honestly, fill me in. Did you actually manage to switch off, or were you still mentally at work the whole time? Speaker_2: Honestly? It was…needed. You practically saved lives all through the pandemic, you deserve a permanent holiday. Are they actually trying to recruit, or are they just expecting you to absorb all the extra workload? Speaker_2: Just expecting me to absorb it, mostly. They’ve posted a job advert, but it’s been up for weeks. I think the pay is a bit low for the level of stress involved, to be honest. Speaker_2: No, thankfully not. Sarah from work is dating him now. Apparently, he’s still the same old Ben. She’s convinced she can “fix” him. It’s painful to watch, honestly. I tried to learn how to make sourdough. Speaker_2: (Laughing) You?! Sourdough is the most millennial, pretentious thing ever. And you're…not exactly known for your patience. Speaker_1: I know, right? It was a disaster. The starter looked like something out of a horror film, and the loaf came out flatter than a pancake. I’m sticking to shop-bought from now on. It was a humbling experience, though. Speaker_2: That’s hilarious. I’m picturing it now. So, are you free next week? There’s that new Italian place opened on Mill Road, I thought we could go and check it out? Proper treat night. Speaker_1: Ooh, yes! That sounds amazing. I’ve been craving pasta. Next week is good. Anything but Tuesday, I've got that networking event for work. Honestly, the thought of small talk with marketing people…gives me hives. Speaker_2: Ugh, networking. The worst. Okay, let’s say Thursday? We can gossip about Sarah and Ben over a tiramisu. Speaker_1: Perfect! That is a plan. Now, more lemon drizzle? I think my mum secretly tried to fatten me up.

Speaker_1: Now then, are you sure you’ve got everything you need for school tomorrow? Physics practical, wasn't it? Speaker_2: Yeah, Mum, I’ve checked three times. Bunsen burner, goggles, the worksheet… all good. Honestly, you fuss more than Miss Harrison. Speaker_3: (Chuckles) Aye, she’s got a point, lad. Your mother always was a worrier. And you were a handful. Speaker_4: (From his armchair, a low rumble of a laugh.) A right little rascal, he was. Always covered in mud. Used to bring the garden indoors, that one. Speaker_1: Oh, don't even *start* on the roses. It took me a week to get all the worms out! Honestly, the state of the garden after you two had been… Speaker_3: Now, now, don’t get yourself all worked up, love. It's a good garden, still. And he was just a lad. Learning about nature, he was. Speaker_1: Learning about destruction, more like! Anyway, have you seen the state of the kitchen? I asked you, Ethan, to put your plate away after tea. Speaker_2: I was finishing my homework! It's due first thing. Speaker_1: Homework can wait five minutes to avoid a mountain of dirty dishes. Honestly, sometimes I think you think the fairies come and do it all. Speaker_4: Fairies? Now there's a thought. Wonder if they'd tackle the hoovering. Speaker_3: (Smiling) You cheeky bugger, Arthur. Trying to get out of your chores again, are you? Speaker_4: A man can dream, can't he? My back’s not what it used to be. Besides, I’ve got a joke for you. Why don’t skeletons ever go on holiday? Speaker_2: (Groaning) Oh no, here we go… Speaker_1: Oh dear. Speaker_3: Go on, Arthur, tell us. Speaker_4: Because they've got no *body* to go with! (A beat of silence, then Speaker_3 bursts into laughter. Speaker_1 rolls her eyes, but a small smile plays on her lips. Speaker_2 hides his face in his hands.) Speaker_1: Oh, Arthur. That was dreadful. Absolutely dreadful. Speaker_3: Oh, it were lovely! You always tell the best bad jokes, Arthur. Speaker_2: Seriously. That was… wow. Speaker_1: Right, that's enough silliness. I’m making a pot of tea. Would you like some, you two? And Ethan, honestly, the kitchen. Five minutes. Just five minutes. Speaker_3: Tea would be lovely, pet. Strong, mind. Speaker_4: And a biscuit, if you've got any of those ginger ones. They're the best. Speaker_2: I’ll get the kitchen done after this level of my game, okay? It’s a really important raid. Speaker_1: (Sighs) Fine. But important raids don’t excuse dirty dishes. And Arthur, no encouraging him.

Speaker_1: Right, so we’re all agreed, bath time first, then we can finish talking about Peter Pan? Honestly, you two have been buzzing about it all afternoon since we finished the film. Speaker_2: But Mummy! Tinkerbell is *so* sparkly! And she’s really brave, even though she’s tiny. Speaker_3: Yeah! And Captain Hook has a hook instead of a hand! That’s really silly. Did he lose it fighting Peter Pan? Speaker_1: He did, actually. The story says he lost it in a fight with Peter Pan, and a crocodile ate the rest of his hand. That’s why he has the hook! Speaker_1: Well, his family had been helped by the hospital before, and he wanted to make sure other children could get better there too. It’s a very kind thing to do, isn’t it? It’s amazing how much money they’ve raised over the years because of Peter Pan. Speaker_2: More than all our Christmas presents? Speaker_1: Oh, definitely more than all our Christmas presents, clever clogs! It’s helped *lots* of children. You know, they made another film a few years ago, called *Pan*? Speaker_3: *Pan*? Is that about Peter before he went to Neverland? Speaker_1: Yes! It’s kind of a prequel, it tells the story of how he got there. It’s not quite as good as the original story, or even the Disney *Peter Pan* film, but it’s… interesting. Speaker_2: I don't remember that one. Was it sparkly like Tinkerbell? Speaker_1: Not *quite* as sparkly, no. It was a bit… darker. More about how Peter became Peter Pan. It tries to explain how he can fly and things. Speaker_3: But everyone knows Peter Pan can fly! He has happy thoughts! Speaker_1: Exactly! That's what makes his story so magical. Actually, there are loads of different films about Peter Pan. And lots about Tinkerbell too – she has her own adventures. Speaker_2: I like the Tinkerbell ones best. She's really a fairy. Speaker_1: She is! And very feisty! Okay, enough Peter Pan talk for now. Bath time. Quickly, before your Dad gets home with ice cream – then *really* all talk of Neverland will have to stop! Speaker_3: YAY! Ice cream! But can we watch Tinkerbell again tomorrow? Speaker_1: We'll see, darling. We'll see. Now, bubbles! Speaker_2: (Giggles) Bubbles and sparkles! Like Tinkerbell!

Speaker_1: Honestly, this M5 is a nightmare already. Even at this time on a Sunday. Reminds me of the old A38, dodging tractors and holidaymakers all the way to… well, everywhere, really.
