It’s just… getting older, you know. Don’t sleep as soundly. Thinking about things. Mostly about making sure you two are alright. And the grand kids, of course. Speaker_3: We’re fine, Dad. Honestly. A bit stressful with the end of term, but that’s normal. And you know how much we appreciate you worrying. Speaker_2: Speaking of stressful, have we finalised Christmas at your place? Are we still doing the usual turkey and all the trimmings? Speaker_1: That’s the plan. Though your Auntie Maureen keeps hinting she’s bringing a vegan nut roast. Speaker_3: Oh, dear. That could be interesting. Speaker_2: We can deal with a nut roast. More importantly, are you still up for a house-warming party once we’re settled into the new place? We were thinking maybe January, before it gets *too* bleak. Speaker_1: Absolutely! A proper knees-up. We’ll invite everyone. Your mum would have loved that new house. It’s a shame she can't see it. Speaker_3: She would have. It's got that lovely garden she always wanted for the grandchildren. Speaker_2: We're hoping so. It is a bit of a project, though. That kitchen especially needs gutting. Speaker_1: Well, you two are good at projects. Remember that disastrous attempt to repaint the bathroom at our old house in Torquay? Speaker_3: (Laughing) Oh don’t! I’m still finding flecks of paint behind the radiator! Speaker_2: Okay, okay, let’s not dwell on past decorating mishaps. We've learned since then. The airport's coming up, isn’t it? Suddenly feeling a bit emotional now… Speaker_1: It always hits you at the airport, doesn't it? Knowing you won’t see them for a while. Drive safe, you two. Give our love to little Emily and James. And remember to text when you land. Speaker_3: We will, Dad. We will. Speaker_1: Right. Focus on the road. And try to avoid any tractors. Speaker_2: (Smiling) No promises, Dad. No promises. Speaker_3: Just think of relaxing on a beach, that will keep you calm. Speaker_1: I am, I am.

Speaker_1: (Sighs, fanning herself with a leaflet) Goodness, it’s warm work, isn’t it? All that shifting of gravel… my hands are aching already. Speaker_2: Tell me about it. I thought my days of heavy lifting were over when I retired from the Building Society. Though, dealing with some of the customers felt like moving mountains at times, mind you. You with the working party then? Speaker_1: Yes, I am. Though ‘working’ feels a bit strong. More like… carefully rearranging. I used to be an artist, you see. Not much call for physical labour in that profession. Spent years running a little gallery in Wells. Speaker_2: Wells, lovely part of the world. My daughter used to take the grandchildren down there. Said the little ones adored the Bishop’s Palace. I’m Arthur, by the way. Speaker_1: Delighted to meet you, Arthur. I’m Margaret. And yes, Wells is rather special. Though I sold up a few years ago. Became… tiring. All the sourcing, the valuations. A Swedish massage is what I really need right now, not more gravel. Speaker_2: Swedish massage, eh? My Brenda – my wife, God rest her – used to swear by those. Said it was the only thing that kept her back from seizing up altogether. She volunteered at the local hospice for years. A truly wonderful woman. Speaker_1: Oh, that’s lovely. It’s so important, that kind of work. I did a bit of work with nursery education, years ago, helping with art classes. The little ones are just so… uncomplicated. It’s a world away from the art market, with all its pretensions. Speaker_2: It is. Though, that reminds me. My granddaughter’s training to be a nursery teacher now. Says she finds the paperwork a nightmare. All these new directives. Still, she’s a strong girl. A bit too opinionated for her own good, if you ask me, but that’s the young generation for you. Expecting equality on a plate. Speaker_1: (Raises an eyebrow) Equality *on* a plate? It's rather a long time coming, isn’t it? I mean, I remember a time when a woman asking for a mortgage alone was practically a scandal. Speaker_2: You’re not wrong there. Though I always treated everyone the same, I like to think. Brenda certainly didn't suffer fools gladly, and she made sure *I* didn’t either. Still, terminology’s all changed, hasn’t it? Can’t say ‘chairman’ anymore, it’s ‘chairperson’. Drives me mad. Speaker_1: It’s a bit silly, yes. But I suppose it’s trying to be inclusive. Have you heard anything more about next year’s ME event? The one they’re holding here? Speaker_2: A little. They’re still trying to get the funding sorted, I believe. Apparently, there’s a push to get more women involved, presenting papers and leading workshops. Speaker_1: Good. It’s about time. Though I do wonder if it will be genuine inclusion, or just… tokenism. They’ll need more than just a few female speakers to convince anyone they’re serious. There are some excellent female archaeologists about. They need to actively seek them out. Speaker_2: You think so? I just thought it was a good thing to have a bit of balance. Though I agree, it’s got to be genuine. Can’t just tick a box and think the job’s done. It’s like that building society again. They’d appoint a woman to a senior position just for PR, then wonder why she wasn’t performing. It's not about gender, it’s about ability. Speaker_1: Precisely. Ability, and opportunity. And being taken seriously. I’ve lost count of the number of times my opinions were dismissed in gallery circles, simply because I was a woman. Stepping back from all that, though, is proving rather… liberating, actually. Perhaps I’ll

Speaker_1: Right, so I was looking at flights again, and honestly, Mum, it’s just… ridiculous. Everything has gone up so much since last time I checked. Speaker_2: Oh dear. To Portugal, is it? Still set on the Algarve? Speaker_1: Yeah, I think so. I mean, I’m open to suggestions, but it felt like a good compromise, you know? Sun, not *too* far to travel, relatively affordable… well, it *was* relatively affordable. Speaker_2: Affordable is a relative term these days, isn’t it? Everything’s gone up. Petrol, the price of a loaf of bread… it's frightening. When your father and I went to Majorca in… oh, goodness, 1985, it was a song. We practically stole the holiday. Speaker_1: (Chuckles) You always tell me that story! But seriously, the flights are looking at nearly four hundred pounds each now. And that's just for the flights! Speaker_2: Four hundred! Goodness me. Have you tried EasyJet or Ryanair? They’re usually the cheapest, even if they are a bit… basic. Speaker_1: Of course, I’ve tried them! They’re the first places I looked. Ryanair wants me to pay extra for a carry-on bag now, can you believe it? It's getting beyond a joke. Speaker_2: Honestly! They squeeze every penny out of you. Remember when baggage was included? Anyway, have you thought about going a bit earlier or later in the season? Maybe June instead of July? Speaker_1: I did. June is a bit cheaper, but the weather’s a bit more unpredictable, isn’t it? I’d rather pay a bit more and guarantee some sunshine. I’m not keen on spending a week huddled in a cardigan. Speaker_2: Fair enough. Sunshine is important. Have you looked at package holidays? Sometimes they can work out cheaper, especially if you include the hotel in the deal. Speaker_1: I had a quick look, but most of them try and stick you in these awful, out-of-the-way places. I want to be near the beach, and somewhere with a bit of life. Not stuck in a concrete block miles from anywhere. Speaker_2: Hmm. You are picky, you know. (Smiling) But you deserve a nice holiday. You work so hard. Have you checked Airbnb for apartments? Sometimes you can find lovely places for a good price. Speaker_1: That's a good shout, actually. I hadn't really considered Airbnb. I always worry about it being a bit… dodgy, you know? But I suppose if you read the reviews carefully… Speaker_2: Exactly. Read the reviews, check the location on a map. And look for places with superhosts. They tend to be more reliable. I used it in Barcelona last year, it was brilliant. A lovely little flat right in the Gothic Quarter. Speaker_1: Okay, I’ll give Airbnb a proper look tonight. Maybe that's the answer. Thanks, Mum. Honestly, you always have good ideas. I was getting so stressed out about it. Speaker_2: No problem, darling. That’s what mothers are for! Now, have you decided what you're taking to the WI meeting next week? Old Mrs. Higgins is demanding my lemon drizzle cake again. Speaker_1: Oh no… not the lemon drizzle cake saga again! I swear, she treats it like a national treasure. I was thinking of taking some of those gingerbread biscuits I made last weekend. Speaker_2: Oh, very sensible. A change is as good as a rest, as they say. And it’ll save me from having to spend the whole afternoon baking.

Speaker_1: Right, so I checked the bank again, and they’ve *still* only authorised eighty quid for the concert tickets. Eighty! Do they think I’m going to sneak into Wembley with eighty pounds? Speaker_2: (Chuckles) Eighty quid, eh? That’s a bit tight, even for standing room. Did you call them, explain the situation? Speaker_1: Yeah, I spent half an hour on hold listening to that awful synthesized music, and then the bloke on the phone just kept repeating their standard security protocols. “Have you used your card abroad recently, sir?” No! “Have you noticed any unusual transactions?” No! It’s just… frustrating. It’s *my* money. Speaker_2: I feel you. Banks are getting worse, honestly. They’re all about protecting themselves, not helping the customer. You should try writing a formal complaint, sometimes that gets things moving. Speaker_1: Maybe. I just want to go and see Arctic Monkeys without having to remortgage the flat. Speaking of frustrating, did you catch the Forest game yesterday? Speaker_2: Oh, don't even *start* me. Absolutely robbed! That penalty decision was unbelievable. The ref was clearly biased. Speaker_1: Totally! I was shouting at the TV. My missus thought I’d lost it. Said I was acting like a proper hooligan. Speaker_2: (Laughing) They don’t understand the passion, do they? It’s a different level. Reminds me of when I was back in Barbados, watching cricket with my grandfather. The atmosphere was electric. Every boundary was celebrated like a national holiday. Speaker_1: Sounds amazing. I’ve never really been to a proper cricket match. It always seemed… slow. Speaker_2: Slow? It’s strategic! It’s a chess match played with a ball and a bat. You just need to understand the nuances. Anyway, enough about sport – how’s work been? Still drowning in essays? Speaker_1: Pretty much. I’ve got this dissertation on post-structuralism to finish, and I’m completely stuck. It’s like trying to explain fog. Speaker_2: (Smiling) Sounds challenging. You always were a bright spark, though. You’ll figure it out. My work’s been… hectic. Had a major incident down at the warehouse last week. Forklift driver reversed into a stack of pallets. Luckily, no one was hurt, but the paperwork was a nightmare. Speaker_1: Oh, blimey. That sounds stressful. You always take it all on your shoulders, don't you? Speaker_2: It's the nature of the job, I suppose. Someone’s got to keep things running smoothly. Speaking of family, have you heard from Auntie Maureen lately? She promised to send photos of little Leo. Speaker_1: I haven't, actually. I’ll give her a ring later. She’s always saying she’s going to, then life gets in the way. She’s a busy woman, that one. Speaker_2: Busy is an understatement! She's got that flower arranging business, managing the grandkids, and volunteering at the church. She never stops. Speaker_1: She’s a legend. I wonder if she watched that Meghan Markle interview? She's fascinated by the royal family. Speaker_2: Oh, I doubt it. She doesn't really do all that celebrity gossip. More interested in what the neighbours are up to, if you ask me. Speaker_1: True, true. Right, I’m going to make a cuppa. Fancy one? Speaker_2: Don't mind if I do. And maybe, just *maybe*, you can explain this post-structuralism stuff to me while we’re at it. I'm intrigued now.

Speaker_1: (A slight crackle on the Skype line) …and then the whole thing just wobbled, you see? Right off its stand. Nearly took the telly with it. Speaker_2: Oh, Arthur! Not the globe again? Honestly, you'd think after all these years you'd find a safer place for it. Is it still in one piece? Speaker_1: Mostly. Bit of a crack across South America, but nothing a bit of glue won't fix. It’s a beautiful thing, that globe. Reminds me of holidays, you know? When we went to… oh, where was it? Not Spain, not Italy… Speaker_3: Yorkshire? You two were always banging on about Yorkshire. That ridiculous little cottage? Speaker_2: It wasn't *ridiculous*, David. It was charming! And the walks were lovely. Though Arthur did nearly break his leg on that one hill… Speaker_1: (Chuckles) Now, that weren’t my leg, Beatrice. That was after the youth hostel trip. Remember that? In the Peak District? That stone staircase… Speaker_3: Oh, God, yes. I remember you both recounting that tale for years. Apparently, a sprained ankle doesn’t stop Arthur from climbing mountains. Speaker_1: I was a young man then! Full of beans. And Beatrice insisted on packing enough for a month in a rucksack barely big enough for a loaf of bread. Speaker_2: Well, someone had to be prepared. You’d forget your head if it wasn’t screwed on, Arthur. Speaking of prepared… did young Emily manage to finish her school project? The one on underground systems? Speaker_3: She did. Quite a good one, actually. She chose the London Underground, naturally. Spent ages researching it. Even made a miniature model with working lights. It was impressive. Though I did have to help her with the history bit – her knowledge before was… limited. Speaker_1: Ah, London Underground. Now *that's* a proper system. Always a bit grubby, mind, but gets you where you need to go. Nothing like the tube we had planned in Norwich. Never happened, did it? Too much fuss. Speaker_2: They talked about it for years. Remember Mr. Henderson at the council? Always going on about 'improving infrastructure.' All talk, that man. He was more interested in his prize-winning roses. Speaker_1: Speaking of gardens… how's yours doing, Beatrice? Are the tomatoes coming along alright? Speaker_2: Slowly. We had a terrible slug infestation. Lost half the seedlings. David’s been trying to build me some sort of barrier, but he’s a teacher, not a gardener. Not quite the same skillset. Speaker_3: Hey! I'm a perfectly capable builder… of poorly constructed slug barriers. It’s a work in progress. How's your knee, Arthur? Still giving you trouble? Speaker_1: It’s a bit achy, son. Nothing a cup of tea and a sit-down won’t fix. Though getting up and down the garden isn’t as easy as it used to be. It's this leg, honestly. The one I didn’t break in Yorkshire. Speaker_2: Honestly, Arthur. It's a miracle you're still standing at all. And don't you start on the Yorkshire stories again. My ears will bleed. Speaker_3: (Laughing) Sounds like a lovely afternoon, you two. Maybe we should come down for a visit next weekend? Escape the Birmingham chaos for a bit. Speaker_1: Now *there's* a thought. You’re always welcome, both of you. We could even dust off the old globe… carefully.

Speaker_1: Right, so I’ve been lookin’ at flights again, yeah? And honestly, they’re just… mental. For what, like, three days in Barcelona? You'd think you were goin' to the moon, the price of ‘em. Are you lookin’ at EasyJet, Ryanair, all the usual suspects? Speaker_1: Aye, all of ‘em. And British Airways just to, like, make me feel properly poor. They’re all just rampin’ up the prices now summer's comin’. It's a conspiracy, I’m tellin’ ya. Speaker_2: Probably is. They know everyone’s desperate for a bit of sun. Have you tried bein’ flexible with the dates at all? Sometimes shifting it by a day or two can make a difference. Speaker_1: I have, a little. But work is… well, work. Hard to get time off. I was hopin’ for the bank holiday weekend, obviously, but everyone and their dog is thinkin’ the same thing. Speaker_2: Yeah, that’s a no-go zone. Speaking of work, I had a proper nightmare today. The entire print run for the new brochure came back wrong. Wrong colours, missin’ pages, the whole shebang. Speaker_1: Oh, no! Seriously? What happened? Did someone mess up the file or…? Speaker_2: It’s a long story, involving a very stressed graphic designer and a printer who clearly needs to invest in a new colour calibration system. I had to spend three hours on the phone, basically yellin’ at people. It was not a good afternoon. Speaker_1: Blimey. Sounds awful. You deserve a big glass of wine for that. And for havin’ to deal with printers in general. They're all cowboys, aren't they? Speaker_2: You have *no* idea. I’m pretty sure they just make mistakes on purpose to see how much they can get away with. Actually, speaking of wine… is that lasagne smellin’ as good as I think it is? Speaker_1: It is! My mum sent us over a massive one. Enough to feed a small army. Help yourself, y’know. Speaker_2: Oh, you’re a star. I’m starvin’. Honestly, after that day, all I want is carbs and comfort. Do you fancy puttin’ somethin’ on after? I was thinkin’ maybe that new true crime doc on Netflix? Speaker_1: Oh, yeah! The one about the art forgery? I've heard good things. Definitely. Though I might need a bit of a lie down afterwards. All this flight searchin’ is givin’ me a headache. Speaker_2: You do that. I’ll get the plates then. And maybe we can strategise about Barcelona prices again later... although, honestly, I'm startin' to think it's just not worth the hassle. Maybe we should just stay local. Have you ever been to that little Italian place near the Mill Pond? Speaker_1: Ooh, the one Dom keeps raving about? No, not yet. But I’ve heard it's proper good. Maybe that’s a better plan than fightin’ for a plane ticket. Speaker_2: Exactly! Sometimes the best adventures are right on your doorstep. Now, lasagne awaits… Speaker_1: Right behind you! And then, art forgers and a lie down. Sounds perfect.

Speaker_1: Honestly, the price of a loaf of bread these days… it’s daylight robbery. Used to be you could get a decent white sliced for… what was it, 40p? Now it’s pushing a pound twenty! Speaker_2: It’s ridiculous, isn't it? I was looking at the cost of pasta sauce yesterday, and even the basic own-brand stuff is almost £1.50. I'm starting to think growing my own tomatoes is the only way forward. Speaker_3: Don’t even *start* me on the supermarkets. I was thinking something… simpler. Maybe just "Maya’s." Or, "The Honeycomb." Speaker_4: "The Honeycomb" sounds lovely. Sophisticated. Reminds me of New York, actually. There's a great little bakery in the Lower East Side called that. Speaker_3: Speaking of names… is anyone ever going to teach me how to properly pronounce your Hebrew name, David? It's drier than a nun’s… well, you get the picture. At least *I* get to sit down. Speaker_1: That's the dream, innit? Sitting down. Or, like, just not having someone yell “Another Jägerbomb!” every thirty seconds. Did you see that new lad, Liam, started at the bar down the road? The one near the train station? Speaker_2: Vaguely. Tall, bit scruffy looking? Saw him through the window once. Apparently he’s a student too. Doing… something. Can’t remember what. Speaker_1: Yeah, that’s him. Apparently he lasted one shift and nearly had a breakdown. Said he didn’t realise how much *running* bartending involved. I said to him, “Welcome to the club, love.” Honestly, people think it’s all shaking fancy drinks and having a laugh. It’s mostly cleaning up spilt vodka and avoiding eye contact with aggressively flirtatious people. Speaker_2: (Laughs) Oh god, sounds horrific. It's tempting to get a part-time job, money's a bit tight. But I don't think I could cope with customer service. I’m terrible with confrontation. Speaker_1: You’d be alright. You’re good at just… being firm. Like when you're arguing about philosophy, you don't back down, do you? You could do that with someone asking for a free drink. "Actually, no. The socio-economic implications of free alcohol distribution are deeply problematic." Speaker_2: (Chuckles) Okay, maybe not. I think I’d just end up crying in the stockroom. Are you still planning on doing a Christmas temp job somewhere? Speaker_1: Yeah, thinking about it. My aunty's trying to get me a job at the garden centre. Which, honestly, is miles better than another bar shift. Just potting plants and telling people what fertilizer to use. Sounds blissful. Though, knowing my luck, it'll be during a blizzard. Speaker_2: Well, at least you wouldn't be dealing with drunk students. Maybe you could get free plants? Speaker_1: Fingers crossed. And a decent wage. I’m saving up for… well, something stupid. Don't ask. Speaker_2: Oh, go on. Spill. Speaker_1: (Hesitates) It’s a… a very expensive vintage record player. I saw one in a shop in Leeds. It’s ridiculous, but I need it. I *need* it. Speaker_2: (Smiling) Okay, that's not stupid. That's a perfectly reasonable thing to spend your money on. Especially after dealing with all those Jägerbombs. You deserve a good record player. Speaker_1: Exactly! It’s self-care. Essential self-care. Speaker_2: Totally. Right, back to Political Theory then. Wish me luck. Speaker_1: Good luck, you’ll need it. And if you ever fancy escaping the library, I'll buy you a coffee. My treat. As a thank you for listening to me moan.

Speaker_1: Right, so, anyone actually *doing* anything exciting this summer? Or is it just going to be a repeat performance of binge-watching boxsets and complaining about the rain? Speaker_2: (Chuckles) Speak for yourself, Mark. I'm off to Majorca! All-inclusive, sun, sea, and a distinct lack of Salford drizzle. First proper holiday in… oh, goodness, I’ve lost count. Speaker_3: Majorca, is it? Lovely spot. Though a bit… rowdy, if you get near the strip. I spent a week in County Clare myself. Quiet, peaceful, mostly sheep for company. Bliss, I tell you. Bliss. Speaker_4: Sheep? Sounds… relaxing, Eileen. I’m attempting to teach my kids the concept of ‘doing nothing’ in Cornwall. It’s proving challenging. They’ve already planned a rigorous schedule of beach volleyball, bodyboarding, and badger watching. Speaker_1: Badger watching? Seriously? Speaker_4: Apparently, it's 'a thing'. My daughter read about it in some wildlife magazine. I suspect it’ll involve a lot of sitting in the dark, waiting for something that probably won’t show up. Speaker_2: Ha! Sounds delightful, David. Reminds me of a ‘wildlife’ holiday I went on once. Ended up staring at a damp patch of grass for three hours, convinced a rare beetle was about to appear. Speaker_3: Oh, the disappointments of nature! Though, you know, sometimes the quiet is reward enough. Last week I saw a robin build a nest right outside my window. Nearly cried, I did. Speaker_1: That *is* sweet, Eileen. I'm contemplating a weekend in the Lake District. Just… walking. Avoiding people. Possibly taking a flask of tea. Speaker_2: Sounds a bit… solitary, Mark? Speaker_1: That's the point, Brenda. After a year of shelving books and politely asking students to be quiet, I need solitary. I need nature. I need a significant amount of tea. Speaker_4: You're preaching to the choir. I’m hoping the sea air will restore some semblance of sanity before September hits. This last semester has been…intense. Speaker_3: University students, eh? Always a handful. Though, I do get a kick out of helping them find that obscure text they need. It's like being a literary detective. Speaker_2: More like a literary shepherd, herding them towards the Dewey Decimal System! Honestly, some of them look utterly lost. Speaker_1: Remember that lad last year who asked where the 'internet books' were? Speaker_4: (Laughing) Oh, don't remind me! I nearly choked on my coffee. Speaker_3: The youth of today! Though don’t be too hard on them. They're just trying to navigate a complicated world. Speaking of complicated, have any of you tried booking a ferry these days? It's a nightmare! Speaker_2: Tell me about it! I nearly had a heart attack trying to get the Majorca flights sorted. Prices are ridiculous this year. Speaker_1: It’s the school holidays, Brenda. Everyone and their dog is trying to escape the country. Speaker_4: It's a conspiracy, I tell you. A conspiracy by the travel companies to fleece us all. Speaker_3: Well, whatever it is, I’m just grateful to be getting away from it all. Even if it means sharing my countryside with a few sheep. Speaker_1: Enjoy the sheep, Eileen. And the lack of students. Speaker_2: And the sunshine! I'll send postcards. Maybe. If I remember. Speaker_4: We’ll hold you to that, Brenda. And good luck with the tea, Mark. You’ll need it, facing the wilds of the Lake District alone.

Speaker_1: Honestly, the refereeing in this game is absolutely shocking. Shocking! That was a clear foul, clear as day. Speaker_2: (Eyes glued to the screen, munching on chips) Mmm? Oh aye, bit soft maybe. He's letting them get away with murder, isn't he? Still, good game though, proper end-to-end stuff. Speaker_1: Good game? They're getting completely overrun in midfield! This game is just stressing me out and I need comfort food. Speaker_2: See? The football gods are telling you something. Speaker_2: No regrets! Just pure, unadulterated fried potato bliss. I’ll even get you some of those onion rings. They're massive. Speaker_1: Onion rings *and* wings? You're enabling my bad habits. Now, watch this, they're building up an attack… Oh, and I’ll get the dips sorted, which ones do you fancy? Garlic mayo or sweet chilli? Speaker_1: Sweet chilli, definitely. And stop analysing the game and focus on Crispy Heaven logistics! We need a plan of attack for those wings. Speaker_2: Right you are. Operation Crispy Heaven is a go. (Both turn their attention back to the TV momentarily, then back to discussing the impending delivery.) Speaker_1: Seriously though, they need to sub that midfielder. He's running around like a headless chicken. Speaker_2: Just let the wings occupy your mind. Wings. Crispy, spicy wings. Speaker_1: You're a terrible influence. Speaker_2: (Grinning) I prefer to think of myself as a connoisseur of fine dining experiences. And a football enthusiast, naturally. Speaker_1: Connoisseur of grease, more like. Speaker_2: A distinction without a difference. Speaker_1: You're impossible. Speaker_2: Lovable, though, aren't I? Speaker_1: (Smiling) Occasionally. Now, about those wings…are they extra large?

Speaker_1: Right, this tea’s proper good, Mum. You’ve outdone yourself. And Grandma, are you alright with your biscuit? Need me to crumble it a bit? Speaker_2: (A slight chuckle) Crumble it? Lad, I've been crumbling biscuits myself for ninety-odd years, I think I can manage. Though, a bit of dunking never hurt anyone, did it? Speaker_3: Don't encourage her, Michael! She'll have the whole thing swimming. Honestly, Mum, you know what happens when you dunk. Speaker_2: Oh, hush you. A little soggy biscuit never killed anyone. It reminds me of when your Grandad…He loved a good dunk, your Grandad did. Always said it was the only way to get a proper flavour release. Speaker_1: He sounds like a man of discerning taste. Back in my day, it was all Bogart and Gable. *Casablanca*, that was a good film. Made you weep, it did. And *Gone With The Wind*. Oh, Scarlett O’Hara! A beautiful woman. Though a bit dramatic, if you ask me. Speaker_3: She’s more of a Morecambe and Wise woman, honestly. She’ll watch anything with Eric and Ernie on. Speaker_2: They were funny lads, those two. Always made me laugh. And they didn't go on for three and a half hours! What’s wrong with a bit of brevity these days? Speaker_1: (Smiling) Fair enough. I’m just…work’s been hectic, you know? Big project at the moment, trying to get everything signed off. It’s all deadlines and meetings. Needed something long and immersive to switch off afterwards. Speaker_3: Sounds stressful. You’re always working, Michael. You need a holiday. Maybe cycle down to Wales, you used to love that. Speaker_1: I’ve been thinking about it, actually. My bike's been gathering dust in the garage. I might just dust it off next weekend. I saw old Mr. Henderson down the road, polishing his classic car again. Makes me feel like I should use mine, or at least the bike, more. Speaker_2: Cars. Horrible things. Always making a racket. I remember when we didn’t *have* cars. Everyone walked, or got on the tram. Much nicer. Though, your Grandad did have a little Austin Seven. Called her Bessie. He was very proud of Bessie. Speaker_3: He was proud of anything that had an engine, bless him. He used to spend hours tinkering with things in the shed. Trying to fix anything and everything. Speaker_1: Sounds like a resourceful man. You’ve always been good with your hands, Mum. Remember that time you built that…what was it? A bird table? Speaker_3: A bird table *and* a greenhouse! Though, honestly, the greenhouse was a disaster. Leaked everywhere, and the tomatoes never ripened. Speaker_2: You get that with tomatoes. Need a good, sunny spot. And a bit of luck. I used to grow the best tomatoes in Withington, you know. Everyone said so. Used to make a lovely tomato sandwich with a bit of white bread and butter. Simple things, eh? The best things. Speaker_1: They are, aren’t they? Simple things. I’m trying to learn to cook properly now, though. I managed a decent curry last week. Speaker_3: Oh? A curry? I hope it wasn’t too spicy. Your Grandma can’t handle spicy. Speaker_2: A little bit of spice is good for you! Keeps you warm. But not too much, mind. I like a bit of flavour, not a fiery inferno. And make sure you use proper spices, not that pre-mixed rubbish.

Speaker_1: Right, Leo, one more bite of pancake, please. Honestly, it’s delicious. Poppy, you’ve barely touched yours! What's wrong? Speaker_2: (Muffled, mouth full) It's...sticky. Speaker_1: Sticky? It's just a little syrup, darling. It makes it nice. Leo, are you enjoying yours? Speaker_3: (Enthusiastically) Yes! It’s the best pancake *ever*! Can I have more syrup, please? Speaker_1: You can have a tiny bit more, alright? Poppy, honestly. You love pancakes usually. Are you feeling okay? Speaker_2: I just… don’t want it right now. Speaker_1: Okay. Well, we’ll put it to one side. It's Pancake Day, you should at least *try* to eat some. It reminds me of being little, my mum always made us pancakes. Though, she wasn't very good at flipping them! They always ended up a bit wonky. Speaker_3: Wonky pancakes! That’s funny! Speaker_1: It was! She'd laugh and say they were 'characterful'. Speaking of school, how was assembly today, Poppy? Mrs. Davies said you both were very well behaved. Speaker_2: It was boring. They talked about...counting. Speaker_1: Counting? Oh dear. Well, that *is* a bit dull, isn't it? Leo, what about you? Did you enjoy assembly? Speaker_3: We sang a song! About…plants! Speaker_1: Oh, lovely! Mrs. Davies is trying to get everyone thinking about Spring. I had a tricky one in my class today. Little Alfie didn’t eat his lunch *at all*. Just pushed it around his plate. It breaks your heart, you know? To think some children don’t even *have* lunch to look forward to. Speaker_2: Sad. Speaker_1: It is very sad. It makes you appreciate what we have, doesn’t it? Right, after pancakes, we need a big teeth-brushing session. And hand washing! You two are like magnets for germs. Speaker_3: But I brushed my teeth this morning! Speaker_1: That's good, but you need to do it after breakfast too. It’s important. You wouldn't want those pancake sugars sticking to your teeth all day. It makes me think of when *I* was little. We didn’t have electric toothbrushes, you know. Just a boring old brush and some toothpaste. Feels like a lifetime ago. Speaker_2: Did you live in Norwich then? Speaker_1: No, I grew up in Dartford, in Kent. It's near London. A very different place to Comberton! When I was your age, my biggest dream was to go to Paris. It seemed so exotic and far away. Speaker_3: Paris! With the Eiffel Tower? Speaker_1: Exactly! We eventually went when I was at university, and it *was* amazing. We’re still planning a family trip one day, aren't we, darling? (To an unseen person - presumably a partner) Speaker_1: Oh, have you checked what’s on at the Festival Hall this weekend? I saw something about a children's performance. And… I was thinking perhaps we could try and go to the Science Museum? It’s a bit of a drive, but I think you two would love it. Speaker_2: The Science Museum is cool! Speaker_3: Can we go to the beach too? Speaker_1: (Chuckles) One thing at a time, my loves. We'll see. Right, back to pancakes. Poppy, just a tiny bite? Think of it as…fuel for a fun weekend! Did you hear that story about Green Knowe? The one where the children visit their great aunt and… (Conversation trails off as Speaker_1 launches into a story, with occasional interjections from Speakers 2 and 3).

Speaker_1: This egg fried rice is… surprisingly good. I was bracing myself for it being a bit oily, but it’s actually really fluffy. Speaker_2: Right? I think we’ve found *the* Chinese. Old Man Wong’s has been consistently solid for, what, a year now? Speaker_3: Easily. Remember when we tried that new place, Golden Dragon, down by the station? That was an absolute disaster. Everything tasted vaguely of dish soap. Speaker_4: Oh god, don’t remind me. I spent the next day regretting my life choices. Anyway, anyone catch the news today? Apparently, old Mr. Henderson passed away. Speaker_1: Oh no! Old Mr. Henderson from number 14? The one with the prize-winning roses? Speaker_4: The very same. Apparently a heart attack. He was a lovely bloke, always had a wave and a chat. Speaker_2: That’s awful. He always used to complain about my cricket practice in the garden, but he did it with a smile. Said it reminded him of his youth. Speaker_3: It’s just… it feels like everyone’s funerals are piling up lately. Old Mrs. Davies last month, and now Mr. Henderson. Makes you think, doesn’t it? Speaker_1: It does. It’s grim. Speaking of grim, have you guys heard from Sarah lately? I haven’t seen her post anything on Facebook in ages. Speaker_2: I messaged her a couple of days ago, just checking in. She’s… dealing with stuff. Apparently, her flatmate, Liam, just up and left. Vanished. Speaker_4: No way! Leaving without a word? What a jerk. Speaker_3: She sounded really upset when I spoke to her last week. Said she felt totally betrayed. He apparently owed a lot of money, and just… ran. Speaker_1: That’s terrible. Poor Sarah. We need to do something for her. Maybe a movie night? Distraction is key. Although, what *is* good at the moment? Everything feels a bit heavy. Speaker_2: I saw the new Wes Anderson film is out. Seems suitably quirky and escapist. Speaker_4: Ooh, good shout. Wes Anderson always delivers. Although, honestly, I’m in the mood for something brainless. Like, aggressively brainless. Speaker_3: You mean like… Bob the Builder? Speaker_4: (Laughing) Don’t mock! Sometimes you just need “Can we fix it?” to soothe the soul. Seriously though, a silly action film would be good. Speaker_1: I’m up for anything, as long as it doesn’t involve existential dread. Oh! And we should definitely get more prawn crackers. These are going fast. Speaker_2: I’ll order another portion. Anyone fancy a dessert menu? I’m eyeing up the banana fritters. Speaker_3: Yes, please! I'm already planning how to justify it. It's for Sarah, right? Emotional support calories? Speaker_4: Absolutely. And it's also research for potential comfort food options for, you know, the inevitable future wave of funerals. Gotta be prepared. Speaker_1: You are morbid. Although...you're not wrong. More fritters for all! Speaker_2: Right, fritters it is. And I’ll text Sarah and see if she fancies joining us for a distraction, even if it just involves us being generally silly. Speaker_3: Good plan. She deserves a night off from the universe being awful. Speaker_4: Agreed. Now, about those prawn crackers…are they sustainably sourced? Just kidding. Mostly.

Speaker_1: Honestly, remembering Auntie Mabel trying to navigate the self-checkout at Sainsbury’s was a highlight. She insisted on scanning *every* item three times. Said she didn’t trust the machine. Speaker_2: (Chuckles, a little raspy) Mabel was a character. Stubborn as a mule, that one. Reminded me of old Mr. Henderson next door, back in Wolverhampton. He’d argue with the postman if a letter was delivered five minutes late. Five minutes! Speaker_3: It's funny, isn't it? How people cling to the old ways. Mum's still convinced everything's better done by hand. Tried to explain the Scan As You Go to her last week… she looked at me like I’d suggested she learn Mandarin. Speaker_1: Oh, the Scan As You Go! Don't even get me started. It's supposed to be quicker, right? But half the time it doesn’t recognise something, or accuses you of stealing a pineapple. Speaker_2: A pineapple? Good heavens. When I was a boy, you were lucky if you *saw* a pineapple! We mostly ate… well, sensible things. Potatoes, mostly. And my mother made a lovely rice pudding. Not these pre-packaged things you get now. Speaker_3: Speaking of sensible, have you seen the price of rice lately? It’s gone up again. I swear, they’re going to price us all out of a decent risotto. Speaker_1: It’s ridiculous. And don't even get me started on new builds and the insurance. We're still battling with the builders over everything at the new house. They say we have to have specific insurance for the underfloor heating because… well, because it’s new. Apparently it’s incredibly sensitive. Speaker_2: Insurance! Back in my day, insurance was simple. Car insurance, house insurance… that was about it. Now you need insurance for your toaster, I wager. Speaker_3: Virtually! I read an article about someone trying to insure their bicycle against accidental damage while learning to ride. Apparently, it was a genuine request. Speaker_1: That *is* a new one. Though honestly, I’m starting to think we’ll need insurance against driverless cars. I saw a report about a test drive where it just… stopped. In the middle of a roundabout. Speaker_2: Driverless cars? Nonsense. Absolute nonsense. People need to drive! Gets the blood flowing, keeps the mind sharp. Though, I suppose air travel’s safer these days. I always worried about flying, you know. All those metal birds… Speaker_3: Statistically, yes, it’s incredibly safe. Though Uncle George swore he knew a pilot who said they routinely flew on autopilot for most of the journey. Speaker_1: He probably did. Remember George and his stories? He once told me he’d accidentally flown a plane upside down over the English Channel. I’m fairly certain that was an exaggeration. Speaker_2: George! Oh, he was a storyteller, that one. Always had a tale to tell. He was always on about Google, too. Said they didn't pay their fair share of tax. Something about shifting profits to Ireland, wasn't it? Speaker_3: Absolutely. It's a complicated system, but essentially, yes. It's all perfectly legal, apparently… though morally questionable. Speaker_1: It’s the same with these big supermarket chains, isn’t it? They make billions, yet still squeeze the farmers and hike up prices for us. Speaker_2: They’ll get their comeuppance one day. Mark my words. Though, I must say, I do enjoy a Rice Krispy Cake now and then. They remind me of being a boy. Simple pleasures, you know? Speaker_3: They’re a bit sickly sweet for me, actually. I prefer something a little more… substantial. I'm thinking about trying to grow some tomatoes this year. Have you started planning the garden yet? Speaker_1: Just a rough sketch. I’m hoping to finally get

Speaker_1: Right, so, Dragon heads need *massive* jaws, don’t they? Yours is looking a little… polite, Leo. Speaker_3: (Muttering) It’s supposed to be a friendly dragon. Not a scary one. Speaker_2: Mine is going to breathe *fire*! I’m drawing sparkly bits, look! (Holds up a drawing covered in glitter glue) Speaker_1: Ooh, very effective. Very fiery. Just try not to get glitter *everywhere*, Elsie, please. Remember last time? It was in my hair for a week. Speaker_2: Sorry, Mummy. But dragons *need* sparkles. It's Chinese New Year! Speaker_3: Chinese New Year is about red envelopes with money in, isn’t it? Speaker_1: It is, but it’s also about dragons and celebrating new beginnings. And delicious food! We’re having noodles tonight, you know, for long life. Speaker_2: Can we have prawn crackers? Speaker_1: Of course. And spring rolls. And maybe a little bit of that sweet and sour chicken you both like. Though not *too* much, we don't want sugar rushes before bedtime. Speaker_3: I don’t really like sweet and sour chicken. Speaker_1: Oh? What *do* you like best, Leo? Speaker_3: Noodles. And… dumplings. And are we still doing drum lessons on Wednesday? Speaker_1: Yes, drum lessons are still on. Though Mr. Davies said you were a little distracted last week. Something about planets? Speaker_3: Uranus is really far away. And it’s blue. Teacher said so. And it has rings, but they're not as good as Saturn’s. Speaker_2: I know Saturn! It has *lots* of rings! Like a princess’s crown! I’m learning a new song on the piano, it sounds like twinkling stars! Speaker_1: That’s lovely, Elsie. You’re getting so good. It was really nice of Mrs. Henderson to say how much you've improved. Speaker_2: She said I play with ‘expression’ now. What does that mean? Speaker_1: It means you put feeling into it! You're not just hitting the notes, you're *telling a story* with the music. Like when you were pretending to be a ballerina when you were playing. Speaker_3: I wish I could learn the drums faster. It’s hard to keep the rhythm. Speaker_1: It takes practice, darling. It's like learning anything new. Remember how hard it was to learn to ride your bike? Speaker_3: I fell over a lot. Speaker_1: You did! But you kept trying, and now look at you, zooming around the park! Elsie, are you still excited about your aerial hoop class this weekend? Speaker_2: YES! I’m going to be a fairy! And I’m going to learn a new trick! I watched Barbie and the Great Adventure, and Barbie does aerial silks, and it looks *amazing*! Speaker_1: Barbie does a lot of amazing things. Though I think your aerial hoop is a bit more challenging than going on a quest with a secret agent. Right, back to dragons then. Leo, maybe a few more teeth? A really long tongue? Speaker_3: (Grumbling) Fine. But it’s still a friendly dragon. Just a friendly dragon with lots of teeth. Speaker_1: Perfect. That’s perfect. Now, who wants to help me chop some spring onion? Speaker_2: Me! Me! I’m good at chopping! (Immediately grabs a plastic knife.) Speaker_1: (Smiling) A *plastic* knife, Elsie. A plastic knife, please. Safety first, even when we’re celebrating Chinese New Year.

Speaker_1: Honestly, this Aperol Spritz is hitting the spot. Needed that after lugging our bags halfway across Rome to this AirBnB. Speaker_2: Tell me about it! That little cobbled street was *not* designed for suitcases with wheels. Though, the AirBnB is gorgeous, isn’t it? That balcony…worth the struggle, I reckon. Speaker_3: Absolutely. And the host left us Prosecco! Which, let’s be honest, has already been partially sampled. Though speaking of struggle, has anyone tried ordering a coffee yet? My Italian’s… rusty, to say the least. I just pointed and hoped for the best. Speaker_4: (With a broad Australian accent) You’re telling me! I walked into a place this morning, tried to ask for a flat white, and the barista looked at me like I’d grown another head. Had to mime a milky coffee, eventually. Apparently, flat whites are a mythical creature here. Speaker_1: Haha, classic. I managed a ‘caffè latte’ reasonably well, but I’m pretty sure they overcharged me. My GCSE Italian is failing me spectacularly. Speaker_2: Mine’s even worse. I spent a year in Spain, so I keep accidentally throwing in Spanish words. It’s a disaster. I asked for ‘agua’ instead of ‘acqua’ and got a very confused look. Speaker_3: Oh, bless you. I’m just sticking to pointing. It's safer. So, dinner plans? I’m starving again already. Saw a tiny trattoria down that alleyway - looked proper authentic. Speaker_1: That sounds good. I’m up for proper authentic. Anything but another pizza, as amazing as they are. Leo, you in? Speaker_4: Yeah, sounds good to me. As long as they have wine. Actually, thinking about it, anyone know what the weather’s doing tomorrow? I was hoping for a bit of sunshine to wander around the Forum. Speaker_2: I checked earlier. Apparently, it’s going to be scorcher. Mid-thirties. Perfect for gelato and avoiding all strenuous activity. Speaker_3: Excellent. I'm packing a giant hat then. It’s a necessity. Speaking of packing, Mum keeps texting me asking if I’ve remembered my scarf. Honestly, it’s Rome in July! Speaker_1: Mothers, eh? Always worrying. Mine’s convinced I’ll get pickpocketed if I so much as look at a souvenir shop. Speaker_2: Mine's on a mission to find me a suitable Italian husband. Sent me a link to a dating app specifically for expats. Seriously. Speaker_4: (Laughing) Oh, that’s brilliant! So, you’re on husband-hunting duty then? I thought you were happy being a free spirit, baking all those incredible cakes. Speaker_2: Don’t get me wrong, the baking is excellent. But apparently, I need someone to "appreciate" my artistry. Mum’s logic, not mine. Speaker_3: Right, well, *my* Mum wants to know if I'm sending photos. She’s promised to show them off to all her bingo friends. The pressure! Speaker_1: The bingo friends are the worst. The absolute *worst*. Right, so trattoria then? Down the alley? Around… eight? Speaker_2: Perfect. And Leo, maybe practice your miming skills for the wine order. Just in case. Speaker_4: (Grinning) Challenge accepted. I'm becoming quite the expert in international non-verbal communication. Though I still reckon I pulled off a pretty convincing flat white request, even if they didn’t understand it.

Speaker_1: Honestly, the planning for Chloe’s hen do is *stressful*. I feel like I'm her mum, not a friend! Speaker_2: Oh, tell me about it! Whose bright idea was it to make friendship bracelets for everyone? My fingers are killing me. Speaker_3: It was Sarah, wasn’t it? She seems to think everyone secretly wants to spend their weekend crafting. Speaker_4: (Laughing) Classic Sarah! Speaker_1: Right, honestly, that was… a day. I need a glass of wine. Did you have a good one, love? Speaker_2: Not bad, not bad. A bit of a slog, actually. Speaker_1: Right, so the story goes, Old Man Hemlock lived in the woods, and he wasn't a *bad* man exactly, but he definitely wasn’t…nice. Did he turn people into frogs? Speaker_1: (Chuckles) No, not frogs. He’d make you lose your way if you were rude to the trees. Or make your apples fall off the branch before they were ripe. Small things. Annoying things. Speaker_2: That *is* mean. Speaker_1: It was. And that's where the good part comes in. There was a little girl, Elara, who lived nearby. Her mum was really sick and needed special berries to get better, berries Old Man Hemlock had all to himself. Speaker_3: Did Elara ask him nicely? Speaker_1: She did. She went to his little hut and asked *very* politely. But he just said no, those berries were for him. Speaker_2: Oh! That’s awful. Speaker_1: It was. But Elara didn't give up. She knew the forest really well, better than Old Man Hemlock even. She figured out that he wasn’t protecting the berries, he was…distracting something. Speaker_3: What was he distracting? A monster? Speaker_1: Not a monster. Something older. There was this creature, called the Gloomwing, that lived in the caves behind his hut. It fed on happiness, and it would drain the colour from everything if it got loose. Old Man Hemlock kept the Gloomwing busy by keeping all the best things for himself - the berries, the shiniest stones, the prettiest flowers. He thought if it was focused on *his* treasures, it wouldn’t bother anyone else. Speaker_2: But that didn't work, did it? Speaker_1: Not really. It just made him a bit grumpy and lonely. Elara realised that if she could give the Gloomwing something *better* than Old Man Hemlock's treasures… something it really liked… she could distract it long enough to gather the berries. Speaker_3: What did she give it? Chocolate? Speaker_1: (Smiling) Even better. Stories. The Gloomwing loved stories. Not scary ones, but stories about kindness and bravery and friendship. She sat outside the cave and told it stories for hours, and the Gloomwing was so captivated, it didn't even notice her sneaking around and collecting the berries. Speaker_2: And then she saved her mum! Speaker_1: She did! And Old Man Hemlock… well, he wasn't quite so grumpy anymore. He realized that sharing actually made him feel *better* than hoarding. He even started helping Elara gather berries for other sick people. Speaker_3: So, it’s better to be good than bad? Speaker_1: It usually is, isn't it? Speaker_1: Honestly, the student feedback this year has been… interesting. Mostly good, thankfully, but one of them said my lectures were “a bit enthusiastic.” A bit enthusiastic!
